nodes.label: Permanent congenital hypothyroidism
nodes.description: A severe and long-lasting form of congenital hypothyroidism that is associated with a lower proportion of premature births (2%) compared to transient congenital hypothyroidism. Patients with permanent CH can have a goitre (55% of cases), a normal sized and shaped thyroid gland (29% of cases), or a hypoplastic gland (16% of cases), which can manifest as global thyroid hypoplasia (3%), a right hemithyroid (2% of cases), hypoplasia of the left lobe (2% of cases), or asymmetry in the location of the two lobes (1% of cases). A disease characterized by defects in iodine organification, Pendred syndrome, thyroglobulin synthesis, sodium iodine symporter, or no determinable cause. It affects 27 patients with a goitre and 14 with a normal sized and shaped thyroid gland. Among these, specific aetiologies were found in 10 patients with a goitre, 1 with Pendred syndrome, 8 with a defect of thyroglobulin synthesis, 1 with a defect of sodium iodine symporter, and none in seven patients. In contrast, among 14 patients with a normal sized and shaped thyroid gland, a specific aetiology was found in only one patient with pseudohypoparathyroidism and two with Down's syndrome. Additionally, two patients with a globally hypoplastic gland had a TSH receptor gene mutation.

nodes.label: MCT8
nodes.description: A cell-membrane transporter gene for thyroid hormone (TH) that, when mutated, causes a syndrome producing severe psychomotor defects in more than 100 males from 26 families. A specific monocarboxylate transporter encoded by the gene located on chromosome Xq13.2, playing an important role in the development of the central nervous system by transporting thyroid hormone into neurons. Mutations or deletions in the MCT8 gene lead to severe psychomotor retardation and biochemical findings consistent with thyroid hormone resistance. A gene or protein involved in transporting T3 in neurons, mutations of which determine a distinct X-linked phenotype of severe psychomotor retardation and consistently elevated T3 levels. The patient had a missense mutation of the MCT8 gene. A specific monocarboxylate transporter identified as a thyroid hormone transporter, crucial for the uptake of thyroid hormone into target tissues. Mutations in this transporter lead to the Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome, characterized by severe psychomotor retardation and elevated serum 3,3',5-tri-iodothyronine levels. A cellular transporter of thyroid hormones important in their action and metabolization. A novel inactivating mutation 630insG in the coding region in exon 1 of MCT8 was identified in a Brazilian boy with thyroid hormone resistance and severe neurologic abnormalities. Neurons are highly dependent on MCT8, while bone tissue, adipose tissue, muscle, and liver are less dependent on MCT8 and may suffer the consequences of exposure to high serum T3 levels. A specific transporter for triiodothyronine (T3), responsible for directed transport of T3 into target cells and for export of thyroid hormones out of thyroid epithelial cells. Genetic disturbances of MCT8 in patients result in a biochemical constellation of high T3 levels in combination with low or normal TSH and thyroxine levels leading to a new syndrome of severe X-linked mental retardation. Mice lacking MCT8 presented only with a mild phenotype, indicating that compensatory mechanisms exist in mice.

nodes.label: Suvorexant
nodes.description: A CNS drug developed with an orexin-based neurotransmitter system as its target, used for treating insomnia. It is a dual orexin receptor antagonist that has recently been approved for the treatment of insomnia. Suvorexant improves subjective total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, and latency to persistent sleep at doses of 10-20 mg. It is generally effective and well tolerated, but further studies are needed to assess its use in patients with a history of addiction and to compare it with other insomnia medications. Suvorexant is the first DORA to be approved for the treatment of insomnia and has demonstrated efficacy at decreasing both time to sleep onset and increasing total sleep time compared with placebo.

nodes.label: Belimumab
nodes.description: A human IgG1λ monoclonal antibody specifically targeting the B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS), an investigational drug used to treat systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It has shown statistically significant results in Phase 3 trials and is currently in late-stage investigation for SLE treatment. Belimumab has been relatively well-tolerated with discontinuation rates and adverse events similar to those of placebo. If approved by the FDA, its US market launch is expected in 2011. A monoclonal antibody targeting B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS), approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for patients with serologically positive systemic lupus erythematosus who have active disease despite standard therapy, based on clinical benefit demonstrated in two large-scale, multicenter phase III trials. A human monoclonal antibody specifically targeting soluble B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS). It was developed by Human Genome Sciences and approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in March 2011 for active autoantibody patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) despite standard therapy. Belimumab promotes B cell survival and is important in immunoglobulin class switching. A fully human monoclonal antibody directed against BAFF, used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus. It has shown overall steroid-sparing ability and benefits on musculoskeletal and mucocutaneous organ systems, suggesting an impact on the clinical management of SLE patients. A fully human monoclonal antibody against B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS), licensed in 2011 for the treatment of autoantibody-positive systemic lupus erythematosus. Clinical trials, such as BLISS-52 and BLISS-76, have demonstrated its safety and efficacy in reducing disease activity when used in combination with standard therapy compared to placebo with standard therapy. It has been found to be safe and well tolerated overall. A monoclonal antibody targeting the soluble human B Lymphocyte Stimulator protein (BLyS), also known as B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and TNFSF13B, which is involved in the selection, maturation, and survival of B cells. It is being studied as a potential therapeutic agent for Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients. An anti-BAFF monoclonal antibody approved by the FDA for use in treating systemic lupus erythematosus. It neutralizes BAFF by interacting with the flap region of BAFF and mimicking the DxL(V/L) motif of BAFF receptors, which disrupts the formation of the more active BAFF 60-mer and favors the induction of the less active BAFF trimer. Its therapeutic activity involves both antagonizing the BAFF-receptor interaction and interfering with BAFF 60-mer formation.

nodes.label: Methotrexate
nodes.description: A commonly used disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriasis, and certain types of cancer. It is a systemic immunosuppressive agent often used as a first-line treatment for severe plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Methotrexate is also used in intrathecal therapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and as a comparator in studies assessing the efficacy of other medications. It has been shown to increase the risk of infections and elevations in transaminase enzymes when co-administered with certain drugs like CP-690,550. Methotrexate is typically administered as single doses of 15-25 mg per week and may be used in combination with other medications such as tofacitinib, ciclosporin, or TNF alpha antagonists like etanercept. It is a standard systemic treatment regimen used for treating atopic dermatitis, but not suitable for long-term treatment due to its unfavorable safety profile.

nodes.label: Pectus excavatum
nodes.description: A congenital chest wall deformity characterized by a sunken or caved-in appearance of the chest, typically affecting the sternum and ribs. It is often caused by an abnormal inward growth of the ribs and breastbone, and can lead to aesthetic and functional debilitation. Pectus excavatum requires surgical correction, with various methods including minimally invasive repair of the pectus excavatum, modified Ravitch repair, and minimized Erlangen repair. It is a common deformity involving the anterior chest wall, associated with respiratory and cardiac abnormalities, and can be broadly divided into symmetric or asymmetric morphology. The Nuss and Ravitch procedures are established methods of surgical correction, and the Haller index, typically evaluated with computed tomography scan, is used to assess the severity of the condition.

nodes.label: Amphiregulin
nodes.description: A mammalian EGFR ligand that increases cancer cell invasion when present in exosomes. It is found in human breast and colorectal cancer cells and is packaged within individual exosomes. Exosomal Amphiregulin increases invasiveness of recipient breast cancer cells 4-fold over TGFα or HB-EGF exosomes and 5-fold over equivalent amounts of recombinant AREG. It displays significantly greater membrane stability than TGFα or HB-EGF. An average of 24 Amphiregulin molecules are packaged within an individual exosome and are rapidly internalized by recipient cells. An EGFR ligand released from airway epithelial cells in response to histamine, causing proliferation and migration of both NHBE cells and human airway smooth muscle cells. It up-regulates its own mRNA expression and causes goblet cell differentiation.

nodes.label: Rosiglitazone
nodes.description: A potent oral antidiabetic agent of the thiazolidinedione class, used for managing Type 2 Diabetes. It works through activation of the peroxisome proliferator-activated nuclear receptor, improving insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues and lowering blood glucose in patients with type 2 diabetes. Rosiglitazone is a PPARγ agonist that has not yet been evaluated in Alzheimer's disease prevention clinical trials. It is marketed as Avandia and has been associated with potential detrimental effects on myocardial events, increased risk of fractures, especially in postmenopausal women, and contraindicated in patients at risk of heart failure. It is an antidiabetic drug belonging to the thiazolidinedione class that has been reported to be associated with increased risks of cardiovascular diseases in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

nodes.label: Striatum
nodes.description: A region of the brain involved in motor control and reward pathways, located within the basal ganglia. It has been studied for its dopaminergic denervation in Parkinson's disease, serotonin transporter-deficient mice, and its terminals forming symmetrical synapses as part of the GABAergic afferents. The striatum has also been evaluated for dopamine transporter availability, PAD2 protein expression, and 5-HT2A receptor up-regulation in certain neurological disorders. It includes the caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens, and has been investigated for its connectivity to other brain structures such as the entopeduncular nucleus, globus pallidus, and substantia nigra.

nodes.label: Deep brain stimulation
nodes.description: A surgical treatment option for tardive dystonia, dystonic cerebral palsy, and certain heredodegenerative diseases involving the stimulation of the posteroventral pallidum. A medical procedure involving the administration of electrical stimulation to specific areas of the brain, used as an alternative treatment for critical neurological conditions with long-lasting clinical benefit. It has been investigated in the treatment of patients who had undergone surgical electrode implants as an emergency procedure to treat acute life-threatening conditions requiring admission to neurological ICU (NICU). Bilateral globus pallidus internus (GPi) DBS was performed in five status dystonicus (SD) patients and unilateral ventralis oralis anterior and posterior (Voa/Vop) nucleus of the thalamus DBS in two post-stroke hemiballismus patients. Bilateral GPi-DBS allowed SD resolution in a time lapse varying from 1 week to 3 months. No clear improvements compared to the baseline clinical condition were observed. Unilateral Voa/Vop-DBS intervention controlled hemiballismus after 10 hours, and the patient was discharged in 2 days. The other patient was transferred from the NICU to the neurosurgery ward after 13 days. No surgical complications were observed in any of the above procedures. A medical procedure involving the stimulation of the globus pallidus externus, with a focus on understanding the effects of programming the higher contacts. A surgical procedure involving the implantation of DBS leads in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus internus (GPi) to treat Parkinson's disease. It is associated with weight changes and improved survival rates. The bilateral STN DBS group gained the most weight after surgery during 6 years of follow-up compared to the bilateral GPi group.

nodes.label: Heerfordt's syndrome
nodes.description: A type of sarcoidosis that affects the salivary glands, specifically the parotid gland, leading to swelling, fever, and uveitis. It is also known as sarcoidosis of the salivary glands and is diagnosed using state-of-the-art ultrasound techniques. The syndrome is characterized by an inhomogeneous nodular appearance of the salivary glands on ultrasound, with areas of hypervascularization. A form of sarcoidosis characterized by uveitis, enlargement of the parotid glands, and optional paralysis of the Nn. facialis. The diagnosis is confirmed by histology. A subtype of clinical presentations associated with sarcoidosis, characterized by the combination of uveitis, parotid gland swelling, and facial nerve palsy. It affects approximately 4.1-5.6% of patients with sarcoidosis and is estimated to occur in 16.9% of patients with radiculopathy associated with sarcoidosis. It is a rare disorder with only 51 documented cases of radiculopathy associated with sarcoidosis and 7 of those cases presenting with Heerfordt's syndrome. A rare manifestation of sarcoidosis characterized by facial nerve palsy, parotid gland enlargement, anterior uveitis, and low-grade fever. It can present as incomplete or complete forms, with the latter including bilateral hearing loss and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Treatment with corticosteroids can improve symptoms such as facial nerve palsy and parotid gland swelling.

nodes.label: PBT2
nodes.description: A metal-protein attenuating compound (MPAC) that targets Cu2(+)-mediated and Zn2(+)-mediated toxic oligomerisation of amyloid-beta (Abeta) seen in Alzheimer's disease (AD). PBT2 is a second-generation 8-OH quinoline derivative of clioquinol, orally bioavailable and performing satisfactorily in toxicology and Phase I clinical trials. It is advancing as a disease-modifying candidate drug for Alzheimer's disease, having shown promise in a Phase IIa, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The trial found that PBT2 was well-tolerated, significantly lowered cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels of amyloid-beta42, and significantly improved executive function on a Neuro-psychological Test Battery (NTB) within 12 weeks of treatment in patients with AD. PBT2 is a metal chaperone with therapeutic potential for Alzheimer's disease, promoting amyloid-β degradation and GSK3 phosphorylation, and improving cognition in AD patients by decreasing Aβ levels and increasing phosphorylation of calcineurin substrates.

nodes.label: Patients
nodes.description: Individuals with deformed rib cages and sternal plates who were treated surgically by the authors' group between 1987 and 2003. A total of 599 patients were treated, with 515 undergoing surgery using the Erlangen minimally invasive repair technique and 84 undergoing surgery at the Freiburg University Medical Center. In the current series, 79 patients underwent surgery using the modified Ravitch method. The mean patient age was 20.5 years (range, 3-54 years), and the rate of postoperative relapses was 5%. Individuals who receive medical treatments or undergo medical procedures, such as infusions, and benefit from shorter infusion durations for increased flexibility, comfort, and convenience. Individuals with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) enrolled in the study, specifically 30 patients with hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related HCC. Eight of these patients had a tumor recurrence. Individuals who have undergone treatment for colorectal cancer with first-line standard chemotherapeutic regimens in combination with bevacizumab. Their CRC tissues are analyzed to explore the correlation between FOXF1 expression and resistance to bevacizumab. Individuals with relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma who have received at least three previous regimens including a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory agent, and an anti-CD38 antibody. A total of 140 patients were enrolled in the study, and 128 received Idecabtagene Vicleucel (ide-cel). At a median follow-up of 13.3 months, 94 of 128 patients (73%) had a response, and 42 of 128 (33%) had a complete response or better. Minimal residual disease (MRD)-negative status was confirmed in 33 patients, representing 26% of all 128 patients who were treated and 79% of the 42 patients who had a complete response or better. The median progression-free survival was 8.8 months (95% confidence interval, 5.6 to 11.6). Common toxic effects included neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, while cytokine release syndrome was reported in 84% of patients, with 5% experiencing grade 3 or higher events. Neurotoxic effects developed in 18% of patients, with 3% experiencing grade 3 effects. Cellular kinetic analysis confirmed CAR+ T cells in 59% of patients at 6 months and 36% of patients at 12 months after infusion.

nodes.label: HIV-1
nodes.description: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1, a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It is transmitted through genital and colorectal mucosal tissues and is the primary target of prevention strategies involving antiretroviral therapy (ART) for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). HIV-1 is treated with drugs such as NNRTIs, RTIs, and monitored for transmitted drug-resistance. It is the focus of various prevention methods, including topical microbicides, vaginal rings, and oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) using drugs like tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dapivirine.

nodes.label: Arginine Vasotocin
nodes.description: A peptide hormone that alters mating calls and decreases call attractiveness in male túngara frogs. It influences the production of advertisement calls, which are acoustic signals used by males to attract females and repel rival males. In anurans, it modulates various social behaviors and affects the rate and production of chucks. A nonapeptide hormone that plays a key role in the regulation of social behavior across vertebrates. It has three neuronal populations described in the preoptic area (POA) of teleost fishes: parvocellular (pPOA), magnocellular (mPOA), and gigantocellular (gPOA). These neurons project to the pituitary and other brain regions, regulating neural circuits underlying social behavior. A neuropeptide that serves as an important modulator of social behavior in addition to its peripheral functions related to osmoregulation, reproductive physiology, and stress hormone release. It is present in greater amounts in males in many brain areas and its presence varies seasonally, with hormonal state, and in males with differing social status. Its social influence is also conserved across herpetological taxa, with significant effects on social signaling and aggression, and may also modulate parental care and social bonding when it is present in these vertebrates. A nonapeptide involved in regulating social behavior, reproductive behavior, and aggressive behavior in many vertebrate species. It is expressed in the hypothalamus, specifically the preoptic area and the anterior tuberal nucleus of teleost fish.

nodes.label: Sonidegib
nodes.description: An oral Smoothened (SMO) inhibitor, also known as LDE225, which is a potent inhibitor of hedgehog signaling. It is a systemic hedgehog inhibitor (HHI) used to treat advanced basal cell carcinoma (BCC), with a primary endpoint assessing the proportion of patients who achieve an objective response to treatment. It is administered orally at two different doses: 200 mg and 800 mg daily. Sonidegib has shown significant efficacy in treating BCC and has been tested in phase I trials for its safety, tolerability, efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and biomarkers in patients with advanced solid tumors. It exhibits exposure-dependent reduction in GLI1 mRNA expression and has an acceptable safety profile in patients with advanced solid tumors. Sonidegib is primarily eliminated through oxidative metabolism of the morpholine part and amide hydrolysis, with metabolites accounting for 4.49% of the dose in excreta.

nodes.label: Astrocyte
nodes.description: A type of glial cell in the central nervous system (CNS) that supports neurons and plays a role in immune cell crosstalk. Astrocytes are the most abundant cell type in the CNS, maintaining homeostasis, providing trophic support to neurons, detoxifying, and performing immune surveillance. They express high levels of the core astrocyte marker GFAP and transcription factors from the NFI family. Astrocyte dysfunction is associated with many neurological disorders. They are involved in regulating synapse formation, controlling neurotransmitter release and uptake, and maintaining extracellular ion balance. Astrocytes have been implicated in the progression of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, and Parkinson's disease. Research focuses on the transcriptional control of astrocyte heterogeneity and the use of human pluripotent stem cell-derived astrocytes for disease modeling.

nodes.label: Chromatin
nodes.description: A tightly packaged structure of DNA and protein within the nucleus of a cell, where the arrangement of different protein complexes along the DNA modulates and is modulated by gene expression. It is a complex structure in eukaryotic cells where DNA is packed, consisting of nucleosomes with DNA wrapped around a histone octamer. Chromatin is folded into higher-order structures through various mechanisms such as repositioning of nucleosomes, packing into more condensed configurations, looping of chromatin fibers, and tethering of chromosomal regions to nuclear structures. It is highly responsive to DNA damage and undergoes specific remodeling to facilitate DNA repair, serving as the context for DNA repair in eukaryotic cells. In metazoa, the nucleoporin ELYS is critical for the recruitment of the essential Nup107/160 complex. FANCL is recruited to chromatin in response to RAD18-mediated PCNA monoubiquitination, where it catalyzes the FANCD2 and FANCI monoubiquitylation.

nodes.label: MTMR2
nodes.description: A myotubularin-related protein that utilizes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) as a substrate and is mutated in type 4B Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, encoding a protein that hydrolyzes both PtdIns3P and PtdIns(3,5)P2. It is a member of the myotubularin family of phosphoinositide-3-phosphatases and is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4B. MTMR2 has a phosphatase domain with a unique structure and a GRAM domain, and its crystal structure provides insights into the specificity of myotubularin phosphatases towards phosphoinositide substrates. It depletes phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI(3)P) and bisphosphate PI(3,5)P2, and associates with MTMR13 in human embryonic kidney 293 cells through coiled-coil sequences. Mutations in MTMR2 cause CMT4B.

nodes.label: Temozolomide
nodes.description: A chemotherapy drug primarily used in the treatment of glioblastoma, often in conjunction with radiotherapy as part of the Stupp protocol. It is an alkylating agent that can be administered in low-dose concurrent with radiotherapy and high-dose as six cycles following radiotherapy. Temozolomide has a weak growth inhibitory effect on all cell lines with an IC50 of 53-226 µM and can be used in combination with other drugs such as STX-0119, BMN 673, olaparib, rucaparib, and NPe6-PDT for GBM-SC-specific therapeutics.

nodes.label: Rituximab
nodes.description: A chimeric, anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody registered for the treatment of B-cell malignancies and refractory rheumatoid arthritis in Australia. It has been used off-label for various diseases, including hematological diseases, systemic connective tissue disorders, and kidney diseases. Rituximab is a B cell-depleting drug that leads to transient stabilization of insulin C-peptide in type 1 diabetes (T1D) and is used in conjunction with systems biology approaches to elucidate mechanisms associated with C-peptide stabilization in clinical trial blood samples from new-onset T1D subjects. It is also used as a treatment option for juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) in children and young people, although it is not licensed for this indication. Common side effects include serious infections and infusion reactions. The level of evidence supporting the use of rituximab for these indications is low, and the cost is very high, making it necessary for further clinical trials, especially in the context of rare diseases.

nodes.label: Conjoined twins
nodes.description: A biological process involving the formation of twins that are connected or fused together, which can occur through various sites of union in the early embryo such as the cranial, caudal, pharyngeal, cloacal, cardiac, and umbilical regions. This process is supported by fusion rather than fission, and is explained by seven possible sites of union in the early embryo. A condition where two embryos develop together, resulting in a single placenta and amnion. This occurs when twinning happens at the primitive streak stage of development, specifically between 13-14 days after fertilization in humans. Conjoined twins are exclusively associated with the monoamniotic monochorionic type of placentation. The highest incidence of this condition is believed to be in humans. Accounts of the anatomical features of commonly encountered varieties of conjoined twins are provided. A rare occurrence in obstetric/pediatric practice, characterized by two individuals sharing a common body. Also known as Siamese twins, they are often born dead, but there are instances where they survive. The case presented involves dicephalus dipud conjoined twins, a specific and uncommon type. A biological process involving the occurrence of two embryos or fetuses that are joined together during development, resulting in various types such as thoracoomphalopagus (28% of cases), thoracopagus (18% of cases), omphalopagus (10% of cases), parasitic twins (10% of cases), and craniopagus (6% of cases). Conjoined twins are more common among females than males, and in nonwhites than whites. No maternal age effect was found. There was no evidence of seasonal or temporal clustering of the cases. A type of twin development where two individuals share a common body, in this case, the infants were joined front-to-front with two faces, each a composite of two twins, each twin having four extremities. They developed from a single zygote, with embryonic tissue dividing incompletely, resulting in twinning anomalies from the 15th to 16th day postovulation.

nodes.label: FANCD2
nodes.description: A protein involved in promoting immunoglobulin gene conversion and DNA repair through a mechanism related to homologous recombination (HR). It is part of a multiprotein complex that includes FancA/C/E/F/G/L and is responsible for DNA damage-induced FancD2 monoubiquitination. A Fanconi anaemia protein that co-localizes with NBS1 and accumulates from mid-S to G2 phase within sites containing single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) intermediates or at sites of DNA damage. It binds preferentially to ssDNA over various DNA substrates and forms foci in vivo. Its stability and function are regulated by MRE11, NBS1, and RAD50. A component of the FA complementation group I (FANCI)-FANCD2 (ID) complex, which is monoubiquitylated by FA complementation group L (FANCL) in response to DNA damage. Monoubiquitylated FANCD2 is stimulated by monoubiquitylated PCNA and is necessary for the recruitment of FANCL to chromatin. A key DNA repair factor involved in the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway, which is monoubiquitinated in response to DNA damage, along with the phosphorylation of FANCI.

nodes.label: c-Myc
nodes.description: A transcription factor and proto-oncogene involved in the regulation of the cell cycle and proliferation mediated by PcG proteins, mainly Bmi-1, in mice and in cell culture experiments. It is one of the four transcription factors, along with Oct4, Sox2 and Klf4, known as the Yamanaka factors, used to generate induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from somatic cells. c-Myc is also a Yamanaka factor involved in maintaining the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells and a target gene of the Notch pathway overexpressed in ependymoma samples. Additionally, it is a protein that interacts with SKIP and Menin to promote HIV-1 Tat transactivation and is stabilized by USP28.

nodes.label: Lewy bodies
nodes.description: Pathological inclusions composed of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein found in the cytoplasm of neurons, associated with Parkinson's disease. They are intracellular aggregates primarily located in the substantia nigra and cortical areas of the brain, and are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease, contributing to its characteristic features and neurodegeneration.

nodes.label: ZSWIM6
nodes.description: A gene whose highly conserved protein domain contains the recurrent de novo mutation associated with Acromelic frontonasal dysostosis. The mutation identified is a heterozygous variant (c.3487C>T [p.Arg1163Trp]), which has not been seen in the 1000 Genomes data, dbSNP, or the Exome Sequencing Project. A gene encoding a protein of unknown function, with a single recurrent heterozygous missense substitution that was previously shown to underlie Acromelic frontonasal dysostosis in four unrelated cases. A gene with a recurrent de novo nonsense variant (c.2737C>T [p.Arg913Ter]) in the penultimate exon, which results in severe-profound intellectual disability and additional central and peripheral nervous system symptoms but no frontonasal or limb malformations. The variant does not trigger nonsense-mediated decay of the ZSWIM6 mRNA in affected individual-derived cells, supporting the existence of a truncated ZSWIM6 protein lacking the Sin3-like domain.

nodes.label: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)
nodes.description: A protein involved in cellular growth, division, and signaling, particularly in the context of colorectal cancer (CRC) carcinogenesis and non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). EGFR is targeted by inhibitors for cancer treatment, and mutations in the EGFR gene, especially activating mutations, are found in ~10-30% of NSCLC patients. Inhibition of mutated EGFR has been a successful cancer targeted therapy for many patients, but resistance to this treatment is common. EGFR is also involved in skin signs, with overexpression in keratinocytes and hair follicles, and is crucial for the normal development and physiology of the epidermis. Inhibition of EGFR in the skin is related to skin toxicities associated with EGFR inhibitors. Additionally, EGFR is involved in the signaling pathway of follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDC-S), with strong expression found on dysplastic and neoplastic FDCs, driving their survival and proliferation primarily via MAPK and STAT pathways.

nodes.label: Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of rectal cancer characterized by stage III disease as determined by endorectal ultrasound (ERUS) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), involving tumors of grade T3/T4 and/or N1. It is an advanced form of rectal cancer that requires careful consideration for treatment timing and often involves neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection. Patients with this condition may be inoperable or require extensive surgery beyond total mesorectal excision (TME). It is a more common form of rectal cancer in China, characterized by locally invasive tumors that can be effectively reduced in size with preoperative neoadjuvant concurrent chemoradiotherapy. The Total Neoadjuvant Treatment for Rectal Cancer has been introduced as a therapeutic option for this type of cancer, which is considered advanced and requires specific treatments like neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) followed by surgical resection.

nodes.label: KRas G12V
nodes.description: A point mutant of the KRas gene with a valine mutation at codon 12, associated with higher metastatic efficiency and aggressiveness in colorectal cancer models compared to KRas G13D.

nodes.label: p16
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene associated with primary glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), located on chromosome 10p and encoded by the INK4a(p16-p14ARF) locus. It is often lost in glioblastomas when p15 protein expression is lost, and is commonly lacking in p16/p15-negative tumors along with p14ARF expression. P16 is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor and shows the most powerful tumor suppressor effects among the three genes studied. It is involved in the inverse correlation with BMI-1 expression, suggesting a role in lung carcinogenesis and regulating the expression of p16 by binding directly to the BRE within the p16 promoter.

nodes.label: Cirrhosis
nodes.description: A chronic liver disease characterized by the replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue, leading to impaired liver function. It can develop as a complication of hepatitis D virus infection without treatment, and is associated with a high risk of advanced liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma. Cirrhosis can be caused by various factors, including viral hepatitis and alcohol abuse, and is often a consequence of long-term liver damage. It is mentioned in the context of HDV-related cirrhosis, CSPH, and is a condition where Bulevirtide is shown to be safe and effective.

nodes.label: VarDict
nodes.description: A novel and versatile variant caller designed for both DNA- and RNA-sequencing data. It accurately calls SNV, MNV, InDels, complex and structural variants, performs local realignments for more accurate allele frequency estimation, and scales linearly with sequencing depth. VarDict is capable of detecting PCR artifacts, performing amplicon aware variant calling for PCR-based targeted sequencing, and identifying differences in somatic and loss of heterozygosity variants between paired samples. It has been used to reprocess The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Lung Adenocarcinoma dataset and called known driver mutations in KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, PIK3CA and MET in 16% more patients than previously published variant calls.

nodes.label: Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer characterized by the spread of tumor cells to distant organs from the original site of the tumor, specifically involving the colon or rectum. It is managed with chemotherapy, including the use of trifluridine/tipiracil (TAS-102, Lonsurf®) for patients who are refractory or intolerant to standard therapies. Survival benefits from bevacizumab treatment in unselected patient populations are modest. It is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in both sexes and is treated with EGFR inhibitors such as cetuximab and panitumumab, especially in patients with microsatellite stability (MSS) and BRAFV600E mutation. Prognosis markers related to miR-7-5p, miR-10a-5p, and miR-143-3p are associated with this type of cancer when treated with bevacizumab plus chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Dapagliflozin
nodes.description: A glucose-lowering agent belonging to the novel class of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes. It inhibits the transporter protein SGLT2 in the kidneys, reducing renal glucose reabsorption, leading to urinary glucose excretion and a reduction in blood glucose levels. It is well tolerated in clinical trials and maintains efficacy for up to approximately 2 years. When used in combination with other antidiabetic drugs, it provides complementary therapy via its unique mechanism of action. A drug used in the management of type 2 diabetes, known for having a low propensity to cause hypoglycaemia, especially when used alone or in combination with metformin. Its unique and complementary mechanism of action makes it an important addition to the therapeutic options for type 2 diabetes, particularly when used as add-on therapy. It has been associated with events suggestive of genital infections and urinary tract infections among recipients, which are believed to be related to its mechanism of action. A new class of oral glucose-lowering drug that inhibits renal glucose reabsorption and promotes glycosuria. It is licensed in the UK for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus in adults as monotherapy when diet and exercise alone do not provide adequate glycaemic control and who are unable to tolerate metformin; or, as add-on therapy, with other glucose-lowering agents including insulin, when these, with diet and exercise, do not provide adequate glycaemic control. Dapagliflozin is marketed under the brand name Forxiga and has been reviewed for its use in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. A sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor used in the management of patients with type 2 diabetes. It reduces renal glucose reabsorption by inhibiting the transporter protein SGLT2 in the renal proximal tubule, leading to increased urinary glucose excretion and reduced blood glucose levels. It is generally well tolerated and has a low risk of hypoglycaemia. Common adverse events include genital mycotic infections. It is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe renal impairment. Dapagliflozin is primarily used as add-on therapy for 24 weeks, but can also be used as monotherapy or initial combination therapy. Numerous clinical trials have demonstrated reductions in glycosylated haemoglobin, fasting plasma glucose levels, and body weight. A sodium glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). It exhibits favorable pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties, effectively reduces glycemic levels, and has beneficial/neutral effects on other risk factors contributing to T2DM metabolic control. It is available under the brand names Farxiga or Forxiga. The use of dapagliflozin is associated with increased risks of genital and urinary infections, episodes of volume depletion, and requires additional data assessment for bladder cancer and cardiovascular safety concerns. An SGLT-2 inhibitor marketed in Europe and Australia, used in the treatment of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. It achieves glycosylated hemoglobin reductions similar to other oral agents and has beneficial effects on major comorbidities associated with T2DM. A specific inhibitor of sodium-glucose cotransporters type 2 (SGLT2), used as a glucose-lowering agent in type 2 diabetes. It inhibits glucose reabsorption in renal tubules, promoting glucosuria, which leads to a reduction in fasting and postprandial glycaemia, a decrease of glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), a minor risk of hypoglycaemia, weight reduction, and a reduction in arterial blood pressure. It is indicated for the treatment of T2DM and reimbursed in Belgium with conditions as add-on to a background glucose-lowering therapy (either metformin or sulfonylurea/repaglinide or metformin plus sulfonylurea/repaglinide or basal insulin plus at least one of these oral glucose-lowering agents). Preliminary results suggest some cardiovascular and renal protection.

nodes.label: Eosinophilic esophagitis
nodes.description: A disease associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease and allergy/atopy, characterized by eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). It involves symptoms of dysphagia and esophageal biopsies with ≥15 eosinophils/hpf. Prospective randomized controlled trials have been conducted to compare the treatment of EoE with acid suppression versus topical corticosteroids. Common in adult patients, with dysphagia improving and esophageal eosinophilic infiltration decreasing with either treatment. There is no difference in the degree of improvement in dysphagia or eosinophil infiltration in patients treated with either topical fluticasone or oral esomeprazole. A chronic inflammatory disease characterized by an increased load of esophageal eosinophils, thickened esophageal walls, and signs of esophageal remodeling. It can be managed with topical corticosteroids like budesonide, which is effective in inducing clinical and histologic remission. A disease characterized by inflammation of the esophagus involving eosinophils, which was the subject of a randomized trial comparing nebulized and viscous topical corticosteroid treatments. The trial involved 25 subjects with incident eosinophilic esophagitis who received budesonide 1 mg twice daily, either nebulized and then swallowed (NEB) or as an oral viscous slurry (OVB), for 8 weeks. A disease characterized by symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and eosinophil-predominant esophageal inflammation. It requires exclusion of other differential diagnoses for esophageal eosinophilia before diagnosis. Most patients are male and have concomitant atopic disorders. Therapeutic options include drugs, diet, and dilation. A relatively new chronic inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration, increasing recognition, and evolving diagnostic and therapeutic aspects. It is associated with dysphagia, food bolus impaction, abdominal pain, feeding disorders, and gastroesophageal reflux-like symptoms. EoE is distinguished from eosinophilic infiltration from gastroesophageal reflux disease and involves complex interactions between food and environmental antigens, stimulating T-helper (Th-2) inflammatory response. Therapeutic options include proton-pump inhibitors, immunosuppressive drugs, elimination diets, and esophageal dilatation. Novel therapeutic approaches targeting chemokines and specific immunologic mechanisms are also being explored.

nodes.label: Aging
nodes.description: Aging is a natural biological process in living organisms characterized by receding bioenergetics, leading to the functional decline of mitochondria and contributing to the decay of mitochondrial health. It is associated with the failure of protective mechanisms and imbalances in key mitochondrial-regulated pathways. Aging is linked to cell death and is an area of interest for scientists involved in identifying new therapies or drugs for human disease. It is also associated with various physiological changes, including declines in stem cell function, and a gradual decline in physiological functions over time, potentially causing age-associated diseases. Aging is studied in the context of replicative senescence, tissue aging, and segmental progeroid syndromes. It is a fundamental process carried out by mitochondria, along with energy production and essential metabolic pathways. Mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) mutations have been proposed to contribute to the progressive nature of common age-related diseases such as cancer, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders. In C. elegans, aging is studied in the context of mitophagy, involving the selective elimination of mitochondria by autophagy.

nodes.label: Nivolumab
nodes.description: An anti-PD-1 antibody used as an immune checkpoint inhibitor in cancer immunotherapy, targeting the programmed death-1 (PD-1) receptor. It has shown long-term survival benefits in patients and is used to block interactions and unleash the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Nivolumab is evaluated in clinical trials for various cancers, including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, head and neck cancers, lymphoma, and several other cancers. It is also used to treat lung adenocarcinoma and can cause immune-related adverse events such as prurigo nodularis. Nivolumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor associated with the risk of elevated transaminases and colitis in patients with cancer.

nodes.label: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
nodes.description: A neuromuscular disorder characterized by reduced quantal release of acetylcholine from the motor nerve terminals, initially affecting proximal muscle weakness, especially gait, and causing autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth, constipation, and erectile failure. It can be treated symptomatically with cholinergic drugs, immunosuppression, immunomodulation, and physical therapy. It is often associated with small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). A case report describes a rare manifestation of this syndrome in ovarian cancer. A disease of neuromuscular transmission characterized by autoantibodies against the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) at the presynaptic nerve terminal, leading to decreased quantal release of acetylcholine (ACh) and resulting in skeletal muscle weakness and autonomic symptoms. Associated with cancer, particularly small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC), in 50-60% of LEMS patients, suggesting an immunological cross-reactivity between the nerve terminal and carcinoma cells due to a shared common antigen (VGCC). Has a strong association with HLA-DR3-B8. In approximately 15% of LEMS patients, no anti-P/Q-type VGCC antibodies are found, indicating recognition of other target(s). Antibodies against synaptotagmin-1 and M1-type presynaptic muscarinic ACh receptor (M1 mAChR) have been detected in both anti-VGCC-positive and -negative LEMS patients. A disease characterized by antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reducing the quantal release of acetylcholine, leading to muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunction. More than half of the affected patients have associated small cell lung cancer. The mainstay of treatment is symptomatic, but immunotherapy is needed in more severely affected patients. 3,4-diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP, amifampridine) is the treatment of choice for increasing muscle strength and resting compound muscle action potentials, with four placebo-controlled trials demonstrating its efficacy. A neuromuscular junction disorder characterized by proximal limb muscle weakness, fatigability, decreased deep-tendon reflexes, and autonomic symptoms. There are two forms: P-Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, often associated with small-cell lung cancer, and NP-Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, a pure autoimmune form. It is a very rare disorder in children younger than age 12 years. The most long-term follow-up of NP-Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome in childhood has been reported in a 25-year-old man who initially presented with the condition at the age of 10 years. The treatment with 3,4-diaminopyridine phosphate has been sufficient to ensure a good quality of life. A pre-synaptic disorder of the neuromuscular and autonomic transmission mediated by antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal. It is a rare and probably under-diagnosed disease with a slow onset and fluctuating clinical signs. LEMS typically involves lower and upper limbs, with proximal muscles being predominantly affected. A significant proportion of patients also have dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system that may include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, impaired sweating, and orthostatic hypotension. Nearly 50-60% of patients with LEMS have an underlying tumour that, in almost all cases, is a small-cell lung cancer. A neurological disorder characterized by primary respiratory failure as the presenting symptom, which is rare. It can occur without associated carcinoma and has been reported to have a rapid respiratory failure as the first manifestation of disease in some patients.

nodes.label: Sclerostin
nodes.description: A bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) antagonist that forms a mutually inhibitory complex with noggin, binds to BMPs with high affinity, and modulates mitogenic activity through BMP sequestration. It is a recombinant protein and is expressed naturally in the rat osteosarcoma cell line, ROS 17/2.8. A cysteine knot protein that directly interacts with LRP5 but not LRP5G171V to modulate Wnt activity. It has been postulated to exert its activity by functioning as a BMP antagonist. Sclerostin is highly related to Wise, which can also modulate the Wnt pathway by binding to LRP5 and LRP6. It physically interacts with Lrp5 and Lrp6 and inhibits the canonical Wnt signaling pathway. Variants of Sost amino acids are used to identify the contact points between Sclerostin and LRP6. An antibody being developed as a novel anabolic agent for the treatment of osteoporosis that targets molecules involved in Wnt signaling. A secreted glycoprotein that alters bone formation and interacts with multiple proteins involved in bone formation and resorption. It was used in a sclerostin affinity capture technique to examine its interactions with bone proteins. An endogenous inhibitor of bone formation, targeted by antibodies in potential new bone anabolic substances for osteoporosis treatment.

nodes.label: COVID-19
nodes.description: A disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, characterized by symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. It has led to a global pandemic, increasing morbidity and mortality rates, and has been associated with severe acute respiratory symptoms. The disease can progress to severe cases requiring hospitalization, especially in vulnerable populations. It has been studied in relation to various factors, including the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and has led to the development of therapeutic antibody cocktails like REGEN-COV for treatment. The disease is managed through symptomatic treatment, and vaccines have been developed to prevent its spread.

nodes.label: Pre-mRNA splicing
nodes.description: A process by which a precursor mRNA (pre-mRNA) is transformed into its mature or functional form, involving the ligation of exons and the excision of introns as branched or lariat RNAs. A biological process involving the removal of introns and joining of exons in pre-mRNA molecules to generate mature mRNA. Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) are involved in this process. A critical step in gene expression that involves the removal of intronic sequences from immature mRNA, leading to the production of mature mRNA that can be translated into protein. It also refers to the process where alternative exons and/or introns are selectively included or excluded, generating mature mRNAs that encode proteins which may differ in function. A processing event involved in shaping protein-coding transcripts during gene expression. It involves the removal of introns and ligation of exons. This process can be initiated and concluded co-transcriptionally, although this is not strictly required. Pre-mRNA splicing is essential for producing mature mRNA, which can be subsequently translated. A biological process during which antisense oligonucleotides like PMOs can induce exon skipping, affecting the reading frame of the DMD primary transcript. A fundamental step in eukaryotic gene expression that systematically removes non-coding regions (introns) and ligates coding regions (exons) into a continuous message (mature mRNA). It is highly regulated and can be highly flexible through a process known as alternative splicing.

nodes.label: TAS-102
nodes.description: A novel oral nucleoside antitumor agent containing trifluridine (FTD) and tipiracil hydrochloride (TPI) at a molar ratio of 1:0.5, used as a DNA synthesis inhibitor for the treatment of gastrointestinal malignancies. It improves overall survival of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients who are insensitive to standard chemotherapies and has been approved in Japan for the treatment of unresectable, advanced or recurrent colorectal cancer that is refractory to standard therapies. TAS-102 extends the median overall survival by approximately 2 months compared with placebo in a randomized phase III trial composed of Asian and non-Asian patients with refractory (or intolerant) metastatic colorectal cancer.

nodes.label: Chemoradiotherapy
nodes.description: A treatment approach involving the combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, commonly used before surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer, glioblastoma, and other types of cancer. It may involve the use of specific drugs such as temozolomide, 5-fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin, and radiation therapy delivered at a certain dose and frequency. The optimal interval between chemoradiotherapy and surgery may vary depending on the type of cancer and the individual patient's condition.

nodes.label: Pyoderma gangrenosum
nodes.description: An orphan disease characterized by severe, albeit rare, clinical manifestations. Treatment options for early stages and mild disease courses involve topical and intralesional therapeutic agents, while systemic therapeutic agents are predominantly used for more advanced cases. Evidence-based study data is available for systemic corticosteroids, cyclosporine A, and infliximab, with the latter particularly effective in patients with concurrent ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. First described by Brocq almost 100 years ago, treatment for Pyoderma gangrenosum remains a clinical challenge, but improvements are anticipated due to further clinical studies, a better understanding of etiopathogenesis, and the use of modern targeted therapies.

nodes.label: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by skin hyperextensibility, dystrophic scarring, and joint hypermobility, also known as classic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS). It is associated with type V collagen mutations, particularly COL5A1 and COL5A2 genes. Over 90% of patients fulfilling all major Villefranche criteria for classic EDS were shown to harbor a type V collagen defect, indicating that this is the major--if not only--cause of classic EDS. A family of multisystemic hereditary connective tissue disorders comprising 13 recognized subtypes, including classical, classical-like, cardiac-valvular, vascular, hypermobile, arthrochalasis, dermopatosis, kyphoscoliosis, brittle cornea syndrome, spondylodysplasia, musculocontractura, myopathy, and periodontal, as designated by the most recent 2017 International classification system. Clinical presentation ranges from mild manifestations such as skin hyperextensibility and joint hypermobility to more severe complications like vascular and organ rupture. Accompanying inflammation may occur in some subtypes, but pathogenic mechanisms are not clearly defined. Evaluation involves clinical examination, family history, laboratory testing, and imaging. Surgical treatment is reserved for complications or emergencies involving vascular or orthopedic injury due to the risk of poor wound healing. An umbrella term for a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of hereditary soft connective tissue disorders mainly featuring abnormal cutaneous texture (doughy/velvety, soft, thin, and/or variably hyperextensible skin), easy bruising, and joint hypermobility. It includes 13 clinical types due to deleterious variants in 19 different genes. Most Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are due to inherited abnormalities affecting the biogenesis of fibrillar collagens and other components of the extracellular matrix. The introduction of next-generation sequencing technologies has improved our knowledge on the phenotypic variability of many Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. A group of hereditary connective tissue disorders, classified into 13 subtypes in the 2017 International Classification. One of the subtypes is classical-like Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome type 2 (clEDS2), caused by biallelic variants in the adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) gene.

nodes.label: Enhanceosome
nodes.description: A higher order nucleoprotein complex consisting of transcriptional activators NF-kappa B (p50/p65), ATF-2/c-jun, IRF-3, IRF-7, architectural protein HMGI(Y), and coactivators p300 and CBP, which is required for the transcriptional activation of the IFN-beta gene by virus infection. It is a complex of transcriptional activators including NF-kappa B, IRF1, ATF2/c-Jun, and the architectural protein HMG I(Y) that enhances transcription of the IFN beta gene in response to virus infection through transcriptional synergy. It is also involved in the activation of transcription from the IFN beta promoter and requires transcriptional coactivators CBP and P/CAF. It includes HMG I(Y), an essential architectural component necessary for its assembly.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Dysfunction
nodes.description: A condition associated with diseases and contributing to the decay of mitochondrial health in aging and age-related metabolic diseases. It involves the failure of protective mechanisms and imbalances in key mitochondrial-regulated pathways. Mitochondrial dysfunction refers to the impaired function of mitochondria, which can manifest in various ways such as increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis disorder, abnormal mitophagy, and changes in mitochondrial morphology and structure. It is associated with the occurrence and development of different chronic liver diseases, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury (DILI), alcoholic fatty liver (AFL), and non-alcoholic fatty liver (NAFL). A condition characterized by impaired function of mitochondria, leading to decreased cellular energy production and increased oxidative stress. It has been associated with metabolic pathologies such as diabetes, obesity, hypertension, neurodegenerative diseases, cellular aging, and cancer.

nodes.label: Microsporidia
nodes.description: A group of obligate, intracellular eukaryotic pathogens that infect animal cells, including humans. They are known for having compact genomes with fewer and highly divergent genes. Microsporidia are believed to have evolved from ancestral sexual fungi and are suggested to be true fungi that descended from a zygomycete ancestor. A large diverse group of intracellular parasites now considered as fungi, particularly prevalent in fish and recognized as important opportunistic parasites in humans. Microsporidia have 99-100% identity with anglerfish microsporidians of the genus Spraguea and very low identity with microsporidians that infect humans. Unicellular fungi that are obligate endoparasites, known to cause infections in nematodes. The only confirmed report of microsporidian infection was that of the 'nematode killer' (Nematocida parisii). Microsporidia are not closely related to N. parisii and differ strikingly in all aspects of infection. They infect the hypodermal and muscle tissues of the free-living marine nematode Odontophora rectangula, and can also infect eggs, suggesting a vertical mode of transmission. A diverse group of obligate, intracellular, eukaryotic, spore-forming parasites that were traditionally considered as protozoans but recently have been reclassified as fungi. They cause systemic infections and keratoconjunctivitis, corneal stromal keratitis, scleritis, and endophthalmitis in the eye. An obligate intracellular protozoan infection, classified under the phylum Microspora, considered an opportunistic infection in humans. It affects 60 transplanted patients worldwide, with 14 species belonging to 8 different genera described. Patients at risk include those infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), HIV serum-negative asymptomatic patients, with poor hygienic conditions, and recipients of bone marrow or solid organ transplantation. A group of obligate intracellular eukaryotes infecting multiple animal lineages, characterized by their large host spectrum and implications in host population regulation. They influence food webs, and accordingly, ecosystem structure and function. Their ecological role is not well understood, and they are present as highly resistant spores in the environment. Different techniques based on direct isolation and/or molecular approaches can be considered to elucidate their role in ecosystems. Genomic data, such as genome architecture, core genome, transcriptional and translational signals, are crucial to better understand the diversity and adaptive capacities of Microsporidia. Understanding of their evolution is currently impaired by limited sampling, suggesting a larger diversity than observed.

nodes.label: E-cadherin
nodes.description: A protein involved in cell adhesion and epithelial plasticity, often repressed by Snail and Suv39H1 in basal-like breast cancer (BLBC), and associated with age of patients and lymph node metastasis in papillary thyroid carcinoma. Its expression decreases during epithelial-mesenchymal transition in breast cancer cells and is a direct transcriptional repressor target of Twist. E-cadherin's downregulation is a crucial event for epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) in embryonic development and cancer progression, and its promoter activity is regulated by DeltaEF1, a transcriptional repressor.

nodes.label: NRAS
nodes.description: A proto-oncogene and one of the three closely related isoforms of Ras proteins, along with HRAS and KRAS, that is frequently mutated in human cancers and has overlapping but distinctive functions with the other isoforms. NRAS mutations are associated with a significantly lower response rate than NRAS wild types and are found in 2.6% (17/644) of the tumours studied, often associated with resistance to anti-EGFR therapies. It is part of the RAS gene family and contains gain-of-function mutations leading to constitutive activity of oncoproteins responsible for tumorigenesis and cancer progression.

nodes.label: Interleukin-18
nodes.description: A ligand that binds to the MC54 protein encoded by MCV, inhibiting interferon-γ production. A proinflammatory and immune regulatory cytokine belonging to the IL-1 family. It was initially identified as an IFN-γ-inducing factor in T and NK cells, involved in Th1 responses. Interleukin-18 is produced as an inactive precursor (pro-IL-18) that is enzymatically processed into a mature form by Casp1. It is expressed by various cell types including macrophages, DCs, microglial cells, synovial fibroblasts, and epithelial cells. The production of bioactive Interleukin-18 is mainly regulated at the processing level. PAMP or DAMP molecules activate inflammasomes, which trigger Casp1 activation and Interleukin-18 conversion. Interleukin-18 has shown anti-tumor activity in different preclinical models of cancer immunotherapy through the activation of NK and/or T cell responses and has been tested in clinical studies in cancer patients. However, its dual role in cancer biology raises critical issues on its therapeutic use in cancer. A proinflammatory cytokine that induces interferon-γ production and plays a crucial role in immune systems. It is involved in the pathophysiology of IgA nephropathy and has higher levels in patients compared to controls. A pro-inflammatory cytokine belonging to the IL-1 family, produced by macrophages, epithelial and dendritic cells, keratinocytes, adrenal cortex, and human platelets. It is produced as an inactive precursor that is cleaved by activated caspase 1 into its mature form. It co-localizes with IL-18BP in α granules inside platelets and is secreted out with different kinetics.

nodes.label: sotorasib
nodes.description: A selective KRAS G12C inhibitor that has been studied in a phase I trial for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and has shown responses in about a third of patients. It is currently in clinical trials, including in combination with other inhibitors, and has received conditional approval as the first targeted therapy for KRAS G12C mutations. Sotorasib is used in combination with Guardant360 CDx for the detection of KRAS p.G12C mutations in NSCLC patients and requires augmentation by tissue testing methodologies as outlined on the approved product label.

nodes.label: Fatigue
nodes.description: A symptom characterized by feelings of tiredness or lack of energy, commonly experienced by patients undergoing various treatments such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and certain medications. It can range from mild to severe in severity and may be more common in specific treatment groups or types of cancer. Fatigue is also a common side effect of vaccines, particularly those administered for shingles. In the context of myotonic dystrophy, it is a symptom of sleep disordered breathing.

nodes.label: EZH2
nodes.description: A core protein of the Polycomb-complexes, encoded by a PcG gene. It is expressed in Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg (H/RS) cells and Hodgkin's lymphoma-derived cell lines, and is associated with the maintenance of cell identity and gene silencing patterns. Together with BMI-1, it is co-expressed in H/RS cells during normal B-cell development in germinal centers. A protein involved in histone methylation, specifically regulating histone H3 lysine 27 methylation. Knockdown of EZH2 caused loss of H3K27me3 but not H3K9me3, indicating that SUZ12 regulates H3-K9 methylation in an EZH2-independent fashion. A chromatin regulator gene/protein that is overexpressed in prostate cancer and plays a crucial role in androgen-stimulated and castration-refractory prostate tumor growth and survival. It is regulated by androgen and strongly expressed in early prostate morphogenesis and during puberty.

nodes.label: Pridopidine
nodes.description: A dopaminergic stabilizer that acts primarily at dopamine type 2 (D(2)) receptors and displays state-dependent behavioral effects. It is a member of the new family of compounds referred to as dopidines, which act as dopaminergic stabilizers. Pridopidine is a substrate for the P450 cytochrome 2D6 enzyme (CYP2D6) and has different half-lives following single dosing versus at steady state. It is used in the treatment of Huntington disease and is administered at doses of 45 mg/day and 90 mg/day in clinical trials. Pridopidine has an acceptable safety profile and is well-tolerated for up to 1 year in patients with Huntington disease. It has been evaluated in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial for its efficacy and safety in managing symptoms of Huntington's disease, with three dosages of pridopidine evaluated: 20 mg, 45 mg, and 90 mg daily for 12 weeks. The 90 mg/day dosage appeared worthy of further study due to its potential improvement in motor function, although the primary analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant treatment effect.

nodes.label: Proteomics
nodes.description: A set of techniques used for the large-scale study of proteins, including 2DE, semi-quantitative image analysis, in-gel trypsin digestion and mass spectrometry. It was used to compare total proteome changes in mouse embryonic fibroblasts knock out for H-ras and/or N-ras. A field of study involving the large-scale analysis of proteins, including data analysis and protein inference. It is the focus of the research and the journal publications mentioned in the text. A scientific approach used to study the presence and abundance of proteins in a biological sample, often involving the use of multiplex proximity extension assays to measure multiple cardiovascular disease (CVD) and inflammatory disease-related biomarkers. A branch of biology concerned with the identification and quantification of proteins, their structures, functions, and interactions. Proteomics technologies are used alongside genomics to generate an immense amount of genomic data on clinical tumors, contributing to the transformation of the cancer landscape and the potential to revolutionize cancer diagnosis and prognosis.

nodes.label: Ubc9
nodes.description: A SUMO-conjugating enzyme, also known as ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme 9, that plays a crucial role in sumoylation and is involved in regulating several critical cellular pathways. It is expressed at high levels in advanced melanomas and its expression correlates with various cancer stages and grades. Ubc9 is also involved in the regulation of nuclear localization and synaptic sumoylation, and it is recognized by phosphorylated substrates through a PKC phosphorylation-dependent increase. Additionally, Ubc9 is a gene or protein that forms noncovalent complexes with a SUMO-like domain of Rad60 (SLD2) and a SUMO-like protein (SUMO), and it is targeted by the HPV E6 protein, which reduces its intracellular quantity.

nodes.label: Sumoylation
nodes.description: A reversible posttranslational modification process that involves the covalent attachment of small ubiquitin-related modifier (SUMO) proteins to target proteins. It regulates a wide variety of cellular processes and plays important roles for numerous viruses during infection. Sumoylation can affect the activity of transcription factors, such as Ets-1 and Tec1, through covalent attachment to lysine residues of target proteins. It is mediated by the sumoylating enzyme Ubc9 and can be regulated by various factors, including E3 SUMO ligases and SUMO proteases. Sumoylation is distinct from ubiquitination in its role in modulating protein-protein interactions rather than targeting proteins for degradation.

nodes.label: Tivozanib
nodes.description: A potent and selective vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, used in a phase I study for Japanese patients with solid tumors and a phase II randomized discontinuation trial for patients with advanced/metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It has demonstrated convincing clinical activity in Phase II and III studies for patients with advanced or metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Tivozanib is a novel tyrosine kinase inhibitor that inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptors-1, -2, and -3 at nanomolar concentrations. It has been studied in pre-clinical settings and Phase I and II clinical trials, including a randomized discontinuation Phase II study and a randomized Phase III study assessing its activity in metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). Tivozanib faces competition in the therapeutic space for mRCC due to the presence of other VEGF-TKIs. It is a potent pan-VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, previously known as KRN-951 and AV-951, and has demonstrated convincing clinical activity in Phase II and III studies for patients with advanced or metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Side effects observed in Phase I studies are generally mild, with hypertension being the most common adverse event. Tivozanib has not yet been approved for regular use.

nodes.label: Fungi
nodes.description: A kingdom of organisms that includes various taxa such as Dikarya, Chytridiomycota, Neocallimastigomycota, Monoblepharidomycetes, Neocallimastigomycetes, Eurotiomycetidae, Lecanoromycetidae, Mycocaliciomycetidae, Acarosporales, Corticiales, Baeomycetales, Candelariales, Gloeophyllales, Melanosporales, Trechisporales, and Umbilicariales. It also encompasses the clade containing Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, classified as subkingdom Dikarya due to the putative synapomorphy of dikaryotic hyphae. A kingdom of eukaryotic organisms, including mushrooms, yeasts, and molds. The Genomicus database has been extended to include this clade, enabling comparative genomic visualization and analysis. A kingdom in the Six-Kingdom System of Life, consisting of multicellular organisms. In the revised system, Fungi is expanded by adding Microsporidia, because of protein sequence evidence that these amitochondrial intracellular parasites are related to conventional Fungi, not Protozoa. Fungi are subdivided into four phyla and 20 classes, and their classification at the rank of subclass and above is comprehensively revised.

nodes.label: Viltolarsen
nodes.description: A phosphorodiamidate morpholino antisense oligonucleotide (PMO) developed through comprehensive sequence optimization and designed to skip exon 53 on the DMD primary transcript. It is used for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and induces de novo dystrophin production. Viltolarsen is administered by weekly intravenous infusion in two dose cohorts: 40 mg/kg and 80 mg/kg. It has received global approval in Japan for the treatment of DMD in patients with confirmed deletion of the dystrophin gene that is amenable to exon 53 skipping and is currently in clinical trials in the USA, Canada, and globally. Viltolarsen can treat approximately 8-10% of the DMD patient population.

nodes.label: PubMed
nodes.description: A database used for the search term 'restless legs syndrome' in combination with various keywords related to mental health and neurology, such as affective/anxiety, antidepressants, anxiety/anxiety disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression/depressive disorder, mood/mood disorder, neuropsychiatric, panic/panic disorder, psychiatric disorder, and psychosis. English-language articles published between January 1993 and May 2013 were retrieved from this database. A database used for searching publications related to Wernicke encephalopathy, thiamine, pediatric, children and adolescents. A database used for conducting a search to identify initial literature sources related to suvorexant and MK-4305. A database searched for studies on enzyme replacement therapies and substrate reduction therapy for treating Gaucher disease. It was used in conjunction with other search methods such as the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register and ClinicalTrials.gov. A scholarly database used for the literature review to identify original studies on C. burnetii DNA presence in ticks. A database used for searching scientific literature, including articles related to Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) and Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA).

nodes.label: Restless Legs Syndrome
nodes.description: A common neurological disorder characterized by an irresistible urge to move the legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, especially during rest or inactivity. It can onset from childhood to old age, with a variable clinical course that may include spontaneous remission. The cause is likely mainly genetic with a dysfunction of iron and dopamine metabolism, exacerbated by peripheral factors such as neuropathy, radiculopathy, and temperature. Secondary forms include iron deficiency, side effects of drugs, renal insufficiency, radiculopathy, and neuropathy. It can also occur during pregnancy, particularly in the last trimester. Treatment options include dopaminergic agents, benzodiazepines, anticonvulsants, and opiates, with dopamine agonists being considered first-line therapy. The effectiveness of other dopamine agonists and dopaminergic agents for children and pregnant women is not currently established.

nodes.label: Bapineuzumab
nodes.description: A humanized anti-amyloid-beta (Abeta) monoclonal antibody being evaluated for the potential treatment of Alzheimer disease (AD), developed as a passive Aβ immunotherapy to accelerate Aβ clearance from the brain. It has been tested in two Phase II trials and is currently under evaluation in four ongoing large Phase III trials. Bapineuzumab has shown a reduction in cortical (11)C-PiB retention compared with both baseline and placebo after 78 weeks of treatment. It has been used in various clinical trials to assess its safety, pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics, and cognitive efficacy, but its clinical use may be limited due to the occurrence of vasogenic edema, especially in apolipoprotein E 4 carriers.

nodes.label: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy
nodes.description: An inherited disorder characterized by the clinical triad of life-threatening progressive cardiomyopathy with conduction defect, early onset joint contractures and slow progressive muscle weakness in scapulo-humero-peroneal distribution. It has two main types of inheritance: X-linked form caused by mutations in the STA gene on locus Xq28 and autosomal dominant form caused by mutations in the LMNA gene on chromosome 1q21. The disease is associated with mutations in the lamin A/C gene, which is a major component of the nuclear lamina. Cardiomyopathy in EDMD is usually noticed after the second to third decade of life, and becomes worse with age. Permanent auricular paralysis occurs frequently and is considered a hallmark of EDMD cardiomyopathy. A rare X-linked muscular dystrophy that is the third most common type, characterized by childhood onset of early contractures, humeroperoneal muscle atrophy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. It has a broad spectrum of clinical severity and patients and carriers are at risk of sudden death. Regular cardiac evaluation is mandatory to assess the risk of cardiac arrhythmias.

nodes.label: Arginine vasotocin
nodes.description: A nonapeptide neuropeptide that is a nonmammalian analog of the mammalian hormone arginine vasopressin (AVP), influencing a wide range of physiological and behavioral responses, including sexual and social behaviors, osmoregulation, stress response, metabolism, blood pressure, and circadian rhythms. It has a mammalian homologue called arginine vasopressin (AVP) and is known to be steroid sensitive and associated with social behaviors in various vertebrate taxa. Its effects on aggression are studied in different species and contexts, but its role in regulating aggression remains unclear.

nodes.label: FOXP2
nodes.description: A gene encoding a forkhead-domain transcription factor, whose disruption causes a severe developmental disorder of verbal communication, involving profound articulation deficits, accompanied by linguistic and grammatical impairments. The gene is expressed in several structures including the cortical plate, basal ganglia, thalamus, inferior olives and cerebellum during brain development, supporting a role for FOXP2 in the development of corticostriatal and olivocerebellar circuits involved in motor control. The homologous pattern of FOXP2/Foxp2 expression in human and mouse argues for a role for this gene in development of motor-related circuits throughout mammalian species. A gene responsible for causing Developmental verbal dyspraxia (DVD) when mutated. It is present on chromosome 7 and has two main types of mutations: hemizygous paternal deletions and translocations interrupting the gene. The maternally inherited FOXP2 is underexpressed compared to the paternally inherited version. A gene associated with hereditary developmental verbal dyspraxia, a condition characterized by primary oromotor verbal dyspraxia. Deficiency in FOXP2 leads to speech delay. The expression patterns of FOXP2 overlap with those of FOXP1 in some areas of the brain, and the two genes can form heterodimers. A gene that expresses a protein involved in regulating the expression of many downstream genes, which may have important roles in nervous system development and function. Mutations in the human FOXP2 gene cause speech and language impairments. The FOXP2 protein is a transcription factor that regulates the expression of many downstream genes.
