An adequate amount of functional FOXP2 protein is thought to be critical for the proper development of the neural circuitry underlying speech and language. A transcription factor that plays an essential role in the development of language and speech. It is covalently modified by both SUMO1 and SUMO3, and its SUMOylation is significantly decreased by SENP2. Human etiological FOXP2 R553H mutation robustly reduces its SUMOylation potential as compared to wild-type FOXP2. The acidic residues downstream the core SUMO motif on FOXP2 are required for its full SUMOylation capacity. SUMOylation may modulate transcriptional activity of FOXP2 in regulating downstream target genes such as DISC1, SRPX2, and MiR200c. A well-studied gene known to play an essential role in normal speech development. Deletions in the gene have been shown to result in developmental speech disorders and regulatory disruption of downstream gene targets associated with common forms of language impairments. The patient had an  approximately 9-kb loss within chromosome band 7q3.1 that contains exon 2 of FOXP2, demonstrating a single copy of this region instead of the normal two copies per diploid gene.

nodes.label: Antibiotics
nodes.description: Medications used to treat bacterial infections, particularly those covering uncommon bacteria, in individuals developing symptoms of meningitis after a dural tear. Medications used to treat bacterial infections, particularly in the management of exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). Antibiotics decrease treatment failure and reduce mortality in hospitalized patients and show effectiveness in the community, especially in patients with severe airflow obstruction. There is uncertainty regarding their value in patients with mild airflow obstruction. Procalcitonin can guide the decision to use antibiotics, and newer broad-spectrum antibiotics may be more effective but should be reserved for patients at highest risk of treatment failure due to concerns about antibiotic resistance. Antibiotic courses of 5 days in duration may be as effective as those for 7 days or more in patients with mild-to-moderate exacerbations of COPD. Topical antibiotics are used as part of prophylactic treatment for EGFRi-associated rash. They are effective in decreasing the incidence of rash when used topically, with a range of 79% to 43% depending on the study group. A category of drugs with more frequent use among diabetics treated orally and on diet only compared to non-diabetics. They were also commonly used among insulin treated diabetics but without significant difference from non-diabetics. A class of drugs usually used to treat the EGFR inhibitor-associated skin rash, with prominent side effects over long-time use. Often used in conjunction with corticosteroids to treat skin toxicity caused by EGFR-TKI. A class of medications used for treating bacterial infections, including those that may cause CNS infections. The study compared the clinical course of children treated with antibiotics to those who received no antimicrobial therapy following basilar skull fractures.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial dynamics
nodes.description: The biological process involving the study of mitochondrial behavior and organization within cells, including the fusion and division of mitochondria, fine regulation of their localization, size, and trafficking. It also involves the maintenance, turnover, and organization of mitochondria within cells, working in conjunction with mitochondrial biogenesis to ensure optimal functioning in response to cellular needs. Mitochondrial dynamics is regulated by various factors such as nutrients availability, bioenergetics demands, and proteins like Parkin.

nodes.label: Histone H3
nodes.description: A type of histone protein involved in the formation of nucleosomes, which are the basic units of chromatin structure. Histone H3 is modified by the addition of a methyl group to lysine 9 or lysine 4, which is recognized by the chromo domain of HP1 proteins. It also undergoes acetylation, phosphorylation, and methylation, playing a role in chromatin-based regulatory mechanisms and epigenetic repression. The ARKS motif is present within the tail of Histone H3.

nodes.label: Resistance to thyroid hormone
nodes.description: A syndrome characterized by raised serum thyroid hormone (TH) levels and raised or inappropriately normal thyrotropin (TSH) levels, where patients exhibit TH resistance in the pituitary and peripheral tissues. A rare autosomal dominant inherited syndrome characterized by reduced end-organ responsiveness to thyroid hormone, leading to elevated serum free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) concentrations and normal or slightly elevated serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) level. Patients with this condition can be classified into three categories based on clinical grounds: generalized resistance (GRTH), pituitary resistance (PRTH), or combined. Mutations in the thyroid hormone receptor (TR) beta gene are responsible for RTH, with 122 different mutations identified in 300 families. No specific treatment is available, but the diagnosis enables appropriate genetic counseling. An autosomal dominant condition of reduced tissue sensitivity to thyroid hormone in which goiter is very frequent and hearing loss occurs in about 20% of patients. It is associated with congenital goiter, elevated free T3 and free T4 concentrations with unsuppressed TSH, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral progressive sensorineural hearing impairment with enlarged vestibular aqueducts. Inner ear malformations are uncommon in this condition. An inherited syndrome characterized by reduced tissue responsiveness to thyroid hormone, with elevated serum thyroid hormone levels in association with a nonsuppressed TSH. It has been identified in more than 400 subjects and appears to be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner in the majority of families. The syndrome is suspected to be caused by an abnormal thyroid hormone receptor (TR), with mutations in the TR beta gene, specifically in the T3-binding domain, being responsible for the disease. The severity of clinical manifestations does not correlate with the degree of hormone-binding impairment. A dominantly inherited disorder characterized by elevated free thyroid hormones in the serum and failure to suppress pituitary thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) secretion with variable refractoriness to hormone action in peripheral tissues. It has two major forms: asymptomatic individuals with generalized resistance (GRTH) and patients with thyrotoxic features, suggesting predominant pituitary resistance (PRTH). The disorder is associated with diverse mutations in the thyroid hormone receptor beta gene, leading to functionally impaired and dominant negative mutant receptors. Recognized features include failure to thrive, growth retardation and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in childhood, and goitre and thyrotoxic cardiac symptoms in adults. The pathogenesis of variable tissue resistance is not fully understood.

nodes.label: Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT)
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving pre-operative chemotherapy and chemoradiotherapy, specifically using six biweekly courses of modified FOLFOX6 followed by pelvic RT with four concurrent cycles of biweekly 5-FU 2600 mg/m2 + LV 200 mg/m2 without oxaliplatin. This results in improved survival and is becoming the new standard of care in locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). It includes induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy using full dose 5FU without oxaliplatin. The study involved 84 LARC patients with a 96% completion rate, experiencing significant toxicities such as neutropenia, diarrhea, and anemia, with two treatment-related deaths.

nodes.label: Cerebellum
nodes.description: A region of the brain responsible for coordinating voluntary muscle movements, maintaining balance, and posture. It is involved in motor control and coordination, and is affected by conditions such as hereditary cerebellar ataxia with peripheral neuropathy and mental retardation, medulloblastoma, and myotonic dystrophy. The cerebellum shows no significant change in OCT3 mRNA concentrations in serotonin transporter-deficient mice and is used as a reference region in various studies, including those evaluating the binding of radioligands and the expression of specific proteins. It is also involved in obsessive-compulsive symptoms in both schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

nodes.label: Amniocentesis
nodes.description: An invasive fetal sampling procedure used in prenatal diagnosis to diagnose fetal genetic or chromosomal conditions, involving the withdrawal of amniotic fluid containing fetal cells for analysis. It is a medical procedure that involves inserting a needle into the amniotic sac to collect fluid surrounding the fetus, which is then analyzed for genetic information. Amniocentesis is typically performed in the second trimester to detect Down syndrome in high-risk pregnancies and is associated with a 1.7% rate of fetal loss when performed after 16 weeks' gestation. It is recommended for pregnant women 35 years of age and older and to women with a history of a fetus with Down syndrome or of a chromosome 21 anomaly. Amniocentesis can lead to procedure-related losses and is often avoided due to its risks, being replaced by less invasive methods such as the integrated test or maternal plasma as the source of fetal DNA.

nodes.label: Marfan syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder affecting connective tissues, characterized by cardiovascular manifestations such as mitral valve prolapse, aortic dilatation, and aortic regurgitation. It is an inherited condition with an autosomal dominant transmission, associated with mutations in the FBN-1 gene on the 15th chromosome. The syndrome has two forms: infantile and classic, with different prognoses and morphological characteristics. The main cause of morbidity is represented by thoracic aortic dissection/aneurysm, which is responsible for 80% of the deaths. Clinical major criteria involve the skeletal and ocular apparatus, the cardiovascular and central nervous system. Diagnosis is based on the identification of major clinical manifestations in at least two organ systems associated with involvement of a third organ system, as defined in the Ghent Nosology.

nodes.label: Thiamine deficiency
nodes.description: A deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B(1)), which can cause Wernicke's encephalopathy (WE), a serious, potentially fatal, neurologic disorder. A condition resulting from insufficient levels of thiamine, leading to Wernicke encephalopathy. It is associated with alcoholics and can be exacerbated by diabetic ketoacidosis. A condition caused by insufficient intake or absorption of thiamine (vitamin B1), leading to Wernicke's encephalopathy. Common causes include alcoholism and gastric disorders. A condition resulting from insufficient thiamine (vitamin B1), which can lead to Wernicke encephalopathy (WE), cardiovascular collapse, and beriberi. It can occur in people with alcoholism, malnutrition, gastrointestinal diseases with malabsorption, or TPN without proper thiamine replacement. Symptoms include ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, mental confusion, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, memory disturbance, and hypotension. A condition associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy, characterized by malabsorption, malnutrition, and malignancies. It can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy, especially when MVI is ceased in the TPN infusion or when an oral multivitamin preparation is given in patients with malabsorption. Thiamine supplementation is essential for treating Wernicke's encephalopathy.

nodes.label: Pregabalin
nodes.description: A medication registered for the treatment of neuropathic pain, indicated as adjuvant therapy in the treatment of epilepsy and for generalized anxiety disorder. Pregabalin is a GABA analogue that binds to the α(2)-δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, leading to a decreased synaptic release of neurotransmitters. A drug used in the study, its ADRs and its use in daily practice were monitored through a web-based intensive monitoring system. The study indicates that Pregabalin is a relatively safe drug, with 11 patients experiencing a serious ADR while using the drug. The most frequently reported possible ADRs correspond with the reactions most frequently reported during clinical trials. A well-known antiepileptic drug used for treating neuropathic pain, along with gabapentin and carbamazepine. It is one of the few drugs registered for this condition. A drug used for the short-term treatment of Restless Legs Syndrome, with level A recommendations based on evidence. An antiepileptic drug (AED) for which data on salivary TDM are sparse or nonexistent. A medication that has been established as effective for up to 1 year in treating Restless Legs Syndrome/Willis-Ekbom Disease (RLS/WED) with Level A evidence. A drug used in the first-line treatment of Restless Leg Syndrome (RLS) alongside dopamine agonists. It is often prescribed for patients with RLS who can adequately control their symptoms with non-pharmacological measures such as massage and warm baths.

nodes.label: Myocardium
nodes.description: The muscular layer of the heart, rich in mitochondria due to their high-energy requirement and particularly vulnerable to mitochondrial defects. It is targeted by antiarrhythmic drugs through sodium-, potassium-, and calcium-channels or beta-adrenergic receptors, and by Class I antiarrhythmic agents through the blockade of the fast-inward sodium channel. The myocardium is involved in acute global myocarditis and can undergo biologically important changes that can be tracked by CMR using native T1 or ECV. It is also used as a reference for global T2 signal intensity ratio compared with skeletal muscle in cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) techniques.

nodes.label: Trifluridine/Tipiracil
nodes.description: A novel, orally active, antimetabolite agent comprised of trifluridine, a thymidine-based nucleoside analogue, and tipiracil, a potent thymidine phosphorylase inhibitor. It is used for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic colorectal cancer who are refractory to or are not considered candidates for current standard chemotherapy and biological therapy in the EU and USA and in unresectable advanced or recurrent CRC in Japan. The approved regimen involves oral twice-daily trifluridine/tipiracil at a dose of 35 mg/m(2) twice daily on days 1-5 and 8-12 of each 28-day cycle. It has been shown to significantly improve overall survival and progression-free survival and was associated with a significantly higher disease control rate than placebo when added to best supportive care in the multinational, pivotal phase III trial (RECOURSE) and a phase II Japanese trial. Common grade 3-4 adverse events include anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. It is associated with an acceptable tolerability profile, with adverse events generally being managed with dose reductions, temporary interruptions in treatment or administration of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor. An antimetabolite agent used in the management of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) for patients who are refractory or intolerant to standard therapies. It is available under the brand name Lonsurf® and is associated with a favorable safety profile, including a low incidence of nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia, and fatigue. A novel form of chemotherapy for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) that has shown clinical benefit in the global, phase III RECOURSE trial, regardless of patient age. It is administered as FTD/TPI 35 mg/m2 twice daily for 5 days followed by 2 days of rest for 2 weeks, with a 14-day rest period. Safety and tolerability data were collected from an expanded-access program (EAP) in the US for patients with mCRC whose disease has progressed on standard therapies. The treatment duration and time to treatment discontinuation were similar to those in the RECOURSE trial. The safety profile in elderly patients was consistent with that in younger patients, with no unexpected safety concerns.

nodes.label: MRI
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique used to visualize the internal structures of the body, particularly the brain and spinal cord. It can provide detailed images of the spine and surrounding structures, help identify specific injuries, and detect abnormalities such as infarcts, atrophy, and hyper intense signal changes with restricted diffusion. MRI has been used in various studies and clinical settings, including evaluating clinicoradiological correlations, studying genetic disorders, and assessing the progression of diseases like Alzheimer's and Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy.

nodes.label: RNA polymerase II
nodes.description: A type of RNA polymerase involved in transcription, specifically associated with pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) processing and elongation. It has a heptad repeat in its carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) that is subject to serine-5 and -2 phosphorylation. An enzyme responsible for transcribing microRNA genes, messenger RNA precursors (pre-mRNAs), and primary miRNAs (pri-miRNAs) into RNA molecules. It is selective in its activity, with alpha-amanitin treatment decreasing the level of pri-miRNAs at a concentration that inhibits its activity. Pol II is physically associated with a miRNA promoter and is the main, if not the only, RNA polymerase for miRNA gene transcription. It is responsible for producing messenger RNA precursors (pre-mRNAs) in eukaryotes, Cryptic unstable transcripts (CUTs) in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and RNA molecules from DNA templates. It binds to the relaxin gene promoter in response to berberine-induced formation of G-quadruplexes, contributing to the up-regulation of relaxin expression. It is involved in transcription and attaches to the nascent RNA during transcription, holding it still attached to the DNA template until the processing events are completed.

nodes.label: Zika Virus
nodes.description: A flavivirus with single stranded RNA, related to yellow fever, dengue, West Nile, and Japanese encephalitis viruses. It is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, primarily by Aedes aegipti, which is widely distributed in Nepal. The virus was first identified in Rhesus monkeys in Uganda in 1947 and in humans in 1952. Outbreaks have been recorded in Africa, the Americas, Asia, and the Pacific. The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared the Zika virus an international public health emergency. A virus belonging to the genus Flavivirus and the family Flaviviridae, known for being transmitted by infected mosquitoes. It was first isolated from a nonhuman primate in 1947 and from mosquitoes in 1948 in Africa. ZIKV infections in humans were sporadic for half a century before emerging in the Pacific and the Americas. Prior to the large French Polynesian outbreak in 2013 and 2014, ZIKV infection was associated with only mild illness. However, this changed with the report of severe neurological complications and the emergence of severe congenital malformations (microcephaly) suspected to be associated with ZIKV. The virus can be diagnosed through virus isolation or detection of ZIKV-specific RNA, but serological diagnosis is complicated by cross-reactivity among members of the Flavivirus genus. A virus that caused an unprecedented outbreak in the western hemisphere from 2015-2018, with Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus being identified as primary and secondary vectors, respectively. The review focuses on identifying secondary vectors capable of transmitting the virus through laboratory vector competence studies.

nodes.label: Dabigatran etexilate
nodes.description: The oral form of dabigatran used in the study, administered at a dose of 220 mg twice daily for 3 days and a final dose on day 4. A drug used as a positive control in the study, its anticoagulant effects were reversed by idarucizumab in a dose-dependent manner. It was used for pretreatment in some participants and its anticoagulant effects were reversed by idarucizumab in a dose-dependent manner. An oral direct thrombin inhibitor included in the Direct-acting oral anticoagulants class, marketed under the brand name Pradaxa by Boehringer Ingelheim. A direct thrombin inhibitor (fIIa) that is now widely prescribed. It binds to the active site of factor IIa (fIIa). A specific substance that directly blocks thrombin and is used as an orally active anticoagulant for thromboprophylaxis following hip or knee replacement surgery. It is also known by the brand name Pradaxa®.

nodes.label: Prednisone
nodes.description: A type of corticosteroid used for treating various medical conditions such as Landau-Kleffner syndrome, CSWS, sarcoidosis, Multiple Myeloma, Molluscum contagiosum, and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It is often used in combination with other drugs and has side effects including weight gain, behavioral change, and hypertension, which are typically few and transient.

nodes.label: Necitumumab
nodes.description: A fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody directed against EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), necitumumab is a second-generation recombinant human immunoglobulin G1 EGFR monoclonal antibody that competitively inhibits ligand binding. It has been studied in various clinical trials for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), both as a single agent and in combination with chemotherapy. Necitumumab has exhibited potential benefits, such as lower hypersensitivity reaction risk compared to cetuximab and equivalent antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity. However, some trials have been prematurely closed or enrollment stopped due to safety concerns, such as an increased risk of thromboembolic events. Necitumumab is currently under development as a treatment for advanced NSCLC and is being tested in two Phase III randomized trials in combination with first-line platinum-based chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Bevacizumab
nodes.description: A targeted therapy used in combination with irinotecan for the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, and a humanized monoclonal antibody against VEGFA. It is used in inhibiting VEGF/VEGFR signaling in various types of cancer, including colorectal, endometrial, and lung cancer. It is also used in combination with chemotherapy, cetuximab, and other anti-angiogenic drugs. Bevacizumab's continued use throughout lines of therapy is being investigated in clinical trials, and its resistance mechanisms are not fully understood.

nodes.label: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
nodes.description: A neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent and intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that are performed in an attempt to relieve anxiety. It is associated with the serotonin (5-HT) neurotransmitter system and its dysfunction. Clinical improvement following treatment with 5-HT reuptake inhibitors can take up to eight to 12 weeks, and most patients do not fully improve. Drugs that potently block serotonin reuptake are effective in the treatment of this disorder, and some patients with OCD may experience remission of OCD symptoms during intoxication with psychedelic drugs that have potent 5-HT2A/2C agonist activity.

nodes.label: Psoriatic arthritis
nodes.description: A condition for which ustekinumab has been investigated as a treatment, alongside psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and relapsing/remitting multiple sclerosis. A chronic inflammatory arthropathy associated with psoriasis, included among the seronegative spondyloarthropathies. It can be clinically subdivided into asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, distal interphalanges predominant, arthritis mutilans, and spondylitis types. It has several unique characteristics, such as enthesopathy, dactylitis and abnormal bone remodeling. Genetic, environmental, and immunological factors are important in its development. The triggering role of physical stress is seen in the 'deep Koebner' phenomenon, which causes inflammation in the synovial membrane and in enthesis, resulting in peripheral arthritis. Cellular infiltrates such as activated T-cells and macrophages are thought to play important roles in the induction of inflammatory and destructive processes in joint tissues, as well as psoriatic skin. New ideas regarding the involvement of the IL-23/Th17 axis have emerged, and the dramatic effects of targeting therapies have highlighted the physiological role of key cytokines in psoriasis. A type of arthritis associated with psoriasis, characterized by joint pain and swelling. Ustekinumab has demonstrated efficacy in treating this condition. A type of arthritis that developed in two patients during ustekinumab treatment for psoriasis. A chronic inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthritis associated with psoriasis. It is a rheumatic disease that has not been fully revolutionized by TNF-α inhibitors, leading to a need for additional treatment modalities. The IL-23/Th17 axis has emerged as an important mechanism in its pathogenesis. Ustekinumab has been shown to be well-tolerated and effective in patients with active Psoriatic arthritis, improving signs and symptoms, inhibiting radiographic progression, and being effective in dactylitis, enthesitis, and skin disease. It also proves to be effective in anti-TNF-α experienced patients. A heterogeneous disease treated with various pharmacotherapeutic agents, including conventional synthetic disease modifying agents (csDMARDs) and novel therapies such as tumour necrosis factor alpha inhibitors, interleukin 12/23 inhibitor (ustekinumab), interleukin 17 antagonists (secukinumab, brodalumab, ixekizumab), and the phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, apremilast. A heterogeneous chronic inflammatory disease with a broad clinical spectrum and variable course, involving musculoskeletal structures as well as skin, nails, eyes, and gut.

nodes.label: Operon
nodes.description: A regulated multigene transcription unit in Caenorhabditis elegans and its relatives, characterized by polycistronic pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) coding for multiple peptides being processed to monocistronic mRNAs. This process involves 3' end formation and trans-splicing using the specialized SL2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle for downstream mRNAs. A type of multigenic transcriptional unit where multiple genes are co-transcribed within a single polycistronic transcript. This phenomenon is observed in C. elegans, where at least 15% of genes are organized into operons, which is quite rare in eukaryotes. A genetic unit consisting of a cluster of genes transcribed together, common in prokaryotes but less so in eukaryotes, especially in nematode worms like Caenorhabditis elegans. The 'one-way street' hypothesis suggests that once formed by chance, operons are very difficult to break due to the potential loss of expression for downstream genes without a promoter. A group of genes organized together in a genome, particularly in the Caenorhabditis elegans genome, containing more than 1000 operons that compose approximately 15% of the protein-coding genes. Operons are found across multiple kingdoms and phyla, from prokaryotes to chordates. In C. elegans, genes within an operon often show poor coexpression and only sometimes encode proteins with related functions. Almost all operon-encoded genes are expressed in germline tissue, but genes expressed during spermatogenesis are excluded from operons. Operons group together along chromosomes in local clusters that also contain monocistronic germline-expressed genes. A biological process where multiple genes share a common promoter to generate a polycistronic primary transcript. In nematode and ascidian genomes, genes in operons make up 15-20% of the coding genome. The identity of genes within operons is highly conserved among species, and they are expressed in germline tissue.

nodes.label: Rectal cancer
nodes.description: A type of colorectal cancer that affects the rectum, with inconsistent results regarding the association with obesity. BMI was positively associated with rectal cancer in men but not in women. The risk increases with a 5-unit increase in BMI, with a per 0.1-unit increase in waist-hip ratio showing an RR of 1.43 in men and 1.20 in women. It is a specific type of colorectal cancer that affects the rectum, associated with high red meat intake, high processed meat intake, and high total red and processed meat consumption. The treatment often involves low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, long-course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection, or short-course neoadjuvant radiotherapy. The optimal timing of surgery following preoperative chemoradiotherapy is a debated topic due to downsizing and repopulation of tumor cells.

nodes.label: TBC1D24
nodes.description: A gene associated with DOORS syndrome, mutations in which were identified in 11 individuals from nine families through exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing. These mutations were found in half of the families with individuals having all five main features of DOORS syndrome. The protein encoded by this gene may play a role in neuronal development and function, as suggested by its expression studies in human fibroblasts and mouse tissues. A gene involved in skeletogenesis, whose mutations can lead to DOORS syndrome and cause diverse phenotypes. It is expressed in mouse phalangeal chondrocytes and calvaria. A gene encoding a component of the BAF complex, identified as causing a clinically similar condition with intellectual disability and cancer predisposition syndrome following the identification of SMARCB1, SMARCE1, SMARCA4, ARID1A, ARID1B, PHF6, and SOX11 mutations. A gene associated with human deafness, mutations of which can cause non-syndromic deafness (DFNB86, OMIM 614617), epilepsy (OMIM 605021), epilepsy with deafness, or DOORS syndrome (OMIM 220500) characterized by deafness, onychodystrophy, osteodystrophy, mental retardation, and seizures.

nodes.label: Migraine
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe headache, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. It can occur with or without aura and can be episodic or chronic. Migraine is associated with changes in calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) levels and is believed to be influenced by CGRP, which plays a major role in its pathophysiology. It can be treated pharmacologically, with novel drugs targeting CGRP signaling, such as lasmiditan, eptinezumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, rimegepant, ubrogepant, and atogepant. These drugs can have both therapeutic and side effects, especially when targeting 5-HT1F receptors and CGRP signaling. Migraine is a common neurological disorder that affects up to 15% of the adult population in most countries, with a higher prevalence in females. It is a highly disabling neurovascular disorder that can lead to significant loss of productivity due to lost time from work or school.

nodes.label: SearchGUI
nodes.description: An open-source graphical user interface used for integrating and optimizing search engines like X!Tandem, MS-GF, MS Amanda, MyriMatch, Comet, Tide, Andromeda, and OMSSA for proteoforms identification.

nodes.label: Taliglucerase alfa
nodes.description: A plant cell-expressed recombinant therapeutic protein approved for Gaucher disease (GD) as an enzyme replacement therapy, administered as a 30 or 60 U/kg dose every other week. It has been studied in multiple phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-dose studies and has demonstrated mean decreases in spleen volume, liver volume, chitotriosidase activity, and chemokine (CC motif) ligand 18 concentration, along with mean increases in hemoglobin concentration and platelet count. The most common adverse events are mild/moderate in intensity and transient.

nodes.label: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
nodes.description: A psychiatric condition characterized by recurrent and persistent thoughts, impulses, or images (obsessions) that cause distress and anxiety, and repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be followed rigidly. The text discusses structural abnormalities in brain regions comprising cortical-striatal-thalamic-cortical loops in pediatric patients with this disorder. A psychiatric disorder characterized by obsessions and compulsions, involving the central serotonergic and dopaminergic systems. Patients with OCD were compared to controls in a study using [123I]-2beta-carbomethoxy-3beta-(4-idiophenyl)tropane (beta-CIT) and a brain-dedicated high-resolution single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) system to quantify dopamine transporter (DAT) and serotonin transporter (SERT) availability. The study found a significantly reduced availability of striatal DAT and of thalamic/hypothalamic, midbrain and brainstem SERT in OCD patients, with a significant negative correlation between severity of OCD symptoms and thalamic/hypothalamic SERT availability, corrected for age and duration of symptoms. A neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent and intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that are performed in response to these thoughts. It is associated with functional deficits in frontostriatal networks, particularly in orbitofrontal regions, and involves alterations in the serotonin and dopamine systems. Pharmacological interventions focus on correcting serotonergic and dopaminergic dysfunctions. A common heterogeneous psychiatric disorder manifesting with obsessions and compulsions. Obsessions are intrusive, recurrent, and persistent unwanted thoughts, while compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to the obsessions. Complications include interpersonal difficulties, unemployment, substance abuse, criminal justice issues, and physical injuries. The disorder involves areas of the brain such as the orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate gyrus, and basal ganglia, and may be due to a malfunction in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit. Neurotransmitters implicated in OCD include serotonin, dopamine, and glutamate. Treatment options include psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy, transcranial magnetic simulation, and in extreme cases, surgery. Exposure and response prevention is the most effective form of psychotherapy, while selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the preferred pharmacotherapy. A behavioral disorder involving the brain serotonin (5-HT) neurotransmitter system, characterized by symptoms such as obsessions and compulsions. It is supported by therapeutic effects found with the semiselective serotonin uptake inhibitor, clomipramine, and studies comparing it with other serotonin uptake inhibitors like desipramine, nortriptyline, fluvoxamine, and fluoxetine. Patients' symptoms improve with clomipramine but worsen when the drug is discontinued or when given metergoline, a 5-HT antagonist. The administration of m-chlorophenylpiperazine (m-CPP), a 5-HT receptor agonist, increases anxiety, depression, and dysphoria, and exacerbates OC symptoms in untreated OCD patients. A relatively common and disabling psychiatric disorder whose pathophysiology is incompletely understood. It involves disruptions in the balance between gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glutamate, contributing to its pathophysiology. The study investigated the role of brain GABA and glutamate concentrations in the anterior cingulate cortex using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). Patients with OCD displayed a higher estimated GABA level and a higher GABA to glutamate ratio than healthy participants, but no significant group differences were observed in the measure of glutamate. A mental health condition characterized by recurrent and intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that are performed to reduce anxiety. Patients with this disorder are not infrequently refractory to treatment with serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

nodes.label: Neutropenia
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by a decreased number of neutrophils in the blood, which are essential for fighting infections. It can be a symptom of various disorders such as WHIM syndrome, Barth syndrome, and Dynamin 2-associated Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, or a side effect of certain treatments like FEC therapy and protein kinase inhibitors. Neutropenia can also be observed in conditions like cardiomyopathy and rheumatoid arthritis. It is typically categorized into grades 1-4 based on severity, with grade 3 and 4 indicating severe cases. Common symptoms include increased risk of infection and illness. Treatment options may include dose modifications, temporary interruptions in treatment, or administration of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor.

nodes.label: Rheumatoid arthritis
nodes.description: A chronic inflammatory autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation of the synovial membrane lining the joints, leading to pain, swelling, and joint damage. It involves cytokine-mediated reactions and critical immune processes, and is associated with citrullination, catalyzed by the enzyme family of peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs). Treatment options include JAK inhibitors such as CP-690,550 and tofacitinib, and rituximab is FDA-approved for treatment. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause atlanto-axial instability, particularly in the form of rotary subluxation due to incompetence of the alar ligament.

nodes.label: Thyroid hormone resistance
nodes.description: A heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by reduced responses of target tissues to thyroid hormone due to defects at the site of hormone action. It is inherited as a dominant trait associated with mutations in the hormone-binding domain of the thyroid hormone receptor. A medical condition characterized by generalized tissue resistance to thyroid hormone, often resulting in euthyroidism with normal or increased thyroid-stimulating hormone levels. Diagnosis can be challenging without careful clinical and biochemical evaluation, and may involve mutation of the thyroid hormone receptor beta gene. A rare syndrome characterized by reduced end organ sensitivity, leading to elevated serum free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) levels, but normal or slightly elevated serum thyrotropin values. Clinical manifestations include goitre without symptoms and metabolic consequences of thyroid hormone excess. It can be classified into pituitary, peripheral, or generalized types based on tissue resistance. Genetic mutations, such as those in the TRbeta gene, cell membrane transporter, and genes controlling intracellular metabolism of thyroid hormone, have been implicated. Differentiation from thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) secreting pituitary adenoma is made by a history of THR in the family. Specific treatment is not often required, with patients with features of hypo- or hyperthyroidism being appropriately treated with levo-triiodothyronine (L-T3), levo-thyroxine (L-T4), dextro-thyroxine (D-T4), or 3,3,5 triiodo-thyroacetic acid (TRIAC). The diagnosis aids in appropriate genetic counselling of the family. A condition where the body is resistant to the effects of thyroid hormones. Characterized by a Brazilian boy with severe neurologic impairment, normal growth during infancy, reduced weight gain, and absence of typical signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Despite treatment with levothyroxine, the clinical picture of the patient did not improve. This condition reinforces the concept that the role of MCT8 is tissue-dependent.

nodes.label: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug
nodes.description: A brown marmorated stink bug, scientifically known as Halyomorpha halys, is an invasive species native to Asia, including countries such as China, Taiwan, Japan, and the Korean peninsula. It was first discovered in Allentown, Pennsylvania, in 1996 and has since spread across wide areas of the Eastern United States. At least 26 states have reported its presence as of October 2010. The bug is known to release chemicals that can cause a slight allergic reaction in fruit crop workers. A pest species that originated from Asia and has become a serious invasive pest in the USA. It was first detected in the USA in the mid 1990s and has since dispersed to over 41 other states. It has spread throughout New Jersey, becoming an important pest of agriculture and a major nuisance in urban developments. The bug's density is strongly associated with urban developments and railroads during its initial establishment and dispersal from 2004 to 2006. It overwinters in multiple habitats and feeds on a variety of plants, which may have reduced the Allee effect, facilitating movement into the southernmost regions of the state by railroads from 2005 to 2008. Its density contracted in 2009 possibly from invading wetlands or sampling artifact. Subsequent invasion from the northwest to the south in 2010 may conform to a stratified-dispersal model marked by rapid long-distance movement, from railroads and wetland rights-of-way. High densities of the bug may be associated with agriculture in southern New Jersey in 2011. An exotic invasive insect species originating in East Asia, known as Halyomorpha halys (Stål) (BMSB), causing significant damage to fruits, vegetables, and other crops throughout most of the Mid-Atlantic states of the U.S. It is also a nuisance pest, entering homes in the fall in search of suitable overwintering sites. A species of stink bug native to eastern Asia and currently invading North America. It utilizes various overwintering habitats with different thermal buffering capacities, including aggregations beneath loose bark on trees, cliff outcroppings, and buildings. The study focuses on the cold tolerance of this species across geographic and temporal scales, particularly in newly invaded regions of North America. A species of insect, specifically an invasive species from Asia, belonging to the Hemiptera: Pentatomidae family. It is capable of causing severe agricultural damage and can also be a nuisance pest when it enters and exits anthropogenic overwintering sites. A species of stink bug originally from East Asia, now established across North America and Europe. It causes significant economic losses to agriculture in the Eastern United States of America and Italy. Its current global range includes North America, Europe, Canada, Switzerland, Italy, France, Greece, and Hungary. The species' expansion has been studied using molecular markers and an Approximate Bayesian Computation approach, revealing that China is the likely source of most non-native populations, with at least four separate introductions in North America and three in Europe. Additionally, there is evidence of a bridgehead event from the Eastern United States to central Italy.

nodes.label: Rheumatoid Arthritis
nodes.description: A chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation of the synovial membranes lining the joints, leading to pain, swelling, and potential joint damage. It is associated with the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and involves genetic factors and specific autoantibodies targeting peptidyl arginine deiminase type 4 (PAD-4). Treatment options include biologics, inhibitors targeting tyrosine kinase known as Janus kinase (Jak), and immunosuppressive regimens. Rheumatoid Arthritis has been studied in relation to its response to TNF-alpha inhibitor treatment, methotrexate, and the use of tofacitinib as a therapeutic intervention.

nodes.label: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)
nodes.description: A type of alpha-herpesvirus that can cause lytic replication and reactivation from latency. It uses the cellular transcriptional coactivator host cell factor-1 (HCF-1) to recruit the lysine-specific demethylase-1 (LSD1) to the viral immediate early promoters. A viral infection that causes acute hepatitis in pregnancy, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. It accounts for 2-4% of all acute hepatitis cases but has high morbidity and mortality rates. Pregnancy is a risk factor for HSV hepatitis, and it can cause symptoms such as back pain, fetal tachycardia, fever, spontaneous rupture of membranes, transaminitis, symptomatic hypotension, pancytopenia, acute liver injury, splenomegaly, pleural effusions, and cardiomyopathy. The virus can be detected through serum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) screening, and treatment with acyclovir can lead to recovery. There is no evidence of neonatal seroconversion.

nodes.label: Bisphosphonates
nodes.description: A class of drugs used for the treatment of osteoporosis, including less potent forms like etidronate and more potent forms. They are antiresorptive agents that work by inhibiting the activity of osteoclasts and reducing bone resorption. Bisphosphonates are used for the treatment of osteoporosis, multiple myeloma-related bone disease, and osteogenesis imperfecta. They are often combined with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and have shown promise in recent studies involving CTX measured in serum. Bisphosphonates are accepted as 'standard of care' for children with osteogenesis imperfecta and are commonly used in postmenopausal women with clinical risk factors for fracture. However, there are potential concerns about long-term suppression of bone turnover associated with bisphosphonate treatment, which may lead to adverse effects such as atypical femoral fractures and osteonecrosis of the jaw, although these cases are extremely rare. Some bisphosphonates, such as zoledronic acid, can also exert stimulating effects on the immune system, potentially leading to anticancer activity against malignant cells.

nodes.label: Immunotherapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses the body's immune system to fight cancer cells, involving the use of monoclonal antibodies, adoptive cell therapy with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, and targeting specific molecules to overcome tumor microenvironment-mediated drug resistance. It has been explored in combination with other therapies such as VEGFR-TKI and has shown promise in treating various types of cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and autoimmune disorders. However, some immunotherapies have failed in clinical trials, particularly those targeting protein accumulation in neurodegenerative diseases.

nodes.label: Fluorouracil
nodes.description: A chemotherapy drug used in various cancer treatments, including metastatic breast cancer, HER2-positive primary breast cancer, and locally advanced rectal cancer. It is often administered in combination with other drugs such as epirubicin, cyclophosphamide, trastuzumab, leucovorin, vinorelbine, cisplatin, paclitaxel, and oxaliplatin. Fluorouracil is also used in the FOLFOXIRI and FEC-75 chemotherapy regimens and as a component of the GONO-FOLFOXIRI regimen. It is an antimetabolite used in cancer chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Hypoxia
nodes.description: A condition characterized by a deficiency of oxygen supply to tissues, which can lead to cellular damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and potential myocardial injury. It disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis, causing calcium overload, acidosis, and oxidative stress. Hypoxia can activate pathways and influence SUMOylation in placental explants, regulate mitophagy, and trigger mitophagy and AMPK activation under chronic conditions, contributing to cardioprotection. It can also cause dysfunctions in mitochondrial dynamics, increases in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species generation and calcium concentration, and decreases in ATP production. In addition, hypoxia can affect the expression and phosphorylation of FUNDC1, influencing mitophagy and CVDs. TgIF1 levels are crucial for parasite survival under hypoxia but not in conventional culture conditions.

nodes.label: Colorectal Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the colon or rectum, characterized by the presence of tumors and an increased risk associated with obesity, particularly among men. It is a common malignancy whose incidence clinicians hope to decrease through the use of natural food compounds in chemoprevention. Risk factors include dietary patterns, body mass index, and genetic mutations such as KRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA alterations. Treatment options include targeted anti-EGFR therapeutics and first-line standard chemotherapeutic regimens in combination with bevacizumab. Colorectal cancer is associated with the activation of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and the expression of tumor-associated trypsinogen inhibitor TATI/SPINK1, which has been shown to be an independent prognostic marker.

nodes.label: 2-hydroxy-dATP
nodes.description: An oxidized form of dATP, 2-hydroxydeoxyadenosine 5'-triphosphate, which induces substitution and deletion mutations in a dose-dependent manner when used in an SV40 origin-dependent in vitro replication system with a HeLa extract. It misincorporates the oxidized nucleotide opposite C, leading to a G.C-->A.T transition including a tandem (CC-->TT) mutation. In Escherichia coli, it elicits G.C-->T.A transversions, but to a lesser extent. Its mutagenicity is enhanced in the presence of 2-hydroxydeoxyadenosine 5'-diphosphate, an inhibitor of the MTH1 protein, suggesting that this protein functions in the hydrolysis of 2-hydroxy-dATP in the replication reaction mixture and probably in living cells. A type of oxidized purine nucleotide analog that is incorporated by DNA polymerase eta opposite template G in addition to template T. A 2-substituted purine nucleotide analog, specifically 2-hydroxy-2'-deoxyadenosine 5'-triphosphate, which was added to a PCR mixture to examine its mutagenic potential. It enhanced the total mutation frequency and induced both transition and transversion mutations. A chemical compound that increases mutation rates in both wild type and mutT strains of Escherichia coli to similar degrees. It is not a substrate of the MutT protein.

nodes.label: Lung cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the lungs, often associated with smoking. It is characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells, and is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide with a 5-year survival rate of less than 20%. Risk and prognosis of lung cancer are associated with the rs1862214 polymorphism in the PDCD5 gene, and the suppression of cell growth and down-regulation of AIMP2-DX2 has been linked to changes in glucose uptake and the EGFR/MAPK signaling pathway. Lung cancer cell lines such as NCI-H520 are used to study the effects of RB knockdown on proliferation and tumor growth. MicroRNA-29 family can normalize aberrant patterns of methylation in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). BHLHB3 is a candidate tumor suppressor in lung cancer, with reduced colony growth likely due to inhibition of cell proliferation. Chronic inflammation and increased expression of COX-2 protein are associated with lung cancer, and the NLRP3 inflammasome is involved in cancer-related inflammation and plays a vital role in regulating the proliferation and migration of A549 cells. SPAG5 has been identified as an oncogene contributing to its progression. Lung cancer has shown significant therapeutic benefits from checkpoint inhibitors like CTLA-4 and PD-1 targeted treatments, and T cells targeting mutated antigens have been associated with clinical immunotherapy responses.

nodes.label: Huntington's disease
nodes.description: A hereditary neurological disorder caused by the expansion of normally polymorphic CTG microsatellites in certain human genes, characterized by progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. It is associated with the pathology and genetics of FUS and TDP-43 forming cytoplasmic inclusions, mitochondrial dysfunction and compromised mitophagy, as well as changes in the levels of neuropeptides and endocannabinoids in the globus pallidus. Huntington's disease is also linked to a reactive microglial response, consequent inflammation, behavioral impairment, mutant huntingtin (mHTT) accumulation, and can impact sleep. There is no cure nor approved disease-slowing therapy for this condition.

nodes.label: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by a temporary reduction in blood supply to part of the brain, leading to neurological symptoms that resolve completely within 24 hours. Patients with a high early risk of stroke are often triaged based on the ABCD(2) score. A condition requiring a systematic intracranial vascular examination in its initial management, as supported by the study. A temporary disruption of blood flow to the brain, often serving as a warning sign for a future stroke. It is used as a baseline condition for evaluating stroke risk and is an independent predictor of stroke recurrence according to the text. A medical condition characterized by temporary episodes of neurological dysfunction due to reduced blood flow to the brain, often serving as a warning sign for future strokes. In this study, patients presenting with TIA were assessed for risk level and managed accordingly. A medical condition characterized by a brief episode of neurological dysfunction due to a temporary reduction in blood flow to part of the brain. In the study, referrals were classified as 'confirmed TIAs' if the stroke specialist confirmed a clinical diagnosis of possible, probable or definite TIA, and 'non-TIAs' if patients had a TIA mimic or completed stroke.

nodes.label: Irinotecan
nodes.description: An anticancer drug primarily used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, often in combination with 5-fluorouracil, targeted therapies like cetuximab or bevacizumab, or other chemotherapy agents such as oxaliplatin. It is a topoisomerase I inhibitor with a common active metabolite, SN-38. Irinotecan's toxicities can be predicted by the phenotyping of DPD activity, and prior UGT1A1 genotyping is recommended to identify patients at high risk of toxicity. It is used in various chemotherapy regimens, including CBI, FOLFOXIRI, FOLFIRI, and TEGAFIRI, and has been tested for its single agent cytotoxic activity and in combination with niraparib in vitro and in vivo. In the context of locally advanced rectal cancer, it is a component of the FOLFOXIRI, mFOLFOX-6, CAPOX, and TEGAFIRI regimens, as well as the Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT) and intensified consolidation treatment for LARC in the ShorTrip Trial.

nodes.label: DNMT3B
nodes.description: A member of the DNMT3 gene family, sharing 48.6% amino acid sequence identity with its mouse orthologue, found in chicken, fish, and humans. An important enzyme involved in modulating the methylation status in mammalian cells. It has a specific polymorphism, the DNMT3B G39179T SNP, which is investigated for its correlation with the susceptibilities of colorectal adenomatous polyps and adenocarcinoma. A de novo DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) responsible for setting genomic DNA methylation patterns, with a significant and distinct flanking sequence preference for target CpG sites determined by the base composition at the -1 and +1 positions flanking the CpG site. A DNA methyltransferase involved in DNA methylation, an essential regulator of transcription and chromatin structure. It has a critical C-terminal catalytic domain and a PWWP domain in the N-terminal region. DNMT3B is alternatively spliced in a tissue- and disease-specific manner and can form self-interactions. Catalytically inactive isoforms of DNMT3B can modulate the activity of DNMT3A-DNMT3L complexes. A de novo DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) involved in establishing DNA methylation patterns during early mammalian development. It requires a DNA cofactor to bind to S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM) and has distinct catalytic properties compared to DNMT3A. Mutations associated with ICF syndrome affect its function, including homo-oligomerization, SAM binding, SAM utilization, and DNA binding. DNMT3L does not interfere with the pathogenesis of ICF syndrome. A DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) present in the bovine oocyte during its growth phase, coordinated with DNA methylation during oocyte development. A gene involved in DNA methylation, with a truncated isoform called DNMT3B7 that is frequently generated in cancer. It suppresses growth, induces differentiation, and alters DNA methylation in human neuroblastoma. A DNA methyltransferase that interacts directly with the H1 C-terminal domain of some, but not all, murine H1 subtypes, leading to the recruitment of DNMT3B and DNA methylation of the H19 and Gtl2 imprinting control regions in ES cells. A gene associated with FSHD2, causing the disease through mutations. A gene involved in the pathogenesis of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy type 2, mutations in which can cause the disease.

nodes.label: Gaucher disease
nodes.description: An inherited autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the absence of β-glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of glucocerebroside and resulting in lysosomal storage disease. Clinical heterogeneity includes prediction of onset of symptoms, affected organs, and severity of signs and symptoms. Treatment options include enzyme replacement therapy, substrate reduction, and pharmacological chaperones. Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant imiglucerase (Cerezyme™) has been safe and effective for visceral symptoms and signs in more than 5000 patients worldwide for over 18 years. It is a genetic disorder characterized by the deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in cells. It has neuronopathic and non-neuronopathic manifestations, with the latter being treated by Taliglucerase alfa. It is a rare, genetic lysosomal storage disorder caused by functional defects of acid β-glucosidase, resulting in multiple organ dysfunction. It has two types, GD1 and GD2, with GD1 being the focus of this text. Clinical manifestations include visceral and hematologic symptoms, and it affects adults. Treatment involves enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) using products like imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, and taliglucerase alfa. It is a chronic condition characterized by classical manifestations that require therapeutic investigations with innovative trial designs and methodology to ensure long-term efficacy and safety.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin-Proteasome System
nodes.description: A system that regulates protein degradation through the covalent linking of ubiquitin to target proteins, leading to protein degradation by the proteasome or other outcomes such as endocytosis, degradation by the lysosome or directing these proteins to specific cellular compartments. A cellular process that regulates protein degradation and cellular functions. It involves the covalent attachment of the small protein ubiquitin to target proteins, serving as a signal for proteasomal degradation or other outcomes such as endocytosis, lysosomal degradation, or cellular localization specification. It plays a role in regulating EMT and multiple signaling pathways. The Ubiquitin-Proteasome System (UPS) is primarily responsible for cellular protein degradation. It involves the use of a short degron, CL1, fused to the COOH-terminus of green fluorescent protein (GFPu) as a reporter protein to analyze UPS function and relative activity. A highly selective post-translational modification process that involves the covalent conjugation of ubiquitin to a substrate protein, leading to the degradation of misfolded, damaged, and excess proteins. It plays a crucial role in the development and function of many tissues and organs, including the inner ear, and is associated with normal hearing and deafness. Impairment of UPS has been linked to altered cochlear development and hearing loss.

nodes.label: Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis
nodes.description: A method for early diagnosis of the genetic status of a fetus using cell-free fetal nucleic acids (cffNA) in maternal blood. It offers an excellent approach for non-invasive prenatal diagnosis, especially for conditions that can be inferred by unique gene expression patterns in the fetus and placenta. A method of prenatal diagnosis that utilizes cell-free fetal DNA found in the maternal plasma of pregnant women to facilitate the detection of specific fetal mutations in single gene disorders. Currently, this testing is limited to paternally derived or de novo mutations due to the presence of background maternal DNA. A diagnostic procedure used for determining fetal sex, rhesus D status, and some single gene disorders without invasively accessing the fetus. It relies on the detection of cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) in maternal plasma. The reliability of the test depends on the amplification of the fetal target being analyzed, as no amplification can be interpreted as either a true negative or a false negative result due to the absence or very low levels of cffDNA. A rapidly evolving field of medical procedures or tests that involves analyzing cell-free DNA in the maternal circulation for various clinical applications, such as fetal sex determination, fetal rhesus D determination, diagnosis of single gene disorders, and screening for aneuploidies.

nodes.label: Schizophrenia
nodes.description: A complex mental disorder characterized by abnormalities in thought, perception, emotion, and behavior, often involving hallucinations and delusions. It is a neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired synaptic connectivity, associated with dysregulation of tau phosphorylation, impaired reelin-signal transduction, and altered GABAergic mRNA expression. Schizophrenia is also linked to changes in neurotransmitter dysfunction, specifically serotonin, glutamate, and dopamine, and is treated with antipsychotic medications. It is a psychiatric disorder with negative symptoms and cognitive deficits, and is associated with social fragmentation and a higher prevalence in homeless populations compared to the general population in Schizophrenia-Spectrum Psychotic Disorders (SSPDs).

nodes.label: KRAS
nodes.description: A RAS oncogene with a lower mutation frequency in myeloid leukemia compared to NRAS but higher than HRAS, exhibiting different leukemogenic potentials in mice. It is a proto-oncogene that is frequently mutated in human cancers and has overlapping but distinctive functions with the other isoforms. KRAS is involved in tumorigenesis of periampullary and ampullary adenomas and carcinomas, with mutations occurring in periampullary tumors, particularly in exons 1 of its first codon. It is associated with colorectal cancer, mutations in which have been confirmed as negative predictors of the response to EGFR-targeted therapies. Wild-type KRAS is present in 53.8% of patients, while KRAS mutants make up 46.2% of the tested patients. The gene is also involved in the epidermal growth factor receptor pathway and is associated with metastatic colorectal cancer, mutations in which can predict a patient's response to the monoclonal antibody cetuximab. KRAS has been the subject of extensive drug-targeting efforts over the past 3-4 decades, with no specific drugs yet approved. However, MRTX849 has been identified as a potent, selective, and covalent inhibitor for the KRASG12C mutation. KRAS has a 'switch I/II pocket' that was previously considered 'undruggable' but has now been shown to be druggable by BI-2852, a KRAS inhibitor that binds with nanomolar affinity to a pocket between switch I and II on RAS. KRAS has been identified as causing approximately 85% of RAS-driven cancers and is a component of the EFR3A-PI4KA signaling axis, targeted by the KRASG12C inhibitor sotorasib.

nodes.label: Niraparib
nodes.description: A poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor, specifically a potent, selective PARP-1 and PARP-2 inhibitor that induces synthetic lethality in preclinical tumor models with loss of BRCA and PTEN function. It is currently under clinical evaluation for the treatment of various types of cancer, including ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancer, and is being tested in phase 3 clinical trials as maintenance therapy in ovarian cancer and as a treatment for breast cancer. Niraparib has shown excellent human pharmacokinetics in phase I clinical trials and promising activity in cancer patients. It is an oral poly(ADP-Ribose) polymerase (PARP) 1/2 inhibitor that has shown clinical activity in patients with ovarian cancer and is known to possess trapping activity, potentiating the cytotoxicity of alkylating agents. Common grade 3 or 4 adverse events include thrombocytopenia, anemia, and neutropenia, which are managed with dose modifications.

nodes.label: CP-690,550
nodes.description: A potent, orally active Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used in clinical trials for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and other autoimmune disease indications. It exhibits 5-100 fold selectivity over JAK2 in cellular assays, despite inhibiting all four JAK isoforms with nM potency in in vitro enzyme assays. CP-690,550 potently inhibits signaling through JAK1 and JAK3, and has been shown to decrease neutrophil counts in RA trials. It returns plasma cytokines, PBNC, and bone marrow myeloid progenitor cells to pre-disease levels at efficacious exposures. The plasma concentration of CP-690,550 at efficacious doses is above the in vitro whole blood IC50 of JAK1 and JAK3 inhibition, but not that of JAK2. A chemical compound used in treatment that leads to decreases in PBNC and is associated with attenuation of inflammation and not suppression of granulopoiesis through JAK2 inhibition. An orally active and selective inhibitor of the Janus kinase (JAK) molecules, used in clinical trials for rheumatoid arthritis. It has shown dose-dependent responses and various side effects including headache, nausea, infections, elevations in transaminase enzymes, changes in lipid profiles, and hematological effects. It is being studied in ongoing Phase III trials for rheumatoid arthritis and potential other indications. A potent and selective Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor identified through optimization within a chemical series, developed for the treatment of autoimmune diseases and organ transplant rejection. It is a potential first-in-class JAK inhibitor.

nodes.label: Riboswitch
nodes.description: A metabolite-binding domain within certain messenger RNAs that serves as precision sensors for their corresponding targets. They control fundamental biochemical pathways in Bacillus subtilis and other bacteria by modulating gene expression through allosteric rearrangement of mRNA structure upon ligand binding. Riboswitches contain sensing 'aptamer' modules, capable of ligand-induced structural changes, and downstream regions, harboring expression-controlling elements. They form tuning fork-like architectures, in which the prongs are held in parallel through hairpin loop interactions, and the internal bubble zippers up to form the purine binding pocket. The bound purines are held by hydrogen bonding interactions involving conserved nucleotides along their entire periphery. Recognition specificity is associated with Watson-Crick pairing of the encapsulated adenine and guanine ligands with uridine and cytosine, respectively. Structured elements typically found in the 5' untranslated regions of mRNAs, where they regulate gene expression by binding to small metabolites. Do not require the involvement of protein factors for metabolite binding. Appear to be pervasive in eubacteria, suggesting that this form of regulation is an important mechanism by which metabolic genes are controlled. Riboswitches are involved in controlling genes responsible for importing or synthesizing thiamine and its phosphorylated derivatives. They form a complex folded RNA with two subdomains, one of which forms an intercalation pocket for the 4-amino-5-hydroxymethyl-2-methylpyrimidine moiety of TPP and another that uses bivalent metal ions and water molecules to make bridging contacts to the pyrophosphate moiety of the ligand. This structure allows the riboswitch to recognize TPP in an extended conformation. The central thiazole moiety is not recognized by the RNA, which explains why the antimicrobial compound pyrithiamine pyrophosphate targets this riboswitch and downregulates the expression of thiamine metabolic genes.

nodes.label: Myotonic dystrophy type 2
nodes.description: A dominantly inherited multisystemic disorder caused by a (CCTG)(n) tetranucleotide repeat expansion in the ZNF9 gene, characterized by genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. It lacks a congenital form and shares several features with DM1, such as the presence of a myogenic program during muscle development and tissue regeneration. It is one of the two known subtypes of myotonic dystrophy, along with myotonic dystrophy type 1. It is characterized by a progressive multisystem genetic disorder affecting about 1 in 8000 people worldwide, and is one of the most frequent forms of muscular dystrophy in adulthood. It is associated with cardiac involvement, often leading to dilated cardiomyopathy and severe arrhythmias, and is also linked to left ventricular non-compaction. Currently, there is no cure for this disease, but supportive management helps to reduce morbidity and mortality, and patients require close follow-up.

nodes.label: NF-kappaB
nodes.description: A family of transcription factors involved in cell proliferation, cell death, cell migration, and cell interactions. Expressed in zones of active neurogenesis in the postnatal and adult mouse brain, including the subventricular zone and the rostral migratory stream. Distinct members include Rel A, p50, Rel B, and c-Rel, with different expression patterns in various cell types such as radial glial cells, migrating neuron precursors, and astrocytic lineage cells. The expression of Rel A and p50 persists into adulthood, suggesting a role in neurogenesis. A transcription factor family involved in the regulation of gene expression, particularly in response to stress, inflammation, and immune responses. It has two activating pathways: the canonical and the alternative. Constitutive activation of the alternative NF-kappaB-activating pathway leads to MMP9 gene induction and potentially the invasive potential of lymphoma cells. The constitutive activation is caused by loss of function mutations within the coding sequence of NF-kappaB inhibitory molecules such as IkappaBalpha or p100. The truncated form of p100, Hut-78, constitutively generates p52 and contributes to the development of T-cell lymphomas. A biological process regulated by polyubiquitin binding proteins, particularly through the binding of NEMO to polyubiquitinated substrates in response to cellular stimuli. Other polyubiquitin binding proteins can antagonize this pathway by competing with NEMO for polyubiquitin. A transcription factor involved in the binding to promoter elements and the activation of miRNA genes in human biliary epithelial cells, particularly in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS). It is composed of the p65 subunit and its activation can be inhibited by SC-514, an IKK2 inhibitor.

nodes.label: PTEN/MMAC1
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene, also known as phosphatase and tensin homolog/mutated in multiple advanced cancers 1. Its inactivation is an important step in the progression of gliomas to end-stage glioblastoma multiforme. A candidate tumor suppressor gene that may be targeted for deletion in association with chromosome 10 LOH, and has been identified through investigations of glioblastomas. It is a protein-coding gene involved in regulating cell growth and division. A novel tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 10q23, mutations of which were described in about 20% of primary glioblastomas and 60% of GBM cell lines. It is involved in the inactivation process of GBM in a subset of cases. A tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 10, specifically close and distally located to the D10S541 locus. Four glioblastomas out of 122 exhibited homozygous deletions at this gene.

nodes.label: Transcription
nodes.description: A cellular process involving the synthesis of RNA from DNA, which is regulated by various factors such as histone methyltransferase complexes, nuclear receptor-mediated interactions, and ubiquitination. It is involved in the production of primary microRNA transcripts (pri-miRNAs) in plants and is essential for the proper development and function of many tissues and organs. Transcription is a complex biochemical process that involves co-transcriptional capping and splicing of the precursor RNA to form the mature mRNA. It is also influenced by nucleosomes and can determine the levels of pri-miRNAs. Additionally, transcription can mediate cohesin translocation or release cohesin from active genes through Wapl.

nodes.label: Thapsigargin
nodes.description: A chemical compound used as an ER stressor that increases ERAD and adaptive ER stress proteins in cardiac myocytes but can also decrease ERAD and increase maladaptive ER stress proteins and cell death when Hrd1 is knocked down. It is also an intracellular Ca2+ mobilizing agent that causes vomiting in the least shrew. Additionally, it is a SERCA inhibitor that reduces the effects of AMPK stimulation on resistance arteries and is used to induce calcium depletion of sarcoplasmic reticular stores, ER stress, and to serve as a negative control for UPR activation.

nodes.label: Pharmacogenetics
nodes.description: The study of how genetic variations affect an individual's response to drugs, particularly in the context of pain treatment.

nodes.label: Fanconi anaemia
nodes.description: An autosomal recessive disease characterized by congenital abnormalities, defective haemopoiesis, and a high risk of developing acute myeloid leukaemia and certain solid tumours. It can be caused by mutations in at least seven different genes and has interaction pathways with other proteins involved in DNA damage repair, such as ATM, BRCA1 and BRCA2. A nosologic entity to which some cases of BGS have been reassigned after demonstration of corresponding cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities. It is not explicitly described in detail in the text. A genetic disorder associated with the FANCD2 protein. A rare, autosomal recessive, genetically complex, DNA repair deficiency syndrome in man characterized by a heterogeneous spectrum of clinical features including stem cell loss, causing progressive bone marrow failure and sterility, diverse developmental abnormalities and a profound predisposition to neoplasia. It involves 15 genes, biallelic disruption of any one of which results in this clinically defined syndrome. The molecular level reveals a fundamental defect in DNA repair underlying this complex phenotype. Cells derived from FA patients spontaneously accumulate broken chromosomes and exhibit a marked sensitivity to DNA-damaging chemotherapeutic agents.

nodes.label: Neurofibromatosis type 1
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by the growth of tumors along nerve tissue, affecting about 1 in 3,000 individuals. It is fully penetrant in adults, meaning that all individuals with the gene will develop the disease, but the severity and frequency of disease features increase with age. The reproductive fitness of NF1 patients is reduced by about one-half. Approximately half of all cases result from new mutations, and the estimated rate of new NF1 mutations is unusually high, although the exact cause remains unknown. An autosomal dominant disease with a prevalence of about 1/3000, characterized by the presence of two or more criteria such as six or more café au lait spots, >2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma, freckling in the axillary or inguinal region, optic glioma, a distinctive osseous lesion like sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of long bone cortex with or without pseudoarthrosis, and a first degree relative with NF1. It has numerous complications and the pathogenesis is not clarified. The NF1 gene, a megagene located on the long arm of the 17th chromosome at the position 17q11.2, is associated with this disease. The mutation rate for NF1-gene is high, with half of all cases of NF1 being from new mutations. The gene protein product - neurofibromin plays an important role in the tumorogenesis as a tumor-suppressor gene. Molecular genetic evaluation for the identification of disease-causing mutations is possible in approximately 20% of patients. Patient care is best done in specialized neurofibromatosis centers. An autosomal dominant condition with a worldwide incidence of approximately 1 per 2500 to 3000 individuals, caused by a germ-line-inactivating mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. The disease is characterized by the presence of neurofibromin, a protein that regulates cell growth. Recent advancements have led to the development of new therapies for managing clinical problems associated with the disease. An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder with an estimated prevalence of about 1/3000. It is characterized by various types of speech abnormalities and is associated with dysfluencies in the speech of individuals affected. Stuttering may occur in some patients, but the dysfluency pattern as a group is not identical to stuttering. A common genetic disorder that affects neurological, cognitive, social, and physical development. It impacts all racial groups and both genders equally, occurring in about 1 in 2,500 to 3,300 individuals in the population. Children with NF-1 experience psychomotor and cognitive impairments affecting their social lives and academic achievements. The incidence rate at birth is about 0.0004 births in the United States and is growing in prevalence. A genetic disorder associated with the most common malignancy, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs). A genetic disorder characterized by the growth of benign tumors along nerve tissue, affecting approximately 1 in 2,000 live births. It is also known as NF1. The prevalence of NF1 in the Finnish population was determined through a retrospective total-population study, yielding a prevalence of 1/4,088 on 31 December 2005 with a 95% confidence interval of 1/4,320-1/3,869. The survival of patients with NF1 was found to be inferior compared to the general population with a hazard ratio of 3.10 (95% CI 2.73-3.53, P < 0.001). When combined with an estimate of NF1 incidence, a prevalence of 1/2,052 (95% CI 1/2,176-1/1,941) was estimated for NF1 in a population aged 0-74 years. A common autosomal dominant disease that occurs in the general population at the rate of 1 in 3000. Many NF-1 patients present with spinal malformations. It is characterized by cervical vertebral scalloping, pedicle deficiencies and dural ectasia (DE). The case involves a 54-year-old female patient who was diagnosed with NF-1 after presenting with gradually increasing swelling and spots on the body that had been present for a long period of time. NF-1 is routinely seen in dermatology practice. Coexistence of NF-1 with vertebral scalloping, pedicle deficiencies and DE rarely occurs. This case is the second reported instance in the literature of NF-1 with a spinal anomaly in the cervical region, and the first reported instance of the coexistence of NF-1 with cervical vertebral scalloping, pedicle deficiencies and DE.
