A monogenic disease within the neurofibromatosis spectrum, with an incidence of 1 in 3000 births. It is characterized by the presence of six or more café-au-lait spots by the age of 12 months in 99% of patients. The disease is associated with a greater tumor burden for the nervous system and is managed in centers of expertise with individualized care and new types of pharmacotherapy. An autosomal dominant disease affecting one in every 3000 individuals, characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations including skin abnormalities and severe vascular damage. It can present cerebrovascular disease (CVD) since childhood, which may include headache, cognitive deficits, aneurysm rupture, and ultimately cause death. The disease is linked to cerebrovascular disorders and has been studied in relation to stroke, Moyamoya disease, vascular diseases, aneurysm, and congenital abnormalities in children and adolescents. Early diagnosis and imaging tests can improve prognosis and clinical outcomes. A genetic disorder characterized by the growth of tumors along nerves throughout the body. It is one of the two types of neurofibromatosis discussed in the text. A multisystem genetic disorder with an incidence of 1 in 3,000, affecting more than one million people worldwide and more than 80,000 in the United States. It is also known as von Recklinghausen disease.

nodes.label: Multiple Sclerosis
nodes.description: A chronic neurological disorder characterized by inflammation, demyelination, and scarring in the central nervous system. It affects approximately five million individuals in Denmark and has been studied through a nationwide, long-term epidemiologic survey in the Danish Multiple Sclerosis Registry. Multiple Sclerosis is associated with excess mortality, characterized by the use of disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) and a median follow-up time of 20.0 years among 1795 people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) diagnosed between 1971-2010. DMTs included in the analyses were interferon and glatiramer acetate. Male sex, higher age at diagnosis, and primary progressive disease course were independently associated with poorer survival. Despite DMT use being associated with better survival, relative life expectancy of pwMS did not change over five decades in Western Finland.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial dysfunction
nodes.description: A condition involving abnormalities in the function of mitochondria, which can lead to various cellular dysfunctions and may have implications for the development of future treatments. It is characterized by impaired mitochondrial function, reduced ATP synthesis, higher levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), imbalanced mitochondrial dynamics, and other detrimental effects, often resulting from mutations in many genes in the nuclear genome that cause dysfunction of mitochondria. Mitochondrial dysfunction can trigger neurodegenerative disorders and is associated with increased apoptosis and necrosis in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative illnesses. It can also worsen following intracerebral hemorrhage, involving impaired ATP production, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and disrupted calcium homeostasis. Strategies such as Mitophagy can protect against mitochondrial dysfunction.

nodes.label: Radiomics
nodes.description: A rapidly evolving field of research concerned with the extraction of quantitative metrics, known as radiomic features, within medical images. These features capture tissue and lesion characteristics such as heterogeneity and shape and may be used for clinical problem solving, often in combination with other types of data like demographic, histologic, genomic, or proteomic data. Radiomics involves a multidisciplinary workflow that includes tumor segmentation, image preprocessing, feature extraction, model development, and validation. It uses various algorithms to extract quantitative features from radiological images, helping in the accurate classification of diseases and playing an integral part in feature selection for the classification problem. Radiomics has been applied within oncology to improve diagnosis, prognostication, and clinical decision support, with the goal of delivering precision medicine.

nodes.label: Craniosynostosis
nodes.description: A medical condition where the sutures between the bones of the skull fuse prematurely, leading to abnormal head shape and growth patterns. It can be caused by single-gene mutations or chromosomal abnormalities, with different prognoses and treatment approaches for each type. Craniosynostosis can be syndromic or nonsyndromic, and may present with various clinical features such as brachydactyly, sensorineural hearing loss, and developmental delay. Specific types include coronal synostosis, bilateral coronal synostosis, and Mercedes Benz pattern craniosynostosis, which involves the sagittal and both lambdoid sutures.

nodes.label: WHIM syndrome
nodes.description: A rare congenital immunodeficiency disease associated with mutations in the chemokine receptor gene CXCR4, characterized by recurrent infections, neutropenia, immunodeficiency, and malignancies. It is caused by heterozygous autosomal dominant mutations of the CXCR4 gene, leading to increased sensitivity of neutrophils and lymphocytes to the unique ligand CXCL12 and an increased accumulation of mature neutrophils in the bone marrow. Symptoms include warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections, and myelokathexis, which refers to the retention of mature neutrophils in the bone marrow. Patients also exhibit impaired CXCR4 internalization and desensitization upon exposure to CXCL12, resulting in enhanced CXCR4-dependent responses such as chemotaxis.

nodes.label: Alzheimer's disease (AD)
nodes.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and changes in behavior and personality. It is associated with the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to toxic signals and neurodegeneration. Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed based on various factors including MMSE score, ADAS-cog score, acetylcholinesterase inhibitor use, modified Hachinski score, and CT or MRI results. It is a ravaging neurodegenerative disorder for which no disease-modifying treatment is currently available, but treatments like aducanumab are being investigated. The disease is also linked to type 2 diabetes and has serious societal implications. Aducanumab is being investigated as a disease-modifying treatment for this condition in patients with mild-to-moderate AD.

nodes.label: Incidental durotomy
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the repair of dural tears intraoperatively using dural stitches and fibrin glue. It does not include mandatory bed rest and allows patients to ambulate according to the natural course after surgery. The study involved 20 cases, with 75% of patients experiencing no symptoms after repair. Dural tears were 1-3 mm in length, and some patients reported headache, nausea, or tinnitus as symptoms. A medical procedure where a dural tear occurs accidentally during spinal surgery, potentially leading to complications such as meningitis.

nodes.label: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
nodes.description: A cellular organelle involved in protein folding, modification, and transport, which can experience stress leading to various diseases when its function is impaired. It forms contact sites with the mitochondrial outer membrane, particularly at the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES), and is crucial for mitochondrial signaling, quality control, and ATP production in cardiac cells.

nodes.label: Colorectal cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the colon or rectum, often involving tumor stem cells and interleukin 22 (IL-22), with international variations in incidence rates. It is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States and the second most common cause of cancer death globally. Colorectal cancer is associated with various risk factors, including physical inactivity, excessive adiposity, hyperinsulinemia, dietary patterns that stimulate insulin secretion, such as high intakes of red and processed meats, saturated and trans-fats, and highly processed carbohydrates and sugars. Protective agents may include certain micronutrients like folate and calcium. Colorectal carcinomas with moderate or strong Bmi-1 expression are more likely to have low levels of INK4 locus proteins (p16INK4a/p14ARF). Colorectal cancer subgroups show specific genetic and epigenetic signatures and display distinctive correlates with overall survival. It is often associated with red and processed meat consumption and can be influenced by modifiable risk factors such as lifestyle, diet, and obesity. Colorectal cancer patients can undergo first-line therapy with bevacizumab and cetuximab combined with chemotherapy, and their circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can be used to monitor therapeutic response and resistance. Experimental studies have explored the potential role of heme iron and heterocyclic amines in its development, but the evidence is not yet sufficient to confirm a mechanistic link between red meat intake and colorectal cancer risk in humans.

nodes.label: International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial (ISAT)
nodes.description: A randomised, multicentre trial comparing the safety and efficacy of endovascular coiling with standard neurosurgical clipping for ruptured intracranial aneurysms judged to be suitable for both treatments. The trial enrolled 2143 patients and analyzed clinical outcomes at 2 months and 1 year, with interim ascertainment of rebleeds and death. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with a modified Rankin scale score of 3-6 at 1 year. A randomised, multicentre trial comparing neurosurgical clipping versus endovascular coiling for treating patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms. The trial involved 2143 patients admitted to 42 neurosurgical centres, mainly in the UK and Europe. Patients were randomly assigned to neurosurgical clipping (n=1070) or endovascular coiling (n=1073). The primary outcome was death or dependence at 1 year (defined by a modified Rankin scale of 3-6), while secondary outcomes included rebleeding from the treated aneurysm and risk of seizures. The trial reported 1-year outcomes for 1063 of 1073 patients allocated to endovascular treatment and 1055 of 1070 patients allocated to neurosurgical treatment. The results showed an absolute risk reduction of 7.4% in favour of endovascular treatment, with a significant early survival advantage maintained for up to 7 years. The risk of epilepsy was lower in patients allocated to endovascular treatment, but the risk of late rebleeding was higher. A study that aimed to assess the long-term risks of death, disability, and rebleeding in patients randomly assigned to clipping or endovascular coiling after rupture of an intracranial aneurysm. The study enrolled 2143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms between 1994 and 2002 at 43 neurosurgical centres and randomly assigned them to clipping or coiling. All UK and some non-UK centres continued long-term follow-up of 2004 patients enrolled in the original cohort. The study recorded all deaths and rebleeding events and analyzed rebleeding by allocation and by treatment received. A trial published in 2002 that has influenced the perception of endovascular treatment of intracranial aneurysms, particularly coiling, gaining progressive recognition. Middle cerebral artery aneurysms were underrepresented in this study, yet it is often used as an argument to favor coiling above surgery in MCA aneurysms. A clinical trial that investigated the differences in incidence and impact of delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) after coiling and clipping in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The trial involved 2,143 patients and used logistic regression analysis to calculate odds ratios (OR) for DCI and poor outcome at 2 months and 1 year.

nodes.label: Interstitial 1q deletion syndrome
nodes.description: A disease characterized by antithrombin III deficiency, which is clinically defined by a patient with microbrachycephaly, high forehead, long philtrum, thin upper lip, downturned corners of the mouth, low set ears with overlapping helix, fifth-finger clinodactyly, small hands and feet, bilateral transverse palmar crease, low total finger ridge count, hypotonia, severe growth and psychomotor delay, mild hypoplasia of corpus callosum, and Arnold-Chiari type 1 malformation. The karyotype shows 46, XY, del(1)(q23q31.2). Coagulation factor V (F5, 1q23) and coagulation factor XIII (F13B, 1q31-q32.1) levels are normal, while antithrombin III (AT3, 1q23-q25.1) serum level and activity are half of normal.

nodes.label: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
nodes.description: A type of tumor associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), characterized by the presence of giant cells in the astrocytes. It is inoperable and life-threatening in some cases, but can be treated with everolimus, leading to a reduction in volume in 75% of patients and no recurrent hydrocephalus in one patient 36 months after initiation. It grows in the subependymal region of the brain and may cause seizure aggravation in children.

nodes.label: Multiple Myeloma
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting plasma cells in the bone marrow, characterized by the presence of abnormal plasma cells and the production of monoclonal proteins. It can lead to various symptoms and complications, including skeletal complications such as pathologic fractures, bone pain, hypercalcemia, neurologic symptoms, and renal insufficiency. Multiple Myeloma is associated with increased morbidity and mortality and remains incurable despite recent advancements in treatment. It involves targeting specific molecules to myeloma cells and overcoming tumor microenvironment-mediated drug resistance. Treatment options vary depending on patient age and eligibility for autologous stem cell transplantation, with induction therapy based on novel agents like bortezomib being considered standard of care for younger patients. Maintenance therapies are also important for prolonging overall survival. Refractory or relapsed MM treatment has improved with the development of second and third generation immunomodulatory agents and proteasome inhibitors, such as pomalidomide and dexamethasone.

nodes.label: Alzheimer's disease
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by the presence of neurofibrillar tangles, which are formed by the accumulation of tau protein, and amyloid plaques. It is associated with cognitive decline, memory loss, and is often diagnosed in later stages of life. Alzheimer's disease is a major public health concern with significant research focused on its prevention and treatment. Several pharmacological strategies have been clinically studied for the primary or secondary prevention of Alzheimer's disease, including antihypertensive agents, statins, conjugated oestrogen, selenium, vitamin E, Ginkgo biloba, cholinesterase inhibitors, anti-amyloid antibodies, active immunisation, selective secretase inhibitors and modulators, microtubule stabilizers, R-flurbiprofen, xaliproden, ONO-2506, FK962, SGS 742, TCH 346, Alzhemed, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, rosiglitazone, leuprolide, interferons, metal-protein attenuating compounds, rasagaline, huperzine A, antioxidants, and memantine. Randomized trial data are available for some of these agents, while others are currently under evaluation in large prevention trials. Imaging modalities such as MRI, PET, and SPECT have the potential to contribute to both the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and assist in the search for more effective treatments. Several AD-related biomarkers have been proposed and evaluated. The use of PET imaging to detect alterations in regional brain metabolism using [(18)F]FDG has enabled more sensitive and accurate early diagnosis of AD, especially in conjunction with traditional medical evaluation. Imaging biomarkers have been shown to correlate with the progression of AD and some have been pursued in clinical trials.

nodes.label: Dystonia
nodes.description: A group of neurological disorders characterized by involuntary muscle contractions leading to abnormal postures and movements. There are currently 13 different forms of dystonia that can be distinguished on a genetic basis, including dystonia types 1-13. Recent advances in dystonia research have led to the discovery of novel dystonia genes and loci, changing classification schemes, and introducing improved and new treatment options. Treatment options include both medical and surgical therapies, with deep brain stimulation being the most recent development. A neurological disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions leading to abnormal movements and postures. It was evaluated in a multicenter prospective study involving 22 patients with primary generalized dystonia. The study assessed the effects of bilateral pallidal deep brain stimulation (DBS) on mood and cognitive performance in these patients. A movement disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions that cause twisting movements and abnormal postures. A disorder characterized by abnormal muscle tone and movement, which may be linked to AIS based on recent studies suggesting a potential role of central nervous system dysfunction in its pathogenesis. A disease process associated with electrophysiologic abnormalities of the globus pallidus externus, characterized by corticopallidal connections. A neurological disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions, causing twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures. It has been treated with deep brain stimulation, with greater clinical impact on trunk and cervical dystonia compared to laryngeal dystonia. Improvements in gait dystonia decreased from 20.9% at 1 year to 16.2% at last assessment, and no patient maintained a fully independent gait. Reduction of BFMDRS-D was maintained for swallowing in 52.9% of patients. A movement disorder linked to aberrant activity of GPe neurons and associated with motor symptoms.

nodes.label: Lichen sclerosus
nodes.description: A chronic inflammatory skin disease that causes substantial discomfort and morbidity, most commonly in adult women, but also in men and children. It affects any skin site, including the anogenital area, oral mucosa, and rarely, the genital area. In the anogenital area, it causes intractable itching and soreness. The exact prevalence is uncertain, and it can occur without symptoms. The disease is more common in women at times of low sex hormone output, and there seems to be a genetic susceptibility and a link with autoimmune mechanisms. The wart virus and the spirochaete borrelia have been suggested but not substantiated as infective triggers. The Koebner phenomenon is known to occur, suggesting that trauma, injury, and sexual abuse have been suggested as possible triggers of symptoms in genetically predisposed people. The treatment of choice for anogenital lichen sclerosus is potent topical corticosteroid ointment for a limited time. Circumcision may be indicated in men, and surgery may be considered in women, to relieve effects of scarring or to treat coexisting carcinoma. Current research aims to identify a treatable cause of lichen sclerosus, to identify patients at risk of scarring and of malignant disorders, and to find target pathways for therapeutic intervention. A chronic inflammatory disease that typically affects the anogenital area, causing intractable itching and soreness. It may also have extragenital involvement in 15 to 20% of cases, and can occur at sites of injury as a Koebner phenomenon. In this case report, it was found at the site of a tattoo with simultaneous genital involvement.

nodes.label: Pendred's syndrome
nodes.description: An autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by congenital sensorineural deafness, goiter, and impaired iodide organification. It is caused by mutations in the Pendred's syndrome (PDS) gene that encodes pendrin, a chloride/iodide transporter expressed in the thyroid, the inner ear, and the kidney. An atypical form of Pendred's syndrome characterized by thyroidal defects, large goiters, short stature, nerve deafness, and mild intellectual impairment. It affects a 52-year-old woman and her 47-year-old brother. Biochemical defects associated with familial goiter are not present in these patients, suggesting an abnormality in thyroglobulin structure may be responsible. A genetic disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing defect and goiter, with a large spectrum of mutations and phenotypic heterogeneity. The diagnosis can be difficult due to the lack of sensitivity and specificity of thyroid signs. The causative gene is PDS. A genetic disorder characterized by bilateral profound hearing loss with residual hearing at low frequencies, goiter diagnosed between the age of 1 to 14 years with a positive perchlorate discharge test, and sometimes associated with normal hormonal and normal perchlorate discharge test results. Patients may develop goiter between 8 and 14 years of age. Relatives of patients with Pendred's syndrome show mild low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss without goiter and normal perchlorate discharge test results in half the cases, and a slight drop in the perchlorate discharge test results with normal hearing and without goiter in the other half. A genetic disorder characterized by familial goiter, congenital deafness, Mondini-type inner ear malformation, goiter, and hypothyroidism. It affects the thyroid tissue, leading to abnormal thyroglobulin messenger ribonucleic acid variants. A genetic disorder associated with congenital neurosensory deafness and goitre, characterized by abnormal discharge of iodide following perchlorate challenge, indicating a defect of iodide organification. It accounts for up to 7.5% of all cases of congenital deafness, but the molecular basis of the association between the hearing loss and the thyroid organification defect remains unknown. A genetic disorder characterized by sensorineural hearing loss and goiter, often associated with defects at the thyroid peroxidase locus on chromosome 2.

nodes.label: Friedreich's Ataxia
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by the expansion of a GAA repeat in intron 1 of the frataxin gene, leading to iron accumulation in the mitochondria and hypersensitivity to oxidative stress. It is the most common genetic cause of ataxia and can be diagnosed through molecular analysis, especially when clinical findings are not clear. A neurodegenerative disorder associated with a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the frataxin (FXN) gene. It is the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia, with a mean age of onset at 16 years. Nearly 95-98% of patients are homozygous for a 90-1300 GAA repeat expansion with only 2-5% demonstrating compound heterozygosity. Compound heterozygous individuals have a repeat expansion in one allele and a point mutation/deletion/insertion in the other. Compound heterozygosity and point mutations are very rare causes of Friedreich's ataxia and nonsense mutations are a further rarity among point mutations. A progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a homozygous GAA repeat expansion mutation in intron 1 of the frataxin gene (FXN), leading to reduced transcription, reduced levels of frataxin protein, mitochondrial iron accumulation, oxidative stress, and cell death, particularly in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) sensory neurons and the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum. It is associated with cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, and skeletal deformities. There is currently no effective treatment for this disease, and patients die prematurely. Recent findings suggest that abnormal GAA expansion plays a role in histone modification, subjecting the FXN gene to heterochromatin silencing.

nodes.label: Imiglucerase
nodes.description: A drug used to treat Gaucher disease, administered to 126 patients in December 2010. It is an enzyme replacement therapy for the treatment of Gaucher disease. One of the three commercially available enzymes for the treatment of Gaucher disease by ERT, produced in different cell systems and undergoing various post-translational or post-production glycosylation modifications to expose mannose residues. A human glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) used for the treatment of Gaucher disease in adults and previously administered to patients in the study before switching to taliglucerase alfa. It is a recombinant human protein and was used as a reference ERT in the Phase 3 trial. A treatment for Gaucher disease that was an alternative in the past before the approval of other treatments. It is mentioned as an option that was available when there were essentially no alternatives, implying its use before the approval of other treatments. A recombinant glucocerebrosidase used in enzyme replacement therapy for the treatment of Gaucher disease, particularly in type 1 Gaucher disease. It has been used for at least two years by some patients before the addition of miglustat. A therapeutic protein used for treatment of patients with type 1 Gaucher disease (GD) before the introduction of taliglucerase alfa. It was studied in the original study and its use preceded that of taliglucerase alfa in patients with GD. An enzyme replacement therapy used for treatment of Gaucher disease (GD) in children and adults. It has been compared to taliglucerase alfa in a multicenter extension study assessing its efficacy and safety in pediatric patients with GD who were treatment-naï¿½ve or previously treated with imiglucerase. The study involved 5 patients switched from imiglucerase. The drug was administered at the same dose as previously treated with imiglucerase every other week.

nodes.label: Aducanumab
nodes.description: Aducanumab is a human monoclonal antibody selective for aggregated forms of amyloid beta, approved by the US Food and Drug Administration on June 7, 2021, as the first disease-modifying treatment for Alzheimer's disease (AD). It is administered through monthly intravenous infusions and is titrated to a dose of 10 mg/kg over a 6-month period. The drug can increase the incidence of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including brain effusion or hemorrhage, and requires dose interruption or treatment discontinuation for symptomatic ARIA or moderate-severe ARIA. It is a human IgG1 anti-Aβ monoclonal antibody currently being evaluated for potential treatment of patients with early Alzheimer's disease.

nodes.label: Astrocytes
nodes.description: A type of cell in the human central nervous system, primarily responsible for iron accumulation in the early affected regions of PSP, highly associated with cellular tau pathology. Astrocytes are key regulators of central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and play a role in neurological and neurodegenerative disorders. They are generated from hiPSCs through a two-step protocol involving a bankable NPC intermediate, low-density passaging, and overexpression of the gliogenic transcription factor NFIA, resulting in the generation of iAstrocytes. Astrocytes are the most abundant type of glial cell in the CNS, displaying unique transcription factor profiles in different regions of the adult brain. They can be modulated by type I interferons (IFNs) and interferon-stimulated gene expression, and are involved in several CNS diseases termed 'interferonopathies'. Astrocytes can be recognized by their expression of glial fibrillary acidic protein, glutamine synthetase, glutamate transporter 1 (GLT1), aquaporin-4, aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 family member L1, and other proteins. They can have varying levels of SOX2 expression and may differ in self-renewal capacity, differentiation status, and phenotypic characteristics. Astrocytes can be activated by hypertension and inhibited by AT1R blockade through Candesartan.

nodes.label: BRAF
nodes.description: A proto-oncogene involved in various types of cancer, particularly melanoma and colorectal cancer, whose mutations can lead to hyper-activation of ERK in melanoma cells, resulting in the down-regulation of MITF protein. BRAF mutations are associated with the development of sessile serrated adenomas (SSAs) in the serrated pathway of colorectal carcinogenesis and are found in 4.7% of tumours studied, often associated with resistance to anti-EGFR therapies. The V600E mutation in BRAF is found in around 5.1% of tested patients with colorectal cancer and is always accompanied by wild-type KRAS. BRAF mutations are also involved in predicting resistance to anti-EGFR MoAb in other cancer models and are included in the list of genes tested for germline variants that associate with somatic mutation of the EGFR pathway. In The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Lung Adenocarcinoma dataset, BRAF is found to have 2% of somatic variants in 7 genes analyzed through next generation sequencing with a 50-gene panel.

nodes.label: Liver
nodes.description: A major organ in the body responsible for metabolism and detoxification, developed by the vertebrate Lhx2. It is involved in the production of triiodothyronine (T3) and is one of the organs affected by Gaucher's disease, characterized by hypertrophy due to the formation of Gaucher cells. The liver is also one of the organs where pathologic findings of hemophagocytosis are typically observed in Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and it is included in the diagnostic criteria for HLH along with the bone marrow and lymph nodes. The liver is the main source of transthyretin production in the body and is involved in the standard treatment of hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (hATTR) through liver transplants. The organ in which the recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vector is delivered to correct phenylketonuria (PKU) in mice, and where the AAV-mediated delivery of the PAL gene is specifically targeted to correct hyperphenylalaninemia in both male and female PKU mice. The liver is also the organ in which the disposition of d-AMPH has been determined in both male and female Oct3 KO and WT mice, and where 3-iodothyronamine (T1AM) is detected at the highest concentration. In C. siamensis, the liver is where Cshepc transcripts are highly expressed. The liver is developed by the vertebrate Lhx2 and has two main cell types: mature hepatocytes and EpCAM-positive cells within ductular reactions that gradually lose EpCAM expression during maturation into hepatocytes. Liver development involves dynamic expression of EpCAM, and liver regeneration is associated with a population of EpCAM-positive cells. The liver is an organ where recently evolved enhancers can be associated with genes under positive selection, and where promoters are partially or fully conserved across species. In dogs, the liver shows adaptive changes of hepatocellular hypertrophy due to drug metabolizing enzyme induction in response to Sotorasib treatment. The liver is also involved in the metabolism of isradipine, a calcium-channel blocker used to treat hypertension in renally impaired patients, and higher drug doses resulted in substantially elevated concentrations for bioconjugates, including HB-10, in this organ.

nodes.label: Atherosclerosis
nodes.description: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the arteries characterized by the buildup of plaque in the inner lining of the arterial walls, leading to narrowed or blocked blood vessels. It is associated with severe threats to human health worldwide and is linked to at least 50% of foam cells in atheromas being derived from vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). The disease involves the presence of oxidized low-density lipoproteins and cholesterol crystals, which can cause lysosomal dysfunction in macrophages, and is associated with endothelial dysfunction and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near the MMP12 gene at chromosome 11q22.3. Atherosclerosis is also related to the presence of circulating leukocytes and can lead to coronary artery disease (CAD) in patients. The condition is investigated for prevention by calcium channel antagonists and is associated with reduced vitality behaviors and elevated hs-CRP and ET levels.

nodes.label: Mitochondria
nodes.description: Mitochondria are cellular organelles primarily responsible for respiration, where catabolism of substrates is coupled to adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis via oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos). They are essential for energy conversion and ATP production, calcium homeostasis, and regulation of apoptosis and stress responses. Mitochondria contain their own DNA that encodes for essential proteins involved in the execution of normal mitochondrial functions. They are involved in various biological functions, including biosynthesis, lipid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, cell signal transduction, and apoptosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction can lead to changes in mitochondrial morphology and structure, and is related to the occurrence and development of different chronic liver diseases. Important organelles responsible for cellular energy production and various metabolic processes. Their dysfunction is strongly related to the progression of cellular aging and is affected by the disruption of proteostasis and Lotus germ extract treatment. Special double-membraned intracellular compartments or 'organelles' commonly known as the 'powerhouses of the cell', responsible for generating the bulk of ATP used to fuel cellular biochemical reactions and synthesizing metabolites for the synthesis of macromolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. Mitochondria were initially thought to have canonical roles in bioenergetics and biosynthesis, but recent evidence suggests they can also act as signaling organelles, influencing diverse physiological and pathophysiological outcomes. Molecular understanding of mitochondrial communication could reveal new therapeutic strategies to improve health and ameliorate diseases. Cellular organelles that play a crucial role in most eukaryotic cells. They are involved in the process of mitophagy, where their quality and quantity are controlled. The outer mitochondrial membrane protein, Atg32, serves as the mitophagic receptor. Organelles commonly associated with adenosine triphosphate (ATP) formation through the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) process. They are responsible for functions such as calcium homeostasis, apoptosis, autophagy, and production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mitochondria sense the microenvironment and can modify the cells to either a pro or anti-inflammatory profile. They undergo morphology changes relying on nutrients' availability and the bioenergetics demands of the cells, in a process known as mitochondrial dynamics, which includes both fusion and fission. Organelles responsible for producing ATP. Their capacity to produce ATP is influenced by the density of the inner mitochondrial membrane and the number of mitochondria per cell. Intracellular organelles involved in energy production, cell metabolism and cell signaling. Essential not only in the process of ATP synthesis, lipid metabolism and nucleic acid metabolism, but also in tumor development and metastasis. They have been demonstrated as the target for cancer treatment and play a unique role in cancer stem cells and the tumor microenvironment. Dynamic organelles of eukaryotes involved in energy production, fatty acid oxidation, ATP production, calcium signaling, cellular apoptosis, and fatty acid synthesis. They are also known as the central hub of the immune system, regulating the innate immune pathway during infection. Mitochondria undergo constant biogenesis, fission, fusion, and degradation, and their dynamics regulate cellular immuno-metabolism. They mediate immune functions such as regulation of reactive oxygen species production, inflammasome activation, cytokine secretion, and apoptosis of infected cells. Several intracellular pathogens target and modulate these normal functions of mitochondria to facilitate their own survival and growth. Mitochondria are cellular organelles responsible for energy production, essential metabolic pathways, apoptosis, and aging. They release vesicles, which contain a functional ATP synthase complex and selectively carry protein cargo enriched for ATP synthase subunits. Mitochondria are involved in organelle-to-organelle communication. The powerhouses of the cell, performing essential functions such as ATP (adenosine triphosphate) generation, metabolism, Ca2+ buffering, and signal transduction. They are especially susceptible to autophagic and mitochondrial malfunction due to their high energy requirements and post-mitotic origin. Subcellular organelles involved in essential cellular functions, including cytosolic calcium regulation, cell apoptosis, and reactive oxygen species production. They are the site of important biochemical pathways, such as the tricarboxylic acid cycle, parts of the ureagenesis cycle, or haem synthesis. Mitochondria are responsible for the majority of cellular ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Membrane-bound cell organelles that supply most of the energy needed for cell function, highly regulated, dynamic organelles capable of altering both form and functionality rapidly to maintain normal physiological events and challenge stress to the cell. Mitochondria are organelles responsible for the maintenance of cellular bioenergetics through the production of ATP. They are also involved in the synthesis of metabolic precursors, calcium regulation, the production of reactive oxygen species, immune signaling, and apoptosis. Mitochondria are fundamental for cellular metabolism and homeostasis. The central hub of ATP production in most eukaryotic cells, responsible for generating cellular power or energy per unit time. Their power, or metabolic rate, is investigated in relation to host cell size. Mitochondria are intracellular organelles traditionally known as 'the powerhouse of the cell,' responsible for energy (ATP) generation through processes such as the electron transport chain, oxidative phosphorylation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and fatty acid β-oxidation. They also regulate several metabolic processes including redox homeostasis, calcium signalling, and cellular apoptosis. Mitochondria are portrayed as multifaceted signalling organelles that ultimately command cells' survival or death. They communicate with other intracellular compartments in homeostasis and pathology-related mitochondrial stress conditions. The molecular mechanisms of mitochondria-mediated signalling can explain mitochondria adaptation to metabolic and environmental stresses to achieve cell survival. Organelles found in the kidney that are the primary source of ATP production and regulate other cellular processes such as redox and calcium homeostasis. They are involved in the Krebs cycle, electron transport system (ETS), oxygen and electrochemical gradient consumption, and have a central role in bioenergetics. Mitochondrial impairment, including functional and structural alterations, has been reported in several kidney diseases. Critical cellular energy resources and central to the life of the neuron, mitochondria are cleared by mitophagy to maintain quality control and homeostasis. They are consumed substantially by mature neurons, which are postmitotic and require highly efficient mitophagy pathways to turnover damaged or dysfunctional mitochondria. Multifunctional organelles found in eukaryotic cells that play a central role in a wide range of life-sustaining tasks such as adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, calcium storage, and coenzyme generation pathways like iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis. Mitochondria contain approximately 1500 proteins or polypeptides. Mitochondria are cellular organelles found in eukaryotic cells responsible for generating ATP under normoxic conditions. They also produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) as a by-product of respiration, which has been associated with dysfunction and disease. Recent studies suggest that ROS production can serve important signaling functions and is an essential adaptive mitochondrial signal triggered by various stressors. Organelles that serve as the powerhouses for cellular bioenergetics in eukaryotic cells, responsible for mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate (ATP) generation, cell signaling and activity, calcium balance, cell survival, proliferation, apoptosis, and autophagy. Essential organelles responsible for energy production, calcium homeostasis, redox signaling, and other cellular responses involved in pulmonary vascular biology and disease processes. Their homeostasis depends on a balance in mitochondrial fusion and fission (dynamics). A cell organelle known as the 'powerhouse of the cell' for its role in ATP production required for numerous cellular activities. It has emerged as an important signaling organelle, mediating signaling pathways that promote protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and regulating innate immunity and inflammation. Mitochondria contain molecules also found in viruses and bacteria, which can elicit innate immune responses if they accumulate in the cytosol. Intracellular organelles responsible for cellular respiration and energy production, specifically ATP generation, with high densities in bee flight muscle and brain to support flight activity and neuronal signaling. An essential intracellular organelle responsible for energy production and conducting various cellular tasks. Mitochondrial dysfunctions and malfunctions lead to many illnesses and are targeted in medication strategies due to their special aspects in the pathophysiology of cancer. They are generally accepted as the authority with respect to ATP production in a cell and are involved in processes such as autophagy, excitotoxicity, and apoptosis. Mitochondria are cellular structures involved in energy production. They are targeted by existing drugs in the treatment and diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders, although their precise formulations are not well understood. A subcellular organelle involved in the pathogenesis of cellular stress, immune responses, differentiation, metabolic disorders, aging, and death by regulating processes such as fission, fusion, mitophagy, and transport. It contains chaperones and proteases that regulate the intrinsic apoptosis pathway through pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins Bax/Bak and Cyt C release, and induces caspase-dependent and independent cell death. It also contains cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc, ferredoxin, and ferredoxin reductase, providing an essential site for steroid hormones biosynthesis. Mitochondria are correlated with mitochondrial integrity, displaying therapeutic implications for inflammatory and immune responses. They can be transferred through cells merging, exosome-mediated transfer, and tunneling through nanotubes. Cellular organelles responsible for energy production, whose molecular mechanisms of interaction with hormones and effects on cellular level, health, and diseases are reviewed in this study. Mitochondria are cellular structures responsible for the metabolic efficiency of cells, providing both ATP and intermediate metabolic products. They play a crucial role in maintaining the energy status and redox homeostasis of eukaryotic cells. Mitochondria also regulate cell survival and death under stress conditions by controlling the cell response or activating the apoptosis process. Their dysfunction is associated with many human diseases and serves as a therapeutic target. Mitochondria are cellular organelles that play a crucial role in cell growth and proliferation by supporting both ATP synthesis and the production of macromolecular precursors. They have two distinct populations based on their dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS): those with cristae and ATP synthase, and those lacking cristae and ATP synthase. The latter contain pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS), which is involved in the reductive synthesis of proline and ornithine. Organelles responsible for ATP synthesis and energy production in cells, containing their own circular, double-stranded DNA that encodes 37 genes. They play a central role in cellular metabolism and energy production, providing approximately 90% of the cells' energy needs through oxidative phosphorylation. Essential organelles in eukaryotic cells responsible for producing ATP through the electron transport chain to supply energy for cellular activities. They also play crucial roles in cellular signaling, stress responses, and the regulation of reactive oxygen species. Mitochondria are known as the cell's powerhouse and play a critical role in cellular energy production. They are involved in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis and responding to hypoxia by activating the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (mtUPR) and mitophagy. Cellular components essential for energy production and regulating oxidative stress, damaged after intracerebral hemorrhage, leading to impaired ATP production, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and disrupted calcium homeostasis.

nodes.label: High Gleason score 8 to 10 adenocarcinoma
nodes.description: The most aggressive and potentially lethal form of prostate cancer, characterized by histologic patterns defined by the 2005 International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP)-modified Gleason grading scheme. It is typically extensive in needle core tissue, with a mean of 4.4 positive cores per case. The study examines the frequency of various gland arrangements and admixtures in needle biopsy tissue, including ill-defined glands with poorly formed lumina, fused microacinar glands, single cells, signet ring cells, cords, cribriform glands, sheets of cells, chains, glomeruloid, comedonecrosis, hypernephromatoid, single file growth, solid cylinders, and nested patterns.

nodes.label: Organic cation transporter 3
nodes.description: A high-capacity, low-affinity transporter that mediates bidirectional, sodium-independent transport of dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, serotonin, and histamine. It is sensitive to corticosterone and is involved in regulating extracellular concentrations of monoamines in the rat brain. A gene that transports serotonin (5-HT) and is upregulated in the brains of mice with constitutively reduced 5-HTT expression. It may mediate serotonergic signaling when 5-HTT expression or function is compromised.

nodes.label: Chemotherapy
nodes.description: A type of cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or inhibit the growth of cancer cells, often in combination with other therapies. It can cause side effects such as new-onset seizures in children, which are managed with medications like gabapentin. Chemotherapy is used in various combinations, including with irradiation, Bevacizumab, anti-VEGF therapy, and immune checkpoint blockade, for different types of cancer and stages. It is a standard treatment for certain cancers, such as glioblastoma and Wilm's tumor, and can be used as a comparison to other treatments in clinical trials.

nodes.label: Human African trypanosomiasis
nodes.description: A parasitic disease caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei, transmitted by tsetse flies. It occurs exclusively in sub-Saharan Africa, usually in rural areas affected by civil conflicts and neglected health systems. Reported cases are fewer than 10,000/year, which classifies it as one of the most neglected tropical diseases. It is fatal if not treated and has to be included in the differential diagnosis of every febrile traveler returning from a game park in East Africa. A neglected tropical disease that affects populations in sub-Saharan Africa, caused by infection with the gambiense and rhodesiense subspecies of the extracellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted to humans by bites of infected tsetse flies. It evolves in two stages, the hemolymphatic and meningoencephalitic stages, with the latter involving central nervous system infection after trypanosomal traversal of the blood-brain barrier. Without treatment, it leads to severe neuroinflammation and is fatal.

nodes.label: Ethanol
nodes.description: A chemical treatment involving exposure of microsporidian spores to ethanol at concentrations between 1 and 70% for 15 minutes, which was found to inactivate the spores. A chemical compound with a molecular formula of C2H5OH, commonly found in alcoholic beverages. In the context of the text, it is associated with an increased abundance of Peptostreptococcaceae and a decreased abundance of Veillonellaceae in polyps group intake.

nodes.label: (-)-OSU6162
nodes.description: A dopaminergic stabilizer used to rescue striatal neurons with normal and expanded polyglutamine chains in the huntingtin protein from exposure to free radicals and mitochondrial toxins. It produces a dose-dependent increase of mitochondrial activity and reduces cell death at concentrations of 3-150 μM. A compound that does not change glutamate toxicity but partially prevents that of H(2)O(2), rotenone, and 3-nitropropionic acid. It increases intracellular levels of BDNF and Bcl2/Bax and decreases those of p-ERK/ERK and CHIP in Q111 cells. It also increases (3)H-dopamine uptake and amphetamine-induced (3)H-dopamine release in E13 mouse mid brain neurons, suggesting potential neuroprotective effects in animal models and patients with HD.

nodes.label: Adenoma
nodes.description: A type of tumor, specifically a benign growth, whose molecular pathogenesis is studied in relation to Ki-ras and p53 genes. The study supports the role of both genes in the progression of adenomas and shows that their molecular pathogenesis differs by anatomic location, age, and mucosal predisposition. A type of tumor that arises from the epithelial cells lining the colon and rectum, characterized by genetic alterations such as mutations in APC, KRAS, FBXW7, TCF7L2 genes and copy number changes in chromosomes 5, 7, and 13. Adenomas have lower mutational rates compared to colorectal cancers and display evidence of multiclonality similar to stage I carcinomas. They are associated with somatic alterations in WNT pathway genes and require deregulation of the WNT pathway for carcinogenesis. A benign tumor that arises from the lining of the colon or rectum. Adenomas can be classified into early-stage adenomas, adenomas without associated foci of carcinoma, and adenomas with associated foci of carcinoma. They can be found in patients with familial adenomatous polyposis and patients without familial polyposis. The presence of ras-gene mutations and allelic deletions of chromosomes 5, 17, and 18 varies depending on the stage and size of the adenoma.

nodes.label: Monoclonal antibodies
nodes.description: Laboratory-produced antibodies used for various purposes, including inhibiting T helper 2-cytokine-mediated inflammatory responses in severe refractory asthma, managing immune-related adverse events, targeting specific molecules such as CTLA-4 or PD-1 proteins, and treating cancer and migraine conditions. They include anti-IgE, anti-IL-5, and anti-IL-4/IL-13 agents, as well as drugs that target CGRP or the CGRP receptor.

nodes.label: Alzheimer disease
nodes.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and changes in behavior and personality. It is associated with amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, and is the most common cause of dementia among older adults. The disease is associated with the abnormal hyperphosphorylation of tau protein and disruption of microtubule network, leading to axonal and dendritic neurodegeneration. It is also linked to the accumulation of β-amyloid (Aβ) plaques in the brain, which can be detected using amyloid PET imaging as a surrogate for β-amyloid pathology. Alzheimer's disease is a complex disease involving the innate immune system, and its pathology does not fit traditional inflammatory or autoimmune models.

nodes.label: Idecabtagene vicleucel
nodes.description: A chimeric antigen-receptor-modified T cell (CAR-T) therapy developed for the treatment of heavily pretreated refractory multiple myeloma patients. It has demonstrated encouraging efficacy and an acceptable safety profile, and was the first CAR-T to gain regulatory approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Preclinical and clinical development is ongoing, with phase III trials underway for two multiple CAR-Ts including idecabtagene vicleucel. A BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy that demonstrated efficacy in triple-class exposed relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients in the KarMMa trial (NCT03361748). It is also the subject of comparison in the KarMMa-RW study. An approved drug used for the treatment of patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) who were previously treated with a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory drug, and an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody. It was compared with ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) in a matching-adjusted indirect comparison study. The study estimated the comparative efficacy of cilta-cel versus ide-cel based on overall response rate (ORR), complete response or better (≥CR) rate, duration of response (DoR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). A bispecific antibody that targets BCMA and has received regulatory approval in the United States for multiple myeloma treatment. A novel chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy targeting B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA), approved by the US FDA for relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) after demonstrating unprecedented results in multicenter trials. It is the first CAR T-cell product approved for myeloma and offers hope for more durable remissions and better quality of life following a single infusion.

nodes.label: Gabapentin
nodes.description: A medication used as an add-on treatment for refractory partial seizures in children with intellectual disability and normal children, and for the adjunctive treatment of partial seizures in patients with epilepsy. It is also considered as an alternative medication in the treatment of Restless legs syndrome (RLS) and used as an antiepileptic drug for the treatment of partial seizures in children. Common adverse effects include somnolence, fainting, ataxia, nystagmus, tremor and headache, but their incidence was low and intensity mild. It is well-tolerated by patients, with the exception of a higher incidence of dizziness in the rapid initiation group. It has been associated with the development of an urticarial rash and irritability in some patients. Skin reactions to gabapentin are considered uncommon, especially compared to other antiepileptic drugs. It is effective in controlling seizures and well-tolerated in children undergoing cancer treatment, with a moderate success rate in seizure control. It has also been used to treat bone pain in bone metastases, specifically neuropathic pain, and to manage overactive bladder in children who do not respond to conventional anticholinergic treatments. It is one of the few drugs registered for the treatment of neuropathic pain and is commonly employed in the treatment of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS), often in combination with L-dopa's sustained release formulation. It has shown promise in improving sleep onset and maintenance in pediatric patients, particularly those with neurodevelopmental disorders. It is a well-known antiepileptic drug used for treating neuropathic pain, along with pregabalin and carbamazepine, and is one of the few drugs registered for this condition. Its active metabolite, gabapentin enacarbil, is used as an anticonvulsant drug off-label to treat refractory insomnia in children.

nodes.label: Bulevirtide (BLV)
nodes.description: A first-in-class HBV-HDV entry inhibitor blocking Na+ -taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTCP), providing very promising efficacy data in Phase II and Phase III trials as well as in preliminary real-life reports. Granted conditional approval by EMA for treatment of compensated CHD at the dose of 2 mg/day by self-administered subcutaneous injections. Evaluated at different doses (2 vs. 10 mg/day) for 24 or 48 weeks, either in monotherapy or in combination with PegIFN. Resulted in 50-83% virological response rates and 45-78% ALT normalization in monotherapy for 24 or 48 weeks. Combination therapy with PegIFN provided synergistic effects. Tolerated well, with only an asymptomatic increase of bile acids as a side effect. A drug that has recently been conditionally approved for the treatment of chronic hepatitis delta (CHD) in Europe. In a single-center study, consecutive patients with HDV-related compensated cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension who started BLV 2 mg/day were enrolled to evaluate its effectiveness and safety. During 48 weeks of BLV monotherapy, HDV RNA declined by 3.1 log IU/ml (p <0.001 vs. baseline), becoming undetectable in 5 patients (23%). A virological response was observed in 14 (78%) patients while a non-response was observed in 2 (11%). ALT decreased to 35 U/L (p <0.001 vs. baseline), normalizing in 83% of patients. A combined response was observed in 67% of patients. Aspartate aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyltransferase levels significantly improved. Concerning liver function parameters, albumin values significantly increased and bilirubin remained stable. LSM significantly improved in patients with virological response, while platelet count was unchanged. None of the patients developed decompensating events or hepatocellular carcinoma. BLV was well tolerated, no patient discontinued treatment and the increase in bile acids was fully asymptomatic. A therapeutic intervention used to treat chronic hepatitis D, specifically a nucleotide analogue that inhibits the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). It is compared to other interventions in the study.

nodes.label: major clinical manifestations
nodes.description: Clinical manifestations that are highly specific for Marfan syndrome, including a combination of four out of eight skeletal manifestations, ectopia lentis, dural ectasia, and dilatation or dissection of the ascending aorta. These criteria are used to confirm the diagnosis of Marfan syndrome in an individual.

nodes.label: Melanocyte
nodes.description: A specialized cell type responsible for producing melanin, involved in skin, hair, and eye pigmentation. Melanocytes originate from the neural crest and migrate to specific target sites during embryonic development. They are regulated by the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), which is a critical regulator of pigment cell development and survival. MITF influences various aspects such as proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, migration, lineage specificity, and differentiation. The canonical Wnt signaling pathway plays a crucial role in melanocyte development and is involved in triggering melanocyte stem cell proliferation. Melanocytes can be generated from human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) in vitro, and their differentiation can be studied using culture supplementation with Wnt3a, SCF, and ET-3. They express markers such as MITF, tyrosinase, SILV, and TYRP1, and contain melanosomes.

nodes.label: Prostate Cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland, often involving lymph node metastasis. It is characterized by high-grade tumors and an increased Gleason score upgrading, and can be managed through various approaches such as active surveillance and nerve-sparing surgery. Prostate cancer can be sporadic, with somatic mutations in genes such as PIK3CA, TP53, EGFR, KIT, KRAS, PTEN, and BRAF. It is the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the USA, with one in every nine men being affected. The most prevalent mutations among patients with prostate cancer are c.1621A>C (rs3822214) in KIT, c.38G>C (rs112445441) in KRAS, and c.733G>A (rs28934575) in TP53 genes. Prostate cancer is also associated with mutations in the KIT gene, presenting in TNM stages II to III, Gleason score ≥ 7, and D'Amico risk. It can include both metastatic and non-metastatic forms, with a specific focus on castration-resistant prostate cancer that has not spread, and is being treated with Darolutamide (NUBEQA™). Prostate cancer increases the risk of Malignant Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC) and often leads to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) if not treated.

nodes.label: Ectopia lentis
nodes.description: A genetically heterogeneous condition characterized by the subluxation of the lens due to the disruption of the zonular fibers. It can occur as an isolated form and is associated with a marked loss in visual acuity and potential ocular complications like cataract, myopia, and retinal detachment. A genetic disorder characterized by the displacement of the lens in the eye, causing various ophthalmic findings such as pupillary abnormality, different types of glaucoma, and progressive hyperopia. It is associated with the p.Arg62Cys mutation of the fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) and was observed in a family with early-onset isolated ectopia lentis. A condition that can either herald underlying systemic conditions or be isolated. It is characterized by a common link in novel genes, particularly the ADAMTS family, which are important in ocular development. The molecular pathogenesis of this condition is being furthered by the expansion in genetics, and the clinical management of it is challenging, especially in addressing surgically induced aphakia in the context of an ectopic capsule. A condition characterized by the displacement of the lens in the eye, often caused genetically and associated with various syndromal disorders like Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria. It can also occur independently (isolated ectopia lentis) due to genetic alterations, most commonly mutations in ADAMTSL4. The management and risk assessment for family members depend on the genetic cause and inheritance pattern.

nodes.label: Social Phobia
nodes.description: A common anxiety disorder characterized by a marked and persistent fear of being observed or evaluated by others in social performance or interaction situations. It is associated with physical, cognitive, and behavioral symptoms such as avoidance. The onset typically occurs in childhood or adolescence, and if left untreated, it can lead to a chronic, unremitting condition with significant functional impairment. Comorbid with other psychiatric disorders like mood disorders, anxiety disorders, and substance abuse/dependence. Despite its prevalence, few people with social phobia seek professional help. A chronic disorder associated with disability and a high relapse rate after short-term therapy, requiring effective treatment continuation for at least 12 months. A specific form of anxiety disorder characterized by intense fear and avoidance of social situations due to concern about being judged or humiliated. It is mentioned in the context of child anxiety disorders and their association with maternal anxiety disorders, specifically for social phobia and separation anxiety disorder. A type of anxiety disorder diagnosed in children aged 8 to 12 years old, with a count of 22 cases in the study. A mental disorder characterized by excessive fear and avoidance of social situations, affecting about 4.5% of the adult general population. It is the most frequent of all anxiety disorders and affects women more frequently than men. Comorbid mental disorders are common, with about half of all individuals with social phobia experiencing at least one such disorder. Adequate treatment is not always received by those affected. A type of phobic disorder characterized by an intense, irrational fear of social situations and interactions. It affects 3.5% of the population in Iceland and is a subset of phobic disorders, which have a lifetime prevalence of 18% in Iceland. A mental health disorder characterized by a fear of social situations, leading to avoidance or enduring them with intense anxiety or distress. It has a high prevalence in the community and tends to have a chronic course. Despite its personal impact, few sufferers seek professional help due to a lack of awareness about the condition among health professionals and the public.

nodes.label: Idiopathic Scoliosis
nodes.description: A multifactorial disorder primarily affecting adolescent girls, characterized by an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine, with unknown genetic causes but with evidence of genetic and environmental influences. It is associated with skeletal length asymmetries and may involve growth conflicts between ribs and vertebrae, leading to deformities. The average age of onset is 10.8 years, and it is often diagnosed based on a Cobb's angle greater than 5 degrees. Pronounced forms of the disease, defined as a curve of at least 11 degrees, can be influenced by a major causal gene, with inheritance described according to a dominant major gene diallele model assuming incomplete sex and age dependent penetrance of genotypes. It is also known as adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS).

nodes.label: Echocardiography
nodes.description: A non-invasive imaging technique used to visualize and evaluate the heart's structure and function, often combined with other imaging modalities such as tissue Doppler imaging, Magnetic Resonance Imaging, and cine CMRI. It is used to assess cardiac function, diastolic function, left ventricular non-compaction, and other cardiovascular manifestations in various conditions, including Barth syndrome, myotonic dystrophy type 2, Marfan syndrome, Noncompaction cardiomyopathy, tafazzin-deficient mice, and patients with Ectopia Lentis. It is also used to measure aortic root diameter, assess mitral valve prolapse and mitral regurgitation, and evaluate cardiac fusion in conjoined twins. Echocardiography is the diagnostic method of choice for isolating Noncompaction cardiomyopathy and is commonly used to study left ventricular structural and functional changes in various patient populations.

nodes.label: Clinical trial
nodes.description: A study or evidence-based approach that evaluates the effectiveness, safety, and impact of various interventions, treatments, or therapies under controlled conditions, often involving human participants. These trials can focus on a wide range of medical conditions, from neurological disorders like Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's disease to infectious diseases like COVID-19 and autoimmune conditions like type 1 diabetes. They may involve the use of new drugs, vaccines, or novel therapeutic approaches, and can compare the results against existing treatments, placebos, or no treatment at all.

nodes.label: Caplacizumab
nodes.description: An anti-von Willebrand factor humanized single-variable-domain immunoglobulin (Nanobody) that inhibits the interaction between ultralarge von Willebrand factor multimers and platelets, used in the treatment of acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (aTTP). Caplacizumab is a bivalent anti-vWF antibody based on camelid single-domain antibodies (sdAbs) or VHHs, also known as nanobodies. It is a potential drug for treating rare blood clotting disorders and may be approved and commercialized in 2018 or shortly thereafter. It is an inhibitor of the glycoprotein-Ib/IX-von Willebrand factor axis, a promising agent under evaluation in large, ideally international, clinical trials for the treatment of autoimmune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and an antiplatelet agent specifically targeting von Willebrand factor.

nodes.label: TFT
nodes.description: A component of the novel nucleoside antitumor agent TAS-102, used to examine its incorporation into tumor- and white blood cell-DNA and its effect on colony formation of mouse bone marrow cells. It is also used to determine its pharmacokinetics and antitumor activity in tumor-bearing nude mice after multiple oral administrations. TFT inhibits proliferations of mouse bone marrow cells and human colorectal carcinoma cells in a dose-dependent manner. The highest tolerable TFT exposure provides the highest antitumor activity, and hematological toxicity may serve as a potential surrogate indicator of TAS-102 efficacy.

nodes.label: Basal Ganglia
nodes.description: A complex brain structure involved in motor control and other functions, consisting of several nuclei including the external globus pallidus (GPe). It is a group of brain regions involved in motor control, reward, and habit formation, which exhibits increased intrinsic inter-regional FC in dancers compared to non-dancers and shows negative correlations with originality and practice intensity in dancers. It includes the putamen and globus pallidus. The basal ganglia is also involved in the integration of information as it is transferred through the brain, with the input from the cerebral cortex being funneled through the striatum to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Injury to the basal ganglia is associated with dyskinetic cerebral palsy and certain behavioral, mood, and cognitive disturbances without motor symptoms.

nodes.label: Major bleeding
nodes.description: A potential side effect that should not be increased when using apixaban compared to warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation who are at increased risk of stroke and for whom warfarin is unsuitable. A potential adverse event associated with anticoagulant therapy. In the ARISTOTLE trial, the beneficial effects of treatment with apixaban were generally maintained across various patient subgroups, and apixaban recipients had a significantly lower risk of major bleeding than warfarin recipients. A risk factor associated with GDF-15 in atrial fibrillation, along with mortality and stroke. Its prognostic value remains consistent despite the presence of N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide and high-sensitivity troponin I. A type of clinical event that occurred in the Apixaban for Reduction in Stroke and Other Thromboembolic Events in Atrial Fibrillation (ARISTOTLE) trial. There were 26 such events in the apixaban group (4.97%/year) and 10 in the warfarin group (1.97%/year) after blinded study drug discontinuation and transition to open-label VKA. A clinical outcome associated with IL-6 beyond clinical risk factors but not in the presence of cardiovascular biomarkers in patients with atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation. A clinical outcome measured in the study, with rates of major bleeding increasing with the number of drug treatments (1.91, 2.46, and 3.88 per 100 patient years for 0-5, 6-8, and ≥9 drugs, respectively). A serious medical event involving excessive bleeding, which can be reduced by the 5 mg twice daily dose of apixaban compared to warfarin in patients with 1 dose-reduction criterion.

nodes.label: Myotubularin
nodes.description: A gene that defines a large family of eukaryotic proteins, initially characterized by the presence of a ten-amino acid consensus sequence related to the active sites of tyrosine phosphatases, dual-specificity protein phosphatases and the lipid phosphatase PTEN. It is mutated in myotubular myopathy and is thought to be primarily a lipid phosphatase, acting on phosphatidylinositol 3-monophosphate, and might be involved in the regulation of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI 3-kinase) pathway and membrane trafficking. A lipid phosphatase with specificity for PtdIns(3)P, mutated in myotubular myopathy and belonging to a family of proteins with significant homology to myotubularin. A cytoplasmic protein that localizes to Rac1-inducible plasma membrane ruffles. It is a phosphatase mutated in X-linked myotubular myopathy, and was shown to dephosphorylate phosphatidylinositol 3-monophosphate (PtdIns3P). It interacts with nuclear transcriptional regulators from the trithorax family. Overexpression of Myotubularin does not affect vesicle trafficking in mammalian cells. Mutation of a key aspartate residue or dominant activation of Rac1 GTPase leads to the recruitment of Myotubularin to specific plasma membrane domains. The recruitment is dependent on the presence of a highly conserved domain named RID. A large disease-associated family of cooperating catalytically active and inactive phosphoinositides phosphatases, encompassing both catalytically active and inactive phosphatases. They dephosphorylate phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns3P) and PtdIns3,5P2, leading to the production of PtdIns and PtdIns5P. These phosphoinositides are signaling molecules involved in vacuolar transport and membrane trafficking. Myotubularins are proposed to be implicated in cellular mechanisms such as endocytosis, and recent observations on their homologues in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans suggest a role in this process. A unique subfamily of protein tyrosine phosphatases that utilize inositol phospholipids as substrates. Contains a subgroup of catalytically inactive proteins that function as adaptors for the active members and play an important regulatory role within the family. A family of phosphoinositide phosphatases that includes several members mutated in neuromuscular diseases or associated with metabolic syndrome, obesity, and cancer. These proteins have been found to regulate various cellular processes such as endocytosis, membrane trafficking, cell proliferation and differentiation, autophagy, cytokinesis, and cytoskeletal and cell junction dynamics. A lipid phosphatase belonging to a large family of conserved enzymes, involved in muscle function. It interacts with catalytically inactive myotubularin-related protein 12 (MTMR12) and its deficiency leads to reduced levels of myotubularin protein in zebrafish and mammalian C2C12 cells. Mutations within the myotubularin interaction domain disrupt binding to MTMR12 in cell culture.

nodes.label: BMI-1
nodes.description: A gene or protein involved in the inverse correlation with the INK4 locus proteins expression (p16/p14ARF), suggesting a possible role in lung carcinogenesis when misregulated. A lymphoid oncogene whose product functions as a transcriptional repressor of the INK4A-ARF tumor suppressor locus. Bmi-1-deficient hematopoietic progenitors are resistant to transformation by E2a-Pbx1; however, the requirement for Bmi-1 is alleviated in cells deficient for both Bmi-1 and INK4A-ARF. The product of BMI-1 functions as a transcriptional repressor. A core protein of the Polycomb-complexes, encoded by a PcG gene. It is expressed in Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg (H/RS) cells and Hodgkin's lymphoma-derived cell lines, and is associated with the maintenance of cell identity and gene silencing patterns. In normal mature B cells, HPC1 expression is not found, suggesting a unique PcG expression profile in H/RS cells. In contrast to Bmi-1 transgenic mice, 27 of 52 BMI-1POS cases of HL reveal strong nuclear expression of p16INK4a. A transcriptional repressor of the Ink4a/Arf locus encoding p16(ink4a) and p14(Arf). Increased nuclear BMI-1 expression was detectable in 41 of 64 (64%) primary melanomas, 117 of 165 melanoma metastases (71%) and 15 of 53 (28%) melanoma cell lines. BMI-1 functions as a transcriptional repressor of the Ink4a/Arf locus. A polycomb factor protein that is expressed in all histologic types of diffuse gliomas and is found to be a novel independent prognostic marker in oligodendroglial tumours. It has a significant correlation with poor survival in World Health Organization grades II-III oligodendrogliomas and oligoastrocytomas. The median survival of patients grouped by low, intermediate or high frequency of BMI-1 immunoreactive tumour cells is 191 months, 151 months and 68 months, respectively. This association is also significant in the Cox multivariate regression model. A gene that is a member of the mammalian Polycomb group family and is involved in causing cell-cycle arrest and derepressing p16INK4a, HOXA9 and HOXC13 mRNA expression in HeLa cells. Overexpression of BMI-1 is associated with human malignancies.

nodes.label: Phthiriasis palpebrarum
nodes.description: A rare cause of blepharoconjunctivitis, often neglected due to its rarity, characterized by lice infestation of the palpabrae, which may present as blepharoconjunctivitis. It is usually seen in lower socioeconomic groups and spreads through sexual contacts, direct contact with linen or clothing. Mechanical removal proved to be effective in treating the disease and preventing its recurrence. It may mimic lid eczema and blepharitis, leading to misdiagnosis. A sexually transmitted disease characterized by chronic conjunctivitis, manifested by gradual pruritus, painless ocular hyperaemia, nasal pterygium, conjunctival hyperaemia, oedema, mild hypertrophy of the palpebral margin, and the presence of numerous creamy oval structures approximately 1 mm in diameter localised in the middle area of the lashes, bloody crusts and a semitransparent deposit in the superior palpebral margin. It can also be misdiagnosed as allergic blepharoconjunctivitis and may represent sexual abuse, especially in children.

nodes.label: Aedes aegypti
nodes.description: A species of mosquito that primarily transmits the Zika virus, dengue virus, and chikungunya virus. It is a primary vector for these diseases and is known for its high vector competence for the imported Zika virus. Aedes aegypti is a main vector for the transmission of Zika and chikungunya viruses, with three evaluated colonies: AeCamp (field), RecL (laboratory), and CqSLab. Its distribution is expected to expand with climate change, potentially leading to a new pandemic of Zika. It is abundant along the U.S.-Mexico border and its ecological behavior in temperate/subtropical desert regions is not well understood. The species is known for its higher competence compared to Ae. albopictus and is used as a model organism in studies involving gut symbiont-derived sphingosine and ZIKV/DENV infection. Aedes aegypti is a species of mosquito that belongs to the family Culicidae, specifically belonging to the genus Aedes and is responsible for transmitting Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika viruses in urban areas. Its population dynamics depend on climate variables such as temperature and rainfall.

nodes.label: Blood samples
nodes.description: Samples collected from individuals with Barth syndrome (BTHS) and healthy controls for the purpose of studying alternative splice variants of TAZ mRNA. The samples were collected, shipped, and processed using a stabilizing medium to ensure consistent expression of various genes. Samples collected from all family members in the study for genomic DNA isolation and mutation analysis of the TYR gene. Samples of blood obtained from patients with STEMI at baseline (0 hour), 6, 24, and 96 hours post PCI for the purpose of measuring cardiovascular and inflammatory biomarkers using multiplex proximity extension assays. Samples collected from patients both before and after microwave ablation (MWA) at 24 h, 72 h, and 1 month intervals to determine the distributions of T-cell subsets including Th17 cells, regulatory Treg-cells, CD4+ T-cells, CD8+ T-cells, and CD3+ T-cells using flow cytometry.

nodes.label: Natriuretic peptide family
nodes.description: A group of hormones produced by cardiomyocytes, including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP).
