They possess similar gene structures and protective effects on cardiovascular physiology such as anti-hypertrophy, anti-fibrosis, myocardial relaxation and blood pressure regulation. The corresponding natriuretic peptide receptors A, B and C mediate multiple effects of natriuretic peptides to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis. Natriuretic peptide receptor-A preferentially binds ANP and BNP, while natriuretic peptide receptor-B is more selective for C-type natriuretic peptides. Natriuretic peptide receptor-C (NPR-C) clears natriuretic peptides from the circulation through receptor-mediated internalization and degradation. A group of three related molecules, including atrial natriuretic peptide, brain natriuretic peptide, and C-type natriuretic peptide, which have similar effects such as causing natriuresis, vasodilation, and suppressing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. C-type natriuretic peptide primarily affects the vasculature by eliciting vasodilation and inhibiting vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation. A family of biological processes involving hormones and neuropeptides, including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), and C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP). These peptides have receptors with at least three subtypes: A-type (GC-A), B-type (GC-B), and C-type (clearance). ANP and BNP are primarily synthesized and secreted by the atria and ventricles, respectively, while CNP is a neuropeptide synthesized by the brain. A- and B-type receptors contain particulate guanylate cyclase and mediate biological functions via cyclic GMP as a second messenger, while C-type receptors are involved in the clearance and metabolism of natriuretic peptides.

nodes.label: Apoptosis
nodes.description: A biological process involving programmed cell death, regulated by mitochondria and characterized by the release of proteins from mitochondria in response to cell stress stimuli. It is a crucial process in maintaining cellular homeostasis and eliminating damaged or unnecessary cells. Apoptosis can be induced by various factors, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and certain chemical compounds. It is also associated with several diseases and pathological conditions, such as neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. The process is regulated by signaling through apoptotic proteins within the Bcl-2 protein family and is influenced by mitochondrial bioenergetic function.

nodes.label: Placebo
nodes.description: A dummy substance or treatment used as a control in various clinical trials and studies, often involving no active ingredients or a substitute with equivalent gastrointestinal risk and adverse event profiles. It is used to compare the effects of new treatments, medications, or interventions, and can be administered in different ways, such as subcutaneously, intravenously, or orally. Placebos can also be used to establish a baseline for comparison with other substances or treatments, such as dexfenfluramine, psilocybin, or erenumab. In some cases, placebos may lead to unexpected results, such as a higher occurrence of Grade 2 rash compared to the tetracycline group or a greater reduction in pain and function improvement compared to treatment groups.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial disease
nodes.description: Mitochondrial disease is a disorder that can result from the presence of heteroplasmy, specifically when it involves combinations of wild-type variants. It can be transmitted through assisted reproduction techniques such as cytoplasmic transfer (CT) and nuclear transfer (NT). A group of genetic disorders characterized by defects in either mitochondrial DNA or nuclear mitochondrial genes, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction. Symptoms can affect a single organ or tissue, or involve multiple systems. There is no cure for the vast majority of mitochondrial disease patients, and a genetic diagnosis is crucial for genetic counselling, recurrence risk calculation, and clinical management. A type of disease that can be detected and mitigated early through the use of an ensemble approach with minimal intervention, as suggested by the text.

nodes.label: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
nodes.description: A non-invasive imaging technique used to visualize internal structures of the body, particularly useful for detecting abnormalities in the brain and spinal cord. MRI is used in various diagnostic procedures, such as evaluating muscle involvement in patients with autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, assessing the presence of enlarged vestibular aqueduct (EVA), confirming the diagnosis of left ventricular non-compaction in the patient with myotonic dystrophy type 2, and identifying paramagnetic substances in the basal ganglia indicating hepatic encephalopathy. It is also used to evaluate the lumen and wall of the aorta, determine the dural sac ratio (DSR) in pediatric patients with Marfan syndrome, and visualize the brain and spinal cord in patients with cerebellar ataxia, Landau-Kleffner syndrome, and gliomas. MRI can help confirm the presence of transverse myelitis in patients following dinutuximab treatment and reveal irregular mixed solid and cystic lesions in the brainstem suggesting brain metastases. Additionally, MRI is used to measure cardiac morphology and detect RV hypertrophy in mice treated with IL-18BP or vehicle and to acquire biomarkers of leg muscles in individuals with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

nodes.label: Tyrosinase
nodes.description: An enzyme involved in the melanin biosynthetic pathway, produced by the tyrosinase gene (TYR) and associated with oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (OCA1). It is a copper-containing enzyme responsible for catalyzing the rate-limiting step in melanin biosynthesis, specifically the hydroxylation of tyrosine to dopaquinone. Mutations in the tyrosinase gene lead to Tyrosinase-related oculocutaneous albinism (OCA1) and a total lack of melanin biosynthesis. It is a key enzyme in melanin synthesis, involved in the processing and sorting of melanogenic proteins and is encoded by the human homologue of the mouse underwhite (uw) gene. Tyrosinase activity is reduced in uw-mutant melanocytes compared to wild-type melanocytes. It is also involved in the differentiation-specific process of pigmentation, regulated by Mitf in melanoblasts and melanocytes. Tyrosinase is a pigment-producing enzyme whose gene is responsible for type IA oculocutaneous albinism and mutations in this gene lead to a severe disease type affecting melanin synthesis.

nodes.label: Systematic Review
nodes.description: A comprehensive evaluation of the benefits and risks of medications and therapies used to prevent fractures in postmenopausal women and men with low bone density (osteopenia) or osteoporosis, including factors that may affect adherence to treatment and monitoring for the identification of those most likely to benefit from treatment. The review was conducted by AHRQ in 2007 and updated in March 2012. A research methodology used to identify, evaluate, and synthesize the available evidence on the vector competence of various mosquito species for Zika Virus. The review was conducted until 15th March 2022, involving searches in multiple databases and assessment of article quality using predefined criteria.

nodes.label: levodopa
nodes.description: A drug used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Its peripheral metabolism is blocked by COMT inhibitors, which increases its plasma half-life and enhances its brain availability. It is administered as an adjunctive agent with tolcapone and entacapone. Motor fluctuations in PD patients can be managed by increasing 'on' time and reducing 'off' time. In patients with more advanced disease, similar benefits are provided, but patients may experience less overall benefit and a greater likelihood of developing dopaminergic adverse events. Adverse events can usually be controlled by levodopa dose adjustments. A drug used in combination with dopa decarboxylase inhibitor for the treatment of Parkinson's disease. It was administered with entacapone in a post-marketing surveillance study to assess patients' responses in a real clinical practice setting. The average daily dose of levodopa was reduced from 510 to 453 mg after the initiation of entacapone treatment. There was a decrease in the mean duration of daily 'off' time from 3.0 to 1.3 h per day during the treatment period. The use of adjunct dopamine agonists decreased from 67 to 59%. The percentage of patients who rated their quality of life as 'very good' or 'good' increased from 12.1 to 51.7% at study end. The most efficacious agent for the treatment of motor features of Parkinson's disease. It has a short half-life, leading to pulsatile stimulation of striatal dopamine receptors and resulting in wearing off, motor fluctuations, and dyskinesias when used chronically. It is often administered with a dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (DDCI) such as carbidopa or benserazide to reduce peripheral conversion to dopamine and increase central bioavailability. It is a precursor to dopamine that is converted to dopamine in the brain via catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT). When administered with a DDCI, its main route of peripheral metabolism is via COMT. A COMT inhibitor can be added to further extend its peripheral half-life and increase central bioavailability.

nodes.label: PARP inhibitors
nodes.description: A class of drugs under clinical development as anticancer therapies, particularly in tumors with DNA repair deficits and in combination with DNA-damaging agents. They potentiate the cytotoxicity of DNA alkylating agents and have been shown to trap PARP1 at DNA single-strand breaks during base excision repair. PARP inhibitors are a class of drugs that block the repair of single-strand breaks, leading to double-strand breaks during DNA replication. They elicit synthetic lethality in cancer with BRCA1/2 loss-of-function mutations that hamper homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks. A class of drugs used to investigate the therapeutic potential of PARP1 inhibition in preclinical models of pediatric high-grade astrocytomas (pHGA) and diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPG). They include veliparib, olaparib, and niraparib. Research tools used in cancer treatment, with the exception of a few tankyrase inhibitors, that mimic the nicotinamide moiety in NAD(+) and block the nicotinamide binding pocket. A class of drugs that target the enzyme PARP and selectively kill HRD cells through a process known as tumor-selective synthetic lethality. They are generally well tolerated and are used as maintenance therapy in Europe and as treatment for advanced recurrent disease in the United States. A type of drug that has been subject to pre-clinical publications and regulatory approval processes, with the first approval occurring ten years before the statement was made. The development and approval of these drugs are expected to continue to be productive in the subsequent decade. A class of targeted therapies approved by the FDA for the management of mTNBC with germline BRCA mutations. They include olaparib (Lynparza) and talazoparib (Talzenna).

nodes.label: Nausea
nodes.description: A common gastrointestinal symptom characterized by an unpleasant feeling in the stomach, often accompanied by the urge to vomit. It can be a side effect of various treatments, such as metformin, dupilumab, and monoclonal antibodies targeting the CGRP pathway, and can also occur as a result of certain medical conditions or injuries. Nausea can range from mild to severe and may be classified into different grades based on its severity. It is a common adverse event observed in clinical trials and can sometimes lead to discontinuation of treatment.

nodes.label: Bupropion
nodes.description: A dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake antagonist present in the Contrave combination therapy. It is used to stimulate central melanocortin pathways, resulting in increased energy expenditure and reduced appetite. A long-acting version of bupropion is a component of the Contrave compound. It is a CNS modulator and a selective central 5-hydroxytryptamine 2C serotonin receptor agonist. A component of the investigational fixed-dose combination drug Contrave, used in conjunction with naltrexone for the treatment of obesity in Phase III clinical trials. A component of the drug combination Contrave, administered at 40 mg/kg/day. It affects hippocampal BDNF mRNA expression and alters D2R mRNA in the caudate-putamen when present in the drug combination. A medication used for major depressive disorder (Wellbutrin®), smoking cessation (Zyban®), and weight loss (in combination with naltrexone ER; Contrave®). It can exacerbate psoriasis, particularly in the United States.

nodes.label: Ropinirole
nodes.description: A newer, non-ergoline dopamine agonist used in the treatment of early Parkinson's disease as a monotherapy. It is effective in delaying the onset of levodopa-induced motor fluctuations and is considered an ideal initial symptomatic medication. A dopaminergic agent used in the treatment of idiopathic Restless Legs Syndrome, periodic limb movement disorder, and Parkinson's disease. It is known as adartrel in the United Kingdom and is recommended as a first-line treatment for restless legs syndrome based on randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials. It is effective in reducing symptoms of restless legs syndrome in the general population and has no serious or common side effects that would limit its use significantly. Rebound and augmentation problems are relatively rarely seen with ropinirole, although properly designed comparative trials are still needed to address this question. It is a dopamine receptor agonist and a treatment for Restless Legs Syndrome licensed in France, often considered as one of the agents of choice for managing its symptoms. It is also used in combination with maintaining a high serum ferritin level to prevent the development of augmentation.

nodes.label: hyperphosphorylation
nodes.description: A process where tau proteins become excessively phosphorylated, leading to their dislodgement from the microtubule surface, potential compromise of axonal integrity, and the accumulation of toxic tau peptides. A process involving the addition of multiple phosphate groups to tau protein, leading to its aggregation into insoluble paired-helical filaments (PHFs) and decreased affinity for microtubules in Alzheimer's disease. A process where tau is excessively phosphorylated, leading to the disruption of microtubules and the formation of paired helical filaments and straight filaments. This process is more pronounced in Alzheimer disease brain tau compared to normal adult brain tau. A process where tau protein is excessively phosphorylated, leading to diminished microtubule-binding capacity, destabilization of microtubules, and enhancement of the formation of paired helical filaments. It is associated with Alzheimer's disease and fetal development. The presence of hyperphosphorylation is not obligatory for the formation of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease.

nodes.label: Oculocutaneous albinism
nodes.description: A group of genetic disorders affecting approximately 1/20,000 people worldwide, characterized by generalized hypopigmentation. It is caused by mutations in genes involved in melanin synthesis, with the most common forms being OCA1 and OCA2, and less common forms including OCA3 and OCA4. These mutations lead to reduced or absent pigmentation in the skin, hair, and eyes, and can result in vision loss. The disease is autosomal recessive and can be associated with common developmental abnormalities of the eye.

nodes.label: Chordoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that serves as the subject of the research described in the text. It is noted that there are no identifiable biomarkers capable of predicting prognosis, and recent research suggests that signal transducers and activators of transcription (Stat3) may be an important prognostic marker in some cancers. The text also mentions the evaluation of Stat3 expression in chordoma tissue microarray and the inhibition of Stat3 signaling cascade in chordoma cell lines using SD-1029. A rare type of malignant bone tumor that arises from the remnants of the notochord. It is a disease that is being studied for potential treatment methods, including differentiation therapy using various chemotherapeutic agents and differentiating agents. A type of cancerous tumor that occurs in the bones of the skull and spine. A rare, slow growing malignant tumor arising from remnants of the fetal notochord. It is characterized by frequent recurrence due to the anatomy of the tumor location and violation of the tumor margins at the initial surgery. There are no effective drugs available for patients with chordoma.

nodes.label: Skin rash
nodes.description: A common adverse reaction experienced by patients receiving erlotinib and other EGFR inhibitors, characterized by skin irritation. It can lead to drug discontinuation or dose reduction, impair quality of life, and put patients at risk of superinfection. Symptoms are diverse, variable, and intermittent, making it difficult to manage with standard treatments. Medical treatment may improve symptoms slowly, and patients may need additional visits to the doctor's office for skin management. A skin symptom that occurs as a side effect of erlotinib treatment in advanced non-small cell lung cancer patients, often leading to dose reduction or drug withdrawal. Isotretinoin and clindamycin show promise in treating this symptom without causing additional adverse events. A side effect of drugs that inhibit epithelial growth factor receptor (EGFR), appearing and worsening with increased severity. It is associated with improved survival rates, especially in patients receiving minocycline. A skin condition caused by EGFR-TKI, particularly when EGFR is highly expressed in the skin. It can be mitigated and eventually disappear after using Pien Tze Huang Unguentum Compositum. Commonly affects the face, head, and back. Antibiotics and corticosteroids are usually used to treat the associated skin rash, but they have prominent side effects over long-time use. An adverse event associated with the use of epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. Minocycline was often administered prophylactically or therapeutically to manage this symptom. In a single-center retrospective analysis, the administration of minocycline for 30 days or longer correlated with good progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) with first-line EGFR-TKIs.

nodes.label: MLL1
nodes.description: A histone methyltransferase involved in the epigenetic maintenance of transcriptional memory and the pathogenesis of human leukemias. It localizes with RNA polymerase II to the 5' end of actively transcribed genes and occupies an extensive domain within a transcriptionally active region of the HoxA cluster. It serves as a start site-specific global transcriptional regulator and participates in larger chromatin domains at the Hox genes. It forms a stable complex with MOF and has a C-terminal domain that interacts with MOF. MLL1 mediates histone methyltransferase activity, specifically for mono-, di-, and trimethylation of H3 K4. It is also involved in transcription activation on a chromatin template in vitro and on an endogenous target gene, Hox a9, in vivo. An H3K4 histone methyltransferase complex that is recruited by p52 on the MMP9 promoter and is associated with Hut-78 in native chromatin-enriched extracts. Its activity on the MMP9 promoter is impaired in p52-depleted HUT-78 cells. A protein involved in the recruitment to the Ink4a/Arf locus and the increase in H3K4 trimethylation during beta-cell regeneration. A histone methyltransferase specific for H3K4 that is required for MDR1 promoter methylation, as knockdown of MLL1 results in a decrease in MDR1 expression. Its overexpression leads to increased MDR1 expression, and its leukemogenic rearrangement, MLL-AF4, is a potential target for circumvention of tumor multidrug resistance. A mammalian homolog of Drosophila trithorax, an H3K4-specific methyltransferase implicated in transcriptional control. Essential for circadian transcription and cyclic H3K4 trimethylation. Forms a complex with CLOCK-BMAL1 and contributes to its rhythmic recruitment to circadian promoters and H3 acetylation. Does not interact with CLOCKΔ19, explaining the dominant negative phenotype of this mutation. A protein containing a SET domain that is part of the core complex of mammalian MLL/SET1 complexes. It has a methyltransferase activity that is stimulated by the Ash2L/RbBP5 heterodimer through coordinated substrate interactions with the MLL1 SET domain. Mutations in the MLL1 SET domain that fail to support overall H3 K4 methylation also compromise SAM binding by Ash2L. The MLL1 SET domain makes direct contacts with the substrates and contributes to the formation of a joint catalytic center with the Ash2L/RbBP5 heterodimer. A histone methyltransferase that interacts with cholecystokinin (Cck) and is necessary for its transcription. A lack of interaction between Cck and MLL1 results in decreased histone H3K4me3 and gene transcription, an effect reversed by lithium.

nodes.label: Apert syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by craniosynostosis, syndactyly, and other congenital anomalies affecting the head and limbs, posing significant challenges for pediatric hand surgeons in reconstructive surgery. It is caused by dominantly acting, allelic mutations of the FGFR2 gene, specifically the Ser252Phe mutation, and can lead to noteworthy abnormalities in vascular anatomy. The syndrome affects both the distal limb bud and craniofacial skeleton, causing endochondral bone growth center malformation and malfunction, as well as ectopic cartilage ossification in soft tissues.

nodes.label: Arabidopsis thaliana
nodes.description: A species of plant used as a representative set for testing the spliced alignment method, consisting of 50 known genes. It is an eukaryote with genomic DNA and protein sequences that can be aligned using the spliced alignment method. A seed plant species used for comparison with Physcomitrella patens. It has an average G/C content of 44% in its CDS and smaller average introns compared to Physcomitrella. It has been used for training support vector machine tools for splice site prediction. A plant species used in genetic research, specifically in the study of natural strains and their nuclear genomes. It has accessions such as Col-0, Bur-0, and Tsu-1, which are examined for sequence variations and polymorphisms. A species of Arabidopsis, a type of plant, used in the study of the CAF1 family and their roles in mediating environmental stress responses. A plant species used in the study to identify nucleoporins, specifically in its nuclear pore complex (NPC). The study involved using an interactive proteomic approach with GFP-tagged nucleoporins and performing subcellular localization analyses. A plant species used in scientific research, specifically for studying the impacts of high ATP supply from chloroplasts and mitochondria on leaf metabolism. It has two organelles, chloroplasts and mitochondria, which are the major ATP producing organelles in plant leaves. The study involves overexpressing Arabidopsis thaliana purple acid phosphatase 2 (AtPAP2) to investigate the effects on plant growth, flowering, seed yield, and biomass at maturity.

nodes.label: Minocycline
nodes.description: An oral tetracycline antibiotic used as a treatment and preventive measure for EGFR inhibitor-induced skin rash. It also has additional anticancer properties like poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition. A second-generation tetracycline antibiotic with a highly lipophilic nature, showing promising results in experimental neurology. Clinically safe and effective as an adjunct to antipsychotic medications. Also used as the tetracycline of choice for multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A medication used in the treatment of mild to moderate rosacea, administered at a dose of 100 mg/day. It has shown comparable efficacy to low-dose isotretinoin for mild to moderate rosacea. A type of oral tetracycline used for the treatment of SSTIs in adult outpatients, known for its common mechanisms of resistance, susceptibility profiles, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. A drug often administered prophylactically or therapeutically to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients receiving epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) for skin rash as an adverse event. It has been found to influence good treatment efficacy with first-line EGFR-TKIs independently of skin rash. In a single-center retrospective analysis, the administration of minocycline for 30 days or longer correlated with good progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) with first-line EGFR-TKIs. A prophylactic medication administered to patients with NSCLC harboring EGFR-activating mutations to manage skin toxicities induced by dacomitinib. More than 90% of patients were perfectly compliant with its administration.

nodes.label: Landau-Kleffner Syndrome
nodes.description: A rare childhood disorder involving seizures and acquired aphasia. Anticonvulsants or the passage of time may control the seizures, but speech recovery is variable, and the aphasia may persist. A type of epilepsy syndrome characterized by progressive neuropsychological impairment related to the appearance of paroxysmal electroencephalograph (EEG) activity. It shares a common pathophysiologic mechanism with continuous spike-wave of sleep (CSWS), acquired epileptic opercular syndrome (AEOS), and benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (BECTS), differing in age of onset, area of primary epileptogenicity, and severity of clinical presentation. A rare childhood disorder characterized by acquired aphasia and epileptiform EEG abnormalities. Common symptoms include hyperactivity, attention problems, and coexisting symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs). Different treatments have been used with varying rates of success, and the effects of antiepileptic drug treatment on acquisition of language have been inconsistent. The literature does not include any reports on the effect of antiepileptic drug treatment on ASD symptoms in patients with LKS. Herein we report a boy with LKS whose ASD symptoms markedly improved in response to antiepileptic treatment. A rare syndrome that typically presents in early childhood with language regression and seizures. It was formerly known as acquired epileptic aphasia. A case report describes a 7-year-old boy who presented with aggressive behavior, difficulty in maintaining posture, and language regression. The diagnosis was confirmed through EEG showing abnormal findings associated with generalized seizure discharge during sleep with more spikes being noted in bilateral frontal and temporal regions. Treatment involved anticonvulsants and steroids, and the patient showed improvement in maintaining posture, walking independently, and linguistic functions.

nodes.label: Wernicke's encephalopathy
nodes.description: A potentially fatal neurological disorder characterized by mental status changes, ocular signs, and ataxia, often associated with vitamin-B1 or thiamine deficiency. It can be caused by various underlying disorders, including malignancy, and may lead to complications such as death from infection. Early identification can be challenging, but thiamine therapy is warranted if any component of the Wernicke's encephalopathy triad is present in an appropriate clinical setting. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation and may include laboratory tests and imaging studies, with prompt treatment typically involving thiamine supplementation.

nodes.label: Chronic Granulomatous Disease
nodes.description: A symptomatic phagocytic defect caused by mutations in genes encoding protein subunits of the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase complex, characterized by a defective intracellular killing of phagocytosed organisms due to a defective oxidative burst in the neutrophils and macrophages. It is inherited in either X-linked recessive or autosomal recessive pattern and is associated with infections by Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species. Common problems in children with CGD include suppurative lymphadenitis, cutaneous abscesses, pneumonia, and diarrhea. A small percentage of children develop autoimmune manifestations such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, colitis, and autoimmune hepatitis, which warrant immunosuppression. X-linked carriers of CGD are at an increased risk of developing autoimmune diseases. Screening tests for CGD include nitroblue-tetrazolium dye reduction test and dihydro-rhodamine assay by flow cytometry. Treatment options include long-term antibiotic and antifungal prophylaxis, hematopoietic stem cell transplant for severe forms, and debatable role of regular interferon-γ injections. Gene therapy is under trial.

nodes.label: Tasimelteon
nodes.description: A melatonin agonist developed by Vanda Pharmaceuticals Inc under license from Bristol-Myers Squibb Co, used for the treatment of insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep disorders. It phase-shifts circadian rhythms, promotes sleep, reduces sleep onset latency, and resets the circadian melatonin rhythm. It has been claimed to be useful in treating depression, particularly those related to circadian dysfunction, and may alleviate sleep problems in depressed patients. It is well-tolerated, does not induce impairment of next-day functioning or dependence, and is considered safe in short-term treatment, although long-term safety requires further evaluation. A new chrono-hypnotic agent that selectively binds to melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors, used for its hypnotic effects. The most advanced drug candidate under clinical evaluation, classified as a high-affinity nonselective MT1/MT2 agonist. An orally bioavailable agonist of the melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors, approved in the US for the treatment of non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder. It is the first US FDA-approved medication for this orphan indication and works by promoting circadian readjustment. A melatonin receptor agonist used for the treatment of insomnia, depression, and circadian rhythms sleep-wake disorders. A new melatonin 1 and melatonin 2 agonist used to improve sleep in blind patients with non-24 sleep-wake syndrome, resetting their circadian sleep-wake clocks. A selective and unique receptor binding profile, Tasimelteon is a potent Dual Melatonin Receptor Agonist (DMRA) with 2.1-4.4 times greater affinity for the MT2 receptor believed to mediate circadian rhythm phase-shifting compared to the MT1 receptor. It has no appreciable affinity for more than 160 other pharmacologically relevant receptors and several enzymes.

nodes.label: Coxiella burnetii
nodes.description: A ubiquitous intracellular bacterium infecting humans and a variety of animals, causing Q fever. It is a pathogen that may be misidentified due to the presence of many Coxiella-like bacteria in ticks. A bacterium responsible for causing Q fever, detected in camels (Camelus dromedarius) and ixodid ticks from Algeria. It is characterized by its ability to infect various mammals, arthropods, and humans, and is used for molecular characterization and detection through serological and molecular assays. An intracellular bacterium that causes Q fever. It has been misidentified as an endosymbiont of ticks, leading to questions about the role of ticks in the transmission of Q fever. An avirulent strain of this bacterium was used in the study to evaluate the vector competence of the African soft tick Ornithodoros moubata.

nodes.label: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)
nodes.description: A preventive measure for HIV that can effectively reduce the spreading of HIV in high-risk populations. It is safe and can prevent high-risk people from HIV infection. The recommended PrEP regimen is daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine combination, and TDF alone can be considered as an alternative regimen for IDUs and heterosexually active adults. It provides a high level of protection against HIV and is even more effective when combined with condoms, ART and other prevention methods. A preventive measure used to reduce the risk of acquiring HIV. It involves taking antiretroviral drugs before potential exposure to the virus. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate combined with emtricitabine is a highly effective oral PrEP agent. A promising biomedical HIV prevention modality involving the daily coformulation of emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. It has not yet been shown to be efficacious in the transgender population due to data limitations. A therapeutic intervention involving the use of emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide or emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV prevention. Evaluated in the DISCOVER trial for its efficacy and safety.

nodes.label: Molluscum contagiosum virus
nodes.description: A common, human poxvirus that causes benign epidermal tumors mainly in children and young adults, and being a common pathogen in immunocompromised individuals. It belongs to the Poxviridae family and encodes various proteins that interfere with cell signaling pathways leading to the activation of NF-κB, a transcription factor crucial for regulation of the immune response, the cell cycle and apoptosis. It is the only member of the Molluscipoxvirus genus and encodes a probable type I topoisomerase enzyme. It can cause localized papules in healthy persons and lead to disseminated infection in immunocompromised patients, and may be present in the blood of severely immunocompromised individuals due to viremia. It infects the basal and suprabasal layers of human epidermis, leading to the formation of phagocytic vacuoles in the basal region that do not fuse with other virus-containing vacuoles or lysosomes. The virus undergoes uncoating stages before ejecting its core into the cytoplasm, often near or associated with centriolar structures, which may interfere with mitosis and involve the excision of gap junction elements.

nodes.label: California
nodes.description: A state in the United States where the study was conducted. A three-year period (1999-2001) overlapping the most recent US census was used for the study. Death certificates were geocoded to the smallest census area available (block group) in California. A state in the United States of America, where Stanford is located. A state located in the western United States where the study was conducted. The study involved collecting adult and nymphal Ixodes pacificus ticks from 24 of 48 California counties over a 13 year period. The risk of exposure to B. burgdorferi sl and B. miyamotoi from adult I. pacificus tick bites is similar in California. The highest risk for both species is found in north and central coastal California and the Sierra Nevada foothill region, and the lowest risk is in southern California. Tick-bite avoidance measures should be implemented in all regions of California.

nodes.label: Christianson syndrome
nodes.description: An X-linked mental retardation syndrome characterized by microcephaly, impaired ocular movement, severe global developmental delay, hypotonia which progresses to spasticity, and early onset seizures of variable types. A new autism-related disorder caused by mutations in the NHE6 protein. A syndromic form of X-linked intellectual disability characterized by microcephaly, severe global developmental delay, autistic behavior, early onset seizures and ataxia. A neurogenetic disorder characterized by nonverbal communication, intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, autism, Angelman syndrome, eye movement abnormalities, postnatal microcephaly, magnetic resonance imaging evidence of cerebellar atrophy, regression, and various medical and behavioral symptoms. It is caused by mutations in the X-linked Na(+)/H(+) exchanger 6 (NHE6) gene.

nodes.label: PTEN (MMAC1)
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 10q23.3. Mutated in approximately 30% of primary (de novo) glioblastomas but rarely in secondary glioblastomas that progressed from low-grade or anaplastic astrocytomas. Mutations were not detected in the analyzed glioblastoma foci, but LOH was observed at one or two flanking markers in six out of eight foci. A tumor suppressor gene located at 10q23.3, which is mutated in multiple malignant tumors including glioblastomas and atypical and anaplastic meningiomas. It is analyzed for loss on 10q, deletion, mutation, and expression. PTEN mutations were detected in 9 of 36 glioblastomas (25%) and complete loss of wild-type PTEN was observed in 7 of these tumors. Although loss of 10q was detected in 14 of the 34 meningiomas investigated, none of these tumors showed evidence of PTEN mutations or homozygous gene deletions. PTEN (MMAC1) is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 10q23. It is mutated in approximately 30% of glioblastomas (WHO Grade IV), particularly in primary glioblastomas. Loss of PTEN function is the most common alteration in primary glioblastomas after overexpression/amplification of the EGF receptor. The gene is involved in several loci associated with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) on chromosome 10. Mutations in PTEN were found in 9 out of 28 (32%) primary glioblastomas and 1 out of 25 (4%) secondary glioblastomas. One primary glioblastoma showed a homozygous PTEN deletion.

nodes.label: NOTCH3 gene
nodes.description: A gene responsible for mutations leading to CADASIL, a genetic disorder causing widespread white-matter lesions, lacunar infarctions, migraine with aura, ischemic strokes, cognitive impairment, and mood disturbances. It contains 34 epidermal growth factor-like repeats in its extracellular domain and has been analyzed in a large group of patients with leukoencephalopathy, revealing several nucleotide alterations, including 20 different mutations, 22 polymorphisms, and 8 genetic variants of unknown pathological significance. The gene has 23 exons, with a cluster of mutations originally reported around exons 3 and 4. Pathogenetic mutations have been identified in exons 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 14, 19, 20, and 22, while no mutations have been found in exons 6 and 8. The entire EGF-like domains region of the gene has been screened for molecular diagnosis of CADASIL. NOTCH3 gene mutations are detected in CADASIL patients, and its analysis is crucial for molecular diagnosis.

nodes.label: SerH3
nodes.description: One of the genes encoding variants of the immobilization antigen (i-ag) at the SerH locus in Tetrahymena thermophila. It is compared with other SerH genes such as SerH1, SerH4, SerH5, and SerH6 in terms of sequences and expression. A gene from Tetrahymena thermophila that encodes a temperature-regulated surface antigen. The DNA sequences of a cDNA clone and the macronuclear genomic fragment corresponding to the functional copy of the SerH3 surface antigen gene were determined. The predicted polypeptide encoded by the SerH3 gene has a molecular mass of 44,415 daltons; one-third of its 439 residues are either cysteine, serine, or threonine. The central half of the polypeptide consists of three homologous domains in tandem array. A temperature-specific surface protein in Tetrahymena thermophila, whose mRNA stability is controlled primarily by a temperature-dependent change. The mRNA of SerH3 is degraded rapidly when cells grown at 30 degrees C are shifted to 40 degrees C, requiring a one-time serine/threonine phosphorylation event at the temperature shift. A regulatory protein involved in rapid SerH3 mRNA decay must be newly and continuously synthesized following the temperature shift. A gene whose mRNA stability is regulated by the product of the RseB locus.

nodes.label: DMD gene
nodes.description: The DMD gene is an X-linked gene responsible for encoding the dystrophin protein, which is essential for structural muscle stability. Mutations in this gene lead to Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) or Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), with genetic defects including deletions, duplications, and point mutations. The gene contains out-of-frame deletion mutations in some patients and has three affected isoforms: Dp427, Dp140, and Dp71. Molecular techniques such as MLPA and whole gene sequencing are used to analyze the gene and identify mutations affecting mRNA splicing and protein functionality.

nodes.label: Asthma
nodes.description: A chronic respiratory disease characterized by inflammation, hyperresponsiveness, and airway obstruction, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It is associated with high prevalence, mortality, and significant direct and indirect costs. Despite guidelines, a large proportion of cases remain uncontrolled, highlighting the need for improved therapeutic strategies. Asthma is mediated by T helper 2 (TH2) cells and involves interleukin (IL)-13 and IL-4, which are crucial in TH2-mediated inflammation and affect immunoglobulin E (IgE) synthesis, eosinophil activation, mucus secretion, and airways remodeling. It is divided into multiple pathophysiologically distinct endotypes based on airway inflammation. Some patients with asthma have refractory forms that do not respond to high doses of inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators or oral corticosteroids. A heterogeneous inflammatory disease where most patients respond to current standard of care including bronchodilators, inhaled glucocorticosteroids and other anti-inflammatory drugs. However, some patients cannot achieve adequate asthma control with standard treatments. It is characterized by the presence of T-helper type 2 (Th-2) inflammation in half of patients with severe asthma, suggesting potential benefits from monoclonal antibody-based treatments. There are two subtypes of asthma being discovered: early-onset, severe IgE-dependent asthma and late onset non-atopic asthma with persistent eosinophilic airway inflammation. A respiratory disorder characterized by inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and airway hyperresponsiveness. Patients with asthma have shown efficacy in response to Dupilumab treatment, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13. A widespread airway disease characterized by chronic airway inflammation, tissue remodeling, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. It is associated with key roles played by interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 in its pathophysiology. A type 2 helper T-cell-mediated disease, often co-occurring with chronic sinusitis and nasal polyposis in the study participants. It was mentioned that 35 out of 60 patients had comorbid asthma. A chronic respiratory disease characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing. It can be uncontrolled, persistent, and may require treatment with inhaled corticosteroids plus long-acting β2-agonist therapy. A disease or disorder targeted by the new mechanism of action interleukin-5 inhibition, which was introduced in the European drug market in 2015. One drug, mepolizumab (Nucala®), has been approved for this purpose. An allergic form of asthma, characterized by bronchial angiogenesis, which has been well documented. It is induced in a rat model using house dust mite allergen (Der p 1; 100 μg/challenge). The study evaluates changes in lung lymphatics and the properties of isolated lung lymphatic endothelial cells. A disease treated by Qi-Wei-Du-Qi-Wan in traditional Chinese medicine and induced by repeated stimulation with Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus (Der p) in mice. The study investigated whether QWDQW alleviates asthmatic symptoms in mice and explored the underlying immune modulatory mechanism. A respiratory disease characterized by increased goblet cell numbers in the airway epithelium, leading to the production of more difficult-to-clear mucus and airway mucus plugging. A chronic respiratory disease characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. IL-31 has been shown to play a relevant role in this condition.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial autophagy
nodes.description: A tightly controlled and highly selective process involving the selective sequestration of mitochondria by autophagosomes and subsequent delivery to lysosomes for destruction. It is essential for myocardial homeostasis and adaptation to stress, and is modulated by mitochondrial fission and fusion proteins, BCL-2 family proteins, and the PINK1/Parkin pathway. It is a core cellular activity involved in cellular quality control, degenerative disease, especially neurodegenerative disease, and cellular remodeling during development. It has strong parallels with xenophagy employed in host defense and converges on receptors in the innate immune system in clinically relevant scenarios. It is a biological process that regulates the mitochondrial network and function, contributing to multiple cellular processes. It involves the replacement of a significant percentage of the mitochondrial mass on a daily basis through mechanisms of mitochondrial quality control, including mitophagy, to maintain a healthy pool of mitochondria, prevent oxidative stress and inflammation, and adapt to the metabolic demand of the cells. It is a cellular process involving the degradation of mitochondria through autophagy, regulated by Shenlian extract to protect mitochondrial function and prevent coronary artery no-reflow. It is a biological process involving proteins such as LC3II/I, P62, PINK, and Parkin, regulated by the PINK/Parkin pathway and can be excessively activated, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction. SL administration prevents the activation of this pathway and inhibits excessive mitochondrial autophagy. It is regulated by SL and the PINK/Parkin pathway, with decreased levels associated with SL treatment. It is a cellular process involving the degradation and recycling of damaged mitochondria, mediated by the Pink1-Mfn2-Parkin pathway, essential for maintaining heart function and affected by the administration of Yi Mai granule (YMG).

nodes.label: Cetuximab
nodes.description: A monoclonal antibody against the EGFR, used as part of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Inhibitors therapy. It is generally well tolerated and does not have severe systemic side-effects. Cetuximab, also known as IMC-C225, is an EGFR inhibitor used in the treatment protocol involving 2 men and 2 women with no previous history of acne. It is used in combination with other EGFR inhibitors like gefitinib and carnetinib. An epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor used to treat non-small-cell lung cancer. It is one of the drugs that have been clinically tested for their effectiveness in treating this type of cancer and has been found to have significant therapeutic benefits for certain subgroups of patients. A monoclonal antibody (mAb) approved for use in Canada as an EGFR-targeting agent for the treatment of gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies. A targeted therapy used in combination with irinotecan for the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. A KRAS mutation confers resistance to cetuximab, reducing treatment options, especially in first-line therapy. A type of anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody, registered for metastatic colorectal carcinoma (mCRC) patients whose tumors express EGFR as determined by immunohistochemistry. An EGFR inhibitor used for the treatment of advanced, metastatic, or recurrent tumours like colorectal carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (SCCHN) and pancreatic cancer. Can cause acneiform rash in 30 to 90% of patients. An anti-EGFR antibody used in the treatment of chemotherapy-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer, often administered in combination with chemotherapy. Its efficacy is influenced by the presence of mutations in genes such as KRAS, BRAF, NRAS, and PIK3CA. A drug whose negative effect on outcome is confirmed by the study, particularly in the context of KRAS mutations. The study shows that additional genotyping of BRAF, NRAS, and PIK3CA exon 20 mutations in a KRAS wild-type population could improve objective response rates. A specific anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody used in targeted therapies and whose efficacy is influenced by the presence or absence of KRAS mutations. A type of anti-EGFR therapy that requires the presence of both wild-type KRAS and wild-type BRAF genotypes for effective treatment of colorectal cancer. A monoclonal antibody used in combination targeted therapies for irinotecan-refractory colorectal cancer, along with bevacizumab. It is part of the CBI and CB treatment regimens in the BOND-2 study. A chimeric anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody studied in combination with different chemotherapy protocols in phase II and phase III trials for patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer. It has shown an absolute overall survival benefit of 1.2 months when added to cisplatin/vinorelbine in the FLEX trial. A monoclonal antibody that has shown significant clinical activity in metastatic colon cancer and is used in combination with chemoradiation for the treatment of locally advanced rectal cancer. Its containing neoadjuvant chemoradiation has not been shown to improve tumor response in recent phase I/II trials. A monoclonal antibody targeting EGFR, often compared with necitumumab in terms of hypersensitivity reaction risk. A drug used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) that is known to be resistant to in patients with KRAS mutations. A monoclonal antibody that produces a statistically significant but clinically modest benefit in the whole study population for advanced NSCLC, when tested in a Phase III randomized trial. No solid data have been produced about predictive factors of efficacy. A first-generation anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of NSCLC. It is one of the drugs joining ramucirumab, necitumumab, and tivantinib in phase III development for NSCLC. A monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. Its effectiveness is predicted by the mutation status of the KRAS gene. A monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of HNSCC, often administered in combination with chemotherapy as palliative therapy. The study evaluated the associations between EGFR polymorphisms and overall survival in HNSCC patients receiving cetuximab-based treatment. The addition of chemotherapy to cetuximab was identified as an independent predictor of overall survival. A monoclonal antibody targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor, used in the treatment of metastatic CRC in combination with other anti-EGFR targeted antibodies. Several recent studies have shown that patients with KRAS mutations in codons 12 and 13 in metastatic CRC do not benefit from anti-EGFR therapy. An Anti-EGFR antibody used to treat metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) along with panitumumab. It was administered to 26 mCRC patients with KRAS wild-type status in this study. An anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody used to treat colorectal cancer, effective when KRAS status is not mutated. A chimeric monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, particularly in combination with first-line chemotherapy and platinum-based chemotherapy. It has been studied in several phase II and phase III trials, including the FLEX trial and BMS099 trial, demonstrating improved survival rates in certain patient populations. Cetuximab has also been investigated in combination with chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced NSCLC. An anti-EGFR drug used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). A drug used in EGFR-targeted treatments for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), its clinical outcomes are strongly predicted by KRAS mutations. A monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) in combination with irinotecan. The study investigates the modulation of plasma EGFR ligands in patients with mCRC during treatment with cetuximab and irinotecan, and explores the clinical implications of plasma levels' variations as potential biomarkers of benefit. An EGFR antagonist used to determine the biological effects on FDC-S cells in vitro. A targeted anti-EGFR therapeutic used to treat metastatic colorectal cancer. It extends survival in only 25% of patients who test wild-type for KRAS. Cetuximab responsiveness is not well defined for KRAS wild-type colorectal cancers, and somatic mutation of the EGFR signaling pathway is a prevalent mechanism of resistance to cetuximab. A drug used for treating metastatic colorectal cancer patients. A chimeric anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody (mAb) with multiple approved indications in HNSCC, including use with radiation therapy (RT) for locoregionally advanced disease, as monotherapy after platinum progression, and with platinum/5-fluorouracil for recurrent or metastatic disease. Under investigation for various unanswered questions regarding optimal use, patient selection, mechanisms of action and resistance, human papillomavirus status on outcomes, and management of skin toxicity and hypersensitivity reactions. A specific type of anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, often combined with chemotherapy. An epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor used in the treatment of various cancers. It can cause acneiform eruptions as a cutaneous adverse event, which are diagnosed as grade II according to the CTCAE v4.0. A monoclonal antibody that targets the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). It has shown improved survival when combined with first-line chemotherapy in patients with nonsmall cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly in those with high EGFR expression. A Southwest Oncology Group study is currently evaluating predictive biomarkers for cetuximab. A drug used in combination with afatinib for the treatment of patients with advanced NSCLC harboring mutated EGFR after progression on first-generation EGFR TKIs. A novel drug, an anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody, often combined with other treatment options for gastrointestinal malignancies. An anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody, one of the main categories of EGFR inhibitors. It is used to treat solid tumors and falls under the class of EGFR inhibitors. A monoclonal antibody (mAb) used in combination therapy for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). It belongs to the class of EGFR-targeting mAbs and was active only in MDA-MB-468 (EGFR amplification) cells. A biologic agent used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. It is one of the three biologic agents approved for first-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. An EGFR-neutralizing antibody used in the treatment of lung cancer. It is ineffective in patients with T790M-mutations within EGFR gene when combined with erlotinib and gefitinib. An anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody used in combination with afatinib in the sequential treatment of NSCLC with EGFR activating mutations. A monoclonal antibody used as a targeted therapy to EGFR, successful in therapeutic scenarios for cancers dependent on EGFR signaling. A monoclonal antibody targeting the Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). A drug used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, often administered in combination with chemotherapy. It is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor (EGFRI) and was used as a treatment for subjects in the study along with panitumumab. A monoclonal antibody against epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) recommended for the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) in combination with conventional chemotherapy. It is associated with skin toxicities including papulopustular rash, xerosis, painful cracks and fissures on the palms and soles of the feet, paronychia, pruritus, and abnormal hair and eyelash growth. A targeted therapy drug used in combination with bevacizumab and chemotherapy in the first-line therapy for advanced colorectal cancer patients. A drug administered to adult patients at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in the calendar year 2012 and 2017, with a comprehensive skin toxicity program evaluated for its association with adherence to prophylaxis guidelines for the prevention of EGFRi-associated cutaneous toxic effects. A drug used in oncology, specifically in the context of EGFR inhibitors. Its dose change or interruption is associated with a 79% reduced likelihood in patients prescribed prophylactic treatment compared to those not prescribed prophylactic treatment. A specific Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor mentioned in the text, used by an African American patient who developed an acneiform rash as a side effect. A chemotherapeutic agent and EGFR inhibitor used in the treatment of colorectal carcinoma. In a prospective study, five patients were using cetuximab. It is often associated with papulopustular (PPL) lesions as a side effect. A drug used in the Binimetinib, Encorafenib, And Cetuximab cOmbiNed to treat BRAF-mutant ColoRectal Cancer (BEACON CRC) study for the treatment of BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer, often combined with encorafenib. An EGFR inhibitor used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, which can induce acneiform rash as a side effect. A monoclonal antibody used in combination with encorafenib for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) with a BRAF V600E mutation, who have received prior systemic therapy. In a clinical trial, the combination of encorafenib and cetuximab was associated with a significantly longer median overall survival (OS), a higher objective response rate (ORR) and longer median progression-free survival (PFS), compared with standard therapy. An EGFR inhibitor that was combined with adagrasib in a phase I/II KRYSTAL-1 trial for treating metastatic colorectal cancer. It demonstrated encouraging clinical activity when used in combination with adagrasib. An antiepidermal growth factor receptor antibody used as subsequent therapy for patients with BRAFV600E-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer. A drug used in the TRESBIEN study (OGSG 2101) as part of a novel combination therapy for patients with early recurrent BRAF V600E-mutated colorectal cancer, during or after adjuvant chemotherapy. A drug used in combination with encorafenib for treating BRAF V600E-mutated colorectal cancer, particularly in cases that have progressed after initial treatment with FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab. A drug approved for the treatment of previously treated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) in combination with encorafenib.

nodes.label: Pentalogy of Fallot
nodes.description: A rare cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by biventricular origin of the aorta above a large ventricular septal defect, obstruction of the pulmonary outflow, right ventricular hypertrophy (tetralogy of Fallot), and an atrial septal defect. Mortality due to syncope, arrhythmia or congestive heart failure is about 75% by the age of 10 years and 97% by the age of 40. A congenital heart disease characterized by a dextropositioned and over-riding aorta, pulmonary valvular stenosis, ventricular and atrial septal defects, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It was diagnosed in a 5-month-old female Korean Sapsaree dog presenting with severe ascites, cyanosis, respiratory difficulty, and exercise intolerance. A rare congenital heart disease characterized by five cardiac abnormalities, including pulmonary atresia, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus. It was diagnosed in an infant who had a positive TORCH test for Toxoplasma gondii and Cytomegalovirus infections, and who had undergone three previous abortions. A congenital cardiac anomaly characterized by a pulmonic stenosis, a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, a right ventricular hypertrophy, and a patent foramen ovale. It was observed in a two-year-old ram during a breeding trial investigating the effects of shortness of the lower jaw. A rare form of congenital heart disease characterized by the association of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) with an atrial septal defect (ASD). It is a leading cause of intracardiac right to left shunt and the commonest type of cyanotic congenital heart disease to cause a brain abscess.

nodes.label: Structured Clinical Diagnostic Interview
nodes.description: An online assessment tool used to evaluate the presence of emetophobia and other conditions in 64 adults. It revealed higher comorbidity rates for depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder compared to general population norms.

nodes.label: Erlotinib
nodes.description: An EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, primarily used in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, metastatic or recurrent tumours like colorectal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, and pancreatic cancer. It can cause acneiform rash in 30 to 90% of patients and is known to have significant therapeutic benefits for certain subgroups of patients with non-small cell lung cancer. It is a first-generation EGFR TKI that patients may progress on before undergoing combination treatment with afatinib plus cetuximab. It is also being tested further with isotretinoin and clindamycin as a potential effective treatment for erlotinib-induced skin rash.

nodes.label: mother
nodes.description: A family member of the index patient who was affected by adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) in the context of Li-Fraumeni syndrome. This information was associated with a combined mutation (R202C) found in the study. The female parent in a family, who may carry the mutated IDS gene responsible for Hunter syndrome. In the described case, she is suggested to have germinal mosaicism, explaining the apparent false negative results in the serum test for her daughter.

nodes.label: α-synuclein
nodes.description: A major protein component of Lewy bodies, implicated in the formation of intracellular aggregates that lead to Parkinson's disease and Dementia with Lewy bodies. It is upregulated in response to chronic oxidative stress and may play a role in neuronal vulnerability. A small synaptic protein associated with familial Parkinson's disease (PD) and the primary component of Lewy bodies. It has been linked to defects in endosomal trafficking and phospholipid biosynthesis, and its overexpression causes cytoplasmic vesicle accumulation in a yeast model of α-synuclein toxicity. It induces aggregation of many yeast Rab GTPase proteins, is enhanced in yeast mutants that produce high levels of acidic phospholipids, and colocalizes with yeast membranes enriched for phosphatidic acid. It expression induces vulnerability to perturbations of Ypt6 and other proteins involved in retrograde endosome-Golgi transport. A small neuronal protein that misfolds and self-associates to form a toxic species, contributing to the development of Parkinson's disease. It is a primary protein in the intraneuronal inclusions present in Parkinson's disease. A protein involved in the formation of aggregates in Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), which initiate in a few discrete regions and spread to larger areas in the nervous system. A protein that is the principal component of Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease. It is known to aggregate and propagate between neurons, playing a central role in PD progression. It can assemble into fibrils, which can be influenced by molecular chaperones such as Hsc70 and Ssa1p. A small protein widely expressed in the brain, involved in the formation of Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). The α-synuclein gene, SNCA, is located on chromosome 4q22.1. Missense mutations such as A53T, A30P, and E46K have been identified, and gene multiplications have also been described. It affects dopamine synthesis and its normal physiological folding state is important for understanding pathological aggregates. A protein known to contribute to the pathogenesis of Parkinson disease, forming oligomeric species with certain conformations being toxic to cells. It is the major component of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, and its oligomers are being investigated for their role in cell death and potential clinical implications. A protein involved in the formation of Lewy bodies, which are intracellular inclusions found in Parkinson's disease. It can interact directly with iron, affecting its solubility and inducing neurotoxicity in vitro. A small-sized, natively unfolded protein that can aggregate and form fibrils, leading to neurotoxicity in Parkinson's disease. It has been suggested that α-synuclein may also have a protective role against oxidative stress. Two forms of α-synuclein are produced: native and Tat-fused (TAT-α-synuclein). Both forms can form fibrils and be cytotoxic at micromolar concentrations. A protein involved in Parkinson's disease pathology, capable of transferring from cell to cell. It can form pathological aggregates known as Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. Recent studies have investigated its cell-to-cell transfer, focusing on the long-distance axonal transport along neurons. A protein associated with Parkinson's disease, forming fibrillar structures within Lewy bodies. A protein involved in Parkinson's disease, with mutations (A53T, A30P, E46K) and multiplication of the gene linked to familial PD. The major protein component of Lewy bodies. A protein that forms aggregates in both the central nervous system and peripheral nervous system, leading to the development of synucleinopathies. Aggregated α-synuclein is thought to spread cell-to-cell and is involved in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease. A protein involved in the pathogenesis of synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. It plays important roles in the release of synaptic vesicles and synaptic membrane recycling in healthy neurons. α-synuclein expression is detected in presynaptic boutons and cell bodies of some neurons, while other neurons either do not or only weakly express the protein. It is colocalized with synapsin, a marker of presynaptic vesicles, but not essential for activity-dependent membrane recycling induced by high potassium treatment. Exogenous supply of preformed fibrils generated by recombinant α-synuclein promotes the formation of Lewy body-like intracellular aggregates involving endogenous α-synuclein. GAD-positive neurons do not form LB-like aggregates following treatment with preformed fibrils, however, exogenous expression of human α-synuclein allows intracellular aggregate formation in these cells. A gene or protein involved in determining the efficiency of intracellular aggregate formation in different neuronal subtypes. A protein involved in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease, expressed heterologously in fruit flies and nematodes. Its expression is thought to be the principal toxic trigger of PD. Administration of spermidine protects against its neurotoxicity. A protein associated with Parkinson's disease, present in plasma biomarkers and positively associated with Mini-Mental State Examination score in Parkinson's disease patients. It is also part of the α-synuclein/Aβ40 ratio.

nodes.label: Exencephaly
nodes.description: A rare and lethal malformation associated with acrania, characterized by the absence of the skull bones and the presence of cerebral tissue often abnormal. It is a severe congenital disorder caused by the incomplete closure of the anterior neuropore during embryonic development, leading to the protrusion of brain tissue through the skull. Exencephaly is considered the most severe form of cranium bifidum and is distinct from anencephaly in that it does not undergo necrosis and early transformation into a residual area cerebrovasculosa.

nodes.label: Melatonin
nodes.description: A hormone primarily produced in the brain and epiphysis, involved in the regulation of various physiological processes, including sleep-wake cycles and bone formation. Its signaling pathway is suspected to be impaired in patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, and its deficiency may be linked to the development of scoliotic deformities. Melatonin is a pineal hormone that alters brain arginine vasotocin immunoreactivity in green treefrogs (Hyla cinerea) and is proposed as a potential target for facilitating seasonal changes in reproductive physiology and social behavior. It is also investigated for its ameliorative potential in mitigating PS-NP-induced mitochondrial damage and neurodegeneration.

nodes.label: Chronic hepatitis D
nodes.description: A disease characterized by a chronic infection caused by the hepatitis D virus, for which management has recently entered a new era. Surrogate markers of treatment efficacy have not yet been well defined for this condition. A form of hepatitis D characterized by ongoing inflammation of the liver, treated with bulevirtide in this study. A chronic viral infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis D virus, which was treated with bulevirtide in a study involving 114 patients from 16 German centers. A disease caused by the hepatitis D virus, treated with bulevirtide as described in the text. A chronic viral liver infection caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV). Bulevirtide is licensed for its treatment. Long-term follow-up of patients discontinuing BLV treatment upon long-term HDV-RNA suppression is studied. A chronic viral infection caused by the hepatitis delta virus (HDV), which requires the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for replication. It is a major focus of the study described in the text. A chronic liver disease caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV), often co-infecting individuals already infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV). The text discusses the use of interferon (IFN) therapy and the combination of IFN and bovine leukemia virus (BLV) as potential treatments for this condition.

nodes.label: Induced Pluripotent Stem (iPS) Cells
nodes.description: Cells generated from somatic cells by ectopic expression of four transcription factors, Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc. They can be derived from amniotic fluid-derived (AF) cells and have the ability to differentiate into three germ layers in vitro and in vivo. The presence of these cells is detected using the alkaline phosphate (AP) assay. Specialized cells that have the ability to differentiate into all three germ layers and can give rise to a variety of cell types. In this study, they are generated from transplantable leukemia cells by overexpressing the MLL-AF9 fusion gene in the presence of doxycycline (Dox). These iPS cells can form teratomas and produce chimeras.

nodes.label: Rash
nodes.description: A common skin reaction associated with various treatments, including epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, and teplizumab. It is characterized by redness, itching, or irritation and can range from mild to moderate. Rash management is crucial for maintaining treatment adherence and minimizing discomfort. It typically resolves without intervention and has a self-limited adverse event profile.

nodes.label: Angiogenesis
nodes.description: A biological process involving the formation of new blood vessels, regulated by various signaling pathways, growth factors, and proteins such as VEGFA, and involved in tumor growth, metastasis, and resistance to bevacizumab treatment. It can be promoted by endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival through the VEGF pathway, and inhibited by anti-ESM1 antibodies. Angiogenesis is also a major target for bevacizumab in suppressing tumor growth and has been established as an effective clinical treatment strategy.

nodes.label: Clinical trials
nodes.description: Research studies conducted to evaluate the safety, efficacy, and optimal use of therapeutic interventions, diagnostic tests, or preventive measures in humans. These trials may involve various medical treatments, drugs, devices, or immunotherapies, and can focus on different conditions such as cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, or genetic disorders. Clinical trials often follow preclinical trials and may lead to the approval of new treatments or therapies. They can be conducted in different phases, each with specific objectives, and may involve human participants who provide informed consent. Adverse events and side effects are monitored and reported during clinical trials.

nodes.label: Lacosamide
nodes.description: A novel anti-convulsant drug that shows efficacy with a wide safety margin in rodent models for epilepsy. It was effective against sound-induced seizures in the genetically susceptible Frings mouse, against maximal electroshock test (MES)-induced seizures in rats and mice, in the rat hippocampal kindling model of partial seizures, and in the 6Hz model of psychomotor seizures in mice. Lacosamide was inactive against clonic seizures induced by subcutaneous administration of the chemoconvulsants pentylenetetrazol, bicuculline, and picrotoxin, but it did inhibit NMDA-induced seizures in mice and showed full efficacy in the homocysteine model of epilepsy. It was also effective in elevating the seizure threshold in the i.v. pentylenetetrazol seizure test at both the median effective dose for MES protection and the median toxic dose for rotorod impairment, suggesting that it is unlikely to be pro-convulsant at high doses. Overall, Lacosamide's anti-convulsant profile appeared to be unique and it displayed a good margin of safety in those tests in which it was effective. A member of a series of functionalized amino acids that were specifically synthesized as anticonvulsive drug candidates. Lacosamide has demonstrated antiepileptic effectiveness in different rodent seizure models and antinociceptive potential in experimental animal models that reflect distinct types and symptoms of neuropathic as well as chronic inflammatory pain. It selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels without affecting fast inactivation and has been identified as a binding partner of collapsin-response mediator protein 2 (CRMP-2). At therapeutic concentrations, it does not inhibit or induce a wide variety of cytochrome P450 enzymes. Safety pharmacology and toxicology studies conducted in mice, rats, rabbits, and dogs have shown that LCM is well tolerated with only minor side effects observed in the central nervous, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and renal systems. Repeated dose toxicity studies demonstrate that adverse events are reversible and consist mostly of exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects on the CNS. No genotoxic or carcinogenic effects were observed in vivo, and LCM shows a favorable profile in reproductive and developmental animal studies. Currently, LCM is in a late stage of clinical development as an adjunctive treatment for patients with uncontrolled partial-onset seizures and as monotherapy in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy. A newer antiepileptic drug with a dual mode of action, selectively enhancing slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels without affecting fast inactivation, and modulating collapsing response mediator protein 2 (CRMP-2). It has a high oral bioavailability of approximately 100% and has shown potent and broad neuroprotective effects in vitro and in vivo animal models. It has demonstrated analgesic activity in various animal models and has potent effects in animal models for a variety of CNS disorders like schizophrenia and stress-induced anxiety. Safety pharmacology and toxicology studies have shown that LCM is well tolerated. Clinical trials have suggested that LCM is a safe, effective, and well-tolerated adjunctive treatment for reduction of seizure frequency in patients with highly refractory, partial seizures. Other potential indications of LCM are being investigated. An epilepsy drug that appears to bind CRMP2 directly with concomitant affects on neural structure. A recently introduced AED licensed for the treatment of refractory partial-onset seizures. An antiepileptic drug (AED) for which there is compelling evidence that salivary TDM can be usefully applied to optimize the treatment of epilepsy. A type of antiepileptic drug that is often initiated in children with refractory epilepsy, alongside topiramate, forming a subnetwork of commonly coadministered drugs.

nodes.label: Glucocorticoid treatment
nodes.description: A long-term daily therapy involving the use of glucocorticoids, such as deflazacort, to extend ambulatory function in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Concerns about side effects often lead to less frequent dosing.

nodes.label: Psoriasis
nodes.description: A chronic autoimmune skin condition characterized by the appearance of red, scaly patches on the skin. Psoriasis patients can experience the Koebner phenomenon, where psoriatic lesions appear in the uninvolved skin as a consequence of trauma. It is a complex systemic immune inflammatory disease involving T-cell differentiation mediated by interleukins 12 and 23 (IL-12/23). Psoriasis is associated with inflammation mediated by cytokines interleukin (IL)-12 and IL-23, and is treated with medications such as ustekinumab, etanercept, and anti-TNF-α agents. It is a common cutaneous disease characterized by scaly erythematous papules and plaques on the scalp and forehead, and groups of clustered erythematous papules with silver scales in the dermatome distributed on the right side of the chest wall.

nodes.label: Protochlorophyllide (Pchlide)
nodes.description: A chemical compound involved in the synthesis of chlorophyll, necessary for the import of POR protein isozyme (PORA). It is used as a substrate for the catalytic reaction of NADPH:protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (POR). A chemical compound involved in the initial stages of chlorophyll biosynthesis, reduced to chlorophyllide (Chlide) by Pchlide oxidoreductase (POR) under light conditions. Accumulates in the dark, mainly in the form of complexes with NADPH and POR, and also as an unbound pigment. Forms ternary complexes with POR and NADPH in etioplasts. A form of protochlorophyll that appears during the desiccoplast-etioplast-chloroplast transformation process in Xerophyta humilis leaves, existing in both photoactive and non-photoactive forms. A photoactive compound bound to protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase in prolamellar bodies (PLBs). Its photoreduction upon illumination leads to the disruption of PLB structures, including enlargement and fragmentation into small balls. The photoreduction of Pchlide is shown in fluorescence spectra. A chemical compound that is reduced to chlorophyllide by the light-dependent protochlorophyllide oxidoreductase (POR) in the chlorophyll biosynthesis pathway.

nodes.label: Chromosome 19
nodes.description: A human chromosome where LOH was found in only one case, indicating its lesser involvement in glioblastoma development compared to chromosome 10. A human chromosome containing the gene encoding for the plasma LDL receptor, which, when mutated, causes Familial Hypercholesterolemia. A human chromosome where the DMPK gene, associated with Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), is located. Chromosome 19 is one of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in humans.
