It is described as short but having a higher relative density of genes compared to other chromosomes. Many genes coding for proteins implicated in the pathogenesis of various human diseases are mapped on chromosome 19. Chromosome 19 is the location of the LDLR gene, which encodes the Low-Density Lipoprotein Receptor (LDLR). Mutations in this gene cause familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). The gene has almost 300 identified mutations.

nodes.label: Restless legs syndrome
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by an irresistible urge to move the legs, often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, especially during rest or at night. It is also known as Willis-Ekbom disease (WED) and can result in considerable sleep disruption. Mood disorders are associated with RLS, and secondary causes need to be excluded. Treatment depends on the severity and frequency of RLS symptoms and may involve non-pharmacological interventions such as lifestyle changes and pharmacological interventions like dopaminergic medication, alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands, and opioids. A range of medical interventions with varied efficacy has been employed, and a statistical negative correlation between serum ferritin and RLS severity of symptoms has been observed.

nodes.label: Total Neoadjuvant Therapy
nodes.description: A therapeutic intervention involving three cycles of induction CAPOX (oxaliplatin plus capecitabine) followed by pelvic radiotherapy and concurrent CAPOX, then three cycles of consolidation CAPOX after radiotherapy. It is used for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer with high risk factors and includes total mesorectal resection (TME) or watch-and-wait strategy based on therapeutic effect and patients' wishes. A novel treatment strategy for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) that involves preoperative chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, as an alternative to preoperative CRT. An optimal protocol for TNT has not yet been established. A therapeutic intervention involving short-course radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy with four cycles of CAPOX (intravenous oxaliplatin [130 mg/m2, once a day] on day 1 and capecitabine [1,000 mg/m2, twice a day] from days 1 to 14) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). It aims to enhance tumor response, reduce recurrence, and improve patient compliance compared to upfront surgery.

nodes.label: Klinefelter syndrome
nodes.description: A sex chromosome disorder commonly diagnosed among males, involving the presence of 47 chromosomes, including two Xs and one Y (47,XXY). It is associated with an increased risk of various malignant diseases, such as germ cell tumors and breast cancers, and is often linked to nonobstructive azoospermia and male infertility. Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by tall stature, immaturity of external genitalia, and testicular dysfunction. It can also be associated with neurocognitive and behavioral phenotypes, as well as vulnerabilities in socio-emotional development. The disorder is one of the sex chromosome aneuploidies observed in infertile males, accounting for 49% of cases. While it is not specifically linked to acute leukemias, it has been shown to be associated with various malignancies. There is a rare variant of Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XY,i(X)(q10), which has an additional isochromosome made of the long arm of the X chromosome and is associated with patients usually being shorter than average height and having normal intelligence. Successful sperm extractions from these patients have not been reported in the literature.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)
nodes.description: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is the genetic material found within mitochondria, responsible for encoding essential proteins involved in the execution of normal mitochondrial functions. It is more prone to be affected by DNA damaging agents compared to nuclear DNA, and accumulated DNA damages may cause mitochondrial dysfunction and drive the pathogenesis of a variety of human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. mtDNA mutations can affect energy production, oxidative stress, and cell survival, which may contribute to aging and/or carcinogenesis. It is also associated with maternal inheritance of Leigh Syndrome due to a point mutation. The quantitative level of mtDNA is related to oocyte cytoplasm maturation and fertilization potential in humans, with insufficient mtDNA potentially leading to abnormal oocyte development and reduced fertility. mtDNA can be altered by metabolic disorders, oxidative stress, or inflammation in the progression and development of various diseases.

nodes.label: Dinutuximab
nodes.description: A monoclonal antibody targeting GD2, developed by United Therapeutics Corporation and the National Cancer Institute for the treatment of neuroblastoma. It is an IgG1 human/mouse chimeric switch variant of murine monoclonal antibody 14G2a, binds to GD2 and induces antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity. It has been approved for use in combination with granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor, interleukin-2 and 13-cis retinoic acid for the treatment of pediatric patients with high-risk neuroblastoma who achieve at least partial response to prior first-line multiagent, multimodality therapy. It is produced by United Therapeutics Corporation (UTC) as Unituxin™. It is a chimeric human-mouse monoclonal antibody that binds to the glycolipid antigen disialoganglioside, highly expressed on the surface of neuroblastoma cells. It is approved in the EU and USA as combination therapy with GM-CSF, IL-2 and isotretinoin for the postconsolidation treatment of patients with high-risk neuroblastoma. It is associated with the development of transverse myelitis as a potential side effect.

nodes.label: Escherichia coli
nodes.description: A type of bacteria commonly used as a model organism in molecular biology research, often used for studying DNA replication processes, mismatch repair systems, and riboswitch regulation. It contains the enzyme DnaQ, which performs the proofreading function in DNA replication, and the protein ExoIX, used as a family member in biochemical characterization studies. Escherichia coli is also used as an expression host for recombinant proteins and to study the effects of various genetic mutations and environmental factors on genome stability.

nodes.label: Koebner phenomenon
nodes.description: A biological process where skin lesions appear in response to certain stimuli, such as trauma, scratching, UV-exposure, and various types of dermatitis. It can be observed not only in psoriasis but also in other diseases, such as lichen planus and some systemic diseases including LE (lupus erythematosus) or sarcoidosis. The pathophysiology involves two steps: a non-specific inflammatory step and a disease-specific step. The inflammatory products released from the first step would be targeted in the second step, involving disease-specific reactions such as those by T-cells, B-cells, autoantibodies, and immune deposits, under the restriction of genetic backgrounds.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Mutations
nodes.description: Mitochondrial Mutations refer to alterations in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) that can be inherited or sporadic. These mutations can lead to simple changes like point mutations, which often occur in mitochondrial tRNA loci, causing mischarging of mitochondrial tRNAs or deletion, duplication, or reduction in mtDNA content. The mtDNA's vulnerability to oxidative modifications, limited presence of DNA damage repair systems, and continuous replication in the cell contribute to its higher susceptibility compared to nuclear DNA. The presence of multiple copies and a specific replication mechanism in cells or tissues can result in heterogeneity, leading to characteristic phenotypic presentations such as heteroplasmy, genetic drift, and threshold effects.

nodes.label: BMAL1
nodes.description: A clock gene that is negatively autoregulated and upregulated by CRY1, CRY2, and PER2. It plays a bidirectional role in transcription, being repressed by BMAL1-CLOCK dimers at high levels by late day. Its negative feedback loop interlocks with the CRY and PER2 negative feedback loop, forming a third positive forward loop. A transcription factor belonging to the bHLH-PAS-containing family, involved in the positive elements of circadian autoregulatory feedback loop. It forms a heterodimer with CLOCK to drive transcription from E-box enhancer elements in the promoters of responsive genes. It is essential for the nuclear accumulation of CLOCK and its degradation. It induces posttranslational modifications and phosphorylation of CLOCK following ectopic coexpression. A gene or protein that plays an essential role in the positive arm of the molecular oscillator in mammals, regulating the circadian transcription feedback loop. It has a C terminus that is involved in determining the balance between circadian transcriptional activation and suppression. The extreme C terminus of BMAL1 contains a domain that controls E-box-mediated circadian transcription rhythmically. The last 43 amino acids (aa) of BMAL1 are required for transcriptional activation and association with the circadian transcriptional repressor CRYPTOCHROME 1 (CRY1), depending on the coexistence of CLOCK protein. C-terminally truncated BMAL1 mutant proteins can still associate with mPER2, suggesting an additional repression mechanism may converge on the N terminus. A basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) PAS domain-containing transcriptional activator that regulates gene expression by interacting with a promoter element termed the E-box (CACGTG), along with another protein called CLOCK. A transcriptional activator involved in the circadian clock mechanism, forms a complex with CLOCK to activate transcription. A protein that forms a complex with CLOCK to regulate circadian transcription and H3 acetylation.

nodes.label: Glioblastoma
nodes.description: A highly aggressive and fatal type of brain cancer, characterized by rapid growth, invasion of surrounding brain tissue, and a poor prognosis. It is the most common and malignant form of primary brain tumor in adults, accounting for up to 50% of brain parenchymal tumors. Glioblastoma is associated with mutations in the p53 gene, deletions in the ink4a-arf locus, and the presence of various molecular genetic abnormalities on many chromosomes. It is managed through surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, with the standard treatment involving maximal surgical resection followed by concurrent chemoradiation therapy and adjuvant TMZ according to the Stupp protocol. Glioblastoma can exhibit whole genome duplication (WGD) and chromothripsis events, with WGD being detected in 11.4% of cases and being significantly associated with TP53 mutation (p = 0.0068). Chromothripsis occurs in 29.3% of cases, mainly affecting chromosomes 7, 9, and 12, with amplification of oncogenes (EGFR, MDM2/CDK4) and homozygous deletion of tumor suppressor genes (CDKN2A).

nodes.label: Tofogliflozin
nodes.description: A new SGLT2 inhibitor, an oral hypoglycemic agent that reduces blood glucose levels by promoting glucose excretion in urine through selective inhibition of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2). It was evaluated for its effects on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of several selected anti-type 2 diabetes mellitus drugs in healthy male volunteers.

nodes.label: Dapivirine
nodes.description: A nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor being developed as a topical microbicide for the prevention of human immunodeficiency virus infection, primarily through gel formulations and intravaginal rings (IVRs). It has been investigated in various clinical trials, including IPM001, IPM008, and the ASPIRE (MTN 020) study, and has shown promise in terms of safety, pharmacokinetics, and anti-HIV activity. Dapivirine is a potent and promising anti-HIV molecule that accumulates mostly at the basal layer of the epithelium infiltrating the upper part of the stroma when delivered through vaginal film codelivery with Tenofovir. It is a poorly-water soluble anti-HIV drug that can be improved in solubility through solid dispersion systems and is used in the development of various dosage forms, such as vaginal rings, gels, and films.

nodes.label: Hunter disease
nodes.description: A rare genetic disorder characterized by the absence of iduronate sulfatase enzyme, leading to the accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfates in various tissues. It affects a karyotypically normal girl in the described case, presenting with symptoms such as developmental delay, macrocephaly, dysmorphic facies, hypotonia, hepatosplenomegaly, mild generalized dysostosis multiplex, mucopolysacchariduria, and Alder-Reilly bodies in peripheral blood leukocytes. An X-linked recessive lethal disease that has recently been observed to occur in high frequency in Israeli Jews as compared with other Caucasian populations. It is used as an example to demonstrate the compatibility of an elevated frequency with genetic drift. A rare X-linked recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency in iduronate sulfatase activity. It was studied in a Neapolitan family and characterized at the molecular level. The delta 139 mutation was identified in the third exon of the gene associated with this disease.

nodes.label: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Inhibitors
nodes.description: A class of drugs targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) used in cancer treatment. They are associated with skin rash as a side effect, which can impact patients' quality of life and the course of cancer treatment. The approach described in this article aims to manage the skin rash associated with these inhibitors through a proactive, grade-based treatment algorithm involving patient education and consultation with dermatologists, oncologists, and pharmacists. A class of drugs used to inhibit the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) in several epithelial tumors, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, and head and neck cancer. They are associated with skin toxicities, particularly a papulopustular rash in the majority of patients. The use of these inhibitors has increased significantly in recent years. A class of drugs that includes anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies such as cetuximab and panitumumab, and first-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as afatinib, gefitinib, and erlotinib. These drugs are used to treat various types of solid tumors and have been shown to extend patient survival. A class of drugs used in cancer treatment, specifically targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Common side effects include rash, which can persist and affect treatment duration. A class of drugs used in cancer treatment that can cause cutaneous toxic effects in up to 90% of patients, negatively affecting quality of life and leading to treatment interruptions.

nodes.label: Albinism
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by a deficiency of melanin pigment in the skin, hair, and eye (oculocutaneous albinism [OCA]) or primarily in the eye (ocular albinism [OA]). It results from mutations in genes involved in the biosynthesis of melanin pigment. The lack of melanin pigment in the developing eye leads to fovea hypoplasia and abnormal routing of the optic nerves, causing nystagmus, strabismus, and reduced visual acuity. A genetic disorder characterized by the partial or complete lack of melanin production, leading to reduced pigmentation of the skin, hair, and eyes. It is associated with mutations in the TYR gene and can manifest as Oculocutaneous Albinism type 1 (OCA1) in humans. A group of disorders characterized by reduced pigmentation, with various types identified by their genetic causes, including Oculocutaneous albinism type 1. The genetics of albinism are complex, involving mutations in multiple genes. A genetic disorder characterized by reduced or absent pigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes, caused by mutations in the TYR gene in humans and Tyrosinase gene in rats. A disease characterized by reduced TYR activity, leading to childhood blindness. It is caused by mutations in the TYR gene and is classified into different types based on the severity of TYR activity, such as OCA1B. Some OCA1B mutations are temperature-sensitive. A genetic disorder characterized by the absence of pigmentation in the skin, hair, and eyes, which is determined by a missense mutation in a highly conserved position of the tyrosinase (TYR) gene deduced protein. It is a major attraction of the Asinara National Park and is caused by disrupting mutations in the TYR gene, such as the c.604C>G; p.His202Asp mutation. A hypopigmentary disorder characterized by limited production or absence of melanin pigment, affecting the skin, hair, and eyes. It includes two main types, OCA1A and OCA1B, with varying degrees of pigmentation. The most frequent and severe form worldwide is OCA1, caused by pathogenic variations in the tyrosinase gene (TYR).

nodes.label: Fanconi anemia
nodes.description: A hereditary chromosomal instability syndrome with cancer predisposition, characterized by bone marrow failure leading to pancytopenia as the main cause of death. Diagnosis is based on cellular hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents and chromosome breakages. Involves at least eight genes, with the gene for complementation group A (FANCA) being defective in the majority of patients. An inherited cancer-susceptibility disorder characterized by genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents, and a prolonged G2 phase of the cell cycle. A human genetic disorder characterized by hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, increased chromosome breakage, and a marked cell-cycle delay with 4N DNA content after introduction of interstrand DNA crosslinks (ICL). It has two complementation groups, A and C, and is studied using FA fibroblasts. A genetic syndrome characterized by aplastic anemia, cancer predisposition and hypersensitivity to DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs). It is associated with proteins called FANCs that are thought to work in pathway(s) essential for dealing with crosslinked DNA. Patients with Fanconi anemia show partial S-phase arrest upon DNA damage, which can be exacerbated by the absence of ATR or NBS1 proteins. A genetic disorder characterized by congenital abnormalities, bone marrow failure, chromosome fragility, and cancer susceptibility. It is associated with eight identified genes that function in the FA/BRCA pathway. Spontaneous genetic reversion can correct FA mutations, leading to somatic mosaicism. Patients can be classified based on the level of FA/BRCA pathway disruption into 'FA core', FA-D2, and an unidentified downstream group. An autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by diverse clinical symptoms, hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, chromosomal instability and susceptibility to cancer. It has at least 11 complementation groups (A, B, C, D1, D2, E, F, G, I, J, L). The genes mutated in 8 of these have been identified. The gene BRCA2 was suggested to underlie complementation group B, but the evidence is inconclusive. A genetic disorder characterized by an increased risk of cancer, bone marrow failure, and congenital abnormalities. It is associated with defects in DNA repair mechanisms, particularly those involving homologous recombination (HR). A recessive syndrome with both autosomal and X-linked inheritance, featuring diverse clinical symptoms such as progressive bone marrow failure, hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents, chromosomal instability and susceptibility to cancer. It has at least 12 genetic subtypes (FA-A, B, C, D1, D2, E, F, G, I, J, L, M) and all except FA-I have been linked to a distinct gene. Most FA proteins form a complex that activates the FANCD2 protein via monoubiquitination, while FANCJ and FANCD1/BRCA2 function downstream of this step. The FA proteins typically lack functional domains, except for FANCJ/BRIP1 and FANCM, which are DNA helicases, and FANCL, which is probably an E3 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme. They are thought to function in the repair of DNA interstrand cross-links, which block the progression of DNA replication forks. A genetic disorder associated with mutations in the FANCJ gene, linked to breast cancer and characterized by genomic instability, particularly in FA-J mutant cells. A genetic disorder characterized by defects in DNA repair mechanisms, particularly affecting the repair of interstrand DNA cross-links. It involves the activation of the Fanconi anemia DNA repair network, which is facilitated by the monoubiquitylation of the FA complementation group I (FANCI)-FANCD2 (ID) complex by FA complementation group L (FANCL), an E3 ubiquitin ligase. An autosomal recessive, cancer susceptibility disorder characterized by diverse clinical features such as short stature, skeletal or skin abnormalities, progressive bone marrow failure, and increased risk of malignancies. It is associated with the development of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in patients. Chromosomal breakage investigation using mitomycin C (MMC)- and diepoxybutane (DEB)-induced peripheral blood cultures can detect clonal chromosomal abnormalities in patients with FA. A genetic disorder affecting the DNA repair pathway, characterized by defects in the Fanconi anemia (FA) protein FANCI and the key DNA repair factor FANCD2. A rare cancer susceptibility syndrome characterized by an incidence of only 1 per 350,000 births, an autosomal recessive disease with three main features: chromosome instability, hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents such as mitomycin C (MMC) and cisplatin, and susceptibility to various cancer types including leukemia and squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck or gynecologic system. The Fanconi anemia pathway plays a key role in repairing DNA cross-linking lesions caused by DNA crosslinking agents. A genetic disorder characterized by progressive bone marrow failure starting in the first decade of life, congenital malformations, endocrine dysfunction, and an extraordinary predisposition to develop cancer. It is associated with the deficiency of the FANCA gene, leading to sensitivity of hematopoietic progenitor cells to DNA-interstrand crosslinking agents and inflammatory cytokines. A genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous recessive disorder characterized by diverse congenital malformations, progressive pancytopenia and predisposition to both hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. It was diagnosed in a 14-year-old boy who initially presented with clinical features of aplastic anemia. A disorder characterized by sensitivity to DNA interstrand crosslinking agents, clinical features of cytopenia, developmental defects, and tumor predisposition. Caused by mutations in at least sixteen FANC genes (FANCA-Q). A rare inherited human disorder caused by mutations in the ERCC1 or ERCC4 genes. It is characterized by an increased risk of bone marrow failure, leukemia, and solid tumors. A genomic instability syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in the ERCC4 gene. A genetic disorder characterized by chromosomal aberrations, hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, and predisposition to malignancy, suggesting a fundamental anomaly of DNA repair. A group of at least five autosomal recessive disorders characterized by both clinical features such as birth defects and hematopoietic failure, and cellular features like sensitivity to cross-linking agents and predisposition to apoptosis. It consists of complementation groups A, B, C, D, and others. A common pathogenetic link among these groups has not been established. A genetic disorder characterized by abnormal G2/M arrest in lymphoblasts after exposure to low doses of DNA cross-linking agents, leading to excessive cell cycle arrest in the G2/M compartment. The disease is associated with mutations in various FA genes that may directly regulate cell cycle checkpoints. A genetic disorder characterized by cellular hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents, such as mitomycin C (MMC), leading to increased cell death, chromosome breakage, and accumulation in the G2 phase of the cell cycle.

nodes.label: PD-1
nodes.description: A protein involved in the PD-1 pathway, which is a checkpoint inhibitor targeting the immune system. It plays a role in preventing excessive immune responses, especially in the context of tumor surveillance and immune tolerance. PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor expressed on T cells that helps regulate their activation and function. It forms a pathway with PD-L1, known as programmed death-ligand-1/programmed death-1 (PD-L1/PD-1), which is a target for therapeutic strategies in cancer treatment. PD-1 is also a crucial immune system regulator that acts as a brake to prevent T-cell overactivation and potential autoimmunity. Tumors can exploit this checkpoint to evade immune detection, but inhibiting it can enhance the body's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells.

nodes.label: Enzalutamide
nodes.description: A new antiandrogen with a dual mechanism of action developed for the treatment of prostate cancer. An experimental intervention tested in clinical trials for treating metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It provides significant overall survival advantages compared to placebo (4.8 months). A drug used in the treatment of prostate cancer, particularly in patients who have received prior docetaxel therapy. It has been shown to improve overall survival and prolong rPFS compared to placebo or best of care. Potential side effects include enzalutamide-induced seizures. A next-generation androgen receptor-signaling inhibitor used in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer, demonstrating significant improvements in survival and important secondary endpoints. It has been evaluated in phase III placebo-controlled trials for non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and is being studied in combination with docetaxel for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer in the ARASENS trial. A novel second-generation androgen receptor antagonist approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It has proven clinical efficacy and good compatibility with minimal side effects. A second-generation anti-androgen therapy used for the treatment of nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It has been shown to significantly decrease prostate-specific antigen progression-free survival and increase metastases-free survival compared to placebo. It is associated with a lower hazard ratio for metastases-free survival when compared to placebo, with a value of 0.29 (95% CI: 0.24-0.35). It is considered an effective treatment for high-risk of progression nmCRPC and is supported by equivalent efficacy and similar risk of adverse effects compared to apalutamide and darolutamide. An androgen inhibitor used to treat prostate cancer, with an effect similar to that of darolutamide in improving metastasis-free survival in men with non-metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer. A standard of care chemotherapeutic used to treat prostate cancer. It is a structural analogue of apalutamide and is susceptible to AKR1C3-mediated resistance. A non-steroidal anti-androgen used in the treatment of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, with a 44% likelihood of maximizing metastasis-free survival according to Bayesian analysis. A drug that may result in improved oncologic outcomes when compared to apalutamide and darolutamide. A next-generation antiandrogen drug and the active ingredient in XTANDI, used to treat advanced prostate cancer. It extends survival times and improves quality of life in patients with advanced prostate cancer. A first second-generation nonsteroidal androgen receptor (AR) antagonist with a strong binding affinity to AR. It can prolong overall survival time, metastatic free survival time, and castration-resistant free survival time for patients with lethal castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), castration-sensitive prostate cancer (CSPC), and has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of both metastatic (in 2012) and non-metastatic (in 2018) CRPC, as well as CSPC (2019). A multiple agent approved for advanced prostate cancer, used for treating the disease. A medication used in the treatment of non-metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC) that has shown improved metastasis free survival (MFS) rates in studies compared to darolutamide but not significantly different from apalutamide. It has a similar and higher MFS rate in indirect comparison with darolutamide. A medication approved since 2018 for the treatment of men with non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (M0CRPC) in conjunction with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). A next-generation androgen receptor inhibitor used in the management of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC), which was found to be significantly more effective than placebo and darolutamide for metastasis-free survival (MFS), and more efficacious for therapy of nmCRPC compared to darolutamide. A novel androgen receptor antagonist used for the treatment of nmCRPC, alongside darolutamide and apalutamide. It is mentioned in comparison to darolutamide regarding adverse events (AEs). A treatment recommended by the NCCN for nmCRPC, often used in combination with a weighted average androgen deprivation therapy comparator.

nodes.label: Meta-analysis
nodes.description: A statistical method used to combine results from multiple studies to draw more robust conclusions. It can be applied to various fields such as evaluating the association between excess weight and cancer risk, assessing the SNP rs11190870's positive association with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, analyzing the relationship between BRAF V600E mutation and tumor response, studying the rs1149048 polymorphism's association with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, evaluating the risk of gastrointestinal toxicities associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, investigating the role of human fatty acid binding protein 2 (FABP2) expression in diagnosing necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), summarizing evidence on dietary factors and colorectal cancer incidence, assessing the effectiveness and safety of long-acting cabotegravir compared to TDF-FTC for HIV PrEP, and analyzing the effects of dopamine agonists on sleep architecture in patients with Restless Leg Syndrome. Meta-analyses often employ statistical models like the random effects model and include systematic searches in databases such as MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library.

nodes.label: Ovarian cancer
nodes.description: A type of malignancy that originates in the ovaries and is often associated with BRCA1 mutations, increasing the risk of developing breast cancer as well. It is characterized by the presence of high-grade serous ovarian cancer, platinum-sensitive relapsed BRCA-mutated (germline or somatic) tumors, and BRCA wild-type patients with other defects in the homologous recombination repair pathway. Ovarian cancer is associated with the upregulation of Annexin A2 mRNA expression and is targeted for early stage detection using the Proseek® technology and improvements in CA125 sensitivity and specificity. There are no FDA approved screening tools for detecting early stage ovarian cancer in the general population. Biomarkers for early detection could significantly improve the survival of patients. Niraparib is currently being tested in phase 3 clinical trials as maintenance therapy in ovarian cancer, and PARP inhibitors such as olaparib, rucaparib, and niraparib are used to treat cells with homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). BRCA mutations are predictive markers for response to PARP inhibitors, and BRCA testing is becoming a routine part of evaluating women with ovarian cancer. Tests for HRD are also being used to evaluate PARP inhibitors in an extended population of non-BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer.

nodes.label: Vorasidenib
nodes.description: A potent, oral, brain-penetrant dual inhibitor of both mIDH1 and mIDH2, used for the treatment of low-grade mIDH glioma. It prevents the accumulation of the oncometabolite d-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and has been shown to inhibit 2-HG production in glioma tissue by >97% in an orthotopic glioma mouse model. A therapeutic alternative that exerts potent dual inhibitory activity against mIDH1/2 towards the treatment of low-grade glioma. It is known to have a strong intermolecular interaction with Val255/Val294 within the binding pockets of both mIDH1 and mIDH2, leading to favorable interactions with binding site residues. This results in a high binding free energy of -28.69 kcal/mol and -19.89 kcal/mol towards mIDH1 and mIDH2, respectively. Upon binding, Vorasidenib triggers systemic alterations of mIDH1 and mIDH2 characterized by restricted residue flexibility and a reduction in exposure of residues to the solvent surface area, ultimately inhibiting crucial interactions of the mutant enzymes and suppressing the production of oncogenic stimulator 2-HG.

nodes.label: Teplizumab
nodes.description: A humanized Fc-receptor non-binding anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D). It targets T-lymphocytes that mediate the destruction of insulin-producing β-cells, leading to preserved C-peptide response, decreased exogenous insulin use, and improved glycemic control. Teplizumab has shown promise in slowing the progression of T1D, particularly in the early stages, and reducing the need for exogenous insulin. It is well-tolerated, with mild and self-limiting adverse effects such as a rash being the most commonly reported. Phase III clinical trials are ongoing to confirm these results and determine the optimal dosage and treatment regimen.

nodes.label: Microsporidia
nodes.description: Obligate intracellular parasites whose evolution from within the fungi has been debated, with some molecular phylogenies suggesting a close relationship to fungi while others place them as a sister group to fungi. Sequencing of beta-tubulins from 3 microsporidia, 4 chytrid fungi, and 12 zygomycete fungi supports the idea that microsporidia evolved from a fungus sometime after the divergence of chytrids. Enigmatic unicellular forms that lack mitochondria and are derived from an endoparasitic chytrid ancestor similar to Rozella allomycis, on the earliest diverging branch of the fungal phylogenetic tree. Microsporidia seem to be involved in the evolution of new mechanisms of spore dispersal, such as polar tube eversion. A group of organisms included in the Fungi kingdom, but no further subdivision of the group is proposed. Obligate intracellular, eukaryotic pathogens that infect a wide range of animals from nematodes to humans, and in some cases, protists. They share a particularly close evolutionary relationship with the zygomycetes and have a unique syntenic gene pair (RPS9-RPL21) present in the vast majority of fungi and the microsporidians but not in other eukaryotic lineages. Two other unique gene fusions (glutamyl-prolyl tRNA synthetase and ubiquitin-ribosomal subunit S30) that are present in metazoans, choanoflagellates, and filasterean opisthokonts are unfused in the fungi and microsporidians. A group of obligate intracellular eukaryotic parasites that infect a wide variety of species, including humans. Microsporidia are analyzed using the DarkHorse software for genome-wide analysis, and their genetic relationships are studied through phylogenetic and LPI-based comparisons with other eukaryotic organisms and fungi. The analysis involves 7 Microsporidia species, including Antonospora locustae, Enterocytozoon bieneusi, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Encephalitozoon intestinalis, Nosema bombycis, Nosema ceranae, and Nematocida parisii.

nodes.label: Apalutamide
nodes.description: A next-generation androgen receptor-signaling inhibitor used in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer, contributing to significant improvements in survival and important secondary endpoints. It has been evaluated in phase III placebo-controlled trials for non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. A novel second-generation androgen receptor antagonist approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It has proven clinical efficacy and good compatibility with minimal side effects. A second-generation anti-androgen therapy used for the treatment of nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It has been shown to significantly decrease prostate-specific antigen progression-free survival and increase metastases-free survival compared to placebo. It is associated with a lower hazard ratio for metastases-free survival when compared to placebo, with a value of 0.28 (95% CI: 0.23-0.35). It is considered an effective treatment for high-risk of progression nmCRPC and is supported by equivalent efficacy and similar risk of adverse effects compared to enzalutamide and darolutamide. An androgen inhibitor used to treat prostate cancer, with an effect similar to that of darolutamide in improving metastasis-free survival in men with non-metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer. An antiandrogen therapeutic that entered the clinic in 2018 for the treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). It induces expression of the enzyme aldo-keto reductase 1C3 (AKR1C3) in prostate cancer cells and is susceptible to AKR1C3-mediated resistance. It has a structural analogue, darolutamide. A non-steroidal anti-androgen used in the treatment of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, with a 56% likelihood of maximizing metastasis-free survival according to Bayesian analysis. A drug that may result in improved oncologic outcomes when compared to enzalutamide and darolutamide. A next-generation antiandrogen drug and the active ingredient in ERLEADA, used to treat advanced prostate cancer. It extends survival times and improves quality of life in patients with advanced prostate cancer. One of the other two second-generation AR antagonists approved by the FDA for the treatment of prostate cancer, along with darolutamide. A multiple agent approved for advanced prostate cancer, used for treating the disease. A medication used in the treatment of non-metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC) that has shown improved metastasis free survival (MFS) rates in studies compared to darolutamide and enzalutamide. A medication approved since 2018 for the treatment of men with non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (M0CRPC) in conjunction with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). A next-generation androgen receptor inhibitor used in the management of non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC), which was found to be significantly more effective than placebo and enzalutamide for metastasis-free survival (MFS), and more efficacious for therapy of nmCRPC compared to darolutamide. A novel androgen receptor antagonist used for the treatment of nmCRPC, alongside darolutamide and enzalutamide. It is mentioned in comparison to darolutamide regarding adverse events (AEs). A treatment recommended by the NCCN for nmCRPC, often used in combination with a weighted average androgen deprivation therapy comparator.

nodes.label: NDC1
nodes.description: A gene encoding a membrane-integral nucleoporin found in metazoan nuclear pore complexes. It is also known as hNDC1 in humans and has been identified as the orthologue to yeast Ndc1p/Cut11p. NDC1 is located at the nuclear pore wall and depletion of its human homolog hNDC1 from human HeLa cells interferes with the assembly of phenylalanine-glycine repeat Nups into NPCs. In Caenorhabditis elegans, loss of NDC1 function causes severe NPC defects and high larval and embryonic mortality but is not ultimately lethal, indicating that NPC assembly is fault-tolerant. A gene or protein that is conserved throughout evolution and has a human homologue. It contains six transmembrane segments in its N-terminal half and has a large soluble C-terminal half of approximately 300 amino acids. The N- and C-termini are inferred to be exposed to the cytoplasm based on charge distribution analysis. It is known to be localized to and important in the assembly of both the nuclear pore complex and spindle pole body in yeasts. Its human homologue contains three FG repeats in the C-terminus and is the known inner nuclear membrane protein, NET3. No vertebrate NDC1 protein localizes to nuclear pores like its yeast counterpart is known. A transmembrane nucleoporin that is required for NPC assembly and nucleocytoplasmic transport. It directly interacts with the nucleoporin ALADIN and is essential for targeting of ALADIN to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) and selective nuclear import.

nodes.label: Corticosteroids
nodes.description: A class of steroid hormones used in the treatment of various conditions, including Landau-Kleffner syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple myeloma, and autoimmune-induced liver injury. They are often used in combination with other medications and can be beneficial in managing symptoms such as inflammation, seizures, and skin rashes. However, they may also cause significant side effects and should be administered with caution, especially in high doses or over prolonged periods.

nodes.label: Mitophagy
nodes.description: A selective type of autophagy that involves the degradation of mitochondria, particularly damaged or dysfunctional ones. It is a cellular process involved in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis and function, regulated by a series of key mitophagy regulatory proteins and signaling pathways. Mitophagy is essential for cellular health, mitochondrial turnover, and the elimination of poorly performing mitochondria. It is implicated in various physiological and pathological situations, including stress, aging, and neurodegenerative diseases. Mitophagy is modulated by mitochondrial fission and fusion proteins, BCL-2 family proteins, and the PINK1/Parkin pathway. It is a critical regulator of mitochondrial quality control and elimination of dysfunctional mitochondria to maintain cellular respiration.

nodes.label: Melanocytes
nodes.description: Cells responsible for producing melanin, found in the skin and eyes. They are affected by the deprivation of survival factors, leading to their apoptosis and contributing to the development of vitiligo. Melanocytes are regulated by the Mitf protein in terms of morphology and migration, particularly by regulating cytoskeleton organization and cell-cell adhesion. They are functional cells generated from mouse and human fibroblasts through direct conversion using a combination of transcription factors MITF, SOX10, and PAX3. Melanocytes maintain a gene expression program ensuring appropriate enzymatic conversion of metabolites into the pigment and transfer it to surrounding cells. They are also involved in the development of malignant melanoma, characterized by the presence of the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), which is essential for their existence and maintains its relevance in melanoma as an important regulator of survival and balances melanoma cell proliferation with terminal differentiation.

nodes.label: Bmi-1
nodes.description: A polycomb family proto-oncogene that is consistently required for the self-renewal of diverse adult stem cells and for the proliferation of cancer cells in the same tissues. It promotes stem cell self-renewal by repressing the expression of Ink4a and Arf, and is involved in the regulation of p16INK4a, p14ARF, h-TERT, and c-Myc expression in primary breast carcinomas. Overexpression of Bmi-1 leads to senescence bypass in human fibroblasts and immortalization of human mammary epithelial cells. It is overexpressed in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cell lines and tumors, and its expression positively correlates with poor prognosis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients. Bmi-1 is also involved in the induction of human telomerase reverse transcriptase activity and reduction of p16(INK4a) expression. Mutational analysis shows that both RING finger and helix-turn-helix domains of Bmi-1 are required for immortalization of normal nasopharyngeal epithelial cells.

nodes.label: Metalloproteinases
nodes.description: A family of endopeptidases that require a zinc ion at their active site for proteolytic activity. They include matrilysins, collagenases, stromelysins, gelatinases, membrane MMPs, and other MMPs. They are produced by tumor cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, polymorphonuclear neutrophiles, and endothelial cells. MMPs facilitate tumor growth by promoting tumor cell proliferation, invasion, migration, and angiogenesis. They can also induce an epithelial to mesenchymal transition and support transendothelial migration. MMPs can degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM) to release peptide growth factors, cleave E-cadherins, and support angiogenesis by releasing pro-angiogenic factors.

nodes.label: Angiotensin converting enzyme
nodes.description: An enzyme responsible for converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a peptide that plays an important role in the central regulation of blood pressure and fluid and electrolyte homeostasis.

nodes.label: SPAG5
nodes.description: A gene whose expression was upregulated in NSCLC and is associated with mitotic spindle formation. A gene identified as regulating a module in male breast cancer that is closely associated with proliferation. A gene or protein involved in cervical cancer, specifically sperm-associated antigen 5. It is upregulated in pelvic lymph node metastasis-positive cervical cancer, relates to poor prognosis, and alters sensitivity to taxol treatment via the mTOR signaling pathway. Its expression is detected using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction, western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. Downregulation of SPAG5 inhibits cell proliferation, growth, migration, and invasion, and affects the sensitivity of cervical cancer cells to taxol dose. A sperm-associated antigen 5 protein that has been identified as an oncogene participating in lung cancer and cervical cancer progression. Its expression level is gradually increased in PCa progression and is significantly associated with lymph node metastasis, clinical stage, Gleason score, and biochemical recurrence. SPAG5 knockdown can inhibit PCa cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and suppress tumor growth and metastasis in vivo. It can be targeted by miR-539, leading to a reduction in expression and reversal of the inhibitory effects of miR-539 on PCa cell proliferation and metastasis. A gene whose copy number aberrations, mRNA transcript expression, and protein expression were investigated for their clinicopathological relevance in relation to breast cancer outcomes. In the METABRIC cohort, SPAG5 gene gain or amplification was detected at the Ch17q11.2 locus in 206 (10%) of 1980 patients overall, 46 (19%) of 237 patients with a PAM50-HER2 phenotype, and 87 (18%) of 488 patients with PAM50-LumB phenotype. High SPAG5 transcript and SPAG5 protein concentrations were associated with shorter overall breast cancer-specific survival. A gene or protein that is amplified on chromosome 17q11.2 in breast cancer, and its transcript and protein products are independent prognostic and predictive biomarkers for combination cytotoxic chemotherapy sensitivity, particularly in oestrogen receptor-negative breast cancer.

nodes.label: Regorafenib
nodes.description: A multikinase inhibitor used as a standard option for second-line therapy and beyond in European and U.S. guidelines for RAS- or BRAF-mutated metastatic colorectal cancers (mCRCs) progressing after first-line treatment, based on the results of the randomized phase III CORRECT trial demonstrating improvement in survival. It was administered daily for 3 weeks of each 4-week cycle until disease progression or other reason in the PREVIUM trial. Common grade 3 adverse effects included asthenia, dysphonia, and hypertension.

nodes.label: Obesity
nodes.description: A chronic medical condition characterized by excess body fat, defined by a body mass index (BMI) of ≥ 30 kg/m², which can lead to various health problems including type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular diseases, and certain types of cancer. It is associated with an increased risk of developing dementia, decreased circulating levels of zinc, and altered expression of zinc-regulatory proteins in the brain. Obesity is managed through lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy, and in some cases, weight loss surgery. It is a major public health problem and a global epidemic that contributes to a number of health complications.

nodes.label: Vessel Dilator
nodes.description: Vessel Dilator is a natriuretic peptide that belongs to the family of natriuretic peptides similar to atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). A vessel dilator is a type of natriuretic peptide that is beneficial in the treatment of congestive heart failure (CHF). It enhances urine flow two- to 13-fold and sodium excretion three- to four-fold for 3 hours after stopping its infusion. It also simultaneously decreases systemic vascular resistance by 24%, pulmonary vascular resistance by 25%, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure by 33%, and central venous pressure by 27%, while increasing cardiac output by 34%, cardiac index by 35%, and stroke volume index by 24% in individuals with CHF. A peptide hormone that significantly improves acute renal failure (ARF) in humans and increases urinary flow and sodium excretion in patients with chronic congestive heart failure (CHF). Its effects last for 6 hours and can be used up to four times per day. A substance used for treating acute renal failure, particularly in ischaemic ARF animal models. It decreases serum creatinine levels from 8.2 0.5 to 0.98 0.12 mg/dL in 6 days when ARF has been established for 2 days before treatment. It also promotes regeneration of proximal and distal tubules after 6 days of treatment. In cancer, it, along with LANP and kaliuretic peptide, decreases up to 97% of human breast, pancreatic and prostate adenocarcinoma cells, as well as small cell and squamous cell lung cancer cells within 24 h. In vivo, it, along with LANP and kaliuretic peptide, completely stops the growth of human pancreatic adenocarcinomas in athymic mice and decreases their tumour volume by 49% in 1 week.

nodes.label: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
nodes.description: A species of yeast commonly used as a model organism for scientific research, particularly for studying various aspects of molecular and cellular functions, such as mRNA turnover, DNA replication, histone modifications, and cell cycle regulation. It is also used for comparing with other yeast species like Schizosaccharomyces pombe and for expressing proteins like OsDRM2. The yeast has a protein called POB1 that binds to DNA polymerase alpha and is involved in DNA metabolism. It has been extensively studied for its replicators, replication origins, and replication-initiation proteins, including the F-box protein Dia2 and the Ctf4p. The yeast is often used in genetic studies to identify potential DNA replication accessory factors and replication-initiation proteins. It is commonly used in studies of mitochondrial respiration and eukaryotic DNA replication.

nodes.label: Darolutamide
nodes.description: A structurally unique androgen-receptor antagonist under development for the treatment of prostate cancer, specifically nonmetastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer (nmCRPC). It has been shown to increase metastasis-free survival among men with nmCRPC compared with placebo, and has potential safety, tolerability, and efficacy advantages for men with nmCRPC. Darolutamide is primarily metabolized via oxidative biotransformation catalyzed by CYP3A4 and identified as a substrate for P-gp and BCRP. It is also being evaluated for its effect on pharmacokinetics and safety in patients with nmCRPC, especially in relation to comedications. The introduction of darolutamide was predicted to increase the total budget by $158,640 in year 1, but this decreased over time to a cost savings of $149,240 by year 5.

nodes.label: Whole Chromosome Instability
nodes.description: A condition that induces senescence and promotes SASP, associated with decreased expression of genes controlling chromosome segregation and cohesin functions. It causes DNA double strand breaks and elevated oxidative stress, but results in low apoptosis. The fate of W-CIN cells is determined by down-regulating the spindle assembly checkpoint component BUB1 and the mitotic cohesin SMC1A, and analyzing senescence features such as SAFs. W-CIN cells acquire a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) characterized by IL1B, CXCL8, CCL2, TNF, CCL27 and other pro-inflammatory factors including a novel SASP component CLEC11A.

nodes.label: Idarucizumab
nodes.description: An antibody fragment binding to dabigatran, used to examine the efficacy in a mouse model of OAC-ICH. It prevents excess intracerebral hematoma formation in mice anticoagulated with dabigatran and reduces mortality. A specific antidote developed against direct thrombin inhibitors. A monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity in a 1:1 molar ratio, used for the reversal of the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 1 trial. A drug used to reverse dabigatran-induced anticoagulation, with immediate and complete effects observed in phase 1 results. It was administered in various doses (1 g, 2 g, 4 g, 5 g plus 2·5 g) to different groups of participants, and was found to be well-tolerated with no serious or severe adverse events reported. It was also found to have no clinically relevant difference in incidence of adverse events compared to placebo. A novel molecule that may provide the most effective and safest way of reversal for dabigatran and other anticoagulants. Currently in premarketing studies. An antibody fragment developed to reverse the anticoagulant effects of dabigatran.

nodes.label: Solanezumab
nodes.description: A humanized monoclonal antibody, also known as LY2062430, being studied as a potential disease-modifying treatment for Alzheimer disease. It is administered in single doses of 0.5, 1.5, 4.0, and 10.0 mg/kg. Safety assessments include gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cerebrospinal fluid analyses at baseline and 21 days after dosing. It increases total amyloid beta (Abeta) in both plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, but no changes in cognitive scores were observed. A monoclonal antibody that binds to β-amyloid (Aβ), a protein involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease. It is currently being investigated in Phase III trials as a disease-modifying treatment for AD. Solanezumab can neutralize soluble Aβ peptides and has shown supportive findings in Phase II trials regarding its safety. It also shows promising cerebrospinal and plasma biomarker changes. An anti-Aβ monoclonal antibody used in the EXPanding alzhEimer's Disease InvestigaTIONs (EXPEDITION) studies for patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD). A humanized anti-amyloid β monoclonal antibody developed as a passive immunization treatment to slow the progression of Alzheimer disease. It is administered via intravenous infusion and has been evaluated in clinical studies involving Japanese and white patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer disease. A monoclonal antibody in clinical trials for Alzheimer's disease, targeting a specific antigen epitope of Abeta. Its anti-amyloid activity is distinct from other antibodies like bapineuzumab, ponezumab, gantenerumab, BAN2401, gammaguard, and octagam. A humanized anti-Aβ monoclonal antibody used in the development of passive immunization strategies for Alzheimer's disease. It targets the midregion of the Aβ peptide and has shown neutralization of soluble Aβ species. Phase II studies have documented a good safety profile, while studies on cerebrospinal and plasma biomarkers have documented good signals of pharmacodynamic activity. An immunotherapeutic agent designed to remove the neurotoxic amyloid β42 protein and prevent amyloid β42-induced neurotoxicity and neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease. Two Phase III trials in AD patients failed to meet endpoints when analyzed independently, but analysis of pooled data from both trials showed a significant reduction in cognitive decline in mild AD patients. It is associated with an increase in plasma amyloid-β (Aβ) levels and a low incidence of ARIA in solanezumab-treated patients. An antibody used as an analog for comparative studies with aducanumab. Its binding properties are directly compared to those of aducanumab to understand their differences in targeting Aβ aggregates. A drug used in a randomized, placebo-controlled, multi-arm trial for dominantly inherited Alzheimer's disease. It engaged its Aβ target but did not demonstrate a beneficial effect on cognitive measures compared to controls. The solanezumab-treated group showed a greater cognitive decline on some measures and did not show benefits on downstream biomarkers.

nodes.label: Metformin
nodes.description: A glucose-lowering agent used for over 40 years in the management of type 2 (noninsulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus, typically reducing basal and postprandial hyperglycaemia by about 25% in more than 90% of patients when given alone or coadministered with other therapies including insulin. Metformin counters insulin resistance and offers benefits against many features of the insulin resistance syndrome by preventing bodyweight gain, reducing hyperinsulinaemia and improving the lipid profile. It does not increase insulin secretion or cause serious hypoglycaemia compared to sulphonylureas. Treatment with metformin from diagnosis also offers greater protection against the chronic vascular complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The most serious complication associated with metformin is lactic acidosis, which has an incidence of about 0.03 cases per 1000 patient-years and a mortality risk of about 0.015 per 1000 patient-years. Major contraindications include impaired renal function, congestive heart failure, hypoxic states, and advanced liver disease. Gastrointestinal adverse effects, notably diarrhoea, occur in less than 20% of patients and remit when the dosage is reduced. Life-threatening risks associated with metformin are rare and could mostly be avoided by strict adherence to the prescribing guidelines. A biguanide medication used for managing Type 2 Diabetes. It was approved in 1995 and accounted for approximately 33% of prescriptions by 2001. A biguanide commonly used in type 2 diabetes, considered safe with minimal side effects. It can cause severe lactic acidosis, especially in patients with renal failure. There is only one reported case of pancreatitis associated with metformin, which was secondary to metformin poisoning and occurred in a patient with renal failure. A pharmacotherapy used as an alternative treatment for impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG), demonstrated to decrease the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in clinical trials. An older oral antidiabetic agent used in the treatment of diabetes, mentioned in the text as a comparison to thiazolidinediones and sulfonylureas. A drug that was not found to differ in use based on race/ethnicity or other demographic variables in the study. An oral glucose-lowering drug used in the management of Type 2 Diabetes. It belongs to the class of biguanides and is commonly used as a first-line therapy. A well-established ingredient of diabetes management, both as a monotherapy in early stages of type 2 diabetes and as adjunct therapy to virtually every other antihyperglycemic medicine available today. It has low potency and a long list of contraindications but remains successful and even expanded experimental use due to its well-established effects on glucose metabolism and benefits on other cardiovascular risk factors. Unlike insulin and secretagogues, metformin does not increase body weight and when used as monotherapy does not likely cause hypoglycemia. The most common adverse effects associated with metformin are mild, transient gastrointestinal symptoms, which are usually self-limiting. These side effects can be minimized by initiating metformin therapy at a low dose and gradually titrating upward, and by taking metformin with meals. Lactic acidosis caused by metformin is rare, and the risk of this complication may be diminished by the observance of prescribing precautions and contraindications that avoid accumulation of metformin or lactate in the body. It has made metformin a preferred combination drug with other oral agents. A commonly prescribed oral hypoglycemic drug used for about 50 years, representing the universal first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes (T2DM). It addresses insulin resistance but not beta-cell dysfunction. When combined with vildagliptin, it offers additive efficacy and complementary mechanisms of action without increasing the risk of hypoglycemia or promoting weight gain. A first-line drug treatment for type 2 diabetes, Metformin is known to cause digestive side-effects such as diarrhoea and vomiting in around 30% of patients. It affects glucose, vitamin B12, and the digestive uptake of bile salts in healthy individuals. Metformin also acts locally in the colon by modifying glucose cell metabolism. Despite various proposed pathophysiological hypotheses, no adequate explanation has been found for its digestive side-effects, and experimental data to explain these patient-dependent adverse effects is lacking. An oral antidiabetic drug used in the management of type 2 diabetes. It is often used as a monotherapy or in combination with other antidiabetic drugs like dapagliflozin. Dapagliflozin has been shown to be noninferior to glipizide in terms of glycaemic control after 52 weeks when used as add-on therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes that is inadequately controlled with metformin. An antidiabetic drug known to be rarely associated with lactic acidosis, a serious condition with a poor prognosis. It was the most frequently associated drug with lactic acidosis in the assessed period. It is reported to cause 18.2% of all 650 adverse drug reactions reported to the national authority. A drug used for glycemic control in patients with T2DM, which had similar effects to Exenatide QW for most goals in treatment-naive patients. A glucose-lowering agent commonly used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, often prescribed as monotherapy or in combination with other glucose-lowering agents. Patients with type 2 diabetes may not tolerate metformin, in which case dapagliflozin can be used as an alternative. A biguanide group oral antidiabetic drug used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and anorexia. It is not recommended for patients with certain risk factors such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, and renal and liver failure. It can cause lactic acidosis, a serious side effect. A commonly used oral hypoglycaemic agent worldwide, known to cause gastrointestinal side effects and lactic acidosis. Long-term use can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency. A medication used as a treatment for type 2 diabetes, often used in combination with sitagliptin as add-on therapy. A commonly prescribed medication used in the treatment of Type 2 diabetes. It is known for its effectiveness in reducing mortality and managing blood sugar levels, but it also has potential adverse effects such as gastrointestinal disorders and lactic acidosis. Its use is recommended as first-line therapy for Type 2 diabetes, although the evidence supporting its efficacy is considered weak. It is less likely to cause hypoglycaemia and does not affect body weight. A drug used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, known to reduce mortality and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality when used as monotherapy. It can cause vitamin B12 deficiency leading to macrocytic anaemia or peripheral neuropathy, and carries a risk of interactions with drugs that impair renal function, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and iodinated contrast media. Renal failure can lead to metformin accumulation and an increased risk of lactic acidosis. Its adverse effects have been extensively studied and are acceptable provided renal function is monitored, especially in situations in which patients are at risk of kidney failure. The harm-benefit balance of metformin monotherapy remains favourable in most patients with type 2 diabetes when dietary measures alone are not sufficient. An anti-type 2 diabetes mellitus drug used in the evaluation of its effects on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of tofogliflozin in healthy male volunteers. A commonly used medication for the treatment of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), often serving as the first-line therapy before considering additional drugs like GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). A commonly used oral antidiabetic drug, often prescribed as the first-line treatment for Type 2 diabetes (T2DM). It is typically used in combination with other antidiabetic drugs such as sulphonylureas (SUs) or dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors when glycaemic control with metformin monotherapy deteriorates. A widely used oral anti-diabetes agent, with considerable benefits over other therapies, but can cause gastrointestinal side effects in 20-30% of people, and 5% are unable to tolerate it due to the severity of these side effects. A biguanide-class drug used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. It increases plasma lactate levels in a plasma concentration-dependent manner by inhibiting mitochondrial respiration predominantly in the liver. It has been contraindicated in moderate and severe renal impairment since its FDA approval due to the risk of toxic metformin levels and metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA). However, the reported incidence of lactic acidosis in clinical practice is very low (<10 cases per 100,000 patient-years). An investigational delayed-release formulation is under development for patients with renal impairment. A medication used to manage type 2 diabetes, specifically affecting metformin plasma levels and the risk of MALA. A commonly prescribed initial oral antihyperglycemic drug for patients with type 2 diabetes, recommended by all clinical guidelines. It is a glucose-lowering medication that helps manage blood sugar levels. An antidiabetic drug that is compared with DPP4i in terms of their risks of cardiovascular diseases and hypoglycemia. A medication used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) that has been compared to other drugs like DPP4i and pioglitazone in terms of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk and other side effects. Metformin users had significantly lower risks for composite CVD risk, myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), and hypoglycemia as compared to DPP4i users. A glucose-lowering agent used in combination with dapagliflozin as a background therapy for T2DM. A biguanide antidiabetic drug used to treat type 2 diabetes, often prescribed as an add-on therapy to insulin in type 1 diabetes patients. It helps lower blood glucose levels by reducing hepatic glucose production and improving insulin sensitivity. A medication used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, particularly in elderly patients. It is available in different doses such as 1000 mg/d, 1500 mg/d, and 2000 mg/d. A medication used for treating diabetes, associated with the development of metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA). It is prescribed judiciously by physicians to prevent MALA development and pay close attention to lifestyle changes in patients at risk for MALA during the COVID-19 pandemic. A widely prescribed medication for the treatment of type II diabetes mellitus. Common gastrointestinal side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and heartburn. It can cause a rare but serious side effect called metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA), which is more commonly reported in patients with chronic renal failure. The first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus for more than 60 years. Associated with metformin-associated lactic acidosis, which is defined as metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate levels in the presence of metformin. A medication used as the first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus, according to the American Diabetes Association. It is considered safe with minimal adverse effects, but can cause gastrointestinal issues. In high doses, it can lead to metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA), especially in patients with kidney dysfunction. A biguanide drug that is the most commonly used first-line medication for type 2 diabetes mellitus due to its outstanding glucose-lowering ability. It peaks at a plasma concentration of approximately 20-30 μM in 3 hours after oral administration of 1 g, mainly accumulating in the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and kidney. Metformin exerts its beneficial or deleterious effect through multiple mechanisms, including AMPK-dependent and several AMPK-independent mechanisms such as restoring redox balance, affecting mitochondrial function, modulating gut microbiome, and regulating signals like FBP1, PP2A, FGF21, SIRT1, and mTOR. A medication used as the first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus. It has been identified as the main driving factor behind the association between low vitamin B12 status and T2DM. It can affect serum vitamin B12 concentrations and may serve as a potential risk assessment tool for vitamin B12 screening in patients with T2DM. A medication used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes, associated with significantly higher risks of incident cellulitis, recurrent cellulitis, foot infections, and amputation compared to no-use in patients with type 2 diabetes. A medication used in the management of type 2 diabetes, known for being safe, effective, and inexpensive. It is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency and is commonly used in Vietnamese patients with type 2 diabetes. The study evaluated the rate of vitamin B12 deficiency in patients treated with metformin and identified factors such as duration of diabetes, duration of metformin use, metformin dose, and hemoglobin levels that are statistically associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. After adjusting for covariates, a metformin dose greater than the median dose remained the only parameter associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. Long-term use of metformin (48 months or more) and a high metformin dose (1000 mg/day or more) are at high risk of experiencing vitamin B12 deficiency and require screening. A widely prescribed, oral, anti-diabetic agent used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM2). It can accumulate in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) or chronic kidney disease (CKD), leading to potentially life-threatening complications such as metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA). It can cause severe hyperkalemia and severe lactic acidosis. A widely used drug in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, known for its dose-dependent blood sugar-lowering effect. It has a positive correlation with the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency when the duration of administration and daily dose increase. Metformin also has immunomodulatory properties, such as anti-inflammatory actions, and can improve insulin sensitivity, potentially reducing the risk of tumor growth in certain cancers. It may have antiviral effects through mechanisms like blocking angiotensin converting enzyme 2 receptor. Potential clinical applications include inflammatory diseases, autoimmune diseases, cancer, and coronavirus disease 2019. A medication used as the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and weight reduction. It has also been shown to be effective in managing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), liver cirrhosis, and various carcinomas such as hepatocellular, colorectal, prostate, breast, urinary bladder, blood, melanoma, bone, skin, lung. Metformin enhances liver health through several mechanisms including reducing reactive oxygen species, nuclear factor kappa beta (NF-κB), liver enzymes, improving insulin sensitivity, and improving hepatic cell lipophagy. However, long-term use of metformin may cause adverse effects like lactic acidosis and gastrointestinal disturbance, and a long-term overdose may lead to a rise in hydrogen sulfide in liver cells. A class of antidiabetic drugs included in the study to investigate the association between sarcopenia and various antidiabetic drugs. The reported odds ratio (ROR) and information component (IC) were analyzed to evaluate the association between sarcopenia and metformin. An oral antihyperglycemic agent approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. It does not enhance insulin secretion and typically does not cause hypoglycemia. Metformin decreases preprandial and postprandial blood glucose concentrations through increased skeletal muscle glucose uptake, reduced gluconeogenesis, and decreased glucose absorption. When combined with maximum dosages of a sulfonylurea, it can synergistically improve glucose control. Potential benefits include weight loss, improved blood flow in patients with peripheral vascular disease, reduced tissue plasminogen activator inhibitor, and improved lipid profiles. Common side effects include gastrointestinal issues like nausea, diarrhea, and anorexia, a metallic taste, and vitamin B12 malabsorption. Lactic acidosis is a rare side effect, especially if metformin is avoided in patients with contraindications to its use. It is generally safe when taken appropriately and may be considered for initial treatment in obese patients who fail dietary measures or cannot tolerate or respond to maximum dosages of sulfonylureas. An antihyperglycemic agent used in the treatment of type II diabetes, with a mean bioavailability of 50-60%. It is eliminated primarily by renal filtration and secretion and has a half-life of approximately 6 hours in patients with type II diabetes. Although the half-life of metformin is prolonged in patients with renal impairment, no specific dosage adjustments have been recommended. This agent has no effect in the absence of insulin. Metformin is as effective as the sulfonylureas in treating patients with type II diabetes and has a more prominent postprandial effect than the sulfonylureas or insulin. When combined with a sulfonylurea, metformin has been shown to exert antihyperglycemic effects in addition to the sulfonylurea with which it is combined. Metformin decreases absorption of vitamin B12 and folic acid, although reported cases of megaloblastic anemia are rare. Cimetidine decreases the elimination of metformin; therefore, the manufacturer recommends a reduced metformin dosage when these agents are combined. A drug commonly used for managing patients with poorly controlled postprandial hyperglycemia, known for its greater postprandial effect compared to sulfonylureas. It has been used in Canada, Great Britain, and the rest of Europe for more than 30 years and was approved for use in the US in December 1994. Metformin is recommended as a first-line agent, especially for obese or hyperlipidemic patients.

nodes.label: Doxycycline
nodes.description: Doxycycline is an antibiotic prescribed in combination with benzoyl peroxide for 3 months to treat the skin lesions caused by EGFR inhibitors. It is effective in managing the rash in patients. A compound used to suppress transgene expression in the rTgTauEC mouse model. Its administration from 18 to 24 months led to the reversal of AChE sprouting, resolution of Gallyas-positive and Alz50-positive NFTs, and abrogation of progressive neuronal loss. An antibiotic used for causal therapy of Borrelia burgdorferi infection, resulting in the disappearance of erythema migrans and psoriasis lesions. A second-generation tetracycline antibiotic with a similar chemical structure and comparable antibacterial spectrum to minocycline. Has shown activity against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infections. Also exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, neuroprotective, immunomodulatory, and other non-antibiotic effects. A type of oral tetracycline used for the treatment of SSTIs in adult outpatients, known for its common mechanisms of resistance, susceptibility profiles, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics.

nodes.label: Contrave
nodes.description: A bupropion and naltrexone combination therapy for the potential treatment of obesity, developed by Orexigen Therapeutics Inc. It is an oral, sustained-release combination of the dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake antagonist bupropion and the opioid antagonist naltrexone. Preliminary data from phase III clinical trials have shown placebo-subtracted weight losses of 3 to 7% and improvements in obesity-related comorbidities and cardiovascular risk factors. The primary adverse effect leading to discontinuation of treatment was nausea.

nodes.label: Pendred syndrome
nodes.description: An autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by sensorineural deafness, goiter, and a partial defect in iodide organification, caused by biallelic mutations in the SLC26A4 gene, which encodes pendrin, a multifunctional anion exchanger. It may lead to thyroid functional disorders of hypothyroidism and is associated with anatomical anomalies requiring a complex clinical evaluation involving endocrine and audiological examinations, radiological diagnostic imaging, and molecular studies of the SLC26A4 gene for complete and accurate diagnosis.

nodes.label: DNA methylation
nodes.description: A biological process involving the addition of a methyl group to the cytosine residue in DNA, specifically at the 5-position, and also to deoxyadenosine residues in DNA. It is a major epigenetic mechanism that regulates long-range gene silencing, genomic imprinting, and transposon silencing. DNA methylation is catalyzed by a family of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), including DNMT 1, DNMT 3a, and DNMT 3b. It plays essential roles in genomic imprinting, gene expression, and embryogenesis, and is involved in the regulation of gene expression and genomic stability. Dysregulation of DNA methylation is associated with various diseases, including cancer, and is influenced by factors such as mutations in DNMT3B and polymorphisms in the DNMT3B gene. DNA methylation is also involved in the transcriptional silencing process, facilitated by the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene, and disruptions in this process can contribute to the phenotypic manifestations of Rett syndrome.

nodes.label: Melanoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that arises from melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing melanin in the skin. It is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of melanocytes and can lead to the formation of tumors. Melanoma cells require the expression of the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) for their development and survival, and are managed by immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).
