They can present themselves with different responses to therapy in the melanocytic (MEL) and the mesenchymal-like (MES) cell states, and can undergo phenotype switching into highly migratory and drug-tolerant dedifferentiated states. Melanoma can arise from mutations that accumulate in melanocyte stem cells, and its mechanisms can be investigated using in vitro differentiation systems of melanocytes from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells). SOX10 has been linked to melanoma initiation and progression, but the molecular mechanisms by which SOX10 guides the appropriate gene expression programs necessary to promote the melanocyte lineage are not fully understood. Melanoma tumor cell lines require wild-type SOX10 expression for proliferation, and SOX10 haploinsufficiency reduces melanoma initiation in the metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (Grm1(Tg)) transgenic mouse model. Stable loss of SOX10 in human melanoma cells leads to cell-cycle arrest, altered cellular morphology, and induction of senescence. Melanoma-initiating cells (MICs) and the anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 contribute to its resistance to single drug BH3 mimetic therapy. The role of Dynamin-Related Protein 1 (DRP-1) in melanoma is being investigated to better understand its regulation of the apoptotic pathway. Melanoma is a solid tumor that has shown significant therapeutic benefits from checkpoint inhibitors like CTLA-4 and PD-1 targeted treatments, and is one of the most immunogenic tumors but can evade anti-tumor immune responses by exploiting tolerance mechanisms, including negative immune checkpoint molecules. It is used as an example to showcase the potential of immuno-oncology therapies to replace conventional radiotherapy regimens.

nodes.label: [18F]altanserin
nodes.description: A radioactive PET ligand used to identify and characterize radiometabolites in the 5-HT2A receptor, with specific applications in positron emission tomography (PET) studies for evaluating 5-HT2A receptor binding and density in humans and animals. It undergoes metabolic processes in plasma, with 38.4% of total plasma activity deriving from unchanged [18F]altanserin 90 minutes after bolus injection. It is a ligand with high affinity for the 5-HT2A binding site and is used as a tracer for 5HT2 receptors binding studies, with selective displacers to test reversibility and selectivity.

nodes.label: Friedreich's ataxia
nodes.description: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a triplet guanine-adenine-adenine (GAA) repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene, leading to decreased levels of the frataxin protein and affecting the formation of iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster prosthetic groups for various metabolic enzymes. It is characterized by a GAA triplet repeat expansion within the frataxin gene, resulting in ataxic gait, cardiomyopathy, and spastic paraplegia. The disease is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS), and neurodegeneration. Current therapeutic options focus on improving mitochondrial function and increasing frataxin expression through pharmacological interventions but are not effective in delaying or preventing neurodegeneration in clinical trials.

nodes.label: Ustekinumab
nodes.description: A fully human IgG1κ monoclonal antibody that targets the common subunit p40 of IL-12 and IL-23, used to treat various immune-mediated inflammatory diseases such as moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. It is administered subcutaneously in doses of 45 or 90 mg as two injections 4 weeks apart, or once every 12 weeks for maintenance therapy. Adverse events are generally mild and the drug is well tolerated in clinical trials.

nodes.label: Trypanosoma brucei
nodes.description: A species of trypanosomatid parasite that causes African trypanosomiasis in humans and domestic animals, with two subspecies, gambiense and rhodesiense. It is an extracellular parasite transmitted to humans through the bites of infected tsetse flies and causes serious neurological disorders if left untreated. T. brucei has a single flagellum that plays important roles in many aspects, especially in the viability of the bloodstream form T. brucei. It has a single flagellum that plays important roles in many aspects, especially in the viability of the bloodstream form T. brucei. The flagellar motility is required for the viability of the bloodstream form T. brucei, suggesting that impairment of the flagellar function may provide a promising cure for African sleeping sickness. It is a parasitic organism that has led to the development of various treatments with important limitations such as acute toxicity and parasite resistance. T. brucei is also used in the study of spliceosomal proteomics, RNA splicing factors, respiratory complex subunits, and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) network.

nodes.label: Ubiquitination
nodes.description: A tightly regulated post-translational modification process involving the covalent linking of the small 76-amino acid protein ubiquitin to target proteins, serving as a signal for various outcomes including proteasomal degradation, endocytosis, lysosomal degradation, or cellular localization specification. It is a versatile tool used by all eukaryotic organisms for controlling the stability, function, and intracellular localization of a wide variety of proteins, often in conjunction with other modifications such as phosphorylation. Ubiquitination is a key regulatory step in target selection and not completely congruent with proteasomal degradation. It involves a series of E1, E2, and E3 enzymes that can ligate ubiquitin to cellular proteins, dictating the turnover of a substrate and the outcome of signaling events such as DNA damage repair and cell cycle. The process is dynamic and reversible, involving the action of deubiquitination enzymes (DUbs) that play diverse and critical roles in cells. Proteins destined for degradation by the proteasome or by lysosomes are deubiquitinated prior to their degradation, allowing ubiquitin to be recycled by the cell, contributing to the steady-state pool of free ubiquitin. Dysfunctional ubiquitination can result in severe diseases.

nodes.label: Insomnia
nodes.description: A sleep disorder characterized by difficulty falling or staying asleep, or both, often affecting adults and pediatric patients, especially those with neurodevelopmental disorders. It can lead to significant annual lost productivity and has been linked to an increased risk of hypertension and vascular diseases. Insomnia can be treated with various medications, including melatonin receptor agonists, small-molecule orexin receptor antagonists, and suvorexant, which helps decrease wakefulness by counteracting orexin activity. The globus pallidus externus (GPe) is a potential target for deep brain stimulation (DBS) to treat insomnia and motor disorders caused by basal ganglia dysfunction.

nodes.label: EGFR
nodes.description: EGFR is a gene and protein involved in various types of cancer, including glioblastoma, colorectal cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is a proto-oncogene and an oncogene commonly overexpressed in malignant gliomas and lung adenocarcinoma. EGFR has a tyrosine kinase domain that is targeted by inhibitors like erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, and neutralizing antibodies like cetuximab and bevacizumab. The T790M mutation within the EGFR gene makes patients resistant to erlotinib and gefitinib. EGFR is also involved in the development of resistance to lorlatinib in NSCLC cells, and its hyperactivation can be blocked by erlotinib to restore sensitivity to lorlatinib. Additionally, EGFR is a molecular target associated with colorectal cancer and is involved in the pharmacologic effects of necitumumab in patients with advanced solid malignancies. It is also co-localized with Receptor mediated endocytosis 8 (RME-8) on early endosomes, indicating their association in endosomal compartments.

nodes.label: Pexidartinib
nodes.description: A selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor against CSF1R, approved by the US FDA in August 2019 for the treatment of adult patients with symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) associated with severe morbidity or functional limitations and not amenable to improvement with surgery. It is a potent inhibitor of CSF1R, KIT, and FLT3, and is being investigated in various malignancies as monotherapy or combination therapy. Pexidartinib has shown an 83% disease control rate, with 52% partial response and 31% stable disease in a recent phase 1 study of patients with TGCT. It is administered as a loading dose of 1000 mg per day orally for the first 2 weeks, followed by 800 mg per day for 22 weeks in the double-blind study part, and then for all patients in the open-label study part. It has been associated with mixed or cholestatic hepatotoxicity, which is an identified risk. Currently available only through a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) Program in the USA.

nodes.label: Phenylketonuria
nodes.description: A genetic disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) in the liver, leading to increased L-phenylalanine in blood, mental retardation, and hypopigmentation of skin and hair. It is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder characterized by the expression of specific genes and can be treated with gene therapy involving the delivery of a human PAH transgene using an adeno-associated virus vector. Phenylketonuria is managed through lifelong dietary restriction of phenylalanine, but this presents problems of adherence for patients. Alternative therapies under investigation include gene therapy to provide copies of wild-type phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) enzyme. It is one of the most common inborn errors of metabolism, affecting around 700,000 people globally and has been managed with a low phenylalanine diet since the 1950s. Mutations in the gene coding for hepatic phenylalanine hydroxylase cause this deficiency, leading to elevated plasma phenylalanine concentrations, cognitive impairment, neuromotor disorders, and related behavioral symptoms.

nodes.label: Hyperthyroidism
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by an overactive thyroid gland, leading to increased metabolic rate and various physiological symptoms. The mutant mice exhibit features of hyperthyroidism, such as decreased body weight, elevated heart rate, raised body temperature, obesity, and skeletal alterations. A condition characterized by the overproduction of thyroid hormones, specifically triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4). It can be further classified into T4+T3 toxicosis and T3 toxicosis. A medical condition characterized by excessive production of thyroid hormones, caused by genetic and environmental factors, and associated with increased risk when polygenetic scores are present. It can be influenced by metabolic parameters and nutritional intakes. A disease characterized by an increased production of thyroid hormones, associated with a higher risk in individuals with high Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) involved in inflammation and immunity, especially when accompanied by low dietary intakes of energy, calcium, seaweed, milk, or coffee.

nodes.label: NF-κB
nodes.description: A protein involved in regulating the expression of a large number of genes involved in inflammation. It plays a key role in the orchestration of the multifaceted inflammatory response, not only in the first pro-inflammatory phase, but also later in the regulation of the resolution of inflammation, when anti-inflammatory genes are expressed and apoptosis is induced. It has two pathways: the canonical, mediated by the p65 and p50 subunits, and the non-canonical, mediated by the subunits RelB, p52 and p50. It is a target for modulating inflammatory responses and can be targeted through various technologies such as small molecules, peptides, or nucleic acids. A protein whose expression is inhibited by oprozomib in dendritic cells. It is involved in the new mechanism of action of proteasome and immunoproteasome inhibitors in DC. A pleiotropic transcription factor present in the cytoplasm of resting cells, associated with inhibitor κB. Upon stimulation by activators such as proinflammatory cytokines and bacterial or viral products, it undergoes phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation, translocates to the nucleus, and regulates the transcription of various genes essential for processes like the immune response, the cell cycle, and apoptosis. It is a good target for poxviral immunomodulation due to its role in these processes.

nodes.label: DNA Methylation
nodes.description: A biological process involving the addition of a methyl group to the cytosine base in DNA, which can lead to changes in gene expression. In human cancer, tumors typically have reduced levels of genomic DNA methylation and contain hypermethylated CpG islands, while normal tissues show overall similar DNA methylation patterns. A major epigenetic modification that plays a crucial role in the regulation of gene expression. It involves the addition of a methyl group to the cytosine residue in DNA, which can affect gene expression without changing the underlying DNA sequence. This process is regulated by DNA methyltransferases such as Dnmt3a, 3b, and 1. Specific epigenetic event that regulates transcription of both rRNA- and mRNA-encoding loci. It is part of the epigenetic mechanisms that control the transcription of ribosomal and mRNA genes in nucleoli and the surrounding non-nucleolar region. A biological process involving the addition of a methyl group to the cytosine base of DNA, particularly at CpG dinucleotides, which plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and maintaining genomic stability. An epigenetic modification involving the addition of a methyl (-CH(3)) group to the cytosine residue in CpG dinucleotides, mainly catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). It plays a crucial role in genomic imprinting, regulating monoallelic expression of imprinted genes, and affecting placental function and embryonic/fetal development. A common DNA modification involving the addition of a methyl group to cytosine (5-methylcytosine (5-mC)), which can occur in CpG dinucleotides and is implicated in the acquisition of the T790M mutation in EGFR codon 790.

nodes.label: Klinefelter's syndrome
nodes.description: A specific syndrome associated with a variety of different sex chromosome anomalies including XXY, XXYY, XXXY and XXXXY. The lastnamed variant is the only one that frequently presents features distinguishing it from the others. A chromosomal abnormality characterized by the presence of an extra X chromosome, denoted as 47, XXY, and is the most common chromosomal aberration associated with chromosomal abnormalities. A disease characterized by a 47,XXY chromosomal pattern, associated with physical abnormalities and potentially involving the X chromosome in the aetiology of schizophrenia. A sex chromosome abnormality affecting approximately 1 in 1000 men, characterized by a higher than average prevalence of sexual offending. It has been suggested that it is associated with an increased risk of sex offending, but research evidence supporting this assertion is limited. The study aimed to conduct a systematic review of published research to establish the prevalence of sexual offending in men with Klinefelter's syndrome. The databases MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE were searched from inception until 31 December 2016 using a range of terms for Klinefelter's syndrome and for sexual offending. All selected papers were examined for quality using the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist. The study identified 53 relevant papers, of which 10 met the inclusion criteria, with all but one being prevalence studies conducted in a prison or hospital setting. The remaining study was a Danish register-based cohort study suggesting an increased risk of sex offending among Klinefelter men, probably established before the diagnosis was made and, therefore, any hormone replacement instituted. There is insufficient evidence to date to support concerns about exceptional risk of sex offending among men with Klinefelter's syndrome. A genetic disorder characterized by an additional X chromosome in males, resulting in a karyotype of 47,XXY. It is associated with an increased risk of certain malignancies, including leukemia, breast cancer, and extragonadal germ cell tumors such as mediastinal germ cell tumors and rarely intracranial germ cell tumors. A genetic disorder characterized by the presence of an extra X chromosome, leading to hormonal imbalances and developmental issues. It is associated with the development of a gonadotropin-secreting tumor and a mediastinal teratocarcinoma in affected individuals.

nodes.label: Atrial fibrillation
nodes.description: A type of arrhythmia characterized by irregular and often rapid heart rate, specifically involving the atria of the heart. It is associated with an increased risk of stroke, especially in patients with a history of previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is an independent risk factor of potentially catastrophic cardioembolic strokes. Patients with AF are often treated with direct oral factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban to reduce the risk of stroke or systemic embolism. It is associated with increased risk of stroke and is the focus of several clinical trials and studies, including ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, and ENGAGE-AF. Atrial fibrillation is a cardiovascular disease associated with comorbid chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The risks of stroke and mortality associated with COPD among patients with atrial fibrillation are not well understood.

nodes.label: Alpha-synuclein
nodes.description: A protein involved in the formation of Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease, which can accumulate in the brains of Parkinson's disease patients and mutations in this gene are associated with familial forms of the disease. The protein exists in various forms, including wild-type, Ala30Pro, and Ala53Thr, and can be fused with enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) for study. It can be truncated to a 27-kDa form upon transfection into mouse cultured primary neurons and can form inclusions when treated with proteasome inhibitors or when its carboxy-terminus is modified by an epitope tag. A protein that can form aggregates leading to the formation of cytoplasmic inclusions, and its carboxy-terminus, when manipulated, can induce inclusion formation, providing a model for studying the pathogenic mechanisms of alpha-synuclein aggregation in Lewy bodies. A protein that appears to be an important structural component of Lewy bodies, point mutations in the alpha-synuclein gene have been linked to rare cases of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. A protein that is a primary component of the fibrillar neuronal inclusions, known as Lewy bodies, which are diagnostic of Parkinson's disease. It forms via discrete beta-sheet-rich oligomers, or protofibrils, and has a gene associated with familial PD. Mutations in this gene can accelerate formation of protofibrils, and changes in cytoplasmic protein concentration could potentially promote formation and stabilization of alpha-synuclein protofibrils. The major component found in Lewy bodies, a protein involved in various cellular processes. It is used as a reference for co-enrichment analysis with other proteins identified in the LB-enriched sample. A protein that forms fibrillar aggregates in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy. It exists in monomeric and oligomeric forms, with soluble oligomers being the pathogenic species leading to neurodegeneration and neuronal cell death. A 140 aa presynaptic protein that belongs to a group of natively unfolded proteins which are unstructured in aqueous solutions. It has two variants studied in the text, the wild-type (WT) protein and A30P. The aggregation rate of Alpha-synuclein is accelerated in the presence of physiological levels of cellular polyamines. A protein that forms the major component of Lewy bodies, Lewy neurites, and filamentous inclusions in multiple system atrophy, Parkinson's disease, and dementia with Lewy bodies. It is involved in the pathogenesis of alpha-synucleinopathies.

nodes.label: Hyperphosphorylated tau
nodes.description: A condition where tau protein is excessively phosphorylated, leading to its polymerization and formation of neurofibrillary tangles. It is associated with low PP2A activity and observed in Alzheimer's disease models. A protein species involved in the pathology of Alzheimer's disease, forming neurofibrillary tangles and neuropil threads, often accompanied by soluble Aβ oligomers. A modification of tau protein characterized by excessive phosphorylation, which contributes to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease. A pathological feature observed in patients with PLA2G6 mutations, supporting a link between PLA2G6 mutations and parkinsonian disorders. A state of tau protein where it is abnormally phosphorylated, found in affected neurons of Alzheimer disease brain. It can be dephosphorylated by protein phosphatases such as protein phosphatase-1, 2A, and 2B in vitro. A condition where tau, the major component of the paired helical filaments of Alzheimer's disease, accumulates in the brains of mice due to the disruption of the calcineurin A alpha gene. This leads to cytoskeletal changes and affects learning and memory.

nodes.label: Radiomic features
nodes.description: Features extracted from computed tomography (CT) scans in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, including 17 tumor intensity statistical features, 16 shape features and 38 textural features. These features are evaluated for their reproducibility and redundancy using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and hierarchical clustering. Features with ICC values greater than 0.75 are considered reproducible. Features extracted from magnetic resonance imaging that can aid in the generation of prediction models for personalized medicine. The robustness of these features is evaluated in a phantom study under various conditions such as signal to noise ratio, region of interest delineation, voxel size change and normalization methods. Many features are found to be non-robust to changing parameters.

nodes.label: Calcium
nodes.description: A mineral supplement and essential nutrient for various physiological processes, often found in dairy products and supplements. It promotes bone health, supports mitochondrial function, and has been implicated in the management of renal lithiasis and colorectal cancer risk. Calcium supplements may raise the risk for cardiovascular disease and kidney stones. It is recommended to meet the daily intake requirement through a calcium-rich diet, with supplements only taken if necessary to reach the RDA goal.

nodes.label: Ixodes ricinus
nodes.description: The most important tick species in Europe, widely distributed and responsible for transmitting the majority of tick-borne zoonotic pathogens. It has bimodal activity patterns with a major peak in the spring. Larvae, nymphs, and adults were collected monthly over 3 consecutive years in Hungary for pathogen screening. A species of tick that serves as a vector for many pathogens of medical and veterinary relevance in Europe, including Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato and tick-borne encephalitis virus. Questing nymph and adult stages were collected at 11 sites in Western Switzerland for this study. A species of tick collected from four locations in the north of the Upper Palatinate in Bavaria for investigation of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato (s. l.). A species of tick that is one of the main vectors for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato in Estonia. It was found to have a lower prevalence of Borrelia infection compared to I. persulcatus, with 8.2% in the studied tick populations. A species of hard tick found in European red squirrels (Sciurus vulgaris) in France, with higher abundance in spring to summer than in autumn to winter. The most important tick species in France, responsible for transmitting Lyme Borreliosis spirochetes. A tick species used in the study to investigate the fate of Coxiella burnetii within putative tick vectors. Adults of this species successfully fed in the feeding system with engorgement rates ranging from 29% to 64%. Nymphs of this species also participated in the study, and 25% of them showed transstadial transmission to the adult stage after feeding on inoculated blood. Females that molted from nymphs fed on inoculated blood excreted C. burnetii of up to 106 genomic equivalents per mg of feces.

nodes.label: BCNU wafer implantation
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the implantation of BCNU wafers during repeat resection for recurrent glioblastoma. It is associated with minor to moderate increases in rates of select complications compared to non-implantation.

nodes.label: Anaplastic astrocytoma
nodes.description: A subtype of astrocytoma with more aggressive behavior compared to low-grade astrocytomas. Can progress to glioblastomas. A type of glioma with a higher frequency of p53 mutations (64.3%) compared to glioblastoma multiforme (25.9%). It is one of the genetic pathways leading to GBM, characterized by a 'progressive' mutation in the p53 gene. A subtype of astrocytoma, characterized by its higher grade of malignancy compared to low-grade astrocytomas. It is a type of glial cell tumor that originates in the supporting cells of the brain called astrocytes. A type of astrocytoma from which secondary glioblastomas can progress, typically affecting younger patients. A type of brain tumor characterized by intermediate growth rate between glioblastoma multiforme and anaplastic oligodendroglioma. It is associated with neurological symptoms and can be diagnosed through CT/MRI imaging. Treatment outcomes include complete response, partial response, stable disease, and progressive course. A type of malignant glioma, which is a primary malignant brain tumor. It is part of the broader category of malignant glioma along with glioblastoma. A grade III astrocytic glioma, intermediate in aggressiveness between low-grade astrocytomas and glioblastomas. It is characterized by increased cell division rate and larger tumor size compared to low-grade astrocytomas.

nodes.label: PTEN
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene located on chromosomal band 10q23, also known as MMAC1 or TEP1. Mutations in PTEN have been detected in various types of gliomas and glioneuronal tumors, with a higher frequency in glioblastomas compared to lower grade gliomas. PTEN mutations were found in 20 out of 142 glioblastomas, 1 out of 7 giant cell glioblastomas, 1 out of 2 gliosarcomas, 1 out of 30 pilocytic astrocytomas, and 2 out of 22 oligodendrogliomas. No PTEN mutations were detected in 52 astrocytomas, 37 oligoastrocytomas, three subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, four pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas, 15 ependymomas, 16 gangliogliomas, and one dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor. Additionally, homozygous deletions of the PTEN gene were detected in 7 glioblastomas that did not have PTEN mutations. PTEN is involved in the AKT pathway, and its downregulation contributes to abnormal nucleus pulposus cell proliferation in intervertebral disc degeneration. It is a lipid phosphatase with a consensus sequence related to the active sites of tyrosine phosphatases, dual-specificity protein phosphatases and the myotubularin family of proteins. PTEN mutations have been studied in glioblastoma cell lines, specifically in the 42MGBA and T98G cell lines, using AAV-mediated gene editing. Correcting PTEN mutations resulted in reduced cellular proliferation, which was Akt-dependent in 42MGBA cells and Akt-independent in T98G cells. PTEN is a known tumor suppressor gene associated with primary glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and located on chromosome 10q. It is involved in the genetic profile of diffuse gliomas and is often mutated or deleted in glioblastoma. PTEN mutations have a dominant-negative effect, suggesting that the aberrant function of PTEN mutation might be more disastrous than deletion, the most frequent genomic event in GBM. PTEN deletions are more prevalent in high-grade gliomas and tend to occur concurrently with CDKN2A deletions.

nodes.label: Qi-Wei-Du-Qi-Wan
nodes.description: A traditional Chinese medicine used to treat chest tightness, cough, shortness of breath, night sweats, frequent urination and asthma in Asia. It is composed of 7 ingredients and has been used in the treatment of asthma for hundreds of years. It exerts an anti-asthmatic effect by inhibiting mast cell degranulation and significantly reduces Der p-induced airway hyperreactivity (AHR), total serum IgE and Der p-specific IgE levels. It also reduces inflammatory cell infiltration and sputum secretion from goblet cells in the lungs, and overproduction of IL-12、IFN-γ、IL-13、IL-4、RNATES、Eotaxin and MCP-1 in lung.

nodes.label: MutL
nodes.description: A protein involved in both methyl-directed mismatch repair (MMR) and very short-patch (VSP) repair in Escherichia coli, sharing functional roles with MutS and MutH. A protein involved in the mismatch repair system (MMR), having homologues widely conserved in almost all organisms. It promotes the endonuclease activity of ttMutS2 at low concentrations. A key protein involved in mismatch recognition within the mismatch repair system (MMR) of Deinococcus radiodurans. Inactivation of MutL leads to similar effects as those observed with MutS1 in-activation. A protein involved in the MMRS of Escherichia coli, acting sequentially with MutS and MutH. The study shows that the mutL gene from Pseudomonas aeruginosa is capable of complementing a MutL-deficient strain of E. coli, and has conserved 21 out of the 22 amino acids known to affect functioning of E. coli MutL. It also interacts specifically with E. coli MutH through its C-terminal region. A protein involved in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) and very-short patch (VSP) repair, interacting with the Vsr repair endonuclease through its N-terminal domain. It forms a complex with MutS and participates in the activation of MutH upon DNA mismatch detection. A component of the MutH-independent MMR system, often associated with DNA mismatch repair. Its knockout results in MMR-deficient strains with similar mutational frequencies and specificity to those with minitransposon insertions in BAS4289. A gene product involved in the mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, specifically in the methyl-directed long patch repair system in Escherichia coli. It is one of three gene products, along with MutS and MutH, that are conserved in higher eukaryotes.

nodes.label: Glycolysis
nodes.description: A metabolic pathway where cells produce energy by breaking down glucose without the need for oxygen, primarily involving the production of ATP. It can be facilitated by mitochondria-to-nucleus retrograde signaling in response to mitochondrial dysfunction and is a major producer of ATP in podocytes, especially in the cortical area of these cells. Glycolysis is also a secondary method by which the heart produces ATP, providing a smaller amount compared to mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. It is a metabolic process involved in energy production, which shifts from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in pulmonary hypertension (PH), particularly in cancer cells initially described and in the context of mitochondrial alterations in PH. Glycolysis is targeted for cancer treatment through manipulation of OXPHOS genes or adjustment of metabolites production in mitochondria. It is a metabolic pathway used by Trypanosoma brucei to produce ATP in the mammalian host, and a biochemical process utilized by trypanosomes that is of particular interest in the search for new antitrypanosonal drugs due to its unique characteristics.

nodes.label: Epirubicin
nodes.description: A moderately emetic chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of various types of cancer, including breast cancer, administered at doses of 120 mg/m2 or 100 mg/m2, often in combination with other drugs and growth factor support (G-CSF). It is an anthracycline drug found to be as effective as doxorubicin at equimolar doses but significantly better tolerated, especially in terms of alopecia, leucopenia, and cardiac toxicity. Epirubicin is a component of the FEC 75 chemotherapy regimen and has been used for treating left breast carcinoma.

nodes.label: Becker muscular dystrophy
nodes.description: A type of muscular dystrophy that is characterized by myopathic abnormalities, associated with an intellectual developmental disorder (IDD) with a global prevalence of 8%, and caused by mutations in the dystrophin (DMD) gene. It is a less severe form of muscular dystrophy compared to Duchenne muscular dystrophy, characterized by the production of internally-deleted dystrophin and an asymptomatic phenotype. It is diagnosed through molecular analyses such as MLPA and whole gene sequencing, and computational algorithms are used to evaluate the impact of DNA variants on mRNA splicing and protein functionality. The diagnostic algorithm used has proven to be accurate for the molecular diagnosis of dystrophinopathies.

nodes.label: LMNA gene
nodes.description: A gene located on chromosome 1q11-q23 that causes both the autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms of Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy when mutated. It has been localized on chromosome 1q11-q23 for the autosomal dominant form and has also been found to be responsible for the less frequent autosomal recessive form of the disease. A gene located on chromosome 1q21, encoding lamin A/C proteins that are located in the inner surface membrane of the nucleus. Mutations in this gene cause autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (AD-EDMD). A novel point mutation of Ser303Pro was found in exon 5 of this gene in the first Japanese case of AD-EDMD. A gene that encodes the intermediate filament protein lamins A and C, which constitute the major scaffolding protein of the inner nuclear membrane. Mutations in the LMNA gene are responsible for the most common etiology of autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD). Animal modeling has helped to identify different mechanisms of disease associated with LMNA gene mutations, including loss of LMNA function leading to nuclear fragility and other defects such as abnormal nuclear function. A gene encoding LaminA and C, mutations in which cause the autosomal dominant form of Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD). A gene that encodes lamins A and C and is responsible for autosomal forms of laminopathies, usually with a dominant transmission. Involved in various conditions such as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, cardiomyopathy, and neuropathy. A gene associated with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, mutations in which can cause the disease, particularly in X-linked and autosomal-dominant forms. A gene encoding lamin A/C, which is involved in the causation of autosomal EDMD2 when mutated. It is located on the autosomal chromosome and is associated with muscle weakness and cardiac abnormalities.

nodes.label: Type 2 diabetes
nodes.description: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to insulin resistance or relative insulin deficiency, often associated with metabolic syndrome. It is managed through various therapeutic interventions, including medication like metformin, dietary changes, and lifestyle modifications. Type 2 diabetes is associated with the human intestinal fatty acid binding protein 2 (FABP2) gene and is influenced by polymorphisms in the FABP2 promoter region. It is a common chronic condition that typically develops after the age of 40 and is often associated with obesity. It is a health complication associated with obesity and is one of the many negative consequences of the disease, along with cardiovascular disease, cancer, and neuropsychiatric disorders. It is treated with medications like sitagliptin, glipizide, insulin glargine, and metformin, and is managed with the use of the combination product Juvisync. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors like Teneligliptin are used to improve glycemic control with a minimal risk of hypoglycemia and weight gain. Rosiglitazone and metformin are commonly used in its treatment, as are metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors like Teneligliptin. It is a progressive disease characterized by impaired glycaemic control, often managed with pharmacotherapy such as sulphonylureas (SUs) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors. It is associated with similar changes in urinary pH, net acid excretion, and ammonium in 24-h urine collections at baseline, even after controlling for dietary factors, and an increased risk for uric acid nephrolithiasis.

nodes.label: Excess Body Weight
nodes.description: A condition characterized by a body mass index (BMI) of 25.00 kg/m2 or higher, which is an established risk factor for diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. It is also associated with an increased risk of certain cancers, such as esophageal adenocarcinoma, kidney, gastric cardia, liver, colon, and gallbladder cancers. The prevalence of excess body weight in Canada has contributed to a substantial cancer burden, particularly in the Prairies (excluding Alberta) and the Atlantic region.

nodes.label: Locally advanced rectal cancer
nodes.description: A stage of rectal cancer characterized by the tumor's localization in the rectum, which is advanced enough to require neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery. It is typically defined by the presence of tumors that have grown beyond the rectal wall but have not yet spread to distant sites in the body. Patients with this condition are often indicated for neoadjuvant concomitant chemoradiotherapy and may be included in clinical trials such as the CoCStom trial. The disease is further classified into stages II, III, and IV, with 4 patients having stage II, 109 having stage III, 15 having stage IV, and 2 unknown stages. It is a type of cancer affecting the rectum that has not spread beyond the rectal wall but has progressed to nearby tissues, and it is treated with preoperative chemoradiation (CRT) followed by surgery approximately 6 weeks later.

nodes.label: Alu
nodes.description: A type of short interspersed repeat element (SINE) found in the human genome, derived from the 7SL RNA gene. In the studied dataset, over 98% of 923,277 Alus were unique when queried at full length, and 97% were still found to be a single copy when the criterion was reduced to half the length of the repeat. A short interspersed repeat element (SINE) derived from the 7SL RNA gene, which exists in the cytoplasm as non-coding RNA and is actively transcribed. It has a bipartite promoter sequence and a poly-A tail for transcription, and its expression is analyzed in the provided text. A type of mobile element that originated in an initial duplication of the 7SL RNA gene prior to the primate-rodent split about 80 million years ago. Alu elements have been selectively retained in the upstream and intronic regions of genes of specific functional classes. They have also shown similar biases in their distribution across functional classes in the human and mouse genomes. A cellular protein that binds small cytoplasmic RNAs in vitro. It is a sequence-homologous interspersed element of unknown function that has expanded in the genomes of humans. A minority of its sequences are expressed as small cytoplasmic RNAs. These RNAs have conserved a secondary structure motif present in signal recognition particle (SRP) RNA despite substantial sequence divergence. A family of repetitive elements in the human genome, related to B1 repeats through a common ancestor. The hypothesis of the monophyletic origin of Alu and B1 repeats suggests that both families originated from a common 7SL RNA-derived retroposing monomeric element.

nodes.label: Koebner phenomenon
nodes.description: The Koebner phenomenon refers to the development of isomorphic pathological lesions in distant wounds of patients with pre-existing cutaneous diseases. It is more frequent in patients with psoriasis but can also occur in the presence of other cutaneous pathologies. A medical condition characterized by the appearance of psoriatic lesions in the uninvolved skin of psoriatic patients as a consequence of trauma. It has been described in numerous diseases and its pathogenesis is not fully understood. Research has focused on identifying possible causes, predisposing and provoking factors, type, site, depth and degree of trauma, the all or none phenomenon, time lag, site preference, medications, inhibition of koebnerization and reverse koebnerization. A well-known entity in dermatology characterized by the formation of psoriatic lesions in uninvolved skin of psoriatic patients after cutaneous trauma. It was first described by Heinrich Koebner in 1876 and is now known to involve numerous diseases such as vitiligo, lichen planus, and Darier disease. The pathogenesis is still obscure but may involve cytokines, stress proteins, adhesion molecules, and autoantigens.

nodes.label: N-Ras
nodes.description: One of the three isoforms of the Ras protein, N-Ras is involved in promoting oncogenesis when mutationally activated at specific codons. It is a small GTPase protein that plays a role in regulating extracellular matrix synthesis, proliferation, and migration in fibroblasts. N-Ras is localized to the Golgi and associated with rasosomes, and it requires farnesylation or geranylgeranylation at the C-terminal CAAX box for proper membrane targeting and activity. It is one of the four highly related isoforms coded by the Ras gene family, along with H-Ras, K-Ras4A, and K-Ras4B, and is expressed in mammalian cells. N-Ras is part of the signaling pathways that control eukaryotic cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation, and it is subject to site-specific regulatory mechanisms, effector pathways, and diverse genetic programs. It is not explicitly described in terms of monoubiquitination or activation mechanisms.

nodes.label: Triple Negative Breast Cancer
nodes.description: A diverse and heterogeneous group of tumors that lack estrogen and progesterone receptors and amplification of the HER-2 gene. They are highly malignant, affecting primarily young patients, and only a subset responds favorably to conventional chemotherapy. The prognosis for this subtype is generally poor, with limited data available from India. A highly aggressive subtype of breast cancer with high grade, limited treatment options, and very poor prognosis. Incidence is higher in the country compared to the western literature and varies in different regions. Significantly associated with young aged patients. There was no association between tumor size and lymph node positivity. A type of breast cancer that represents approximately 15-20% of breast cancers. It is characterized by the absence of oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and amplification of the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) gene. TNBC is an heterogeneous group of tumours with a distinctly aggressive nature, higher rates of relapse, and shorter overall survival in the metastatic setting compared with other subtypes of breast cancer. Currently, cytotoxic chemotherapy is the only treatment option for TNBC due to the absence of well-defined molecular targets. A type of breast cancer (BC) that does not express the oestrogen and the progesterone receptors and the human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 (HER2). It is characterized by the absence of positive markers for classification and is the most aggressive form of breast carcinomas. Clinical and epidemiological data suggest that it may represent multiple clinical entities rather than a single disease. It is associated with tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and has implications for prognosis and treatment response.

nodes.label: Trastuzumab Deruxtecan
nodes.description: An antibody-drug conjugate used as a potential treatment for metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer. It has been associated with a high objective response rate and long median progression-free survival in phase II trials, but also causes serious side effects in some patients. An antibody-drug conjugate consisting of an anti-HER2 antibody, a cleavable tetrapeptide-based linker, and a cytotoxic topoisomerase I inhibitor. It has shown efficacy in patients with HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer. In a phase 2 trial, it was compared to chemotherapy in patients with HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer, with an objective response reported in 51% of the patients in the trastuzumab deruxtecan group compared to 14% in the physician's choice group (P<0.001). The most common grade 3 or higher adverse events were a decreased neutrophil count, anemia, and decreased white-cell count. A next-generation antibody-drug conjugate composed of a monoclonal anti-HER2 antibody and a topoisomerase I inhibitor, an exatecan derivative (DX-8951f), which has shown favorable outcomes in HER2-positive heavily pretreated breast cancer patients and promising efficacy in patients with HER2-negative/low-expressing disease. It was granted accelerated approval by the US Food and Drug Administration for advanced or unresectable HER2-positive breast cancer pretreated with at least two HER2-targeting treatment lines based on recent clinical trials.

nodes.label: Gaucher's disease
nodes.description: A rare inherited inborn error of metabolism caused by mutations in the gene encoding the lysosomal enzyme glucocerebrosidase, GBA. It involves the metabolism of the lipid metabolism-derived substrate, glucocerebroside. The accumulation of glucocerebroside substrate in macrophages due to loss of enzyme function leads to the formation of Gaucher cells, causing hypertrophy of the spleen and liver, hematological disorders, skeletal malformations, and neurological symptoms. The disease is subdivided into three types that differ in their symptoms, severity, and prognosis. Patients of any age can be affected but those of a younger age have a poor prognosis often dying in infancy. As a genetic disorder, the incidence of the disease is variable on a global scale. Enzyme replacement therapy is the therapy of choice and has demonstrated good efficacy in treating the visceral and skeletal symptoms of Gaucher's disease. A rare autosomal-recessive disorder due to a confirmed lysosomal enzyme (glucocerebrosidase) deficiency, characterized by clinical features such as splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, bone events including avascular necrosis, bone infarct, or pathological fracture, splenectomy, and Parkinson's disease. It has four types: type 1, type 2, perinatal-lethal type, and type 3. The birth incidence rate is estimated at 1/50,000, and the prevalence at 1/136,000.

nodes.label: SLC26A4
nodes.description: A gene associated with thyroid function abnormalities, mutations in which lead to larger thyroid volume, higher serum thyroglobulin levels, and greater radioiodine discharge after perchlorate compared to patients without mutations. The gene responsible for encoding pendrin, a new anion exchanger involved in iodide transport by thyrocytes and regulating ion and fluid transport by the endolymphatic sac epithelium. Defects in this gene can lead to Pendred syndrome. A gene that encodes pendrin, an anion exchanger located in the cochlea, thyroid, and kidney. Mutations of SLC26A4 cause an enlarged vestibular aqueduct, nonsyndromic deafness, and deafness as part of Pendred syndrome. A gene encoding pendrin, a protein involved in the development of Pendred syndrome. Mutations in this gene, specifically biallelic mutations, cause Pendred syndrome. The text describes the sequencing of this gene and identifies two mutations, one novel (p.T537P) and one recurrent (p.H723R), in a compound heterozygous state in a patient with Pendred syndrome. A gene encoding the multifunctional anion transporter protein pendrin, associated with Pendred syndrome through biallelic mutations. A gene encoding pendrin, a transporter accomplishing anion exchange, expressed in inner ear, thyroid gland, kidneys, lung, liver and heart. Mutations of this gene underlie Pendred syndrome.

nodes.label: SOX9
nodes.description: A transcription factor located near the susceptibility locus on chromosome 17q24.3, involved in defining the astroglial cell fate and expressed almost exclusively by astrocytes in the adult brain, except for ependymal cells and neurogenic regions. It is also expressed by neural progenitor cells and reactive astrocytes in various settings. SOX9 is used as a nuclear marker to identify astrocytes and serves as an astrocyte-specific nuclear marker in all major areas of the CNS outside of the neurogenic regions. It activates astrocyte genes in combination with NFIA and oligodendrocyte genes in combination with SOX10 during maturation. SOX9 expression is regulated by PITX1, with increased expression observed during early astrocyte differentiation.

nodes.label: NBEAL2
nodes.description: A gene that encodes a BEACH/ARM/WD40 domain protein and is mutated in gray platelet syndrome (GPS), causing defects in the biogenesis of platelet α-granules. NBEAL2 is expressed as a unique combination of transcripts in megakaryocytes and platelets from individuals with GPS. It localizes to the dense tubular system (endoplasmic reticulum) in platelets. A gene encoding a BEACH protein involved in the development of platelet α-granules and vesicular trafficking. Mutations in this gene cause gray platelet syndrome. A gene responsible for gray platelet syndrome, mutations in which lead to macrothrombocytopenia and deficiency of alpha (α)-granules in platelets. It has two alleles, and biallelic mutations are associated with almost complete absence of platelet α-granules. A gene that, when mutated, can lead to mild laboratory abnormalities in platelet phenotype. A protein involved in the biogenesis of platelet α-granules, acting independently of VPS33B/VPS16B at a later stage of α-granule biogenesis in Nbeal2(-/-) mice. A gene that encodes a multidomain scaffolding protein with a putative role in granule ontogeny in human platelets. Mutations in this gene underlie gray platelet syndrome (GPS).

nodes.label: GDAP1
nodes.description: A gene associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, specifically involved in the development of both axonal and demyelinating forms of the disease. Mutations in this gene can lead to various phenotypes including axonal, demyelinating, and intermediate forms in autosomal recessive Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease patients and a later disease onset and milder phenotypes in autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease patients. A gene associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, particularly in its autosomal dominant form (ADCMT). Mutations in GDAP1 can lead to both ADCMT and ARCMT, although the latter is less common. GDAP1 mutations are involved in ganglioside-induced differentiation, affecting mitochondrial morphology and function. A gene associated with recessive intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (RI-CMT).

nodes.label: ARISTOTLE trial
nodes.description: A randomized controlled trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), with a particular focus on subgroups of patients with and without previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). The trial enrolled 18,201 patients at 1034 clinical sites in 39 countries between December 19, 2006, and April 2, 2010. The primary efficacy outcome was stroke or systemic embolism, analyzed by intention to treat. The primary safety outcome was major bleeding in the on-treatment population. The median duration of follow-up was 1.8 years (IQR 1.4-2.3). The trial demonstrated that apixaban is superior to warfarin for reduction in stroke or SE risk in patients with AF.

nodes.label: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
nodes.description: A heterogeneous group of genetic motor and sensory neuropathies, which can be further classified into demyelinating and axonal forms based on the primary site of damage. It is a common neurogenetic disorder characterized by heterogeneity, posing challenges for genetic diagnostics. It can be classified into different types based on electrophysiological criteria, such as very slow motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) (<15 m/s), slow MNCV (15-25 m/s), intermediate MNCV (25-45 m/s), and normal MNCV (>45 m/s). It can also be divided into dominant (DI-CMT) and recessive types (RI-CMT) based on inheritance pattern. Several genes are associated with different types of CMT, including GJB1 with X-linked DI-CMT, MPZ, INF2, DNM2, YARS, GNB4, NEFL, and MFN2 with autosomal DI-CMT, and GDAP1, KARS, and PLEKHG5 with RI-CMT. The GDAP1 gene mutation Glu222Lys is associated with a certain trait of inheritance in CMT disease.

nodes.label: Sickle cell anemia
nodes.description: A genetic blood disorder caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene, leading to the replacement of glutamic acid residue by valine at the sixth position of the beta-chain of hemoglobin. This results in the formation of sickle hemoglobin, which polymerizes inside red blood cells under low oxygen tension, causing a drastic decrease in red cell deformability and micro-vascular occlusion, potentially leading to serious crises.

nodes.label: Oculocutaneous albinism type 1
nodes.description: An autosomal recessive genetic disorder affecting both the eyes and skin, characterized by reduced or absent melanin production due to mutations in the tyrosinase gene (TYR). It is associated with various clinical findings, including primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) and affects the eye developmental process. The disorder is divided into two subtypes, OCA1A and OCA1B, with different prevalence rates among patients. Mutations in the tyrosinase gene were found in 47% of patients, while no mutations were identified in 53% of patients. The most serious and common type of Oculocutaneous albinism, characterized by defects in melanin production.

nodes.label: DMD
nodes.description: A form of Duchenne muscular dystrophy characterized by severe muscle weakness and degeneration, occurring in 90.6% (423/467) of patients with gene deletion and duplication. A shorthand term for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The study focused on predicting LV dysfunction and the timing for echocardiography in patients with DMD. A progressive wasting disease of skeletal and cardiac muscles, representing one of the most common recessive fatal inherited genetic diseases with a yearly incidence of 1:3500-1:5000. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene that encodes the membrane-associated dystrophin protein. Equivalent to Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The genetic abbreviation for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a common lethal muscle-wasting disorder affecting young boys caused by mutations in the DMD gene. A rare, genetic disease caused by mutations in the DMD gene resulting in an absence of functional dystrophin protein. It is another name for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a common inherited disease with a worldwide incidence of 1 in 3,500 male births, characterized by mutations in the dystrophin gene leading to deletions of one or more exons in over 65% of patients.

nodes.label: Cephalothoracopagus
nodes.description: A rare variety of conjoined twins where they are fused with their heads, thoracic and upper abdominal cavities.

nodes.label: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
nodes.description: A heritable connective tissue disorder characterized by joint pain, swelling and instability, spinal deformity, and various musculoskeletal problems. It includes various types such as classic, hypermobility, vascular, kyphoscoliotic A/B, arthrochalasis A/B, dermatosparaxis, and a recessive form caused by tenascin-X deficiency. The disease is caused by mutations in genes encoding fibrillar collagens and collagen-modifying proteins, leading to impaired biosynthesis and enzymatic modification of collagen. It can present with clinical overlap with Marfan syndrome and be associated with mutations in the FBN1 gene. Diagnostic investigation often involves biopsy of the skin. The rare vascular type (Ehlers-Danlos type IV) is associated with spontaneous innominate artery pseudoaneurysm rupture and requires accurate diagnosis and tailored management. The disease involves a COL3A1 gene mutation and can lead to arterial rupture, vascular fragility, and death from vascular rupture or bowel perforation.

nodes.label: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
nodes.description: A disease characterized by abnormal thickening of the heart muscle, specifically the left ventricle, often leading to progression towards dilation, left ventricular dysfunction, and refractory heart failure. It can be familial, affecting multiple family members, and is associated with mutations in various genes such as phospholamban promoter region, alpha-myosin heavy chain (alphaMyHC), TNNC1, and beta-myosin heavy chain. It is also associated with myocardial fibrosis and can lead to sudden cardiac death. In some cases, it can be caused by a single R403Q missense allele for cardiac alpha-myosin heavy chain.

nodes.label: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration
nodes.description: A heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by neurodegeneration associated with brain iron accumulation, involving mutations in the PLA2G6 gene. Clinical features include progressive cognitive and motor skill regression, axial hypotonia, four limb spasticity, bulbar dysfunction, strabismus, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, optic atrophy, and changes consistent with increased iron deposition in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Brain imaging demonstrates cerebellar cortical atrophy and gliosis. Novel corpus callosum changes are also reported. A group of neurodegenerative disorders including conditions known as atypical neuroaxonal dystrophy, Karak syndrome and early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism with cognitive impairment, caused by recessively inherited mutations of the PLA2G6 gene.

nodes.label: Osteoporosis
nodes.description: A disease characterized by decreased bone density and strength, leading to an increased risk of fractures. It is more prevalent in postmenopausal women and can be exacerbated by increased bone turnover. Treatment options include pharmacological agents such as bisphosphonates, hormone replacement therapy, selective estrogen receptor modulators, and calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Osteoporosis is a significant public health issue with a high prevalence and is managed through various therapeutic agents and lifestyle modifications.

nodes.label: Diabetes
nodes.description: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to defects in insulin production, action, or both. It is a major risk factor for various health conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, cardiovascular diseases, and certain types of cancer. Diabetes is managed through various treatments, including lifestyle modifications, medications, and insulin therapy. It is a significant global health issue, especially in aging populations and those with changing lifestyles. Certain medications, such as those used to treat hypertension, can increase the risk of its development. Diabetes is also associated with other medical conditions, such as obesity, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.

nodes.label: Dyskeratosis congenita
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by premature telomere shortening, caused by mutations in the telomerase complex genes DKC1, TERC, TERT, and NOP10. It can manifest in different forms due to these mutations. An inheritable bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by reticulated hyperpigmentation, dystrophic nails and oral leukoplakia. Also known as Zinsser-Cole-Engman syndrome. Hematologic manifestations usually do not appear in childhood but later in early adulthood. Patients are also prone to carcinomas, particularly of the head and neck. The disease has X-linked or autosomal dominant/recessive inheritance. Early childhood variants (Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome) are associated with immunological abnormalities in the form of low T- and B-cell numbers. Four genes, namely DKC1 (codes for dyskerin), TERC and TERT (code for telomerase) and NOP10, have been implicated in the pathogenesis; the short telomeres provide a marker for genetic linkage studies. Treatment options include androgens, with or without granulocyte colony stimulating factor, and stem cell transplantation from matched sibling donor, which requires modified nonmyeloablative conditioning protocols due to the patients' predisposition to pulmonary and hepatic complications. A multisystem inherited syndrome exhibiting marked clinical and genetic heterogeneity, characterized by mucocutaneous abnormalities, bone marrow failure, and a predisposition to cancer. It is principally a disease of defective telomere maintenance, with patients usually having very short telomeres. It has been unified with several other disorders, including Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson and Revesz syndromes, as well as a subset of patients with aplastic anemia, myelodysplasia, leukemia, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This wide spectrum of diseases can be regarded as disorders of defective telomere maintenance, known as 'the telomereopathies'.

nodes.label: Cohesin
nodes.description: A protein complex involved in organizing mammalian genomes into chromatin loops and topologically associated domains, playing important roles in gene regulation and recombination. It binds to specific sequences defined by CTCF and can be loaded onto DNA elsewhere before extruding chromatin loops until encountering CTCF-bound DNA. Its recruitment to CTCF sites is not fully understood. It accumulates at transcription start sites of active genes and in regions at 3'-ends of active genes in the absence of CTCF and Wapl, suggesting its relocation by transcription or Wapl-mediated release. A complex that topologically encircles chromosomes, mediating sister chromatid cohesion for accurate chromosome segregation during cell division. It also participates in DNA repair and gene transcription. Its binding is maximal at replication origins and extends outward to occupy active genes and regulatory sequences.

nodes.label: Postmenopausal osteoporosis
nodes.description: A major public health problem in aging women, characterized by a high burden related to the consequent fractures. It is a type of osteoporosis that affects women after menopause, which can be prevented and treated through interventions such as estrogen replacement, selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), or bisphosphonates. It involves monitoring bone mineral density (BMD) and considering risk factors for treatment decisions. It is a disorder characterized by decreased bone mass and density, which can be prevented by the use of bisphosphonates like alendronate and ibandronate. It is more common in women after menopause and is the focus of the study evaluating the effects of denosumab. It is a condition characterized by changes in bone metabolism and clinical complaints, not a well-defined disease but summarizing women with different severities, with the only common feature being the deficiency of estrogen.

nodes.label: Prostate cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the prostate gland, characterized by the presence of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels ranging from 1 to 78 ng/ml and clinical stages B, C, and D. It can have higher, similar, or lower levels of CB compared to stefin A, with higher levels potentially indicating an aggressive variant. Prostate cancer cases with Gleason histologic scores between 3 and 10 can exhibit aggressive variants, even though higher scores are typically associated with more aggressive forms. The disease is characterized by the presence of cancerous cells in the prostate gland and is associated with upregulation and overexpression of DVL1, a human counterpart of the Drosophila dishevelled gene, and alterations of the DVL1 gene. The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is involved in its carcinogenesis, and DVL1 overexpression may contribute to its progression. Prostate cancer can progress through four stages: prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, well-differentiated tumors, early poorly differentiated tumors, and late poorly differentiated tumors. It is studied in the transgenic adenocarcinoma of mouse prostate (TRAMP) model and involves various stages of disease progression, including primary prostate cancers and metastatic prostate cancer, which exhibit different patterns of DNA hypomethylation and CpG island methylation. Prostate cancer has two grades: low-grade and high-grade. Finasteride has been found to reduce the incidence of low-grade prostate cancer but paradoxically increase high-grade cancer due to increased sensitivity and improved performance of prostate specific antigen levels to detect all grades of prostate cancer. Ubc9 expression is increased in primary tumors compared to their normal tissue counterparts and decreased in metastatic tumors compared to their corresponding normal and primary adenocarcinoma tissues. Aloe-emodin suppresses prostate cancer progression by targeting mTORC2. Prostate cancer is a heterogeneous disease where the previous concept of 'hormone resistance' has been changed by a new generation of hormonal therapies that have proven efficacy in the castration-resistant setting. Androgens play a crucial role in the whole clinical course of prostate cancer, even when a patient meets castration-resistance criteria. The development of abiraterone showed how important and clinically meaningful can be to achieve the lowest possible levels of testosterone, and androgen receptor overexpression, mutation, or enhanced crosstalk with other pathways, which can also be targeted with new agents tested in the last few years. Prostate cancer is being treated with Orteronel, a novel hormonal therapy that inhibits the 17,20 lyase activity of the enzyme CYP17A1, important for androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenal glands and prostate cancer cells. Clinical trials have shown that Orteronel treatment leads to reduced prostate-specific antigen levels and more complete suppression of androgen synthesis than conventional therapies. Adverse events include fatigue and febrile neutropenia when used in combination with docetaxel. Prostate cancer is also characterized by the presence of androgen-independent prostate cancer (AIPC) and androgen-dependent prostate cancer (ADPC) subtypes, with AIPC showing lower miR-26a expression compared to ADPC. The Gleason score remains the most reliable prognosticator in men with prostate cancer. Prostate cancer patients have significantly lower scores in moderate activity and total physical activity compared to the control group, and higher scores for kinesiophobia and the total kinesiophobia score. The FACIT-F and total FACT-P score are significantly lower in PCa than the control, and kinesiophobia negatively affects patients' functional status and overall quality of life.

nodes.label: Tick-borne pathogens
nodes.description: A group of pathogens transmitted by ticks, including bacteria (Anaplasma, Rickettsia, Coxiella, and Borrelia), protozoa (Babesia and Theileria), and viruses (Orthonairovirus, tick-borne encephalitis virus, and louping ill virus) that affect wildlife and domestic animals in Europe. Some of these pathogens are zoonotic and can cause serious, sometimes fatal, problems in human health.

nodes.label: Parkin
nodes.description: A protein that is recruited to damaged mitochondria by PINK1 during mitophagy. It ubiquitinates a broad range of outer mitochondrial membrane proteins, leading to the degradation of damaged mitochondria through autophagy. A gene or protein that regulates mitochondrial quality control reactions, including the autophagic removal of depolarized mitochondria (mitophagy), and is mediated by protein ubiquitinations which may be counteracted by deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs). It is overexpressed in HeLa cells and its translocation to depolarized mitochondria is studied after siRNA-mediated silencing of each DUB. A ubiquitin ligase that is recruited by the mitochondrial protein kinase PINK1 upon activation, participating in the regulation of mitophagy pathways, particularly in response to mitochondrial depolarization in mammalian cells. A gene or protein that functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, primarily known for its role in regulating the removal of defective mitochondria via mitophagy. It has been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics, and mitochondria-derived vesicle formation. Parkin is commonly described as a cytosolic E3 ubiquitin ligase but has also been detected in other cellular compartments, including the nucleus, where it regulates transcription factors and acts as a transcription factor itself. Overexpression of Parkin has been demonstrated to delay ageing, protect against cellular senescence and neurological disorders associated with ageing, and suppress tumour growth. A core component of the mitophagy process, mutations in which are linked to Parkinson's Disease. It is involved in the PINK1/Parkin pathway during stress-induced mitophagy, and has been studied in vitro in different cell types. It is also implicated in the circadian control of mitochondrial physiology. A protein involved in the mitophagy process, specifically in the ubiquitination of damaged mitochondria for degradation. Its expression is significantly increased after intracellular infection with Staphylococcus aureus in bovine macrophages. A protein that is recruited by PINK1 to the outer mitochondrial membrane in healthy individuals, activating it to attach ubiquitin proteins to the mitochondrial membrane. Mutations in the gene encoding parkin are linked to hereditary PD, leading to less efficient mitophagy.

nodes.label: dapivirine
nodes.description: A nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) being evaluated as a vaginal microbicide for its ability to inhibit Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1) infection. It has shown potent dose-dependent inhibitory effects against a broad panel of HIV-1 isolates from different clades and is well tolerated by epithelial cells, T cells, macrophages, and cervical tissue explants. A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor currently in development as a microbicide for HIV PrEP, metabolized differently in colorectal tissue and vaginal tissue. A microbicide used in combination with darunavir in the development of a combination microbicide vaginal ring for the reduction/prevention of sexual transmission of HIV. It has a melting temperature that is reduced by darunavir in a concentration-dependent manner. Serum concentrations range between 10^1 and 10^2 pg/mL in macaques, while vaginal fluid levels range between 10^3 and 10^4 ng/g. It shows similar concentrations in each tissue type compared to darunavir. An investigational drug used in a vaginal ring for preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV infections in women in Africa. Two large efficacy trials demonstrated its efficacy and safety.

nodes.label: Levodopa
nodes.description: A dopamine precursor used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS), Levodopa is studied for its effects on midbrain dopamine neurons and its modulation by Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). It is commonly administered as an adjunct to COMT inhibitors like tolcapone and entacapone to provide PD patients with increased 'on' time, decreased 'off' time, and improved motor scores. Dopaminergic side effects, such as dyskinesia, should be controlled by adjusting the dose of levodopa and not the COMT inhibitor. Levodopa is known to cause augmentation of symptoms, especially under prolonged therapy, and long-term administration is associated with the development of motor complications. It is a precursor to dopamine, which is involved in the pathophysiology of RLS, and its efficacy has been well-documented over the short term.

nodes.label: DNMT1
nodes.description: Synonym for DNA methyltransferase 1, a gene or protein involved in biological functions such as methylation of DNA and transcriptional repression, which is crucial for embryonic stem (ES) cell survival and epigenetic regulation. It contains a catalytic residue that, when mutated, affects its ability to rescue phenotypes of Dnmt1-null ES cells. A cytosine-DNA methyltransferase protein that increases significantly during carcinogen exposure and is associated with the detection of promoter hypermethylation of 5 to 10 genes in each transformed cell line. It is also involved in the de novo methylation of tumor suppressor genes and reduced DNA repair capacity, which together seem causal for transformation of lung epithelial cells. One of the three DNA methyltransferases responsible for establishing and maintaining DNA methylation, along with DNMT3A and DNMT3B. It is involved in the coordinated action of the DNMT family. A DNA methyltransferase protein that is involved in the maintenance of methylation marks in cell-specific patterns in virtually all mitotic cells of the body. It is most highly expressed in postmitotic neurons and is found to be positive in approximately 30% of NeuN-immunopositive neurons in the motor cortex, piriform cortex, striatum, CA1 region of the hippocampus, dentate gyrus, and basolateral amygdala. A DNA methyltransferase that maintains methylation patterns during development and mediates transcriptional repression by directly binding to HDAC2. It is highly expressed in immune cells and required for the differentiation of CD4+ into T regulatory cells. Mutations in this gene cause autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, deafness and narcolepsy (ADCA-DN) and hereditary sensory neuropathy with dementia and hearing loss (HSAN1). A DNA methyltransferase that interacts directly with the H1 C-terminal domain of some, but not all, murine H1 subtypes, leading to the recruitment of DNMT1 and DNA methylation of the H19 and Gtl2 imprinting control regions in ES cells. A gene/protein involved in regulating DNA methylation maintenance during DNA replication. It is activated by UHRF1 through its RFTS domain in complex with ubiquitin. DNMT1 is localized onto replication foci via histone H3 ubiquitination at Lys18 and/or Lys23, recognized by the RFTS domain. The UHRF1 N-terminal ubiquitin-like domain (UBL) also binds directly to DNMT1, affecting its enzymatic activity. DNMT1 binds to ubiquitinated histone H3 catalyzed by UHRF1 RING domain, crucial for its subnuclear localization and maintenance of DNA methylation.

nodes.label: Fluorodopa (FDOPA)
nodes.description: An analogue of L-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-dopa) used to assess the nigrostriatal dopamine system in vivo with positron emission tomography (PET). It is used in conjunction with an inhibitor of catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), such as entacapone (OR-611), to reduce the plasma 3-O-methyldopa (3OMFD) fraction and evaluate its contribution in kinetic models of FDOPA uptake. FDOPA/PET quantitation is complicated by the presence of the 3-O-methyldopa (3OMFD) fraction in brain and plasma.

nodes.label: Sorafenib
nodes.description: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor primarily prescribed for the management of metastatic kidney cancer, with a good safety profile but can cause dermatological adverse effects, including a specific hand-foot skin reaction (HFSR) affecting at least 30% of patients. It is also used in the treatment of NSCLC and as a comparison agent in a pivotal randomized Phase III trial evaluating the front-line use of tivozanib in patients with metastatic clear cell RCC. Sorafenib is an inhibitor of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) and is used as initial targeted therapy for patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). It is marketed under the brand name Nexavar by Bayer.

nodes.label: Orteronel
nodes.description: A naphthylmethylimidazole derivative, specifically the 6,7-dihydro-5H-pyrrolo[1,2-c]imidazole derivative (+)-3c, Orteronel is a potent and highly selective 17,20-lyase inhibitor. It is an investigational, oral, nonsteroidal, selective, reversible inhibitor of 17,20-lyase used in phase I/II trials for treating metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Orteronel inhibits the production of androgenic hormones and has been tested in patients with progressive, chemotherapy-na�ve, metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, and serum testosterone <50 ng/dL. It has been shown to cause pancreatitis as a side effect.

nodes.label: Group A
nodes.description: A group of patients who underwent surgical resection <8 weeks after neoadjuvant CRT. The group consisted of 105 patients, 76.5% of whom were male and 23.5% female. The mean age was 57.8 years. The rate of sphincter preserving surgery was 82.7%, and the postoperative complication rate was 28.8%. The pCR rate was 71.4%. The nodal downstaging rate was 46.7%. One of the two groups in the study, assigned to receive induction chemotherapy using three cycles of fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin before fluorouracil/oxaliplatin CRT (50.4 Gy). The group had a pCR of 17% in the intention-to-treat population.

nodes.label: Enhancer
nodes.description: A type of DNA element that can increase the rate of transcription of a nearby gene, often functioning as a conserved non-coding element and transcribed in extant species of Olfactores. It is a biological process that causes a high level of transcription and activation of chromatin structure at target genes, leading to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, and affects histone methylation at K4, K9 and K36 in distinct ways depending on the methylation level and the location in the locus. Enhancers are located at gene regulatory regions, can be far away from the gene they affect, and are identified and characterized through sequence comparison between multiple mammals. They play a crucial role in regulating gene expression by controlling the accessibility of DNA to transcription factors and RNA polymerase, and are analyzed using deep learning and cross-species chromatin accessibility profiling to understand their function and build explainable models.

nodes.label: SerH locus
nodes.description: A locus in Tetrahymena thermophila with genes encoding variants of the major cell surface protein known as the immobilization antigen (i-ag). It is highly polymorphic and raises questions concerning functional equivalency and selective forces acting on its multiple alleles.

nodes.label: DNA replication
nodes.description: A cellular process involved in the replication of DNA molecules, which is regulated by various proteins and complexes such as And-1/Ctf4, Mcm10, and DNA pol alpha. It involves the identification and study of replication origins and initiation proteins, and is essential for DNA synthesis and sister chromatid cohesion. DNA replication is a primary mechanism for maintaining genome integrity in eukaryotes and is often influenced by other cellular processes such as DNA repair and recombination.
