It is a dynamic process involving frequent switches between DNA polymerases and the coordination of various proteins to initiate, elongate, and process Okazaki fragments. DNA replication is also influenced by histone chaperones through chromatin assembly, disassembly, and histone exchange. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the absence of POB1 leads to defects in mitosis, chromosome loss, genetic recombination, and sensitivity to UV radiation and temperature changes. DNA replication is a complex series of cell-cycle-regulated events involving the faithful replication of eukaryotic chromosomal DNA, incompletely understood and analyzed through the reconstitution of DNA replication free in solution with purified proteins from budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

nodes.label: Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis
nodes.description: A rare disease that occurs mainly in women of reproductive age, characterized by recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax and progressive dyspnea. It is diagnosed through pulmonary biopsy and is associated with bilateral thin-walled cysts on chest computed tomography. Treatment involves video-assisted pleurectomy, bulla resection, and bulla coagulation. It can be a differential diagnosis for young women with diffuse bilateral bullous emphysema or tuberous sclerosis. A progressive cystic lung disease associated with infiltration of atypical smooth muscle-like cells. It has both sporadic and tuberous sclerosis-related forms, with pulmonary manifestations like spontaneous pneumothorax being the primary events leading to diagnosis in most cases. The age range of women afflicted with this disease is broader than previously appreciated, and the degree of pulmonary function can be quite variable, with one-third of subjects having normal spirometry at enrollment into the registry.

nodes.label: AZD7442
nodes.description: A drug consisting of tixagevimab-cilgavimab, also known as Evusheld, manufactured by AstraZeneca, used for intramuscular administration to reduce SARS-CoV-2 infection and severe disease in immunocompromised individuals. A combination of two long-acting monoclonal antibodies, tixagevimab [AZD8895] and cilgavimab [AZD1061], authorized for the prevention and treatment of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). It requires methods capable of quickly characterizing resistance to support resistance monitoring, which led to the development of a biolayer interferometry (BLI) assay to screen the binding of its components to SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins. A drug consisting of two components, tixagevimab and cilgavimab, used in the BLI assay to screen SARS-CoV-2 spike trimer variants.

nodes.label: Aedes albopictus
nodes.description: A species of mosquito from the family Culicidae, specifically belonging to the genus Aedes, known as a secondary vector for Zika virus (ZIKV) and dengue virus (DENV), showing comparable vector competence to Aedes aegypti after antibiotic treatment or intrathoracic injection. It is a main vector for arboviruses such as dengue, Zika virus, and chikungunya, and is of Asian origin, showing exophilic behavior, and can be found in subtropical and temperate areas. It uses genetic and environmental resources to adapt to the environment through survival mechanisms like embryonic dormancy.

nodes.label: BNIP3L
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene, located at 8p21, which is one of the high frequent regions of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in lung carcinoma. The gene product can interact with antiapoptotic proteins such as Bcl-2, Bcl-x(L), E1B19K, promoting apoptosis. The expression and structure of this gene were studied in 4 lung cancer cell strains and 30 tissues, revealing that BNIP3L protein was not detected in A549, NCI-H460, NCI-H446, except for NCI-H520, where the protein expression level was slightly lower than that in immortal bronchial epithelial cell strain HBE4-E6/E7. BNIP3L protein was observed in 46.7% (14/30) lung cancer tissues, while 100% (12/12) in normal lung tissues. The difference was significant in statistics (P< 0.05). BNIP3L mRNA was detected in all lung cancer cell strains and 73.3% (22/30) of lung cancer tissues. There was no significant difference in the amount of BNIP3L mRNA between lung cancer tissues and their paired normal lung tissues (P> 0.05). No point mutation was detected in all 6 exons of BNIP3L gene in 4 lung cancer cell strains and 30 tissues. A gene or protein whose expression is down-regulated in lung cancer, potentially influencing the occurrence and/or development of the disease. Its transcription may be partially responsible for this down-regulation, while variations in gene structure do not appear to be the cause of its inactivity in lung cancer.

nodes.label: Macrophages
nodes.description: A type of white blood cell that is part of the immune system and is involved in various biological processes such as the inflammatory response, hemophagocytosis, and tumor microenvironment modulation. Macrophages are targeted by enzyme replacement therapy in Gaucher disease and are involved in the immune response against pathogens, cellular debris, and Candida albicans infection. They can produce interleukin-31 and are associated with the production of nitric oxide and inflammatory cytokines. In the context of tumor microenvironment, macrophages can be polarized into M1 or M2 subtypes, with M1 macrophages associated with pro-inflammatory cytokines and antitumor immune responses and M2 macrophages linked to anti-inflammatory cytokines and tumor growth promotion.

nodes.label: FBN1
nodes.description: The fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) is associated with predominant ectopia lentis and marfanoid habitus in Chinese patients. It contains 65 exons and flanking intronic sequences, which were amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and screened for mutations by direct DNA sequencing. Three novel mutations and four known mutations were identified in FBN1, including c.203G>T in exon 2, c.502T>C in exon 5, c.2096G>C in exon 16, c.364C>T in exon 4, c.1633C>T in exon 13, c.1879C>T in exon 15, and c.4588C>T in exon 37. Cysteine substitution is highly related to ectopia lentis (EL). A gene located at chromosome 15q, specifically at position 15q21. It encodes fibrillin-1, a protein involved in the development of ectopia lentis. A recurrent mutation, R240C, has been identified in this gene, which is associated with isolated ectopia lentis and has been reported in multiple families and individuals, including one with classic Marfan syndrome. A gene responsible for encoding fibrillin-1, a protein involved in the development and maintenance of connective tissues. Mutations in the FBN1 gene are associated with Marfan syndrome and can lead to phenotypic variability within families. Additional mutational analysis of the FBN1 gene can aid in the diagnosis of MFS. The fibrillin-1 gene, which codes for a protein involved in the development of Marfan syndrome and related diseases. A novel mutation was identified at nucleotide position c.1759, leading to a substitution of Cysteine for Arginine at codon 587 (C587R). This mutation was not present in any unaffected family members. A gene associated with Ectopia Lentis, a disease characterized by the abnormal positioning of the lens in the eye. Mutations in FBN1 are found in 25% of patients with Ectopia Lentis, including four novel mutations not previously reported as causing classical Marfan syndrome. One additional patient was found to have an FBN1 mutation previously reported in classical MFS. The median age of diagnosis for Ectopia Lentis associated with FBN1 mutations is 35 years. FBN1 is less commonly associated with Ectopia Lentis than ADAMTSL4. A gene screened for in the patient, but not found to be the cause of craniosynostosis and ectopia lentis. A gene associated with ectopia lentis, particularly in cases of early onset and autosomal dominant inheritance. Mutations in this gene, such as c.1948 C>T (p.Arg650Cys), can cause ectopia lentis and are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. The gene is involved in the development and maintenance of connective tissue, which is consistent with the manifestations of Marfan syndrome. A gene encoding for fibrillin 1, a component of the extracellular matrix, linked to Marfan syndrome and similar clinical phenotypes. Mutations within this gene are associated with familial adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.

nodes.label: Glioblastoma multiforme
nodes.description: A highly aggressive and malignant subtype of glioma, characterized by its heterogeneous appearance under the microscope, rapid growth and invasion of surrounding brain tissue, and a poor prognosis despite multimodal therapy. It is the most common and most severe form of primary brain cancer in adults, associated with a median survival of less than 1 year. Glioblastoma multiforme is studied in the context of molecular analysis of tumor suppressor genes and protein overexpression, and is often compared to anaplastic astrocytomas in terms of CDKN2A gene deletion. It can be divided into genetic subsets based on EGFR amplification and TP53 mutation, and is associated with homozygous deletions of the CDKN2 (p16/MTS1) gene.

nodes.label: MeCP2
nodes.description: A protein encoded by the methyl-CpG-binding protein-2 gene, which plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression through its interaction with DNA and histones. Mutations in this gene are commonly associated with Rett syndrome but can also be linked to other neuropsychiatric phenotypes. MeCP2 is an abundant chromatin-associated protein and a methyl-CpG-binding protein that is involved in transcriptional repression, developmental silencing of imprinted genes, and neural transcription factor functions. It interacts with various factors such as YY1, ATRX, cohesin, and histones to regulate gene expression and neuronal responses. Mutations in the MeCP2 gene can lead to Rett syndrome and other neuropsychiatric phenotypes, while its restoration can reverse neurologic deficits in mouse models.

nodes.label: Tuberous sclerosis complex
nodes.description: An autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by inactivating mutations in either the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, characterized by the development of multiple, benign tumors in several organs throughout the body, including the brain, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, and skin. Lesions associated with this condition can result in seizures and epilepsy, mental retardation, autism, and renal and pulmonary organ system dysfunction, as well as other complications. It is associated with the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway and can cause symptoms such as seizures, intellectual disability, and skin lesions. Everolimus is used as a systemic treatment for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs) associated with this condition.

nodes.label: Depression
nodes.description: A mental health condition marked by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and a loss of interest in activities. It is associated with various psychiatric disorders, sleep problems, and increased levels of sputum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) AUC in lung cancer patients. Depression can also increase mortality in adults with chronic kidney disease and diabetes.

nodes.label: daughter
nodes.description: The female offspring in a family, who may inherit the mutated IDS gene from her mother. In the described case, she appears to be a carrier of Hunter syndrome based on the serum test, despite having a negative result initially. This could be explained by her mother's germinal mosaicism.

nodes.label: Positron emission tomography (PET)
nodes.description: A medical imaging technique used to visualize and quantify various biological processes and receptors in the body, such as 5-HT2A receptors, amyloid-beta plaques, and adenosine A1 receptors. It involves the use of radiolabeled compounds and the detection of emitted positrons to create images of receptor distribution and density. PET is also used to assess metabolic activity in the brain and to study the nigrostriatal dopamine system.

nodes.label: Type 1 diabetes
nodes.description: A chronic autoimmune disease characterized by a decline in C-peptide production, resulting from a chronic autoimmune process continuing for years after presentation. The study tested the effect of teplizumab treatment on the decline in C-peptide production in individuals with type 1 diabetes after the new-onset period. The disease was prevalent among the participants in the trial, with 58 individuals having type 1 diabetes. An organ-specific autoimmune disease characterized by selective destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells by T-cell-mediated inflammation, leading to the metabolic instability that defines the disease. A chronic autoimmune disease characterized by progressive destruction of the pancreatic beta cells, leading to a lifelong dependence on insulin. It is associated with an increased morbidity and mortality from diabetes-related complications and a significant treatment burden. A form of diabetes where the body does not produce insulin. It is more commonly diagnosed in winter. It is commonly associated with other autoimmune diseases such as coeliac disease and thyroid disease. Individuals with childhood-onset type 1 diabetes also had significantly higher rates of Addison's disease, coeliac disease, and thyroid disease. An autoimmune condition characterized by the destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells by immune cells, leading to a chronic inability to regulate blood glucose levels. It is well-characterized in childhood and is associated with the presence of two or more autoantibodies to the islet antigens insulin, GAD, IA-2 or ZnT8 in early childhood. The risk factors and progression rate from multiple islet autoantibody positivity to onset of symptoms are less clear in adults and not fully understood. A chronic autoimmune endocrinopathy characterized by the depletion of pancreatic beta cells and exogenous insulin dependence, with increasing incidence. Despite technological advances in insulin delivery, disease control remains suboptimal, while previous immunotherapy options have failed to prevent T1D. Teplizumab, an immunomodulating monoclonal antibody, was approved to delay or prevent T1D. In participants with new-onset T1D, teplizumab delayed C-peptide decline, improved glycemic control, and reduced insulin demand for a median of 1 or 2 years. Studies in at-risk relatives of patients showed a decrease in T1D incidence during 2 years of follow-up. Mild to moderate adverse effects were reported, including transient rash, cytopenia, nausea, vomiting, and infections.

nodes.label: Molluscum contagiosum
nodes.description: A viral infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, characterized by skin lesions. It is associated with the production of interleukin-18 (IL-18) binding protein (MC54L) by the human poxvirus that causes this disease. A benign contagious disease caused by a poxvirus, characterized by the proliferation of the virus within keratinocytes and the formation of intracytoplasmic Molluscum bodies. It is a common clinical condition, but histologically has not been reported from the Mymensingh region. Diagnosis can be made easily through histological examination, and patients suspected of having this disease are recommended to undergo such examination to exclude other similar types of lesions. Commonly affects the trunk. A viral skin condition characterized by the appearance of pearly lesions on the surface of the skin. It is common in children and can be contracted during sexual activity in adults, potentially indicating the need for diagnostic testing for other, more serious sexually transmitted infections. A viral infection of the skin and mucous membranes caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, which can be acquired through skin-to-skin contact, such as during play, in a swimming pool, or through sexual contact. It is rare in younger children but becomes common during adolescence and young adulthood. Vertical transmission of molluscum should be considered for all infantile cases of molluscum. A human disease caused by a poxvirus, which can be as benign as human diseases caused by other poxviruses. A common skin and mucosal disease of viral origin caused by molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) of the poxvirus family. It is challenging to diagnose due to its unusual clinical presentation. A common skin disorder primarily affecting young children, caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV). It can be treated with various methods such as cryotherapy, curettage, or topical therapies, but these often require multiple sessions, can be ineffective, and cause pain. In the study, a single session of pulsed dye laser treatment was found to be successful in treating recalcitrant Molluscum contagiosum lesions without recurrence and with good tolerance by the subjects. A common superficial skin infection caused by the poxvirus, Molluscum Contagiosum virus. It is characterized by the presence of multiple lesions, with the most common cases seen being children with multiple lesions and adults with genital lesions. The infection is seen by many types of practitioners and can be treated with various methods such as cryotherapy and curettage. Guidance on treatment considerations and infection control is valuable due to the prevalence of this infection. A persistent skin infection caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) in immunocompetent individuals, often spread by contact with lesions. The incidence rate for this disease in children <5 years old was highest in the West and East regions among American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) children. It has been associated with atopic dermatitis (AD), eczema, eczema or dermatitis, impetigo, and scabies. A viral infection caused by a DNA virus of the poxvirus group, common in children, sexually active adults and HIV-seropositive patients. It is characterized by the presence of multiple flesh-coloured papules spread over the entire skin surface, surrounded by a white halo, and infected cells with intracytoplasmic inclusions in an acanthotic epidermis. The halo could be due to the secretion of a protein by molluscum contagiosum inhibiting inflammation around this MC. A very common benign self-limiting cutaneous viral infection caused by molluscum contagiosum virus. It tends to take a chronic course and is usually not responsive to various treatments in immunocompromised patients. In advanced stages of immunosuppression, giant or verrucous forms of MC may occur. It is self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals but can be severe and prolonged when associated with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection. The widespread and refractory mollusca of HIV disease occur especially on the face. A viral infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum poxvirus, which may act as an opportunistic pathogen in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It is associated with unusual clinical manifestations in AIDS patients. A disease caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) that affects both children and adults.

nodes.label: Hypertension
nodes.description: A common trait associated with metabolic syndrome, characterized by persistently high blood pressure levels, which can increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases. It is often linked with insulin resistance/hyperinsulinaemia and can be a side effect of certain treatments, such as Prednisone, protein kinase inhibitors like fostamatinib, or drugs used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Hypertension is also a grade 3 and 4 treatment-related adverse event observed in the phase II randomized discontinuation trial involving tivozanib and a common adverse event in studies involving Taliglucerase alfa and regorafenib. It is one of the core traits of the metabolic syndrome, along with elevated blood pressure and hyperglycemia.

nodes.label: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)
nodes.description: A gene or protein involved in the treatment of various types of cancer, including advanced, metastatic, or recurrent tumours like colorectal carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (SCCHN) and pancreatic cancer. It is a protein kinase that is aberrantly expressed in malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) and promotes their pathogenesis. EGFR is also frequently expressed in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and serves as a marker of poor prognosis in this patient population. It is involved in normal and pathological mammary gland development, with essential roles in signal transduction. Over-expression of EGFR ligands is associated with poorer clinical outcome in breast cancers. EGFR is targeted by small molecule inhibitors like gefitinib and monoclonal antibodies in anti-EGFR therapy for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), leading to skin toxicities. It is also involved in the epidermal growth factor receptor pathway, which is targeted by tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) as a standard-of-care treatment for EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

nodes.label: CADASIL
nodes.description: A hereditary cerebrovascular disease leading to accumulating neurologic deficits and dementia, associated with nucleotide substitutions and deletions in the Notch3 gene. It is characterized by recurrent ischemic stroke, cognitive decline, psychiatric disturbances, and migraine. The disease involves mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, particularly missense point mutations around exons 3 and 4, leading to the loss or gain of a cysteine residue in the gene. Genetic testing is the gold standard for diagnosis, and it is primarily caused by missense mutations in the NOTCH3 gene. There is no approved treatment for migraine prophylaxis in CADASIL, but acetazolamide has been anecdotally reported to be effective.

nodes.label: Anxiety disorders
nodes.description: A group of mental health conditions characterized by excessive, irrational fear and worry. In the study, twelve African-American adolescents with anxiety disorders were randomly assigned to either CBT or a group attention-support control condition (AS-Control). Diagnostic interviews were conducted at pre- and posttreatment, and adolescents completed self-report measures of anxiety. At posttreatment and among those who attended more than one treatment session, 3/4 adolescents in CBT no longer met diagnostic criteria for their primary anxiety disorder, compared with 1/5 in AS-Control. Clinician ratings of impairment and self-report levels of overall anxiety were significantly lower at posttreatment in CBT compared with AS-Control. Teenagers in both groups reported lower levels of social anxiety from pre- to posttreatment. A group of neuropsychiatric disorders involving abnormal fear and anxiety, for which organic cation transporters (OCTs) are attractive candidates due to their involvement in monoaminergic signalling. A psychiatric disorder that co-occurs with depression in adolescents, present in 23.37% of cases. It is a type of comorbid condition associated with depression. A group of mental health disorders that carry a significant increased risk due to RLS/WED. A group of psychiatric disorders characterized by excessive fear and worry. After puberty, females are more prone to anxiety disorders compared to males. It is associated with an increased risk in individuals with sex chromosome aneuploidies, including Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, XYY syndrome, and XXX syndrome.

nodes.label: Astrocytoma
nodes.description: A type of glioma, specifically a brain tumor originating from astrocytes, which are star-shaped glial cells in the central nervous system. Astrocytomas can be classified into different grades based on their aggressiveness, with higher grades indicating more aggressive and rapidly growing tumors. They include both low-grade and anaplastic subtypes, with low-grade astrocytomas capable of progressing to anaplastic astrocytomas and then to glioblastomas. The study examines the expression of NFIA protein in astrocytomas and its association with clinical outcome in pediatric malignant astrocytomas. Astrocytoma exhibits higher prevalence of TP53, PTEN, and CDKN2A alterations compared to other tumor subtypes.

nodes.label: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis
nodes.description: A serious condition with a poor prognosis, associated with metformin, a common antidiabetic drug. It requires hospitalization and has a mortality rate of 25.4%. The predictors of death include low arterial blood pH and absence of acute renal failure. Risk minimization measures are taken at the national level to prevent this serious complication. A condition associated with the use of metformin, characterized by elevated plasma lactate levels and a mortality rate approaching 50%. It typically requires elevated plasma metformin concentrations and a secondary event or condition that further disrupts lactate production or clearance, such as cirrhosis, sepsis, or hypoperfusion. A severe and infrequent adverse event associated with metformin, characterized by a metabolic acidosis. It has an elevated mortality rate ranging from 50-80% and requires early diagnosis and specific treatment for favorable outcomes. A severe adverse effect of metformin characterized by metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate levels in the presence of metformin. There is no consensus regarding the role of metformin in its onset. A rare but life-threatening complication of metformin use, characterized by lactic acidosis. It was successfully managed in a case involving concurrent cardiogenic and vasoplegic shock using ECPella (concurrent use of VA-ECMO and Impella). Early recognition, aggressive hemodynamic support with ECPella and early hemodialysis can be life-saving. Monitoring of both lactate and SvO2 trends can help understand the response to treatment.

nodes.label: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
nodes.description: A genetic disorder affecting the heart muscle, characterized by thickening of the heart walls and often leading to symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, and irregular heartbeats. It can be caused by mutations in various genes involved in calcium handling and cardiac muscle function, such as sarcomere genes, cardiac troponin C (cTnC) gene, and alpha-myosin heavy chain. It is a type of cardiomyopathy that is inherited and characterized by abnormal enlargement and thickening of the heart chambers, leading to reduced pumping efficiency. Mouse models of this condition have been generated by introducing specific mutations into the alpha cardiac myosin heavy chain (MHC) gene.

nodes.label: Metabolic syndrome
nodes.description: A cluster of metabolic risk factors including dyslipidaemia, hypertension, abdominal obesity, microalbuminuria, endothelial dysfunction, and markers of inflammation and hypercoagulability. It is associated with impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), impaired fasting glucose (IFG), and progression to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and cardiovascular disease. A common complex trait consisting of the clustering of abdominal obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and dysglycemia. It is found in about 25% of the population in the United States and is associated with an increased risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. A cluster of conditions, including hyperglycaemia, that increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes. Rimonabant has favourable effects on aspects of the metabolic syndrome. A traditional definition of the metabolic syndrome that includes increased susceptibility to dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and hypertension. It is associated with obesity. A cluster of conditions including insulin resistance, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol levels, and increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, linked to mutations in the myotubularin family of phosphoinositide phosphatases. A cluster of metabolic disorders including insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and obesity. It is considered an important factor linking obesity to colorectal cancer (CRC). A condition characterized by the presence of at least three out of five dysmetabolic traits including abdominal obesity, hypertension, low plasma HDL-cholesterol, high plasma glucose, and high triglycerides. It has been associated with an increased risk of several age-related chronic diseases, including breast cancer. Metabolic syndrome is reversible through lifestyle changes and interventions to decrease its traits in BC patients should be implemented in BC clinics. A cluster of the most dangerous heart attack risk factors including diabetes, raised fasting plasma glucose, abdominal obesity, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure. It has become a major global threat to human health. A condition characterized by the concurrent presentation of multiple cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia and hypertension. It has been suggested that some of these risk factors can have detrimental effects on the skeletal muscle while others can be a direct result of skeletal muscle abnormalities, showing a two-way directionality in the pathogenesis of the condition. A condition that interacts with polygenetic risk scores (PRSs) and influences hyperthyroidism risk. A cluster of symptoms characterized by symptoms that may arise from a deficit in the bioenergetic role of mitochondria for ATP homeostasis.

nodes.label: One-and-a-half syndrome
nodes.description: A rare neurological syndrome characterized by a lateral gaze palsy in one direction and internuclear ophthalmoplegia in the other. It is caused by a unilateral lesion of the dorsal pontine tegmentum, involving the ipsilateral paramedian pontine reticular formation, internuclear fibres of the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus and, usually, the abducens nucleus. Clinically, it presents with symptoms such as diplopia, oscillopsia, blurred vision, facial nerve palsy, hemiparesis, and unilateral hemihypoaesthesia. The syndrome is often associated with stroke or multiple sclerosis and can be diagnosed through MRI, which reveals an infarct in the pons. The cause of the infarct can be a basilar artery dissection, bilateral vertebral artery dissection, or unknown. A clinical disorder featuring extraocular movements characterized by horizontal conjugate gaze palsy with internuclear ophthalmoplegia. It usually results from a unilateral lesion of the midbrain and is commonly caused by multiple sclerosis in young women. In the reported case, it was associated with acute myeloblastic leukemia. A symptom associated with internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), referring to unilateral gaze palsy. It is mentioned that 16% of patients with unilateral INO experienced this symptom. A symptom characterized by binocular diplopia on lateral gazes, as observed in the reported case of a 43-year-old male patient. A neurological disorder characterized by the combination of ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia. It can be accompanied by 7th and 8th cranial nerve palsy, which is then called 16-and-a-half syndrome.

nodes.label: B1
nodes.description: A type of short interspersed repeat element (SINE) found in the mouse genome, derived from the 7SL RNA gene. In the studied dataset, over 73% of 365,377 B1s were still found to be a single copy when the criterion was reduced to half the length of the repeat. All single and multi-copy sequences have been mapped and documented. A short interspersed repeat element (SINE) derived from the 7SL RNA gene, similar to Alu, existing in the cytoplasm as non-coding RNA and being actively transcribed. It shares characteristics with Alu such as having a bipartite promoter sequence and a poly-A tail for transcription. A type of mobile element that originated in an initial duplication of the 7SL RNA gene prior to the primate-rodent split about 80 million years ago. B1 elements have been selectively retained in the upstream and intronic regions of genes of specific functional classes. They have also shown similar biases in their distribution across functional classes in the human and mouse genomes. A cellular protein that binds small cytoplasmic RNAs in vitro. It is a sequence-homologous interspersed element of unknown function that has expanded in the genomes of mice. A minority of its sequences are expressed as small cytoplasmic RNAs. These RNAs have conserved a secondary structure motif present in signal recognition particle (SRP) RNA despite substantial sequence divergence.

nodes.label: Ivacaftor
nodes.description: A drug used in combination with lumacaftor to treat cystic fibrosis (CF). A drug used for the treatment of cystic fibrosis as both monotherapy and combination therapy with lumacaftor. It is administered twice daily and is extensively converted in humans to major metabolites M1 and M6. It has two deuterated analogs, CTP-656 (d9-ivacaftor) and d18-ivacaftor, which were synthesized and tested for pharmacological and metabolic effects. A component of the combination therapy Orkambi®, used to potentiate mutations like c.3700 A>G in the CFTR gene. A component of the combination drug Orkambi, used for treating cystic fibrosis by reversing the effects of the defective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein. A small molecule or modulator approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to treat cystic fibrosis patients with certain CFTR mutations. It is known by the brand name Kalydeco. A drug used in combination therapy for cystic fibrosis, specifically targeting the processing defect of F508del-CFTR. It has a lipophilicity of 10 μM and can negatively impact the stability of F508del-CFTR and other membrane localized solute carriers (SLC26A3, SLC26A9, and SLC6A14).

nodes.label: Natriuretic peptides
nodes.description: A family of peptides including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP), dendroaspis natriuretic peptide (DNP), and urodilatin. They are synthesized from polypeptide precursors and their activities are strictly associated with endothelins. They can inhibit endothelin-1 (ET-1) production and stimulate natriuretic peptide synthesis. A family of structurally related peptides, products of at least three genes, which share a common, 17-membered, internal disulfide ring. They include three major subtypes: A-, B-, and C-type natriuretic peptides, each present in various tissues in multiple N- and C-terminally extended or shortened forms. The C-type peptide CNP is the major brain-derived peptide. Original studies examining the endocrine actions of the natriuretic peptides using A-type (ANP) or B-type (BNP) isoforms might have underestimated some of their biopotency or failed to detect the full spectrum of the family's bioactivity. Hormones mainly secreted from the heart, with important natriuretic and kaliuretic properties. Include four different groups: atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP), and dendroaspis natriuretic peptide (DNP). Each group has its own characteristic functions. Natriuretic peptides are a group of chemicals that appear after their receptors in vertebrates. They are known only in vertebrates and are associated with three transmembrane receptors, NPR1, NPR2 and NPR3, in mammals. These peptides are believed to have appeared later than their receptors during animal evolution. Peptide hormones involved in the regulation of blood pressure, water-mineral balance and multiple metabolic processes. Eight natriuretic peptides have been described so far: ANP, BNP, CNP, DNP, urodilatin, uroguanylin, osteocrin, musculin. They have three receptors: NPR-A, NPR-B and NPR-C. Determination of natriuretic peptide concentration in plasma is used in the diagnosis and treatment of heart failure and pulmonary embolism. Research results indicate that the determination of natriuretic peptides concentration in plasma may also be important in the acute coronary syndromes, subclinical complications of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. The concentration of natriuretic peptides is changing in many diseases. Beneficial effects of natriuretic peptides have led to the production of drugs that are their synthetic derivatives. These drugs are mainly used among patients with heart failure. Research is currently underway on the efficacy and safety of other synthetic natriuretic peptides. A family of three biologically active peptides consisting of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain (or B-type) natriuretic peptide (BNP), and C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP). ANP and BNP are secreted by the heart and act as cardiac hormones, while CNP is an endothelial peptide. The manuscript reviews their production, action mechanisms, effects, and clinical applications.

nodes.label: Pre-exposure prophylaxis
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the use of tenofovir/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) to prevent HIV transmission. It is expected to be available in the Netherlands, but guidelines are needed before its introduction due to concerns about renal function and antiretroviral resistance. A medical procedure or test involving the use of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate in combination with emtricitabine for HIV-1 prevention. It has been shown to be efficacious for HIV-1 prevention. A medical procedure involving the use of emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate to prevent HIV infection. It is highly effective, with only two reported cases of infection with a multidrug-resistant virus under adequate long-term adherence. The Amsterdam PrEP project is a demonstration project of daily and event-driven PrEP. A strategy to reduce HIV incidence, involving the use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine, adopted by WHO. It requires optimal adherence to be effective, posing a challenge for certain at-risk populations. A medical procedure involving the administration of oral medications such as tenofovir (TFV) disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine daily to prevent human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) acquisition in both men and women with sufficient adherence. It is effective when adhered to properly, but its adherence-efficacy relationship in cisgender women has not been well established.

nodes.label: Atopic Dermatitis
nodes.description: A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by itching, redness, and scaling. It is associated with type 2 helper T-cell (Th2)-mediated inflammation and is inadequately controlled by topical treatments. The disease is associated with increased levels of IL-4 and IL-13 cytokines and involves an overexpression of Th2 cytokines, particularly IL-4 and IL-13. It is a focus of ongoing research for potential therapeutic approaches, with several clinical trials recruiting participants. Common chronic inflammatory skin disease with high prevalence rates in adults and even higher among children, affecting up to one-third of adults with moderate-to-severe disease. It is a moderate-to-severe form of the disease and is inadequately controlled by topical treatments. Patients with this condition participated in a phase II, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study and a 52-week, double-blind extension study involving nemolizumab injections. A skin condition characterized by inflammation, itching, and redness, often associated with a pathway of immunoglobulin E (IgE) sensitization and involving proinflammatory cytokines such as chemoattractant receptor-homologous molecule expressed on TH2 cells (CRTH2), IgE, thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), and several monoclonal antibodies that block key cytokine pathways in the innate immune response. A skin condition treated with Dupilumab in clinical trials, characterized by signs and symptoms such as pruritus, symptoms of anxiety and depression, and an impact on quality of life. Trials involve patients with this condition and are funded by Sanofi and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. A chronic skin condition characterized by inflamed, itchy skin that tends to recur. It is a moderate-to-severe form of the disease and is inadequately controlled by topical treatments. It is a common inflammatory dermatologic disease clinically characterized by intense itch, recurrent eczematous lesions, and a chronic or relapsing disease course. It involves epidermal barrier dysfunction, skin microbiome abnormalities, and cutaneous inflammation. Inflammatory mediators such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, IL-31, IL-33, IL-17, IL-23, and thymic stromal lymphopoietin are involved in AD development. A skin condition characterized by inflamed, itchy skin that often leads to dry, red, scaly rashes. It is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that can cause severe itching and discomfort. An inflammatory skin disease characterized by skin inflammation and pruritus, often treated with anti-IL-31RA antibodies like nemolizumab.

nodes.label: Systemic lupus erythematosus
nodes.description: A chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and damage to various organs and systems in the body, including the skin, joints, kidneys, and central nervous system. It involves the production of autoantibodies against the patient's own tissues, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, joint pain, and skin rashes. The disease can affect multiple organs including the kidneys, lungs, and central nervous system. It is associated with the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), an increased risk of developing endothelial dysfunction, and premature cardiovascular disease. Systemic lupus erythematosus is a remarkably heterogeneous autoimmune disease characterized by serum protein patterns associated with organ damage and lupus nephritis, and it includes various phenotypes such as severe forms. It is also mentioned as a non-Mendelian disorder characterized by an up-regulation of type I interferon signaling, suggesting potential relevance to type I interferonopathies.

nodes.label: Six-Kingdom System of Life
nodes.description: A revised classification system of life that divides organisms into six kingdoms: Bacteria, Protozoa, Animalia, Fungi, Plantae, and Chromista. It uses extensive intermediate high-level categories like infraphylum to avoid splitting organisms into an excessive number of kingdoms and phyla. The circumscriptions of the kingdoms Bacteria and Plantae remain unchanged since Cavalier-Smith (1981). The kingdom Fungi is expanded by adding Microsporidia, and fungal classification at the rank of subclass and above is comprehensively revised. The kingdoms Protozoa and Animalia are modified based on molecular phylogenetic evidence, and several new higher level groupings are made in the animal kingdom, recognizing only 23 animal phyla.

nodes.label: CXCR4
nodes.description: A chemokine receptor gene associated with WHIM syndrome, mutations in which lead to truncating mutations in the cytoplasmic tail domain and dysregulated signaling by the mutant receptor. It is a G protein-coupled receptor encoded by a gene with inherited heterozygous autosomal dominant mutations in the WHIM syndrome. The gene is responsible for encoding the protein involved in the pathogenesis of WHIM syndrome, mutations in which lead to CXCR4 hyperfunction, resulting in increased responsiveness to its unique ligand CXCL12. The protein is involved in CXCL12-promoted internalization and desensitization, whose dysfunction is associated with WHIM(WT) leukocytes. It is regulated by GRK3 and its attenuation and desensitization are impaired in WHIM(WT) cells, leading to enhanced chemotaxis. The protein is also involved in several biological processes such as bone marrow hematopoiesis, cardiogenesis, angiogenesis, neurogenesis, and implicated in clinical pathologic conditions like WHIM, HIV infection, tumor metastatization, and autoimmunity. Pharmacologic agents that modulate CXCR4 expression/function are already available and promise a wide range of future clinical applications. The most common truncation mutation in WHIM syndrome is CXCR4(R334X), which truncates the C-terminus by 10-19 amino acids. Validated as the molecular target in the disease by Mendelian genetics. CXCR4-selective antagonists have been developed, and CXCR4 haploinsufficiency enhances engraftment of transplanted hematopoietic stem cells in mice.

nodes.label: Heerfordt syndrome
nodes.description: A rare autoimmune disorder associated with sarcoidosis, characterized by peripheral facial palsy, uveitis, and exophthalmos. It can present with bilateral swelling of the eyelids and parotid glands, and may progress to involve the facial nerve. It can be diagnosed based on clinical symptoms and may coexist with pericardial effusion. A gallium scan can be helpful for diagnosis, showing increased uptake of Ga to the ophthalmic lesion, parotid glands and hilar lesions. Prednisolone may be used for therapeutic trials, especially for facial palsy. It can be diagnosed based on symptoms and physical examination results of the patient, and may involve small fiber neuropathy (SFN) manifesting as refractory facial pain.

nodes.label: Sigmoid volvulus
nodes.description: A disease characterized by the twisting of the sigmoid colon, which can lead to bowel compromise and potentially necrosis. It has a spectrum of imaging findings, with a classic appearance absent on approximately one half of scanograms and one fourth of CT scans. The use of new imaging signs, such as the X-marks-the-spot sign and the split-wall sign, may improve diagnostic confidence. A rare cause of intestinal obstruction in the pediatric age group, characterized by rotation of the redundant sigmoid colon about its narrow mesenteric base, leading to vascular compromise and large bowel obstruction. Predisposing factors include Hirschsprung's disease, congenital anomalous fixation of the colon, and chronic constipation. A medical condition characterized by the twisting of the sigmoid colon, often leading to symptoms such as abdominal distension. Diagnosed through characteristic radiographic signs including the coffee bean sign, steel pan sign, whirl sign, and a beak-shaped transition point. Treated with colonoscopic decompression and detorsion. A medical condition characterized by the twisting of the sigmoid colon, leading to intestinal obstruction. It is a common cause of abdominal diseases presenting at the emergency department, accounting for a relevant percentage of cases. Treatment typically involves early endoscopic devolvulation (ED) followed by elective surgery as definitive treatment. Recurrence rates can be high, with up to 86% of cases experiencing a recurrence after ED, increasing the risk of complications such as intestinal ischemia or perforation, urgent surgery, and mortality. A rare disorder in children characterized by recurrent episodes, associated with Hirschsprung disease, neurodevelopmental disorders and chronic constipation. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, tenderness, vomiting, and signs of peritonitis indicating a gangrenous sigmoid. It can lead to more complications and has a recurrence rate of 38-57% after non-operative treatment.

nodes.label: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato
nodes.description: A group of related bacteria including Borr. afzelii, Borr. burgdorferi sensu stricto, Borr. garinii, Borr. lusitaniae, and Borr. valaisiana, which are tick-borne zoonotic pathogens. The minimum prevalence in Ixodes ricinus was 2.5% in Hungary. A group of related bacteria that are pathogens of medical and veterinary relevance, transmitted by the vector Ixodes ricinus. Investigations have been conducted on these bacteria in Europe. A complex of spirochetes including various genospecies such as B. afzelii, B. garinii, B. valaisiana, B. bavariensis, and B. burgdorferi s.s., which are the causative agents of Lyme borreliosis. The prevalence of this complex in tick populations in Estonia was estimated to be 9.7%. An expected tick-borne pathogen detected in the study, belonging to the Borrelia genus.

nodes.label: Restless Leg Syndrome
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by uncomfortable sensations in the legs and an irresistible urge to move them, often worse at rest and in the evening. Its pathogenesis is unknown, but recent developments have highlighted the role of genetic markers, neurotransmitter dysfunction, and iron deficiency. It can be exacerbated by long-term dopamine agonist therapy and may affect the quality of life of patients. A common neurological disorder characterized by uncomfortable sensations in the legs and an irresistible urge to move them, often worse at rest and in the evening. Its pathogenesis is unknown, but recent developments have highlighted the role of genetic markers, neurotransmitter dysfunction, and iron deficiency. It can be exacerbated by long-term dopamine agonist therapy and may affect the quality of life of patients. A neurological disorder characterized by an irresistible urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations. It is the focus of the systematic review and meta-analysis regarding the effects of dopamine agonists on sleep parameters.

nodes.label: Aortitis
nodes.description: An inflammatory process involving one or more layers of the aortic wall, including the internal elastic lamina, tunica media, and adventitia. It can be caused by multiple mechanisms, and its clinical features are usually nonspecific. A high index of suspicion is required for making the diagnosis. Noninvasive imaging studies are increasingly used, but angiography remains the gold standard for confirming aortic involvement. Pathologic examination can aid in clarifying the diagnosis when tissue is available. Treatment depends on the underlying cause, with infectious aortitis responding to appropriate antimicrobial therapy and noninfectious, immune-mediated aortitis requiring immunosuppressive therapy. Surgical intervention may be necessary due to delays in diagnosis. A chronic, progressive disease manifestation associated with large vessel vasculitides, most notably giant cell, Takayasu arteritis, and a newly described entity, isolated aortitis. It can lead to aneurysm formation and symptoms associated with branch vessel occlusion, but aortic dissection is rare and usually a late complication of smoldering, incompletely treated disease.

nodes.label: Gefitinib
nodes.description: A first-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor used as a targeted therapy for EGFR-dependent cancers, particularly in the treatment of lung cancer. It is effective in second and third-line treatments following chemotherapies but is ineffective in patients with T790M mutations within the EGFR gene. Gefitinib is known to cause acquired resistance due to the T790M mutation and may lead to the induction of resistance in some cells over time. It is used in combination with other EGFR inhibitors like carnetinib, cetuximab, and afatinib. Common side effects include acneiform rash in 30 to 90% of patients. It is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) used in combination therapy for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and as a targeted therapy for NSCLC with EGFR-activating mutations. It blocks the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and reduces tumor incidence, size, and metastasis in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma by targeting TOB1 expression and causing cell cycle arrest predominantly at the G1 phase through TOB1 nuclear translocation and its interaction with cyclin D1.

nodes.label: Osteogenesis imperfecta
nodes.description: A systemic heritable disorder of connective tissue characterized by bone fragility. It is caused by mutations in either of the genes encoding the pro-alpha1 or pro-alpha2 chains of type I collagen (COL1A1 or COL1A2), or mutations involving the enzyme complex responsible for posttranslational hydroxylation of the position 3 proline residue of COL1A1. Mutations in LEPRE1 and cartilage-associated protein can also cause autosomal recessive osteogenesis imperfecta, leading to a moderate to severe clinical phenotype that is often indistinguishable from osteogenesis imperfecta types II or III. A genetic disorder characterized by bones that break easily, often from minimal trauma. It is caused by mutations in genes involved in collagen production, such as COL1A1, COL1A2, CRTAP, and LEPRE1. There are two new genes, CRTAP and LEPRE1, that have been defined in patients with recessive severe or lethal osteogenesis imperfecta types. Diagnostic concerns involve testing procedures, either skin biopsies or DNA analysis. Bisphosphonates have been accepted as 'standard of care' for children with osteogenesis imperfecta, but questions remain as to the selection of patients for treatment, effectiveness in fracture prevention, which bisphosphonates should be used, and the duration of treatment. Orthopedic intervention includes the immediate treatment of fractures, the treatment of scoliosis, and the use of intramedullary rods. Current experience suggests that DNA analysis is a better test for diagnosis as compared with dermal biopsy. There are no standardized guidelines for initiating bisphosphonate treatment in children, and recent data suggest either intravenous or oral bisphosphonates are effective, but differences exist between different bisphosphonates. There is a paucity of evidence-based data regarding the effectiveness of bisphosphonate treatment in fracture prevention. A heterogeneous group of inherited disorders of bone formation, resulting in low bone mass and an increased propensity to fracture. Exhibits a broad spectrum of clinical severity, ranging from multiple fractures in utero and perinatal death to normal adult stature and low fracture incidence. Extra-skeletal features include blue sclera, hearing loss, skin hyperlaxity, joint hyperextensibility, and dentinogenesis imperfecta. Often associated with mutations in the COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes, showing an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. Six other genes, CRTAP, LEPRE1, FKBP10, PP1B, SP7/Osterix (OSX), and SERPINH1, are associated with autosomal recessive forms of OI. Other rare phenotypes have also been described. A group of inherited connective tissue disorders characterized by bones that fracture easily. It can present as a syndromic form, such as Bruck syndrome, or as an isolated condition. Mutations in the FKBP10 gene can cause both Bruck syndrome and isolated osteogenesis imperfecta. A rare connective tissue disorder characterized by bone fragility and low bone density. Most cases are caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in either COL1A1 or COL1A2 gene encoding type I collagen, but autosomal recessive forms have been identified. A genetic disorder commonly known as 'brittle bone disease' that was traditionally considered a bone disorder caused by collagen mutations. Recent genetic discoveries have revealed that most cases are due to autosomal dominant type I collagen defects, while rare, mostly recessive, forms are due to defects in genes whose protein products interact with collagen protein. There are several types of osteogenesis imperfecta, including types V, VI, VII-IX, X, XI, and XII, each associated with specific genetic mutations and affecting bone mineralization, collagen post-translational modification, collagen crosslinking, folding, chaperoning, osteoblast development, and collagen maturation/processing. A heritable disorder of connective tissue characterized by abnormalities in the synthesis of type I collagen, leading to fragile bones. Various mutations affecting normal synthesis of type I collagen have been reported in this condition.

nodes.label: Coxiella burnetii
nodes.description: A bacterium that causes Q fever, an obligate intracellular pathogen responsible for a vector-borne zoonosis. It primarily infects a wide range of animal species including mammals, birds, reptiles, and arthropods. Transmission is mainly airborne, but ticks may act as vectors and play an important role in the natural cycle of transmission of coxiellosis among wild vertebrates and livestock. Livestock are the primary source of C. burnetii infection in most Q fever outbreaks, which occur mainly through inhalation of contaminated particles. Many cases of Q fever are linked to exposure to wildlife, highlighting the potential role of changes in human-wildlife interactions in the emergence/re-emergence of Q fever. C. burnetii infection is of public and veterinary health and economic concern due to its potential for rapid spread and highly infectious nature. It has a worldwide distribution and was discovered in 1935.

nodes.label: Polypharmacy
nodes.description: The use of multiple medications simultaneously, particularly common in older patients. It increases the risk of drug interactions with statins, which can lead to adverse effects such as elevation of liver enzymes and skeletal muscle abnormalities. Frequent administration of multiple medications during treatment, which may lead to severe adverse events in patients with Barth syndrome. The concurrent use of multiple medications by patients, defined as the use of ≥5 drugs. It was observed in 76.5% of the patients in the ARISTOTLE trial, associated with increased mortality, stroke or systemic embolism, and major bleeding rates. The concurrent use of multiple medications, often associated with increased comorbidity, more interacting drugs, increased mortality, and higher rates of thromboembolic and bleeding complications in patients with atrial fibrillation. The concurrent use of multiple medications, specifically defined as taking 6 or more medications. Approximately 35% of study patients reported polypharmacy. DM1 patients with polypharmacy were significantly younger (mean 55.0 years) compared to DM2 (59.0 years) and FSHD (63.2 years) and had shorter disease duration (mean 26 years) compared to FSHD (26.8 years) and DM2 (34.8 years). The concurrent use of multiple medications, particularly common in patients with age-related comorbidities, which may increase drug-drug interaction (DDI) risks.

nodes.label: Aagenaes syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by severe neonatal cholestasis that usually lessens during early childhood and becomes episodic, and chronic severe lymphedema. Synonymous with Cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome. A specific syndrome characterized by neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis and lymphoedema in feet and legs, named after the Norwegian paediatrician Øystein Aagenaes who described the syndrome in 1968. It is autosomal recessively inherited and the gene is located to 15q, but not yet identified. The condition is particularly frequent in the southernmost part of Norway with an estimated gene frequency of about 3%. The only known form of hereditary lymphedema associated with cholestasis, also referred to as Lymphedema-cholestasis syndrome. A form of idiopathic familial intrahepatic cholestasis associated with lymphedema of the lower extremities. It is named after the Norwegian pediatrician Oyestein Aagenaes, who described the syndrome in 1968. The presence of lymphedema is likely the predisposing factor for development of recurrent infections in such patients. A rare congenital cholestatic syndrome that resembles the symptoms of congenital cholestasis, including intermittent oedema in childhood. It is associated with an increased risk of developing advanced hepatocellular carcinoma in adolescence. Aagenaes syndrome, also known as lymphoedema cholestasis syndrome 1 (LSC1), is characterized by neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis that often lessens and becomes intermittent with age, and severe chronic lymphoedema, mainly affecting the lower extremities. It is an autosomal recessively inherited condition with the gene located on chromosome 15q. A rare genetic disorder characterized by infantile cholestasis and lymphoedema, transmitted from a mother to her child in a dominant manner, as indicated by the family pedigree. It is distinct from typical cases involving Norwegian ancestry.

nodes.label: Bromodomain
nodes.description: An approximately 110-amino-acid module found in many chromatin-associated proteins, particularly in histone-acetyltransferase (HAT)-associated transcriptional co-activators like P/CAF (p300/CBP-associated factor). It has a unique left-handed up-and-down four-helix bundle structure and can interact specifically with acetylated lysine. A domain found in the GCN5 protein, which is involved in the solution structure and acetyl-lysine binding activity. It has a left-handed four-helix bundle topology with two short additional helices in a long connecting loop. The bromodomain forms a specific binding pocket for the acetamide moiety of peptides containing an N(epsilon)-acetylated lysine residue, with modest affinity (K(D) approximately 0.9 mM). It also binds the small ligands N(omega)-acetylhistamine and N-methylacetamide, confirming specificity for the alkyl acetamide moiety. A domain found in proteins of the BET family, responsible for recognizing acetylated chromatin. The bromodomain is present in two copies in BRD2 (BD1 and BD2). The BRD2 BD1 protein forms an intact homodimer in the crystal, with a buried hydrophobic core region at the interface. A domain found in many chromatin-associated proteins and in nearly all known nuclear histone acetyltransferases (HATs). It is present in BRD7 and plays an important role in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional activation. The solution structure of BRD7 bromodomain has been determined by NMR spectroscopy, and it contains the typical left-handed four-helix bundle topology. A protein domain found in chromatin-associated proteins and histone acetyltransferases, responsible for binding acetyl-lysine motifs and playing a crucial role in regulating protein-protein interactions in histone-directed chromatin remodeling and gene transcription. A protein domain found in BET family proteins, specifically in Brd2. It consists of two tandem bromodomains (BD1 and BD2) that bind the acetylated histone H4 and are responsible for mitotic retention on chromosomes. The BD2 domain is monomeric in solution and has a unique pi-helix (piD) in the ZA loop that forms part of the acetyl-lysine binding site. The BET family bromodomains may share a common characteristic in having additional secondary elements in the long ZA loop.

nodes.label: Tofacitinib
nodes.description: An oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used for the treatment of moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA), with a potency of approximately 3.5 mg BID in clinical studies. It demonstrates efficacy and safety comparable to other disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and is associated with infections, malignancies, elevations in serum creatinine and lipids. It is an oral treatment option for RA patients who have an inadequate response or intolerance to methotrexate. Tofacitinib is also used in the treatment of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

nodes.label: Barth syndrome
nodes.description: A rare, X-linked recessive genetic disorder affecting only boys, characterized by growth retardation, cardioskeletal myopathy, chronic or cyclic neutropenia, and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. It is caused by mutations in the tafazzin (TAZ) gene, leading to cardiolipin deficiency and resulting in respiratory chain dysfunction. Clinical manifestations include cardiomyopathy, neutropenia, skeletal muscle weakness, and growth delay. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent the progression of heart failure. There is no specific treatment, and current therapy is primarily palliative, focusing on managing organ-specific complications during disease progression.

nodes.label: Overall survival
nodes.description: A measure of the length of time from a defined point in time, such as the start of treatment or diagnosis, until death, often used to assess the effectiveness of treatments or prognostic factors in various types of cancer and other medical conditions. It can be analyzed in molecularly defined subgroups of patients and may be influenced by factors such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or specific drug regimens.

nodes.label: Angiogenin
nodes.description: A type of RNase homologue with roles in human pathologies, for which therapeutic agents are being developed to control its activities. A 14-kDa plasma protein with angiogenic and ribonucleolytic activities, which binds specifically to aortic smooth muscle cells, activates second messenger pathways, and inhibits their proliferation. It exists in both native and iodinated forms, with the latter being used to study internalization through receptor-mediated endocytosis. The protein is processed into fragments with molecular masses of 14 kDa, 8.7 kDa, 10.5 kDa, and 6.1 kDa after internalization. A potent blood-vessel-inducing polypeptide with a molecular weight of 14,000 that has a unique ribonucleolytic activity. It was first isolated from the conditioned medium of tumor cells and later purified from normal plasma. Angiogenin has the potential to induce neovascularization, but its activity should be strictly controlled due to its role in angiogenesis. It interacts with cell-surface receptors and extracellular matrix of endothelial cells, and its ribonucleolytic activity and cell binding property can be inhibited by ribonuclease inhibitor. Divalent copper, a modulator of angiogenesis, also influences its overall activity. A small basic protein with a molecular weight of 14,120 used as a complexing agent for heparin-derived oligosaccharides larger than decasaccharides. It forms ionic complexes with an inhomogeneous hexadecasaccharide fraction. A protein identical to the degranulation inhibitory protein (DIP) with a molecular weight of 14 kD. It is involved in angioplastic processes.

nodes.label: Study
nodes.description: A research investigation involving various methodologies such as randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and systematic reviews, evaluating the efficacy, safety, and associations of different interventions, treatments, and factors on health outcomes, including genetic changes, seizure management, vulvodynia, HIV prevention, fracture risk prediction, TIA management, diabetes treatment, rectal cancer treatment, mosquito species for Zika virus infection, dietary patterns and colorectal cancer risk, postoperative morbidity, dietary patterns and colorectal cancer staging progression, surgical outcomes, and treatment outcomes for pectus excavatum patients.

nodes.label: Denosumab
nodes.description: A fully human monoclonal antibody to RANKL with pharmacologic attributes similar to Osteoprotegerin, used to treat osteoporosis, bone metastases, and other bone-related conditions. It has a significantly longer half-life, offering less frequent administration and a rapid onset of action. Denosumab has been shown to reduce bone turnover, improve bone density, and provide good tolerability. It is a potent antiresorptive drug that increases bone mineral density and bone mass, leading to increased bone strength. Long-term treatment with denosumab results in a continued almost linear increase in total hip and femoral neck BMD beyond 3 years up to 8 years. Denosumab may cause a generalized urticarial reaction and facial angioedema in some patients, requiring desensitization.

nodes.label: FDA
nodes.description: The United States Food and Drug Administration is a federal agency responsible for ensuring the safety and effectiveness of medications, devices, and food products. It approves drugs for use, regulates their safety and effectiveness, and has recently approved several antibody drugs for treating various cancers, as well as eteplirsen and golodirsen for DMD exons 51 and 53 skipping respectively. The FDA also granted conditional approval for sotorasib in May 2021.

nodes.label: Hyperglycemia
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by high blood sugar levels, often associated with diabetes and contributing to acidic conditions in the brain that can activate asparaginyl endopeptidase and lead to the etiopathogenesis of Alzheimer disease. It is a symptom of various conditions, including Type 1 Diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and diabetic ketoacidosis, and can be a side effect of certain medications or treatments. Hyperglycemia is associated with endothelial dysfunction and increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

nodes.label: EP-DNN
nodes.description: A deep neural network-based architecture developed in this paper for predicting the presence and types of enhancers in the human genome. It uses features such as expression levels of histone modifications at the peaks of functional sites and their adjacent regions. It has superior accuracy and takes less time to make predictions compared to other computational models. EP-DNN is a developed method that has high accuracy of prediction for the operational region of enhancer prediction for all four cell lines studied. It outperforms DEEP-ENCODE and RFECS. A deep neural network-based global enhancer prediction algorithm used to predict enhancers based on chromatin features in different cell types. It uses a DNN-based architecture to extract enhancer signatures and is trained using p300 binding sites as enhancers and TSS and random non-DHS sites as non-enhancers. EP-DNN has a validation rate of 91.6% and performs better than DEEP-ENCODE and RFECS.

nodes.label: PIK3CA
nodes.description: A gene encoding a protein that antagonizes the function of the PTEN protein in the PI3K/Akt pathway, with mutations identified in glioblastomas, periampullary and ampullary adenomas and carcinomas, colorectal cancer, and lung adenocarcinoma. Mutations are primarily found in exons 9 and 20, with exon 20 mutations associated with a worse outcome compared to wild types. PIK3CA mutations have a frequency of 14.5% in studied tumors, 21% in colorectal cancer patients, and 72.2% in pure TNACs. It is one of the 8 genes analyzed for mutation patterns in glioblastoma multiforme and is involved in known driver mutations identified by VarDict in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Lung Adenocarcinoma dataset.

nodes.label: Panitumumab
nodes.description: A fully human monoclonal antibody targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), approved in the United States and Europe for the treatment of refractory metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). It is used in the Skin Toxicity Evaluation Protocol with Panitumumab (STEPP) study as part of the pre-emptive treatment regimen, which includes the use of skin moisturizers, sunscreen, topical steroid, and doxycycline. Panitumumab is an anti-EGFR drug used in the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) and is often combined with chemotherapy, particularly in patients with KRAS wild-type tumours. It can cause acneiform rash in 30 to 90% of patients and is used in EGFR-targeted treatments for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). Clinical outcomes are strongly predicted by KRAS mutations.

nodes.label: Autophagy
nodes.description: A cellular process involved in the degradation and recycling of damaged or unnecessary cellular components, including mitochondria. It is a lysosome-associated process regulated by the CLEAR network and is involved in maintaining cellular homeostasis, energy production, and cellular recycling. Autophagy is also associated with mitochondrial autophagy, mitophagy, and the clearance of long-lived or damaged organelles. Dysfunctions in autophagy are linked to various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, cardiomyopathies, and sarcopenia.

nodes.label: Belzutifan
nodes.description: A specific HIF2α inhibitor that has shown signs of efficacy in kidney cancer, particularly in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), with an objective response rate of 25% in 55 patients. A hypoxia-inducible factor-2α (HIF2α) inhibitor that has been approved by the FDA for treating von Hippel-Lindau disease-associated renal cell carcinoma, central nervous system hemangioblastomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. A HIF-2α inhibitor mentioned as a possible new approach in subsequent lines of therapy for renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It is discussed in the context of the 2021 ASCO Genitourinary Cancers Symposium. A small molecule used for the treatment of renal cell carcinoma associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. It is also known as MK-6482. An oral small molecule inhibitor of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-2α developed by Peloton Therapeutics for the treatment of solid tumours, including renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with clear cell histology (ccRCC) and von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease-associated RCC. It received its first approval in the USA in August 2021 for the treatment of patients with VHL disease who require therapy for associated RCC, central nervous system (CNS) haemangioblastomas or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (pNET), not requiring immediate surgery.

nodes.label: KCNJ2
nodes.description: A gene encoding an inward rectifier potassium channel, specifically the Kir2.1 channel, involved in causing Short QT syndrome through gain-of-function mutations. This gene is also associated with atrial fibrillation and is located near the susceptibility locus on chromosome 17q24.3. Gain-of-function mutations in this gene lead to a shortening of the action potential duration.

nodes.label: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
nodes.description: A hereditary cerebrovascular disease leading to accumulating neurologic deficits and dementia, associated with nucleotide substitutions and deletions in the Notch3 gene. A genetic disorder characterized by cerebral arteriopathy, subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, with a predominant inheritance pattern of autosomal dominance. It is associated with mutations in the Notch3 gene, leading to various clinical manifestations and MRI findings such as white matter hyperintensities, lacunar infarcts, and microbleeds. The prevalence of certain symptoms and MRI abnormalities may vary among populations, including the Korean population. A genetic disorder characterized by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, causing widespread white-matter lesions associated with lacunar infarctions in various subcortical areas. It leads to migraine with aura, ischemic strokes, cognitive impairment, and mood disturbances. CADASIL is considered a unique model to study subcortical ischemic vascular dementia. Magnetic resonance imaging markers associated with cognitive and motor disabilities include the number and severity of lacunar infarctions and cerebral atrophy. Mood disturbances, present in 10% to 20% of patients, may be linked to ischemic lesions in the basal ganglia or frontal white matter. A genetic disorder characterized by cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy, associated with headache symptoms. The diagnostic criteria for any type of migraine in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, second edition (ICHD-II) require that the disturbance is not attributed to another disorder. A cerebrovascular disease caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, characterized by loss or gain of a cysteine residue in the gene. It involves a cluster of mutations around exons 3 and 4, and has been associated with several genetic variations in both coding and intronic regions. The disease has been identified in 14 familial forms, with causative mutations found in exons 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 14, 19, 20, and 22 of the NOTCH3 gene. Exons 6 and 8 have not shown any pathogenetic mutations. A disease caused by mutations within the NOTCH3 gene, characterized by cerebral arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. Associated with the gain or loss of a cysteine amino acid in the first twenty-four exons of the NOTCH3 gene.

nodes.label: Dracorhodin perchlorate
nodes.description: A red pigment, specifically an anthocyanin, that induces apoptosis in A375-S2 cells through the activation of caspases and the upregulation of p53 and p21(WAF1) proteins. It also affects the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and activates JNK and p38 MAPK pathways. The drug's effects can be modulated by various inhibitors, such as SP600125, SB 203580, PD98059, CH-11, wortmanin, and genistein. An anthocyanin red pigment that induces apoptosis in HL-60 cells, leading to cell death through the activation of caspases -1, -3, -8, -9, and -10, and the degradation of caspase-3 substrates such as ICAD and PARP. It also up-regulates the expression ratio of mitochondrial proteins, Bax/Bcl-XL, and induces the phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, and p38 MAPK. A chemical compound that exhibits growth inhibitory and pro-apoptotic effects on human prostate cancer cell line PC-3. It is administered in different concentrations (10-80 μmol/L) and time periods (12-48 h) to evaluate its impact on cell viability, proliferation, and apoptosis. A chemical compound that inhibits PI3K/Akt and NF-κB activation, up-regulates the expression of p53, and enhances apoptosis. It induces apoptotic cell death in cancer cells, specifically in SGC-7901 cells, by mediating cell cycle arrest and inducing apoptosis through upregulation of p53 and inhibition of PI3K/Akt and NF-κB activation. It also suppresses IGF-1-induced phosphorylation of Akt and TNF-induced NF-κB transcriptional activity. A synthetic analogue of the antimicrobial anthocyanin red pigment dracorhodin, reported to induce apoptosis in human prostate cancer, human gastric tumor cells, human melanoma, and human breast cancer cells through mitochondrial pathways. It dose and time-dependently inhibits the growth of MCF-7 cells and regulates the expression of Bcl-2 and Bax, leading to decreased mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) and release of AIF and cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, further activating caspase-9 and ultimately causing apoptosis.

nodes.label: MITF
nodes.description: A transcription factor that is essential for normal melanocyte development and regulates expression of several pigmentation genes, including SILV and MLANA. It encodes a protein that is recognized by the melanoma diagnostic antibody MITF (D5) and binds to conserved DNA sequences in the promoter/enhancer regions of SILV and MLANA genes. A transcription factor that is essential for the survival of pigmented cells. High levels of MITF drive melanocyte differentiation, while lower levels are required to permit proliferation and survival of melanoma cells. MITF is phosphorylated by ERK, which stimulates its activation but also targets it for degradation through the ubiquitin-proteosome pathway. Oncogenic BRAF up-regulates MITF transcription through ERK and the transcription factor BRN2. In melanoma cells, MITF is required downstream of oncogenic BRAF for the regulation of key cell cycle regulatory proteins such as CDK2 and CDK4. However, in melanocytes, BRN2 is not expressed, indicating that MITF regulation is a newly acquired function of oncogenic BRAF that is not performed by the wild-type protein. A marker gene expressed by melanocytes, involved in the regulation of melanogenesis and melanosome biogenesis. A master regulator of melanocyte development, differentiation, migration, and survival, directly regulating the transcription of genes involved in pigmentation which are selective to the melanocyte lineage. It also controls expression of genes which are expressed in multiple cell lineages and may play differential roles in activating vs. maintaining gene expression patterns. A transcription factor that, along with TFEB, is recruited to lysosomes by interaction with active Rag heterodimers. It is not further described in the text.
