Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor, a protein regulated by the EMT transcription factor ZEB2 to control melanocyte differentiation. Loss of ZEB2 results in downregulation of MITF levels. A transcription factor involved in the direct conversion of mouse and human fibroblasts to functional melanocytes. It is one of the three factors identified in the study. A transcription factor associated with melanoma oncogene and lysosomal master regulator TFEB, involved in endolysosomal biogenesis and Wnt signaling. It has the highest phylogenetic conservation of three consecutive putative GSK3 phosphorylation sites in animal proteomes. A transcription factor that is the master regulator of the melanocyte lineage, involved in transcription, DNA replication and repair, and chromatin organization. It interacts with a PBAF chromatin remodeling complex comprising BRG1 and CHD7, and is actively recruited to a set of MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) at active enhancers by combinations of MITF, SOX10, TFAP2A, and YY1. MITF-BRG1 interplay plays an essential role in transcription regulation in melanoma. A transcription factor and the 'master regulator' of melanocyte development. MITF is considered necessary for the induction of the melanocyte lineage, similar to TFAP2 paralogs. It binds to the promoter of TRPM1, a pigmentation gene, and its activity is required for the expression of certain pigmentation genes. In mouse embryos with Wnt1-Cre-mediated deletion of Tfap2a and Tfap2b in the neural crest, MITF is still present, suggesting its importance in melanocyte development. The expression of Trpm1, a pigmentation gene, is not TFAP2A-dependent, implying that additional TFAP2 paralogs function redundantly to drive melanocyte differentiation, which is consistent with previous results from zebrafish. A lineage-specific transcription factor that, along with TFAP2 paralogs, directly regulates effectors of terminal differentiation in melanocytes. A key transcription factor for melanocyte development and differentiation. Regulates expression of numerous pigmentation genes to promote melanocyte differentiation and maintain cell homeostasis by controlling genes encoding proteins involved in apoptosis and the cell cycle. Loss-of-function mutations cause Waardenburg syndrome type IIA, while amplification or specific mutation can be an oncogenic event in melanomas. A gene product that influences MEL enhancer function in the melanocytic (MEL) state of melanoma cells, working together with SOX10 to achieve high levels of activity.

nodes.label: Chlamydia trachomatis
nodes.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, which was prevalent among the African HIV-1 seronegative women enrolled in the ASPIRE trial, affecting 12% of the participants. A bacterium responsible for causing cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), often transmitted through sexual contact. A bacterial infection that can lead to cervicitis, urethritis, and infertility. It is characterized by a high prevalence of DNA and seroprevalence among women attending infertility and gynecology clinics in Hunan, China. The most prevalent genotype is E (27.5%). C. trachomatis omp1 sense mutation is associated with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) with an odds ratio of 6.033. C. trachomatis DNA is significantly associated with CIN, while pgp3 antibody is not. A sexually transmitted infection (STI) associated with anorectal infections in female sex workers (FSWs) and female non-sex workers (NSW) in Ecuador. It is detected in conjunction with Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) and Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) in anorectal swabs. A disease or disorder detected at high prevalence in the anorectum of female sex workers (FSWs), suggesting the possibility of missing significant infections if only genital testing is provided. A sexually transmitted bacterial pathogen that can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and other reproductive sequelae when it ascends to the upper genital tract. It is the focus of the study investigating cervicovaginal microbial features and their impact on its spread. A bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, which can lead to various symptoms including lower abdominal discomfort, salpingitis, pelvic peritonitis, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome. It can also cause chronic infection in the uterus, leading to peritonitis when the uterine cavity is examined.

nodes.label: Body mass index (BMI)
nodes.description: A measure used to assess body fat based on weight and height, categorized as normal (less than 25 kg/m²), overweight (25-29 kg/m²), and obese (³ 30 kg/m²). It is used to estimate the prevalence of overweight and obesity in each country of the European Union, assess the risk of various diseases and mortality associated with obesity, and categorize individuals as underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese. Higher BMIs were associated with an increased risk of early-onset CRC among women and an increased risk of FASN-negative colorectal cancer compared to normal BMI.

nodes.label: Human African Trypanosomiasis
nodes.description: Another name for African Sleeping Sickness, a parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei (gambiense or rhodesiense), and one of the declared neglected tropical diseases. A parasitic infection caused by two species of trypanosomes, Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and rhodesiense, transmitted by the tsetse fly. It eventually affects the central nervous system, resulting in severe neurological symptoms and without treatment, death is inevitable. An endemic parasitic disease of sub-Saharan Africa, caused by two subspecies of protozoa belonging to Trypanosoma genus: T. brucei gambiense and T. brucei rhodesiense. It involves the inhibition of papain-family cysteine proteases rhodesain and TbCatB, which are essential for parasite survival and play a role in immunoevasion and iron acquisition by the parasite. A fatal disease caused by two subspecies of the genus Trypanosoma, namely Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense and Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, with limited therapy options due to the availability of only five non-adequate drugs. A neglected tropical disease caused by infections due to Trypanosoma brucei subspecies, including Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, and is associated with genetic factors such as IL1 gene polymorphism. A disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei, also known as sleeping sickness, which leads to serious neurological disorders and is fatal if left untreated. It is associated with the development of various treatments with important limitations such as acute toxicity and parasite resistance. A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by the tsetse fly insect vector (Glossina spp). It has been a significant public health issue affecting the poorest and most vulnerable communities in Africa. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established a dedicated 2021-2030 roadmap for its elimination. Since 2018, less than 1000 cases are detected annually.

nodes.label: Progression-free survival (PFS)
nodes.description: A measure of the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death, used to evaluate the effectiveness of therapies in clinical trials, particularly in oncology. It refers to the length of time during and after treatment when the disease does not worsen, and is often used as a primary or secondary endpoint in clinical trials to assess the efficacy of a therapeutic intervention. Higher PFS percentages indicate better treatment outcomes.

nodes.label: Hippocampus
nodes.description: A brain structure located in the medial temporal lobe, involved in memory formation, consolidation, and spatial navigation. It contains the dentate gyrus, with granule cells essential for memory function. The hippocampus shows reduced glucose metabolism in Alzheimer's disease despite elevated PiB uptake. It is also involved in emotion and has serotonergic system expression differences in Mecp2-/y mice. The hippocampus is a specific brain subregion most relevant to Alzheimer's disease, exhibiting important radiomic features including shape, GLSZM, and GLDM. It is one of the regions where both Aducanumab and scanning ultrasound reduce the total plaque area in APP23 mice. The hippocampus is where hyperphosphorylated tau accumulates, cytoskeletal changes occur, and CNA alpha -/- mice exhibit deficits in learning and memory.

nodes.label: Non-small cell lung cancer
nodes.description: A type of lung cancer characterized by the absence of small cells, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. It is the most common type of lung cancer and is associated with wide-ranging survival rates and treatment outcomes. Non-small cell lung cancer can be targeted by various treatments, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, PARP1/2 inhibitors, and KRAS G12C inhibitors. It can also be investigated in the context of its treatment with compounds like dehydrocostuslactone (DHE) and lorlatinib. Genetic mutations, such as EGFR T790M, KRAS G12C, and ERCC1 deficiency, can influence the development and treatment of non-small cell lung cancer.

nodes.label: Pain therapy
nodes.description: A medical procedure focused on the treatment of pain in pediatric oncology patients, which involves the use of various drugs and pharmacological interventions. It is a priority for all patients, especially critically ill children, due to their vulnerability and limited understanding. The therapy takes into account the subjective experience of pain, which depends on age, pain experience, and the environment. Diagnostic and therapeutic procedures are performed under analgesia and sedation for a given drug scheme by a pediatrician experienced in intensive care.

nodes.label: Glutamate
nodes.description: An excitatory neurotransmitter involved in learning and memory. Glutamate dysfunction has been implicated in the neuropathology of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) within the cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit. A neurotransmitter involved in obsessive-compulsive symptoms (OCSS) and its abnormalities have been suggested by neuroimaging, neuropsychological, and neuromotor abnormalities. Atypical antipsychotics can induce OCSS, pointing towards the possible roles of glutamate and serotonin. Dopamine may be responsible for the beneficial role of antipsychotics in the treatment of OCD. An excitatory neurotransmitter that has been found to be dysregulated in Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. Recent evidence suggests that this dysregulation may contribute to the pathophysiology of the disorder. An amino-acid neurotransmitter whose level is reduced in the hippocampus of pR5 mice, and whose turnover is increased in the cerebral cortex via the pyruvate carboxylation pathway. A neurotransmitter involved in the pathophysiology of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). It was measured using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) in the anterior cingulate cortex of patients with OCD and healthy community volunteers. The study found that patients with OCD displayed a higher estimated GABA level and a higher GABA to glutamate ratio than healthy participants, but no significant group differences were observed in the measure of glutamate. A neurotransmitter involved in the communication between neurons. Imbalance in its level relative to GABA may contribute to the pathophysiology of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. A neurotransmitter, a neuro-chemical marker that was predicted to be depressed in subjects with Havana Syndrome. It is one of the neuro-chemical markers linked to neuropsychological constructs in the network model.

nodes.label: Landau-Kleffner syndrome
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by language disorders, including disability in understanding spoken words, inarticulation, decreased amount of speech, auditory verbal agnosia, sensory aphasia, auditory agnosia, and word deafness. Patients may show sequential and sometimes hierarchical language disorders beginning with sensory aphasia, followed by auditory agnosia, and finally word deafness during their disease process. During long-term follow-up (20 to 30 years), all patients showed marked recovery in language without any intellectual handicap, but with some disability in spoken language, auditory verbal perception, and a discrepancy between Wechsler Verbal and Performance IQ scores. It is also associated with paroxysmal EEG abnormalities, more pronounced during sleep, acquired aphasia typically of receptive type, and epileptic seizures in three-quarters of cases. Additional features include behavioral disturbances that may present with autistic features, cognitive regression of varying degrees, and sometimes motor difficulties, indicating the pervasive nature of the disorder. The epileptic activity, as manifested by the EEG, seems responsible for the pervasive dysfunction. Treatment with antiepileptic drugs is often ineffective, while ACTH and corticosteroids are currently regarded as the best therapy, and surgical treatment by subpial transection is being actively studied.

nodes.label: Myotonic dystrophy type 1
nodes.description: A multisystemic myotonic disorder characterized by genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, located at chromosome 19q 13.3. It is a dominantly inherited multisystemic disorder caused by the pathological expansion of a (CTG)(n) triplet repeat in the DMPK gene. It is characterized by fetal cells being deficient in differentiation ability compared to unaffected controls. It is one of the two known subtypes of myotonic dystrophy, along with myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2), and is one of the most frequent forms of muscular dystrophy in adulthood. Clinically, it is characterized by a high variability of muscular and extramuscular symptoms, often causing a delay in diagnosis. It is a progressive multisystem genetic disorder affecting about 1 in 8000 people worldwide, with no cure currently available. Supportive management helps to reduce morbidity and mortality, and patients require close follow-up.

nodes.label: Rett syndrome
nodes.description: An X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder that typically manifests in females after the first year of life, causing mental retardation and autistic behavior. It is characterized by incessant hand movements such as wringing, twisting, or clapping. Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene, which assists in the transcriptional silencing process via DNA methylation. The pattern of X inactivation determines phenotypic severity, with favorable skewing potentially sparing patients from severe symptoms. MECP2 mutations can manifest in a broader array of phenotypes than classic Rett syndrome, including mild learning disabilities or severe neonatal encephalopathies of unknown cause.

nodes.label: Integrin-linked kinase (ILK)
nodes.description: An essential protein involved in extracellular matrix (ECM)/integrin signaling, bridging integrin and slit diaphragm signaling, and transmitting ECM signaling through integrin receptors. It plays a crucial role in cell-ECM-adhesion, specifying nephrin and alpha-actinin-4 distribution, maintaining slit diaphragm integrity and podocyte architecture, protecting the mammalian heart against cardiomyopathy and failure, and terminating liver regeneration. ILK is also involved in bone resorption and signal transduction pathways. Its disruption can lead to various abnormalities such as impaired healing, histologic abnormalities, increased cell proliferation, hepatomegaly, and abnormal shape changes in cells.

nodes.label: Dementia with Lewy bodies
nodes.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the presence of Lewy bodies, which are formed by the accumulation of α-synuclein into intracellular aggregates, leading to symptoms of dementia and parkinsonism. It is associated with more severe autonomic failure compared to Parkinson's disease (PD), and is linked to multiple system atrophy through alpha-synuclein inclusions.

nodes.label: GATA-1
nodes.description: A zinc finger transcription factor and a central mediator of erythroid gene expression, interacting with multiple proteins including FOG-1, EKLF, SP1, CBP/p300 and PU.1. A direct physical interaction between GATA-1 and FOG-1 is essential for normal human erythroid and megakaryocyte maturation in vivo. A protein that forms distinct activating and repressive complexes in erythroid cells. It is essential for the generation of erythroid, megakaryocytic, eosinophilic, and mast cell lineages. GATA-1 acts as an activator and repressor of different target genes, such as erythroid genes, and mediates cell proliferation and early hematopoietic gene repression. It interacts with the essential hematopoietic factor Gfi-1b, the repressive MeCP1 complex, and the chromatin remodeling ACF/WCRF complex, as well as the known GATA-1/FOG-1 and GATA-1/TAL-1 complexes. FOG-1 mediates GATA-1 interactions with the MeCP1 complex, linking specific GATA-1 partners to distinct aspects of its functions. A hematopoietic transcription factor that is essential for erythroid differentiation. Its functions include upregulating erythroid genes, repressing alternative transcription programs, and suppressing cell proliferation. It interacts with various factors such as Gfi-1b, FOG-1, TAL-1, Gfi-1b, FOG-1, MeCP1, Ldb-1, Eto-2, Lmo4, and CdK9 in erythroid cells.

nodes.label: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
nodes.description: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to insulin resistance or relative insulin deficiency, pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, or both. It is associated with various complications such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetic nephropathy, and end-stage renal disease. Management includes lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapies like metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin), and other oral agents, and may progress to insulin therapy. It is the primary indication for metformin as a first-line medication and is managed with a multifactorial therapeutic approach to minimize long-term complications and optimize glycemic control.

nodes.label: Dystrophin
nodes.description: A large cytoskeletal protein involved in maintaining muscle cell integrity, particularly in striated muscle, and encoded by the dystrophin gene. Mutations in the dystrophin gene can lead to deletions, point mutations, or duplications, causing dystrophinopathies such as Duchenne's and Becker's muscular dystrophies. Dystrophin is a membrane-associated protein that, when absent, results in numerous cellular defects including mechanical instability of the sarcolemma, increased influx of extracellular calcium, and cell signaling defects in dystrophin-deficient striated muscle. Its expression is determined in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and is not found in most patients, confirming the diagnosis. Golodirsen, an exon-skipping therapy, has been used to increase dystrophin production in DMD patients, demonstrating a significant increase in dystrophin protein expression and sarcolemmal localization at week 48.

nodes.label: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
nodes.description: A class of drugs used in cancer treatment that target specific immune system proteins, such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1, to restore the capability of the immune system to attack cancer cells and stop their growth. These inhibitors can be used alone or in combination with other cancer treatments like surgery, radiation, or chemotherapy. They are known to have fewer side effects compared to traditional chemotherapy drugs, but may still cause fatigue, skin rashes, fever, cardiotoxicity, and inflammation in the intestines or lungs. A type of immunotherapy that involves blocking immune checkpoints to enhance the body's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells.

nodes.label: Zika virus
nodes.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus that primarily affects humans and can cause mild symptoms such as fever, rash, and joint pain. However, it can lead to severe complications in pregnant women, including fetal microcephaly and an increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome. The virus is transmitted by the Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes and can also be sexually transmitted. It has caused significant public health concerns, especially in the Americas, leading to large outbreaks and affecting millions of people. The virus has significant neurotrophic properties, but further research is needed to understand its mechanisms of pathogenesis.

nodes.label: PLA2G6
nodes.description: A gene encoding a calcium-independent group VI phospholipase A2, which is mutated in neurodegenerative disorders with high brain iron, including infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (INAD), neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), and the related Karak syndrome. A gene responsible for infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, neurodegeneration associated with brain iron accumulation, and Karak syndrome. It has been identified as the causative gene for early-onset PARK14-linked dystonia-parkinsonism. Mutations in this gene can lead to early-onset l-dopa-responsive parkinsonism with dementia and frontotemporal lobar atrophy. Two novel compound heterozygous PLA2G6 mutations were detected in the study: patient A carries p.F72L/p.R635Q, while patients B1 and B2 carry p.Q452X/p.R635Q. All three patients exhibited early-onset l-dopa-responsive parkinsonism with dementia and frontotemporal lobar atrophy. SPECT in patient B1 revealed frontotemporal lobar hypoperfusion, and MRI in patient A showed iron accumulation in the substantia nigra and striatum. A gene that encodes a group VIA calcium-independent phospholipase A2 beta enzyme, which selectively hydrolyzes glycerophospholipids to release free fatty acids. Mutations in this gene have been associated with disorders such as infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type II and Karak syndrome. It was also identified as the causative gene in a subgroup of patients with autosomal recessive early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism. A gene whose normal activity leads to lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction and subsequent mitochondrial membrane abnormalities when lost. It is associated with neurodegeneration and has a knockout fly model for further study.

nodes.label: Bulevirtide
nodes.description: A first-in-class entry inhibitor developed by MYR GmbH for the treatment of chronic hepatitis delta virus (HDV) and chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections. It is a small lipopeptide agent that specifically binds to the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) bile salt transporter and HBV/HDV receptor on the surface of human hepatocytes, inhibiting HDV and HBV entry. Bulevirtide has received conditional authorization of use from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and has been submitted for approval in the United States. It is a promising new therapeutic option for hepatitis D virus infection. Bulevirtide was recently approved in the European Union (EU) for the treatment of chronic HDV infection in HDV RNA positive adult patients with compensated liver disease. It is used in combination with pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN) and as monotherapy in the study. Bulevirtide is a medication that blocks the entry of HDV into hepatocytes and is administered subcutaneously at 2 mg per day or 10 mg per day for 144 weeks. Patients in the control group received no treatment for 48 weeks followed by 10 mg per day for 96 weeks. Bulevirtide has shown potent activity against multiple laboratory strains spanning all HBV/HDV A-H/1-8 genotype combinations and the most diverse collection of HDV clinical samples tested to date, including HBV/HDV genotype combinations less frequently observed in the clinic.

nodes.label: Mitf
nodes.description: A murine transcription factor involved in melanocyte development, studied alongside Pax-3 using a transgenic mouse model and two murine coat color mutants, Splotch (Sp) and Mitf(mi). A mutation in this gene is present in the Mitf(mi) mouse model, and it is required for the survival of melanoblasts up to the migration staging area in neural crest development. A gene that facilitates the survival of the melanoblast in a gene dosage-dependent manner within and immediately after emigration from the dorsal neural tube, and may also directly or indirectly affect the rate at which melanoblast number increases during dorsolateral pathway migration. A basic helix-loop-helix-leucine zipper transcription factor whose M isoform is restricted to neural crest derived melanocytes and is essential for the development of these cells in vertebrates from mammals to fish. It is involved in the differentiation of medaka blastula derived stem cells into melanocytes when expressed in embryonic stem (ES) cell lines. A basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that plays an essential role in the differentiation of the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and neural crest-derived melanocytes. It is expressed at lower levels in pigmented epithelial RPE-like cells compared to neural crest-derived melanocytes. Overexpression of Mitf in cultured quail RPE causes cells to develop into neural crest-like pigmented cells, suggesting that it is sufficient for the proper differentiation of crest-like pigmented cells from retinal cells. A target of SOX10, involved in the negative regulation of Sox10 in McSCs. Haploinsufficiency for Mitf exacerbates Tg(DctSox10) hair graying, suggesting that MITF participates in the negative regulation of Sox10 in McSCs. A transcription factor important in melanoma development and progression, associated with a distinct transcriptional program and poor patient survival in metastatic melanoma. Loss of Mitf is marked by MITF promoter hypermethylation and loss of melanocyte-specific gene expression. It is involved in the phenotype switching of melanoma cells into highly migratory and drug-tolerant dedifferentiated states. In this study, depletion of SOX10 in Mitf-methylated melanoma cells using CRISPR/Cas9 supports the findings related to this gene.

nodes.label: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for preventing HIV-1 transmission before potential exposure. It primarily involves the use of drugs like tenofovir (TFV) disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine (FTC) in the form of Truvada. A medical procedure or test involving the topical application of anti-HIV drugs to the mucosal sites of infection for preventing HIV infection. A medical procedure used for the prevention of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. It involves the use of medications such as Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)/emtricitabine (FTC) and other antiretroviral agents from different drug classes like integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTI), nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI), and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI) as potential therapies. A method of using antiretroviral medications, specifically the combination of emtricitabine-tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (FTC/TDF), to prevent the acquisition of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). It requires patient and provider acceptance, adherence, and retention in care during periods of high-risk behaviors. A key component of the HIV prevention strategy in the US, which has been demonstrated to be highly effective in preventing HIV acquisition among individuals at risk. It involves the use of two PrEP medications: emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Truvada®; F/TDF) and emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Descovy®; F/TAF). Both medications have been found to be efficacious and well tolerated.

nodes.label: ABCG1
nodes.description: A gene involved in the expression of mRNA in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of 100-km ultramarathon runners, whose expression levels were measured by real-time quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). A human ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter that removes excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues. It has a cryo-EM structure reported at 4 Å resolution in an inward-open state, featuring sterol-like density in the binding cavity. It is compared structurally with ABCG2 and ABCG5/G8 to understand mechanistic differences and substrate specificity. Benzamil and taurocholate inhibit its ATPase activity when reconstituted in liposomes, while Ko143 does not.

nodes.label: Pendrin
nodes.description: A 780-amino acid protein encoded by the SLC26A4 gene, functioning as a multifunctional anion exchanger involved in iodide transport by thyrocytes, apical Cl(-)/HCO3(-) exchange in intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct, and regulating ion and fluid transport by the endolymphatic sac epithelium. It is also expressed in the inner ear, thyroid, and kidney, and mutations in the SLC26A4 gene underlie Pendred syndrome.

nodes.label: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
nodes.description: An acute, life-threatening disease characterized by enhanced platelet aggregation, disturbed microcirculation, and organ dysfunction. A life-threatening and debilitating disease characterized by acquired, anti-ADAMTS13 antibody-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which historically had a fatal prognosis but is now managed with daily therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE). Despite this, relapses occur in up to 40% of patients and refractory disease with fatal outcomes still occurs, typically within the first days of management. The introduction of rituximab has been a major breakthrough in TTP management, with routine recommendation during the acute phase and increasing use as frontline therapy, leading to high response rates in the following weeks. In more severe patients, salvage strategies typically include twice daily TPE, pulses of cyclophosphamide, as well as splenectomy in the more desperate cases. A medical condition characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and a consumptive thrombocytopenia, resulting from severe deficiency of ADAMTS13. It requires standard of care treatment involving plasma exchange and immunosuppression, and poses a significant risk of relapse and long-term complications associated with significant morbidity and even mortality.

nodes.label: Menin
nodes.description: A protein encoded by the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) tumor suppressor gene, Menin is an integral component of MLL1/MLL2 histone methyltransferase complexes specific for Lys4 of histone H3 (H3K4). It acts as a transcriptional coactivator of the nuclear receptors for estrogen and vitamin D. A protein that interacts with SKIP and c-Myc to promote HIV-1 Tat transactivation. It is required for HIV-1 transcription but not for MLL1 or H3K4me3. A subunit of MLL1/MLL2-containing histone methyltransferase complexes that trimethylate histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3), encoded by the MEN1 gene.

nodes.label: Methyl-directed mismatch repair (MMR)
nodes.description: A type of DNA repair mechanism that affects the stability of CTG repeats in Escherichia coli, generating slipped structures during replication, causing single triplet expansions and contractions. It is a biochemical process in Escherichia coli and related enteric bacteria that repairs replication errors, involving proteins such as MutS, MutL, and MutH. It is more efficient during exponential growth compared to very short-patch (VSP) repair. It is a biological process involving the repair of mismatched DNA, detected using MMR-proficient or MMR-deficient E. coli strains carrying a lac +1 frameshift mutation expressing hMLH1 proteins. It is a system in bacteria that maintains genome stability by repairing mismatches in DNA sequences that have been methylated. Defects in this system, particularly mutations in mutS, lead to higher mutation frequencies and increased resistance levels in mutator strains. It is involved in the control of genotoxicity of O(6)-alkylG adducts in Escherichia coli and is involved in the coordination with the canonical MTase repair of O(6)mG:T mismatches. It is one of two mismatch repair pathways in E. coli that converts G:T mispairs to native G:C pairings, along with very short patch repair (VSPR). It is a biological process involving the mismatch repair protein MutS and the gene or protein Thermotoga maritima MutL (TmL) to assist in the initiation of the methyl-directed mismatch repair response in various organisms ranging from prokaryotes to eukaryotes. It is a specific type of mismatch repair that recognizes O(6)-mG:T replication intermediates and triggers sensitivity to methylating agents. It is involved in the mutS/L operon, which is essential for methyldirected mismatch repair activity.

nodes.label: Endometrial carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the female genital tract, characterized by infiltrating tumors and myometrial invasion. It is the most frequent among infiltrating tumors of the female genital tract, with myometrial invasion representing an increase in the rate of recurrences and a decrease in survival. A type of cancer affecting the endometrium, the lining of the uterus. The study analyzes the expression levels of various immune checkpoint molecules in tissue samples from patients with this disease to detect the immunosuppressive environment of endometrial carcinomas. A type of cancer involving the endometrium, characterized by abnormal angiogenesis and increased expression of factors such as VEGF-A, TSP-1, COX-2, PGE2, and aromatase (P450arom). MicroRNA-101 levels are reduced in this disease.

nodes.label: Epilepsy
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by recurrent seizures, which can affect patients of all age groups, including children, adults and the elderly. It is associated with various syndromes such as Landau-Kleffner syndrome, Tuberous sclerosis complex, and can be a symptom of conditions like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. Epilepsy can present with different types and frequencies of seizures and may require monotherapy or polytherapy for management. It is also observed in genetic disorders like NF1 and NF2, where it can be related to specific mutations or tumors. Some forms of epilepsy may be pharmacoresistant and can involve cognitive impairments.

nodes.label: Apixaban
nodes.description: A direct factor Xa inhibitor, developed by Bristol-Myers Squibb and Pfizer for the prevention and treatment of thrombotic disorders. It is used as a new oral anticoagulant in patients with atrial fibrillation, found to be safe and effective in reducing stroke risk. Compared to warfarin and other drugs in clinical trials for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, it has shown numerically superior results in some studies and a lower risk of major hemorrhage. Apixaban is also used for the treatment of thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and has a half-life of about 12 hours. The normal dosage is 5 mg orally twice daily, but it may be reduced based on individual factors of the patient. It is a reference standard for evaluating the efficacy and safety of other anticoagulants in the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism in patients with atrial fibrillation.

nodes.label: Hypophosphatemic rickets
nodes.description: A disease characterized by hypophosphatemia, involving the overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), and associated with mutations in genes such as phosphate-regulating gene with homologies to endopeptidases on the X chromosome, dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1, and ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1. It can be caused by activating mutations in the FGF23 gene, leading to autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, or inactivating mutations, resulting in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets 1, and autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets 2. Iron deficiency may affect the phenotype of autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets by regulating FGF23 production. Treatment options include activated vitamin D metabolites and oral inorganic phosphate salts, but identification of the causative mutation can be useful for diagnosis and prognosis. A familial disorder characterized by severe early signs of rickets and delayed growth, with a mode of inheritance that is autosomal dominant. It affects both a father and his son, with plasma 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D and PTH levels being normal and no hypercalciuria present. Treatment with vitamin D (40,000 U/day) in the father and 1 alpha hydroxyvitamin D (1 microgram/day) in the son leads to complete cure of rickets and catch-up growth.

nodes.label: Transient Ischemic Attack
nodes.description: A medical condition involving temporary reduction of blood flow to part of the brain, often serving as a warning sign for future ischemic strokes. Patients with this condition were enrolled in the study at 16 North Carolina hospitals, presenting within 24 hours of symptom onset. A medical condition characterized by temporary reduction of blood flow to part of the brain, leading to symptoms such as weakness, numbness, or confusion that last for a short period of time before resolving completely. It is also known as TIA. A medical condition being studied for risk stratification using the ABCD2 score and its modifications. Patients with this condition are evaluated to determine their risk category based on various factors such as age, blood pressure, clinical symptoms, duration of symptoms, and diabetes. A medical condition characterized by a temporary reduction in blood flow to part of the brain, leading to symptoms such as weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking. It can be followed by a stroke or recurrent TIA. A medical condition characterized by temporary disruption of blood supply to the brain, leading to symptoms such as weakness, numbness, or confusion that resolve within 24 hours. A medical condition characterized by temporary neurological symptoms due to reduced blood flow to the brain, often serving as a warning sign for future strokes. A medical condition characterized by temporary disruption of blood flow to the brain, leading to symptoms similar to stroke but without permanent damage. It is associated with extracranial stenosis (ECS) and intracranial stenosis (ICS) as independent risk factors for stroke.

nodes.label: Mitosis
nodes.description: A type of cell division in which the cell nucleus splits into two daughter nuclei, followed by the division of the cell cytoplasm. Cohesion has to be dissolved during this process, partly mediated by the protease separase and controlled by Wapl. It is a stage in the cell cycle where the cell's chromosomes are divided into two sets, preparing the cell for division into two daughter cells. In metazoa, it is characterized by nuclear pore complexes disassembling and reassembling at the end of the process, leading to a reforming nuclear envelope. It is regulated by MITF, along with DNA replication and repair, for which MITF directly regulates a set of genes. It is also associated with the reduction of the 28-kDa cleaved coilin fragment levels and the excision of gap junction elements in response to Molluscum contagiosum virus infection.

nodes.label: TP53
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene that plays a crucial role in preventing uncontrolled cell growth and promoting apoptosis. Mutations in TP53 can lead to cancer development, particularly in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), and colorectal cancer. It encodes a protein involved in sustaining cellular homeostasis via different signaling pathways and is often mutated or deleted in malignant gliomas. TP53 mutations are evaluated through molecular techniques such as single-strand conformational polymorphism, array-comparative genomic hybridization, and fluorescence in situ hybridization. Germline mutations in TP53 are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome and increase the risk of developing various types of cancer, including adrenocortical carcinoma and breast cancer. In the studied cohort, 3 out of 213 women with HER2+ breast cancer (1.4%) were found to carry a TP53 mutation, among these carriers, two met Chompret criteria for LFS, but none met classic LFS criteria.

nodes.label: PINK1
nodes.description: A protein associated with the outer mitochondrial membrane that recruits parkin to activate it for attaching ubiquitin proteins to the mitochondrial membrane, playing a crucial role in regulating mitophagy pathways in mammalian cells, especially in response to mitochondrial depolarization. Mutations in the gene encoding PINK1 are linked to hereditary PD, leading to less efficient mitophagy. It is involved in the PINK1/Parkin pathway during stress-induced mitophagy and contributes to the age-related increase in GV oocytes collected during ovarian aging.

nodes.label: MutS
nodes.description: A protein involved in mismatch repair (MMR) systems, including methyl-directed MMR and very-short patch (VSP) repair, working with MutL and MutH. It exists as dimers and tetramers in solution and is highly homologous to MutS2 in Thermus thermophilus HB8. MutS is a component of the MutH-independent MMR system and is targeted to the replisome by DnaN clamp zones, facilitating repair by disengaging from the replisome following mismatch detection. Increasing the concentration of MutS within the cell can bypass the dependence on DnaN, indicating a secondary mode of detection in vivo.

nodes.label: NETosis
nodes.description: A process involving the formation and release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which can be induced by immunogenic complexes composed of MMP-9 and anti-MMP-9, as well as anti-MMP-9 autoantibodies.

nodes.label: Down syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, distinctive physical features, developmental delays, and an increased risk of certain medical conditions. It is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 and can be detected through various screening methods, including maternal serum screening tests, amniocentesis, and CVS. Prenatal screening and diagnosis are recommended to identify this condition in fetuses. The detection rate for Down syndrome using screening tests ranges from approximately 40% to 96% at a 5% false-positive rate.

nodes.label: TYR gene
nodes.description: A gene responsible for encoding tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the production of melanin pigment. Mutations in this gene lead to OCA1. The human gene associated with type 1 oculocutaneous albinism (OCA1), mutations in which lead to reduced or absent pigmentation of skin, hair, and eye. Various mutations causing OCA in humans have been identified throughout this gene. A gene responsible for the production of tyrosinase enzyme, which is essential for melanin synthesis. Mutations in this gene lead to Oculocutaneous albinism type1A. It is located on chromosome 11 and its coding region is amplified using eight sets of primers for bidirectional direct sequencing mutation analysis. The TYR gene encodes the enzyme tyrosinase involved in the metabolic pathway of melanin synthesis. It has been reported that 230 mutations in this gene are responsible for oculocutaneous albinism type 1 worldwide. Five exons in the TYR gene were sequenced to search for the gene carriers in the family and in the non-related individual. Mutations identified in the TYR gene include G47D, 1379delTT, and compound heterozygote for G47D and D42N mutations. A gene associated with the production of tyrosinase, mutations in which were studied in the context of Oculocutaneous albinism type 1. Three previously unidentified alleles were discovered in this gene. A gene located at position 11q14.3 on the human chromosome, encoding tyrosinase, which is expressed in melanocytes and controls the biosynthesis of melanin. Mutations in this gene can lead to the development of nonsyndromic oculocutaneous albinism.

nodes.label: Myotonic dystrophy
nodes.description: A hereditary neurological disorder caused by the expansion of normally polymorphic CTG microsatellites in certain human genes, characterized by myotonia, progressive muscle wasting, and cataracts. It has two forms: myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) and myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2). DM1 is caused by an expansion of a CTG repeat in the 3' untranslated region of the myotonin-protein kinase (DMPK) gene on chromosome 19, while DM2 is caused by an expansion of a CCTG repeat in intron 1 of the cellular nucleic acid-binding protein (CNBP) gene on chromosome 3. It is a genetically determined disease with autosomal dominant mode of inheritance, affecting multiple systems including the central and peripheral nervous systems, heart muscle, and endocrine system. Symptoms include myotonic symptoms, muscular weakness, muscular atrophy, cataract, endocrine disorders, cognitive dysfunctions, intellectual and personality disturbances, and sleep-disordered breathing with nocturnal hypoventilation, obstructive, central and mixed apneas and hypopneas. It is a common adult muscular dystrophy, with two types, DM1 and DM2, that are often discussed jointly despite sharing many clinical and molecular features. It is a progressive multisystem genetic disorder with clinical and genetic features in common, including surveillance for arrhythmias and left ventricular dysfunction, both of which occur in a progressive manner and contribute to morbidity and mortality.

nodes.label: Entacapone
nodes.description: A highly potent, reversible, peripherally acting catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitor used as an adjunct to L-dopa in the treatment of Parkinson disease (PD). It is administered at a dose of 200 mg in combination with each scheduled L-dopa/dopa decarboxylase inhibitor dose, ranging from 3 to 5 doses daily. It is a purely peripheral COMT inhibitor with lower potency than tolcapone, used in the treatment of motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson's disease, particularly the 'wearing-off' phenomenon. It provides increased 'on' time, decreased 'off' time, and improved motor scores. Unlike tolcapone, it does not cause explosive diarrhea or liver dysfunction, and no monitoring is required. Metabolites of entacapone may cause discoloration of the urine. It is also used in the treatment of Restless Legs Syndrome and as a medication in the study to investigate its effects on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of apomorphine in Parkinson's disease patients experiencing severe motor fluctuations. The first catechol-O-methyl transferase inhibitor marketed in Japan for the treatment of Parkinson's disease, approved in April 2007.

nodes.label: Group B
nodes.description: A group of patients who underwent surgical resection ≥8 weeks after neoadjuvant CRT. The group consisted of 48 patients. The rate of sphincter preserving surgery was 77.6%, and the postoperative complication rate was 14.3%. The pCR rate was 75%. The nodal downstaging rate was 66.7%. One of the two groups in the study, assigned to receive consolidation chemotherapy after CRT. The group had a pCR of 25% in the intention-to-treat population and a higher compliance with CRT compared to group A.

nodes.label: KRAS mutation
nodes.description: A genetic mutation in the KRAS gene, specifically associated with resistance to cetuximab-based treatment in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) patients. It has been identified as a marker of resistance to cetuximab-based treatment in mCRC patients. A mutation in the KRAS gene, which is unambiguously linked to a lack of response to targeted therapies such as anti-Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) antibodies like cetuximab or panitumumab. The presence of KRAS mutations is a mandatory prerequisite for treating metastatic colorectal patients with these therapies. A genetic alteration identified as a negative predictive biomarker of Anti-EGFR antibodies in metastatic colorectal cancer. It affects the efficacy of Anti-EGFR antibodies in mCRC patients.

nodes.label: p53
nodes.description: A tumor suppressor gene associated with glioblastomas through frequent mutations, located on chromosome 17p and involved in the development of gliomas. It is a protein that plays a role in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, and is regulated by posttranslational modifications such as phosphorylation or ubiquitination. The p53 gene is implicated in at least two genetic pathways leading to GBM, one de novo without p53 mutation and another 'progressive' with p53 mutation. It is a known tumor suppressor gene that, when inactivated, can be used in conjunction with transgenic mice expressing inducible KrasG12D. The wild-type form of p53 is necessary for the effectiveness of oridonin, and over-expression of E6 from HPV-16 can suppress p53, leading to loss of sensitivity to oridonin-induced growth inhibition and apoptosis. P53 is also involved in the molecular pathogenesis of adenomas and Mantle-cell lymphoma (MCL), and is targeted for degradation by RING1 through direct interaction and ubiquitination.

nodes.label: CRAFFT
nodes.description: The CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble, 1999) is a brief screening instrument developed for adolescents to measure AUD and SUD. It consists of six questions that assess various aspects of alcohol and substance use, such as car use, relaxation, alone time, forgetting, friends, and trouble. The CRAFFT has been found to be a good screening instrument for gradations of alcohol and substance misuse, including problem use, abuse, and dependence. Its sensitivities range from 0.61 to 1.00, specificities from 0.33 to 0.97, and internal consistency values from 0.65 to 0.86. It also demonstrates high test-retest reliability.

nodes.label: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
nodes.description: A type of scoliosis that affects adolescents and is characterized by a curvature of the spine, with no known cause. It is associated with certain genetic factors and can be influenced by promoter polymorphism of matrilin-1 gene. It includes three subtypes: double curve pattern, Cobb angle ≥ 40 degrees, and thoracic curve. It is a common disorder with strong evidence for genetic predisposition, characterized by the presence of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) on chromosomes. It is associated with low melatonin levels and has been studied in relation to melatonin-related receptors and mutations. It is a complex disorder with a strong genetic predisposition, characterized by a curvature of the spine that typically appears during adolescence and has no known cause. It is associated with directional and regional differential growth, particularly during the pubertal growth spurt, and is controlled by many genes, as well as by hormones and signalling molecules. It is a disease characterized by spinal deformities that typically presents during adolescence and has been associated with the two traditional estrogen receptor genes, ESR1 and ESR2. It is also known to be related to the severity of curvature in AIS patients through the presence of certain tag single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the GPER gene. It is a disease that affects adolescents, occurring between two and ten times more frequently in females than in males, with an unknown cause and genetic underpinnings. It can be inherited and may be influenced by genetic factors, with males potentially requiring a greater number of susceptibility genes to develop the deformity. It is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal curvature of the spine in adolescents, which was studied in 126 patients and 197 healthy controls from independent Hungarian pedigrees. It is associated with loci in CNTNAP2 and CHL1 gene.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin
nodes.description: A small 76-amino acid protein involved in the process of ubiquitination, where it is attached to lysine on a target protein. It is a central molecule in proteosome-mediated protein degradation, serving as the second major component of Lewy bodies and is used for post-translational modifications such as ubiquitination. Ubiquitin can form homotypic chains, such as K48-linked polymers, and branched chains, which are produced in response to specific signals and essential for cellular and organismal homeostasis. It is also used as a marker for Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, and is involved in various cellular processes including DNA repair, protein kinase activation, and mitophagy. It is regulated at the level of both addition and removal of ubiquitin from target proteins.

nodes.label: ANCCA
nodes.description: A chromatin regulator gene/protein that is overexpressed in prostate cancer and plays a crucial role in androgen-stimulated and castration-refractory prostate tumor growth and survival. It is regulated by androgen and strongly expressed in early prostate morphogenesis and during puberty. It emphasizes bromodomain protein ANCCA as a potential therapeutic target against prostate cancer.

nodes.label: Sulfonylureas
nodes.description: A class of oral antidiabetic agents that stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, commonly used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus for 5 to 10 years or longer. They serve as the foundation of oral pharmacologic therapy and can delay the need for insulin or aid in achieving glycemic goals when used in combination with other agents. They are often used in combination with other oral agents and may cause weight gain, a safety concern that limits their optimal application. A class of second-line glucose-lowering medications used in Denmark, Norway, and Sweden for treating type 2 diabetes. They were the most common second-line treatment after metformin in these countries in 2013. A class of oral medications used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. They work by improving insulin secretion and are one of the four different classes of oral medications available for diabetes treatment.

nodes.label: ClinicalTrials.gov
nodes.description: A registry and results database for clinical studies run by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH), providing information about clinical trials conducted worldwide. It allows researchers, patients, and the public to search for and find information on health studies, including those evaluating the effectiveness of treatments for various conditions, and tracks and shares information about clinical trials.

nodes.label: HIV
nodes.description: A viral infection that attacks the immune system, specifically the CD4 cells (T cells), which help the immune system fight off infections. It reduces the number of these cells, making it difficult for the body to fight off infections and diseases. It can be treated as a chronic disease through antiretroviral therapy (ART) and can be prevented and transmitted among high-risk people, especially in high-risk populations such as men who have sex with men (MSM), heterosexually active men and women, HIV-uninfected partner in serodiscordant couples and injection drug users (IDUs). Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine combination is recommended for high-risk populations and can provide a high level of protection against HIV when combined with condoms, ART and other prevention methods. It is also a disease targeted by pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for transmission prevention, and medications like Dapivirine, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide are used for HIV prevention.

nodes.label: Inflammation
nodes.description: A biological process involving the body's response to infection, injury, or irritation, characterized by various cellular and molecular changes, including the recruitment of immune cells and the release of inflammatory mediators. It is associated with the cardinal signs of redness, heat, swelling, and pain, and can lead to loss of function if uncontrolled or unresolved. Inflammation plays a role in containing and resolving infection, as well as in several pathological processes, such as intervertebral disc degeneration, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. It is also implicated in cancer development, metabolic syndrome, and autoimmune diseases. Interleukin-31 (IL-31) has been shown to play relevant roles in various conditions associated with inflammation.

nodes.label: Wernicke encephalopathy
nodes.description: A neurological disorder caused by thiamine deficiency in the central nervous system, characterized by a triad of confusional symptoms, ocular alterations and ataxia. It can develop in alcoholics with diabetic ketoacidosis, suggesting that metabolic decompensation is essential in its onset. A rarely diagnosed neurological disorder caused by vitamin B1 deficiency, characterized by a typical triad (confusion, oculomotor disturbance and ataxia) in the classical form, but often only confusion is present. It can be frequently observed in subjects with chronic alcohol consumption and may accompany different pathological states, including end stage malignant diseases such as advanced gastric cancer. A medical condition caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, characterized by encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction and gait ataxia. It is generally considered to be a disease of adult alcoholics, but can occur in the pediatric population and in non-alcoholic conditions. The classic triad of symptoms is not always present. It is a medical emergency, and delay in its recognition and treatment may lead to significant morbidity, irreversible neurological damage or even death. An acute neurologic disorder characterized by a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and mental confusion, often associated with alcoholism and malnutrition, gastrointestinal diseases with malabsorption, and total parenteral nutrition (TPN) without proper replacement of thiamine. Early diagnosis and treatment with thiamine in the acute stages can reverse neurologic and cardiovascular abnormalities.

nodes.label: Pain
nodes.description: A subjective experience that can have various meanings, including being a naturalistic symptom of disease or a symbol used in a metaphorical context. It can be associated with conditions such as Restless Legs Syndrome, vulvodynia, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome hypermobile type (hEDS), and can be managed with treatments like paracetamol, NSAIDs, and codeine, with considerations for contraindications. It is also a common but often ignored symptom in COVID-19 patients, and early and adequate treatment with detailed pain assessment may reduce the risk of pain chronicization and mood dysregulation.

nodes.label: Esco2
nodes.description: A gene or protein involved in cohesin acetyltransferase activity, regulating SAC and kinetochore functions via maintaining H4K16 acetylation during mouse oocyte meiosis. Its depletion leads to precocious polar body extrusion, escape of metaphase I arrest, loss of BubR1 from kinetochores, impaired spindle assembly, and chromosome alignment, as well as increased incidence of defective kinetochore-microtubule attachments, resulting in aneuploid eggs. It binds to histone H4 and acetylates H4K16 both in vivo and in vitro. An ESCO2 protein that acts as an N-acetyltransferase targeting the SMC3 subunit of the cohesin complex, involved in Roberts Syndrome (RBS) and transcriptional dysregulation. A gene or protein that exerts transcriptional regulation of cx43 through modification of Smc3 bound to the cx43 promoter.

nodes.label: Dupilumab
nodes.description: A fully human monoclonal antibody that blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13, shown to be effective in patients with asthma and elevated eosinophil levels. It is administered subcutaneously at a dose of 300 mg once weekly. Dupilumab is used to treat moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic asthma, or raised serum periostin levels. It has been evaluated as monotherapy and in combination with topical glucocorticoids. Dupilumab has shown promise in reducing asthma exacerbations and improving respiratory symptoms and lung function in patients with difficult-to-control asthma. It has received US FDA breakthrough therapy designation for atopic dermatitis and is making unprecedented advances towards highly effective control of this debilitating disease.

nodes.label: Acneiform side effects
nodes.description: A group of side effects that manifest as skin rashes resembling acne, specifically affecting the face, upper trunk, and back. These side effects are commonly observed in patients receiving EGFR inhibitors and can be treated with various medications such as emollients, topical steroids, and antibiotics.

nodes.label: Dabigatran
nodes.description: A direct oral anticoagulant used for the treatment of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and for the prevention of systemic embolism in non-valvular atrial fibrillation. It is a thrombin inhibitor, specifically mentioned as dabigatran etexilate (DE), and is known as Pradaxa. It can be reversed using idarucizumab and has shown superiority to warfarin in preventing ischemic stroke and a significant reduction in intracranial bleeding in the RE-LY study at a 150 mg dose. Its medical cost reduction associated with usage instead of warfarin was estimated to be -$179 in a patient year for patients aged <75 years.

nodes.label: H-Ras
nodes.description: A protein involved in the induction of senescence through retroviral gene transduction, and in the suppression of p16Ink4a by Bmi-1 after the introduction of H-Ras through transient transfection with cationic liposome. One of the three isoforms of the Ras protein, occupying a different microdomain within the plasma membrane and being present and active in endomembranes. It is subject to site-specific regulatory mechanisms, effector pathways, and diverse genetic programs, and is affected by posttranslational modifications such as binding to membranes, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination. A protein isoform of the Ras gene family, one of the four highly related isoforms coded by the Ras gene family, along with N-Ras, K-Ras4A, and K-Ras4B. It is part of the signaling pathways that control eukaryotic cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation. One of the three closely related Ras proteins expressed in mammalian cells, along with K-Ras and N-Ras. It is involved in promoting oncogenesis when mutationally activated at specific codons. A member of the Ras isoforms, which regulate cellular growth and survival and are often activated by somatic mutation in human tumors. Oncogenic lesions can occur in H-Ras within individual tumors. A Ras isoform contributing to about 1% of human cancers. Requires farnesylation or geranylgeranylation at the C-terminal CAAX box for proper membrane targeting and activity. A Ras isoform that is activated by monoubiquitination and ubiquitination at Lys-117 accelerates intrinsic nucleotide exchange, thereby promoting GTP loading.

nodes.label: Sarcoidosis
nodes.description: A chronic, multisystem disorder characterized by the formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in various organs and tissues, including the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, eyes, and salivary glands. It is a systemic inflammatory disease of unknown cause, associated with infectious agents and genetic components. The diagnosis is confirmed by histology, and treatment typically involves glucocorticoids. Sarcoidosis can present with symptoms such as swelling, fever, uveitis, and facial nerve palsy, and may lead to the development of Heerfordt syndrome.

nodes.label: Statins
nodes.description: A subclass of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, statins are effective in both the primary and secondary prevention of ischaemic heart disease. They are well tolerated except for two uncommon but potentially serious adverse effects: elevation of liver enzymes and skeletal muscle abnormalities, which can range from benign myalgias to life-threatening rhabdomyolysis. A class of lipid-lowering drugs that have been implicated in causing complications either in monotherapy or in combination therapy. Adverse events occur more often with statins that are metabolized via the CYP enzyme system and its 3A4, 2C9 or 2C19 paths. They may cause myopathy, up to rhabdomyolysis with ensuing acute renal insufficiency. When combined with fibrates, they may cause serious complications and should be avoided when possible. A class of drugs that inhibit the activity of HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme involved in cholesterol synthesis. They have been studied for their efficacy in Alzheimer's disease prevention. At least four large prevention trials involving statins are currently underway. Cholesterol-lowering drugs extensively used in cardiovascular prevention. Their most well-known adverse effect is muscle damage, including rhabdomyolysis. Several cases of peripheral polyneuropathy have been published or reported by pharmacovigilance centres, affecting about one patient in 10 000 treated for one year. Risk factors include renal failure and diabetes. Statins are a class of drugs that inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarylcoenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. They cause intracellular cholesterol depletion and upregulate the expression of LDL receptors, leading to lower plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels. Although generally well-tolerated, they may cause adverse effects such as myopathy, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, impaired myocardial contractility, and autoimmune diseases. However, the benefits of statins in reducing cardiovascular events outweigh the risks. A class of medications used to lower cholesterol levels, which may protect against incident dementia in elderly subjects. A class of drugs used in the immediate starting treatment for transient ischemic attack (TIA) patients to reduce the risk of stroke within 90 days. A class of medications known to have cutaneous adverse effects, including the induction of autoimmune diseases like systemic and subacute lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, polymyositis, lichen planus pemphigoides, and the drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). Also reported as a triggering factor of psoriasis. A class of drugs used to treat high cholesterol levels, which have not been effective in controlling the condition in some patients. A class of drugs widely used to prevent major cardiovascular events by lowering serum cholesterol. They have pleiotropic effects, which include cholesterol-independent effects that may protect against cardiovascular disease and other pathologies such as cancer. Statins are also associated with adverse effects like myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, liver damage, and type 2 diabetes. In vitro and animal studies show that statins can inhibit histone deacetylase activity, increase histone acetylation, and affect histone and DNA methyltransferases, leading to changes in gene expression, including tumor suppressor genes and genes with anti-atherosclerotic actions. Statins also influence the expression of microRNAs that suppress proteins involved in tumorigenesis and vascular function. Alterations in microRNA expression have been observed in statin-induced muscle and liver damage, suggesting an epigenetic component to some adverse effects. A type of medication that is a substrate for breast cancer resistance protein and organic anion transporter proteins, and may have a clinically relevant effect on comedications when co-administered with darolutamide. Specifically, a subgroup analysis was conducted in statin users versus nonusers. Drugs that are widely prescribed in high-risk patients for cerebrovascular or cardiovascular diseases. They are usually safe and well tolerated, but may cause neuromuscular side effects such as muscle-related adverse events including cramps, myalgia, weakness, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, peripheral neuropathy, and neuromuscular junction dysfunction. The incidence of neuromuscular complications associated with statin use is expected to increase due to the more widespread use of statins. Pharmacogenomic and environmental studies may help predict neuromuscular complications due to statin exposure, leading to a more personalized therapeutic approach. HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly known as statins, are the primary treatment choice for cardiovascular diseases, which stand as the leading global cause of mortality. They offer various pleiotropic effects, including improved endothelial function, anti-inflammatory properties, reduced oxidative stress, anti-thrombotic effects, and the stabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. However, their usage can be accompanied by a range of adverse effects such as the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus, muscular symptoms, liver toxicity, kidney diseases, cataracts, hemorrhagic strokes, and psychiatric complications.

nodes.label: Beta-clip fold
nodes.description: A diverse group of protein domains characterized by the presence of two characteristic waist-like constrictions that bound a central extended region. It includes enzymes like deoxyuridine triphosphatase and the SET methylase, carbohydrate-binding domains like the fish antifreeze proteins/Sialate synthase C-terminal domains, and functionally enigmatic accessory subunits of urease and molybdopterin biosynthesis protein MoeA. The study reconstructs its evolutionary history using sensitive sequence and structure comparison methods and further classifies it into two major groups based on structural comparisons.

nodes.label: Acneiform eruptions
nodes.description: A type of skin reaction characterized by eruptions resembling acne, which can be induced by epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors. It is a common cutaneous side effect of these drugs and can be treated with oral isotretinoin. A skin condition characterized by inflammatory lesions resembling acne, caused by the use of epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors, specifically cetuximab. It is diagnosed as grade II according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v4.0.

nodes.label: Heart failure
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by the heart's inability to pump blood effectively, leading to decreased cardiac output and inadequate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues. It is associated with neurohormonal activation, vasoconstriction, increased blood pressure, increased afterload, and impaired diastolic function at the myocyte level. Heart failure can occur with systolic dysfunction and is indicated as a result of targeted ablation of ILK from the murine heart and its spontaneous occurrence in the absence of ILK. It is a chronic condition affecting approximately 5.7 million people in the United States alone, characterized by impaired cardiac function leading to decreased ejection fraction and increased sensitivity to natriuretic peptides, with high mortality rates. Management includes the use of drugs like sacubitril valsartan and medications such as angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, β-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists.

nodes.label: Natriuretic peptides
nodes.description: A family of proteins that participate in the integrated control of intravascular volume and arterial blood pressure. They differentially bind distinct classes of receptors that signal through different mechanisms. The natriuretic peptides include atrial natriuretic peptide, brain natriuretic peptide, and C-type natriuretic peptide. Membrane-bound, guanylyl cyclase-coupled natriuretic peptide receptors (A- and B-types) mediate natriuretic peptide effects through the production of 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). C-Type natriuretic peptide receptors, which lack the guanylyl cyclase domain, alter target cell function through G(i) protein-coupled inhibition of membrane adenylyl cyclase activity, and also serve to clear circulating natriuretic peptides. Cardiac and vascular peptides with vasodilatory, diuretic, natriuretic, anti-inflammatory, antifibrotic and antimitogenic actions, involved in normal pressure and volume homeostasis and in the defence against excessive increases in overload-related factors, vasopressive and cardiotoxic factors and their impact on the heart, blood vessels and brain. They are metabolized by NPR-C and by enzymatic degradation by neutral endopeptidase. Levels of natriuretic peptides, mainly brain natriuretic peptide, correlate with left ventricular hypertrophy and with the severity of heart failure, and are reduced by effective treatment, making them useful as diagnostic and prognostic tools. Genetic manipulation studies confirmed their importance in these functions. Four major natriuretic peptides have been isolated: atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP), and Dendroaspis-type natriuretic peptide (DNP). They play an important role in the regulation of cardiovascular homeostasis maintaining blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume. The classical endocrine effects of natriuretic peptides include modulating fluid and electrolyte balance and vascular smooth muscle tone, and autocrine and paracrine actions that involve regulating coronary blood flow, myocardial perfusion, proliferative responses during myocardial and vascular remodeling, and cytoprotective anti-ischemic effects. They are mediated by the specific binding of these peptides to three cell surface receptors: type A natriuretic peptide receptor (NPR-A), type B natriuretic peptide receptor (NPR-B), and type C natriuretic peptide receptor (NPR-C). NPR-A and NPR-B are guanylyl cyclase receptors that increase intracellular cGMP concentration and activate cGMP-dependent protein kinases. NPR-C has been presented as a clearance receptor and its activation results in inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial dysfunction
nodes.description: A condition associated with Parkinson's disease, characterized by dysregulation of the mitochondria. It is linked to the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease through molecular genetics discoveries. Mutations in gene products that associate with the mitochondria, such as PTEN-induced kinase-1 (PINK1) and PARKIN, can cause mitochondrial dysfunction. It is also related to other conditions like Barth syndrome, heart failure, and ototoxicity, and can be alleviated by Hippo-YAP signaling in response to copper (Cu) stress.

nodes.label: Parkinson's disease
nodes.description: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective aggregation of alpha-synuclein in the form of filamentous inclusion bodies, specifically in the form of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites. It is associated with the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia. The disease is marked by the presence of Lewy bodies, which are neuropathological hallmarks associated with the death of dopamine neurons. It can be familial or sporadic and is associated with certain neuronal types in the adult human central nervous system. Alpha-synuclein is the primary component of these Lewy bodies, and mutations in the alpha-synuclein gene are associated with familial forms of the disease. The pathology of Parkinson's disease involves neurotoxicity triggered by alpha-synuclein aggregation, although some evidence suggests a protective role of alpha-synuclein against oxidative stress.

nodes.label: Sacubitril/valsartan
nodes.description: A pharmaceutical drug used for the treatment of chronic heart failure. A novel cardiovascular combination agent that combines neprilysin inhibition with angiotensin II receptor antagonism, used to increase endogenous natriuretic peptides while inhibiting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. It has been studied in the treatment of hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in blood pressure reduction in hypertensive patients with and without HFpEF and a reduction in hospitalizations and mortality for patients with HFrEF. It is approved to reduce hospitalization and risk of cardiovascular death for patients with HFrEF in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II-IV. The most common side effect is hypotension, and it is more costly than generic angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor antagonists. A molecular combination of sacubitril and valsartan, marketed under the brand name Entresto, used for reducing the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in patients with chronic heart failure (NYHA Class II-IV) and reduced ejection fraction. It is typically administered alongside other heart failure therapies, instead of an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin-receptor blocker (ARB). Possible side effects include hypotension, angioedema, impaired renal function, and elevation in serum potassium levels. The drug should not be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding, in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), and in combination with aliskiren in patients with diabetes. A medication used for treating ischemic cardiomyopathy, consisting of two active ingredients: sacubitril and valsartan. It is marketed under the brand name Entresto by Novartis, headquartered in Cambridge, MA. The medication can cause profound hypotension in patients undergoing heart transplantation, potentially leading to acute kidney injury and requiring dialysis and a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit. A drug combination used in a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study to evaluate its effects on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) in dogs with cardiomegaly secondary to myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD). It is also known as Entresto.

nodes.label: Daratumumab
nodes.description: A novel, high-affinity, therapeutic human monoclonal antibody against the unique CD38 epitope with broad-spectrum killing activity, used in the treatment of multiple myeloma. It targets the CD38 molecule on the surface of cancer cells, leading to the activation of the complement system and the induction of apoptosis in cancer cells. Daratumumab has a favorable safety profile as monotherapy in patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma and demonstrates significant single-agent activity. It is being studied in combination therapy and has shown promising results in recent clinical studies.

nodes.label: KRAS gene
nodes.description: A gene that belongs to the RAS gene family and encodes a membrane-bound 21-kd guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-binding protein. Mutations in this gene, particularly at codon 12, are associated with the development of lung adenocarcinomas (ADCs) and confer a growth advantage to airway epithelial cells. These mutations also affect atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, the precursor of ADCs, and can lead to an unfavorable response to certain molecular-targeting therapies. Patients with ADCs affected by mutations have a significantly higher risk of postoperative disease recurrence. A gene involved in colorectal carcinogenesis, mutations in which can be detected in more than 30% of all patients with colorectal cancer (CRC). In particular, mutations in codons 12 and 13 are associated with lack of benefit from anti-EGFR therapy in metastatic CRC. Seven known mutations of the KRAS gene in codons 12 or 13 were tested in 44 CRC samples from the Croatian population, revealing a mutation incidence of 27%. These mutations include Gly12Val (GGT>GTT), Gly12Asp (GGT>GAT), Gly13Asp (GGC>GAC), Gly12Ser (GGT>AGT), and Gly12Cys (GGT>TGT).
