A gene that is commonly mutated in colorectal villous adenomas and in situ carcinomas compared to carcinomas. Mutations in this gene were found in 61.9% of 134 adenomas, 67.8% of 84 in situ carcinomas, and 31.6% of 171 carcinomas. The presence of somatic mutations in this gene is more likely in tubulovillous and villous adenomas, as well as both the benign and malignant parts of in situ carcinomas, than in colorectal carcinomas, particularly in non-mucinous and microsatellite stable tumors. A gene associated with poorer prognosis in primary colorectal cancer when mutated, particularly in codons 12 and 13. Its mutations are considered early indicators of CRC progression and are analyzed through direct sequencing or Luminex assay. A gene that, when mutated, plays a central role in tumorigenesis and is mutated in 30-40% of all colorectal cancer patients. The study involved collecting 80 colorectal cancer tumor tissues and sequencing the KRAS gene using automated sequencing technologies to explore the prevalence of KRAS gene mutations in the Saudi population. Mutations were found in four different codons: 12, 13, 17, and 31, with most occurring in codon 12. Two novel mutations, c.51 G>A (S17R) and c.91 G>A (E31K), were also identified in four and three patients, respectively.

nodes.label: BRAF V600E mutation
nodes.description: A specific genetic mutation found in approximately 5% of colorectal cancer (CRC) cases, characterized by an extremely poor prognostic factor. It is associated with a negative prognostic role in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), leading to a median Progression Free Survival of 4-6 months with first-line conventional treatments. This mutation is often associated with cancer and can be targeted by verumafemib for treatment. In mCRC, it makes patients eligible for treatment with encorafenib in combination with cetuximab, resulting in a significantly longer median overall survival (OS), a higher objective response rate (ORR) and longer median progression-free survival (PFS) compared with standard therapy in a clinical trial. It is also a target for the BRAF inhibitor encorafenib in combination with cetuximab and is associated with poor prognosis in mCRC tumors, for which there are no specifically targeted first-line treatment options.

nodes.label: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)
nodes.description: A method used to individualize and optimize the drug management of patients with epilepsy by monitoring the concentration of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in blood (serum/plasma) or saliva. It involves summarizing key pharmacokinetic characteristics of each AED, discussing the use of other biological matrices like saliva, and providing indications for salivary AED TDM. A practical protocol is described to enable optimal and effective application in the clinical setting.

nodes.label: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration
nodes.description: A neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid deposition in the brain, which can be diagnosed using (18)F-florbetaben and PET. It is distinguished from Alzheimer disease using (18)F-florbetaben. Only 9% of patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration show cortical binding with (18)F-florbetaben. A group of clinically, neuropathologically and genetically heterogeneous disorders with overlaps between the neurodegenerative mechanism and the clinical phenotype, characterized by frontal and temporal lobar atrophy. A neurodegenerative disease associated with TDP-43 inclusions.

nodes.label: Sideritis scardica Griseb.
nodes.description: An endemic species of the Balkan Peninsula, Sideritis scardica Griseb. is used in traditional medicine as a loosening agent in bronchitis and bronchial asthma, against the common cold and lung emphysema, in the treatment of inflammation, gastrointestinal disorders and coughs, and as an active constituent of dietary supplements for the prevention of anemia. It has become very popular and widely advertised herb in Europe.

nodes.label: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and degeneration, affecting males primarily. It is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to deficiency of the protein dystrophin. The disease is associated with a lack of dystrophin in all muscle types, including smooth muscle, which may contribute to a poor vascular smooth muscle vaso-constrictive response. It is a rare disease with a frequency of less than 1/2000, but it is one of the most common myopathies observed in all populations. The most common cause of death in DMD patients is cardiac and respiratory failure. Current pharmacological and other treatment methods do not lead to full recovery. It is a severe and incurable X-linked neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene (DMD), which forms a complex spectrum. It is one of the diseases included in the Chinese Genetic Disease Registry. The disease is diagnosed through molecular analyses such as MLPA and whole gene sequencing, and computational algorithms are used to evaluate the impact of DNA variants on mRNA splicing and protein functionality. The diagnostic algorithm used has proven to be accurate for the molecular diagnosis of dystrophinopathies.

nodes.label: Tyrosinase (TYR) gene
nodes.description: The gene associated with oculocutaneous albinism type I, analyzed for mutations in two families through PCR and sequencing techniques. The mutations include R278X, 929insC, IVS4+3A>T, and G253E. A gene responsible for encoding the tyrosinase enzyme, which plays a crucial role in melanin synthesis. Mutations in this gene were identified in Chinese families with oculocutaneous albinism type 1, leading to various functional impairments of the tyrosinase enzyme. A gene responsible for producing the enzyme tyrosinase, which is involved in the production of melanin pigment. Mutations in this gene can lead to oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (OCA1). A gene responsible for encoding the tyrosinase enzyme, mutations in which lead to oculocutaneous albinism (OCA). This gene is examined in the study involving 30 unrelated Iranian OCA1 patients and 100 healthy individuals using PCR-sequencing. Two novel pathogenic mutations, p.C89S and p.H180R, are detected in two OCA1 patients, while common non-pathogenic polymorphisms R402Q and S192Y are found in 17.5% and 35% of the patients, respectively. A gene that codes for the tyrosinase protein, which is involved in the production of melanin. A missense mutation in a highly conserved position of this gene causes albinism in donkeys and is a strong candidate to identify the causative mutation of the albinism in Asinara white donkeys. The gene was sequenced from 13 donkeys and seven single nucleotide polymorphisms were identified, including the c.604C>G; p.His202Asp mutation.

nodes.label: Lewy bodies
nodes.description: Pathological structures composed primarily of alpha-synuclein (α-syn) that are a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), characterized by filamentous inclusions associated with neurodegeneration. They are detected by staining with antibodies directed against amino-terminal and carboxyl-terminal sequences of alpha-synuclein and are believed to originate in the olfactory bulb or peripheral autonomic nervous system and spread to other brain regions.

nodes.label: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
nodes.description: A clinical triad of gait disturbance, dementia, and urinary incontinence combined with radiographic findings of ventriculomegaly and laboratory findings of normal cerebrospinal fluid pressures. First described by Hakim and Adams in 1965, it is estimated to be the cause of about 5% of cases of dementia and is one of the few reversible causes of dementia. Accurate diagnosis and identification of responders to treatment are important for increasing the rate of success to treatment. A neurological disorder characterized by clinical signs involving gait disorders, urinary incontinence, and dementia, associated with aspects on brain imaging that are consistent with this hypothesis and also normal or slightly increased intracranial pressure. It is diagnosed based on the Adams and Hakim triad and may require surgical shunt for improvement. A frequently missed clinical entity characterized by a symptom triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia, known as Hakim's triad. It typically occurs from the 6th decade of life onwards and can be effectively treated with early therapy.

nodes.label: Citrullination
nodes.description: A posttranslational modification involving the conversion of peptidylarginine to peptidylcitrulline, catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), which has gained significant interest in biomedicine due to its impact on protein structure and function. It is associated with the development of rheumatoid arthritis in some populations and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders, brain-specific prion diseases, and cancer. The process involves the enzymatic deimination of peptidylarginine in a calcium concentration-dependent manner, leading to the abolition of positive charges in native protein molecules and causing significant alterations in their structure and functions. The identity and function of citrullinated proteins in vivo remain largely unknown despite increasing scientific interest.

nodes.label: Off-label use of rituximab
nodes.description: The use of rituximab for purposes other than those approved by regulatory agencies. It was analyzed in a retrospective study involving 101 cases from January 2007 to December 2009 in two tertiary hospitals. The indications for prescribing rituximab were primarily hematological diseases (46%), systemic connective tissue disorders (27%), and kidney diseases (20%). Available evidence supporting rituximab treatment for these indications mainly came from individual cohort studies (53.5% of cases) and case series (25.7%) The response among the patient cohort was variable depending on the specific disease. The level of evidence supporting the use of rituximab for these indications was low and the cost was very high. The use of rituximab for indications outside of its approved uses, such as B-cell malignancies and refractory rheumatoid arthritis. There has been growing interest in using off-label rituximab for various diseases, and a total of 364 instances of off-label rituximab use was recorded in the national database over a 6-month period. The level of evidence for the use of rituximab was determined for each off-label indication.

nodes.label: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
nodes.description: A severe inherited arrhythmic disease manifesting with salvoes of exercise-induced bidirectional and polymorphic tachycardias. An arrhythmogenic disease that manifests as syncope or sudden death during high adrenergic tone in the absence of structural heart defects. Primarily caused by mutations in the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2). Enhanced SOICR, but not altered FKBP12.6 binding, is a common mechanism by which RyR2 mutations cause arrhythmias. A disease characterized by exercise-induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in humans, which was modeled in mice through the generation of knock-in mice with mutations introduced into RyR2, resulting in leaky channels and causing exercise-induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Three mouse models were used to explore the role of diastolic SR Ca2+ leak in atrial fibrillation. A disease characterized by mutations in cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2) that cause a distinctive form of Ca(2+) release dysfunction, leading to arrhythmias. It is associated with mutations such as RyR2-V2475F. A hereditary cardiac channelopathy characterized by syncope and/or sudden death related to motion. It involves alterations in T waves and tall U waves in right chest leads on electrocardiograms (ECGs). The mode of its onset is bidirectional and/or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (bVT and pVT), which can be captured by Holter easily. Beta blockers are a safe and effective remedy for suppressing its attacks. A disease caused by mutations in the ryanodine receptor 2 (RYR2) gene, associated with a gain-of-function mutation in the cardiac Ca(2+) release channel ryanodine receptor and characterized by both catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

nodes.label: Natriuretic Peptide Family
nodes.description: A group of structurally similar but genetically distinct peptides with many favorable physiological properties that have emerged as important candidates for development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic agents in cardiovascular diseases. The NP family includes atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP, 28AA), urodilatin (INN: Ularitide, 32 AA), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP, 32AA), C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP, 22AA), and D-type natriuretic peptide (DNP, 38AA). They share common features and exhibit tissue distribution of gene expression as well as functional and pharmacological characteristics. The primary sites of synthesis of the NP are the heart and brain; additional extra cardiac and extra cranial sites include intestine and kidney. Membrane-bound guanyl cyclase-coupled NP receptors (NPR) (A- and B- types) are generally implicated in mediating NP effects via the production of cyclic GMP as the intracellular messenger. NPR-C lacking the guanyl cyclase domain may influence the target cell function through inhibitory guanine nucleotide (Gi) protein, and they likely also act as clearance receptors for circulating peptides. NPs are identified as regulatory diuretic-natriuretic substances responsible for salt and water homeostasis and as hormones lowering blood pressure. A complex biological process involving at least three endogenous peptides (atrial natriuretic peptide, brain natriuretic peptide and C-type natriuretic peptide) and three receptors (the atrial natriuretic peptide-A receptor (guanylyl cyclase A), the atrial natriuretic peptide-B receptor (guanylyl cyclase B) and the clearance receptor). This system is involved in the control of blood pressure, body fluid homeostasis and vascular remodelling as a cardiac hormone and local regulator.

nodes.label: Nucleotide excision repair
nodes.description: A macromolecular event involved in DNA repair, which shares many components with the lagging strand DNA synthesis machinery. A universally used biological process for recognizing and removing many types of DNA damage. In eubacteria, the NER system typically consists of UvrA, UvrB, UvrC, the UvrD helicase, DNA polymerase I, and ligase. When DNA damage blocks transcription, the transcription-repair coupling factor (TRCF), the product of the mfd gene, recruits the Uvr complex to repair the damage. A broader DNA repair pathway that includes the transcription-coupled DNA repair (TCR) subpathway. It is a process by which cells repair damaged DNA by removing a segment of DNA containing the damage and replacing it with new DNA synthesized from the undamaged template strand. The transcription-independent 'global' NER pathway repairs lesions more slowly compared to TCR. A DNA repair mechanism consisting of machineries such as excinuclease protein UvrABC endonuclease, multi-enzymatic complex which carries out repair of damaged DNA in sequential manner. It is a part of the pathogenicity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A DNA repair pathway in which ERCC1-XPF nuclease is a core component. It involves the removal of damaged nucleotides from the DNA strand, followed by the insertion of new nucleotides to restore the strand's integrity. ERCC1-XPF nuclease specifically nicks DNA at junctions between double-stranded and single-stranded DNA. A DNA repair process involving the protein encoded by the ERCC4 gene, which forms a complex with ERCC1 and is required for the 5' incision during nucleotide excision repair.

nodes.label: Invadopodia
nodes.description: Membrane protrusions that localize enzymes required for ECM degradation, used by metastatic tumor cells for organizing the cellular actin cytoskeleton to form membrane protrusions and using proteolytic enzyme(s) for ECM degradation. A cell structure involved in the formation and function, according to the proposed stepwise model. Extracellular matrix-digesting actin-rich protrusions formed by primary rat aorta vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) when expressing activated versions of Src, Cdc42 and Rac1, or a kinase-dead but open form of the p21-activated kinase (PAK1). These structures are morphologically similar to the invadopodia formed by highly invasive tumor cells and are enriched in known markers such as cortactin and tyrosine-phosphorylated cortactin, containing matrix metalloproteinases MMP-9 and MT1-MMP and the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR). Formation of invadopodia by Src depends on Cdc42, Rac, and ERK, but not on p38 MAPK. Formation by kinase-dead PAK1 requires Src and ERK activity and a direct interaction with the exchange factor PIX. Matrix-degrading membrane protrusions found in invasive carcinoma cells, involved in the assembly and maturation stages regulated by cortactin phosphorylation. Actin-rich membrane protrusions of tumor cells that are thought to initiate the local migration and invasion during cancer metastasis.

nodes.label: LMNA
nodes.description: A gene located on chromosome 1q11-q23 that encodes two proteins of the nuclear lamina, lamins A and C, produced by alternative splicing. Mutations in this gene cause autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy. A gene located at 1q21 that encodes lamins A/C, nuclear membrane proteins associated with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, familial dilated cardiomyopathy, and familial partial lipodystrophy. A gene encoding lamins A and C through alternative splicing, which are involved in Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy. The gene is associated with nine missense mutations and two small in-frame deletions, with most mutations affecting the central rod domain common to both lamins A/C. A gene that encodes A-type nuclear lamins, intermediate filament proteins associated with the inner nuclear membrane, and is involved in causing Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy when mutated. A gene encoding A-type lamins, a protein of the inner membrane of the nuclear envelope, involved in causing autosomal dominant Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy when mutated. A gene encoding for lamin A/C, located at 1q21.2-q21.3. Mutations in this gene can cause Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD), especially in the autosomal dominant form, which is more common and often more severe than the X-linked form. Lamin A/C is involved in the histological and histochemical levels of EDMD. A gene located on chromosome 1 that encodes for lamin A/C protein, and carries a heterozygous mutation (c.1622G>A) associated with Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy in the proband.

nodes.label: EpCAM
nodes.description: A transmembrane glycoprotein that is frequently and highly expressed on carcinomas, tumor-initiating cells, selected tissue progenitors, and embryonic and adult stem cells. It is detected in fetal liver, including cells of the parenchyma, and is lost in mature hepatocytes during liver development. EpCAM can be switched on and off through various strategies and its functions include cell-cell adhesion, proliferation, maintenance of a pluripotent state, regulation of differentiation, migration, and invasion. These functions can be conferred by the full-length protein and/or EpCAM-derived fragments, which are generated upon regulated intramembrane proteolysis. The spatiotemporal localization of EpCAM in immature liver progenitors, transit-amplifying cells, and mature liver cells impacts the regulation of EpCAM functions. A type I transmembrane glycoprotein overexpressed in human epithelioma but with relatively low expression in normal epithelial tissues. It is targeted by an immunotoxin for potential use in cancer therapy. A gene or protein involved in the study of papillary thyroid carcinoma, specifically expressed within the cytoplasm and nucleus of tumor cells, and correlated with follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma and extrathyroidal extension. Epithelial Cell Adhesion Molecule, a protein involved in physiology and pathology of the epithelium, specifically in regulating cell growth through interactions with other cell-cell contact molecules like E-cadherin and claudins, and crosstalk with Wnt and TGF-beta signaling. It also modulates trans-epithelial migration processes of white blood cells. Mutations of the EpCAM gene lead to disturbances of epithelial homeostasis and cellular differentiation from the stem cell compartment. In the intestinal tract, EpCAM mutations contribute to congenital tufting enteropathy. Tumor cells display increased EpCAM expression often correlated with the loss of strict basolateral localization. Many tumors show enhanced regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP) of EpCAM leading to the formation of extracellular EpEX and intracellular EpICD fragments which mediate proliferative signals to the cell. Detection of EpCAM fragments can be validated by sensitive enzyme-linked immune-sandwich assays (EpEX) or by immunohistochemistry (EpICD). A stem cell landmark protein identified by western blotting in drug-resistant cells.

nodes.label: Atopic dermatitis
nodes.description: A chronic skin condition characterized by symptoms such as itching, redness, and dryness. It can be exacerbated by stress and may lead to psychological stress due to social isolation and discrimination. The severity of the disease is assessed using the Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) index. Salivary cortisol levels are used as a biomarker to evaluate stress in patients with atopic dermatitis. A severe form of atopic dermatitis associated with Sezary syndrome, reported to have the phenomenon of a white halo around Molluscum contagiosum. A chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by dry, itchy skin and is often associated with sensitizations against Malassezia species in the variant of head and neck dermatitis. Current studies focus on systemic treatment approaches, particularly targeting Th2 polarized inflammation and itch with novel biologicals or small molecules. A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by aberrant barrier function and immune activation, resulting in symptoms such as pruritus and visible disease. Standard therapies have been insufficient, leading to the exploration of novel therapeutics like dupilumab. Clinical trials have shown marked improvement in patient symptoms and changes in the molecular signature of diseased skin, with reduction of both inflammatory and proliferative markers. Dupilumab has received US FDA breakthrough therapy designation for atopic dermatitis and is making unprecedented advances towards highly effective control of this debilitating disease. A complex skin disease often associated with other diseases of the atopic diathesis, characterized by chronic cutaneous inflammation and immune deviations. It may result in higher susceptibility of the skin to environmental factors. There is a high unmet medical need to define immunologic endotypes of AD due to its significant implications on upcoming stratification of the phenotype of AD and the resulting targeted therapies in the development of precision medicine. A skin condition characterized by inflammation, itching, and dryness, often leading to eczema. It is a type of atopic or allergic disease driven by interleukin-4 and interleukin-13, type 2 cytokines. The disease can be moderately to severely controlled by topical treatments, but some patients may require additional interventions like dupilumab. A widely acquired, relapsing inflammatory skin disease for which biological therapies are used, particularly in patients with moderate-to-severe cases.

nodes.label: Metabolic Syndrome
nodes.description: A complex disorder characterized by multiple metabolic abnormalities including high levels of HDL-cholesterol, plasma glucose, Type 2 diabetes, abdominal obesity measured by waist to hip ratio, and diastolic blood pressure. It is associated with an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, and is often accompanied by symptoms such as overweight or obesity, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, and dyslipidemia. The presence of metabolic syndrome is determined by the phenotypic expression of certain traits such as waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, glucose, HDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides, which are assessed and adjusted for age and sex. It has both strong environmental and genetic contributions and is studied in various populations, including Indian Asian men. Supervised or partially supervised exercise training is recommended as an initial adjunctive step in its treatment.

nodes.label: Fibrolamellar carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of carcinoma characterized by activation of protein kinase A, a kinase composed of catalytic and regulatory subunits. It is associated with the Carney complex and can be caused by both a heterozygous 400-kb deletion leading to the fusion of DNAJB1 and PRKACA and by loss of function of the PRKAR1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. A type of cancer that can be part of the Carney complex, characterized by inactivating PRKAR1A mutations instead of the DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion gene found in sporadic fibrolamellar carcinomas, which provides an alternate means for activation of protein kinase A. A rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma that occurs in children and young adults without underlying liver disease. The diagnosis is based on morphological characteristics of the tumor, supplemented by immunohistochemistry and/or genetic testing. A characteristic DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion gene has been associated with FLC. A type of liver cancer representing approximately 0.85% of liver cancers, associated with DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion transcript RNA coding for the catalytic domain of protein kinase A and overexpression of Aurora kinase A (AURKA). Patients with incurable, measurably confirmed FLC, aged >12 years, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-2 or Lansky 70-100, and adequate organ function were eligible for the study.

nodes.label: Potassium
nodes.description: A nutrient identified as a shortfall nutrient by the Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2010 Advisory Committee. It has been found to have a moderate body of evidence associating its intake with blood pressure reduction in adults, which influences the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease. Adequate dietary potassium also has a protective effect on age-related bone loss and reduction of kidney stones. Its benefits depend on organic anions associated with potassium as occurs in foods such as fruits and vegetables, in contrast to similar blood pressure-lowering benefits of potassium chloride. Low potassium-to-sodium intake ratios are more strongly related to cardiovascular disease risk than either nutrient alone. A nutrient that has been implicated in the management of renal lithiasis. Foods rich in potassium increase urinary citrate because of its alkali content.

nodes.label: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
nodes.description: A disease characterized by abnormal curvature of the spine in adolescents, affecting girls more commonly. It is a complex genetic disorder that results from the interaction of multiple gene loci and the environment, and its exact cause is unknown. Genetic studies have revealed that certain SNPs in genes like LAPTM4B and IGF1 are associated with susceptibility to and curve severity in AIS. The condition is studied in both white and Japanese patients, and its genetic contributions have been difficult to identify. It is associated with genetic predisposition and can progress if not treated effectively.

nodes.label: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
nodes.description: A major form of lung cancer accounting for about 85% of all lung cancer cases, characterized by the presence of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) rearrangements in 2-5% of patients, leading to the development of oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) for treatment. It is a type of lung cancer that is not classified as small cell lung cancer and is often associated with EGFR mutations. Patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC develop acquired drug resistance to EGFR TKIs. NSCLC is treated with various therapies such as EGFR inhibitors, PD-1 inhibitors, chemo-, radiation, and adjuvant-therapies. It is also characterized by the expression of Bmi-1 protein, with tumors showing moderate or strong Bmi-1 expression being more likely to have low levels of p16 and p14ARF. MicroRNA-21 (miR-21) post-transcriptionally down-regulates the expression of PTEN and stimulates growth and invasion in NSCLC, suggesting that this may be a potential therapeutic target in the future treatment of NSCLC. NSCLC cells exposed to lorlatinib acquire hyperactivation of EGFR, which can be blocked by erlotinib to restore sensitivity to lorlatinib. HER3-DXd shows broad effectiveness in HER3-expressing cancers, including NSCLC. A 55-year-old man was diagnosed with this condition and received treatment involving combined immunochemotherapy with pembrolizumab, carboplatin, and pemetrexed.

nodes.label: Overall Survival
nodes.description: A measure of the total time from treatment until death due to any cause, often used as an endpoint in clinical trials to assess the effectiveness of medical interventions. It can refer to the time from random assignment, treatment initiation, or the start of a medical treatment until death. In some studies, it has been shown that certain treatments, such as enzalutamide, abiraterone, and cabazitaxel, can improve overall survival compared to placebo or best of care.

nodes.label: Lorlatinib
nodes.description: A potent, brain-penetrant, third-generation inhibitor of ALK and ROS1 tyrosine kinases with broad coverage of ALK mutations, used to treat ALK-positive non-small-cell lung cancer, including those with CNS metastases and progression after ALK-directed therapy. It is administered at a dose of 100 mg orally once daily continuously in 21-day cycles and has shown substantial overall and intracranial activity in treatment-naive patients and those who had progressed on crizotinib or other ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

nodes.label: Senescence
nodes.description: A state of permanent cell cycle arrest associated with aging and various stressors, characterized by the expression of senescence-associated features (SAFs) and the secretion of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which includes pro-inflammatory factors such as IL1B, CXCL8, CCL2, TNF, CCL27 and CLEC11A. It can be triggered by reduced c-Myc signaling, mitogenic signaling, or hypoproliferative signaling imbalances, and is often induced by tumor suppressor genes as a response to DNA damage or other stressors. Senescence is evaluated in relation to the proliferative potential of primary keratinocyte cultures from young and old healthy donors, and from young patients with inherited defects leading to premature aging. It is also characterized by the aging or inactivation of cells, particularly HUVECs, leading to the release of cytokines and chemokines that promote tumor growth. Senescence can be induced by W-CIN, RING1 depletion, SOX10 ablation, and Berberine Derivative B68 targeting BMI1.

nodes.label: Dyskeratosis Congenita
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by progressive and fatal bone marrow failure, caused by mutations in the DKC1 gene. It can lead to a more severe allelic variant known as Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome. A rare and fatal congenital syndrome characterized by the triad of reticular skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy and mucosal leukoplakia, and the predisposition to bone marrow failure and malignancies. Mutations in DKC1 gene encoding dyskerin are responsible for this condition. A rare inherited multisystem disorder characterized by the triad of abnormal skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy and mucosal leucoplakia. It has an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern in approximately 40% of the patients. A multi-system disorder characterized by abnormalities of the skin, nails, and mucous membranes, and often associated with bone marrow dysfunction. It has six identified genetic subtypes, including X-linked recessive, autosomal dominant, and autosomal recessive. These subtypes are caused by defects in genes that encode components critical for telomere maintenance, such as dyskerin, TERC, TERT, NOP10, NHP2, and TIN2. Dyskeratosis Congenita and related diseases can now be regarded as disorders of 'telomere and stem cell dysfunction'. A rare inherited disorder characterized by the early onset of reticulate skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, and mucosal leucoplakia. Bone marrow failure develops in over 80% of cases and is the main cause of early mortality. The DC1 gene responsible for the X linked form of dyskeratosis congenita has been mapped to Xq28. An inherited disorder characterized by skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy and mucosal leucoplakia. It is suggested that the major form is X-linked, with a high incidence of bone marrow failure and early mortality. The DKC1 gene, located within Xq28, is responsible for the X-linked form of the disease and has a key role in normal cell biology.

nodes.label: Warfarin
nodes.description: A traditional oral anticoagulant used for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), often compared to newer drugs like apixaban and rivaroxaban in clinical trials. It is a vitamin K antagonist that requires regular monitoring of its anticoagulant intensity and has a target International Normalized Ratio (INR) range of 2.0-3.0. Warfarin has been the standard therapy for stroke prevention in intermediate- to high-risk AF patients but has been limited by several factors such as narrow therapeutic windows, drug-drug and drug-food interactions, and hemorrhagic complications. It is also used as a comparator in phase 3 randomized trials evaluating the efficacy of novel oral anticoagulants like dabigatran, rivaroxaban, and apixaban.

nodes.label: Hunter syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by profound iduronate sulfatase deficiency, which has been found in cultured fibroblasts, serum, lymphocytes, and tissues of two clinically affected girls. It is an X-linked disease, with the patients being karyotypically normal and having normal fathers. The mothers' fibroblasts were cloned but did not reveal mosaicism, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. An X-linked recessive disorder, characterized by a deficiency of the enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase (IDS), leading to the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in various tissues. It is associated with intellectual disability, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and organomegaly. Genetic counseling is important for identifying heterozygotes, and serum assays for IDS activity can detect carriers with 91.7% accuracy.

nodes.label: Monkeypox
nodes.description: A zoonotic illness caused by the monkeypox virus, an Orthopoxvirus in the same genus as the variola, vaccinia, and cowpox viruses. It has caused sporadic infections and outbreaks mainly restricted to some countries in west and central Africa since the detection of the first human case in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1970. The 2022 outbreak has been primarily associated with close intimate contact and most cases have been diagnosed among men who have sex with men. The incubation period ranges from 7 days to 10 days and most patients present with a systemic illness that includes fever and myalgia and a characteristic rash, with papules that evolve to vesicles, pustules, and crusts in the genital, anal, or oral regions and often involve the mucosa. Complications that require medical treatment occur in up to 40% of patients and include rectal pain, odynophagia, penile oedema, and skin and anorectal abscesses. Most patients have a self-limited illness; between 1% and 13% require hospital admission and the case-fatality rate is less than 0.1%. A diagnosis can be made through the presence of Orthopoxvirus DNA in PCRs from lesion swabs or body fluids. Patients with severe manifestations and people at risk of severe disease could benefit from antiviral treatment such as tecovirimat. The current strategy for post-exposure prophylaxis or pre-exposure prophylaxis for people at high risk is vaccination with the non-replicating modified vaccinia Ankara.

nodes.label: Short QT syndrome
nodes.description: A newly described clinical entity characterized by the presence of a short QT interval associated with cardiac tachyarrhythmias including sudden cardiac death at a young age in otherwise healthy individuals. It is linked to mutations in KCNH2 in familial forms and a mutation in KCNQ1 in a sporadic form of the disease. The disease is clinically heterogeneous, with a wide range of symptoms varying from atrial to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. It is a rare genetic disease with a risk of sudden cardiac death, characterized by a lack of adaptation of the QT interval during treadmill testing and a shortened QTc interval of less than 300 to 320 milliseconds. It is caused by missense mutations in KCNH2 (HERG) and KCNQ1 genes and is associated with an increased incidence of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The treatment of choice for symptomatic patients is the implantable cardioverter defibrillator, and quinidine has been shown to be efficient in prolonging the QT interval and normalizing the effective refractory periods in some patients.

nodes.label: Osteogenesis Imperfecta
nodes.description: An inherited bone fragility disorder most commonly associated with autosomal dominant mutations in the type I collagen genes, particularly in collagen type I alpha 1 (COL1A1) and collagen type I alpha 2 (COL1A2). It can also be caused by autosomal recessive mutations in various genes, including the BMP1 gene. Symptoms include increased bone mineral density in some cases and recurrent fractures, hypermobility, and no evidence of dentinogenesis imperfecta in others. There are different types of BMP1 mutations associated with OI, ranging from mild to severe and progressively deforming skeletal phenotypes. Bone material density is very high in some cases, leading to concerns about anti-resorptive therapy. A genetic disorder characterized by brittle bones and multiple causative defects, which has led to the identification of critical cellular and bone tissue mechanisms. Investigations into common pathways in osteogenesis imperfecta could yield new mechanistic insights into clinical therapies for patients.

nodes.label: Cholinergic innervation
nodes.description: The process of cholinergic innervation involves the distribution of cholinergic markers such as acetylcholinesterase, choline acetyltransferase, and nerve growth factor receptors in the basal ganglia of the human brain. This includes the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and subthalamic nucleus. The striatum, specifically the putamen, caudate, olfactory tubercle, and nucleus accumbens, display the highest density of cholinergic varicosities. The red nucleus and subthalamic nucleus follow with the next highest density, while the globus pallidus and ventral tegmental area show intermediate density and the pars compacta of the substantia nigra shows low density. The basal forebrain is the primary source of this cholinergic innervation, with NGFr-positive axons being more pronounced in the putamen than in the caudate. A process involving the transmission of nerve impulses from cholinergic neurons outside the basal forebrain, primarily located in the upper brainstem, to various structures including the latter three structures and parts of the globus pallidus.

nodes.label: Cauda equina syndrome
nodes.description: A neurological disorder characterized by single or double-level compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots located in the dural sac, leading to polyradicular symptomatology including low-back pain, saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, motor weakness of the lower extremities, chronic paraplegia, bladder dysfunction, and impairment of impulse propagation. It can be caused by non-neoplastic compressive etiologies such as herniated lumbosacral discs, spinal stenosis, spinal neoplasms, and non-compressive etiologies like ischemic insults, inflammatory conditions, spinal arachnoiditis, and infectious etiologies. A relatively uncommon condition typically associated with a large, space-occupying lesion within the canal of the lumbosacral spine. Characterized by varying patterns of low back pain, sciatica, lower extremity sensorimotor loss, and bowel and bladder dysfunction. Pathophysiology remains unclear but may be related to damage to the nerve roots composing the cauda equina from direct mechanical compression and venous congestion or ischemia. Treatment involves urgent surgical decompression of the spinal canal. A well-described neurological condition caused by compression of the lumbosacral roots, often due to a herniated disc, tumor, infection, or hematoma. It can manifest as chronic low back pain, perineal numbness, bladder incontinence, and associated pain complaints. Surgical decompression has shown high success rates for symptomatic cysts, particularly in the setting of acute cauda equina syndrome secondary to a lumbar synovial cyst.

nodes.label: UvrC protein
nodes.description: A protein involved in the nucleotide excision repair mechanism, part of the UvrABC endonuclease complex and helps to repair the damaged DNA of M. tuberculosis.

nodes.label: Trastuzumab deruxtecan
nodes.description: A HER2-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, also known as DS-8201, consisting of a humanized antibody against HER2, a novel enzyme-cleavable linker, and a topoisomerase I inhibitor payload. It has been evaluated for safety and tolerability in patients with advanced breast and gastric or gastro-oesophageal tumours in a phase 1 dose-escalation study. The recommended doses for expansion are 5.4 or 6.4 mg/kg. It has a manageable safety profile and shows preliminary activity in trastuzumab emtansine-pretreated patients with HER2-positive breast cancer and heavily pretreated patients with HER2-positive gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer. It is used in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer, gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction cancer, and has been associated with interstitial lung disease and myelosuppression as notable toxic effects.

nodes.label: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
nodes.description: A severe, X-linked recessive, neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to absent full-length dystrophin protein. It is the most common form of muscular dystrophy, affecting mainly young boys and characterized by progressive muscle weakness, degeneration, and central nervous system involvement. Diagnostic and treatment guidelines have been published recently. It is evaluated using the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) in clinical trials to assess drug efficacy. The mean age of onset is around 3.2 years, with a mean presentation age of 7.2 years. The disease can be diagnosed through genetic testing or muscle biopsy. The incidence is one in 5000 live male births worldwide. It affects both skeletal muscle and the heart, and is associated with a higher prevalence of epilepsy (6.3% - 12.3%) than in the general pediatric population (0.5-1%).

nodes.label: Everolimus
nodes.description: An orally administered inhibitor of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), used to treat subependymal giant cell astrocytoma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. It has been shown to significantly reduce the volume of the largest subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) in patients with TSC in phase II and III trials. Commonly, the starting dosage is 3.0 mg/m² or 4.5 mg/m² depending on the trial. It is titrated to tolerability to achieve target trough concentrations of 5-15 ng/mL. Clinical trials have demonstrated significant reductions in SEGA volume and decreased seizure frequency. It is also used to treat epilepsy and growth in children under 3 years of age with subependymal giant cell astrocytoma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Adverse events are mostly grade 1 or 2, and no patients discontinued treatment because of adverse events. The most common adverse events are mouth ulceration, stomatitis, convulsion, and pyrexia.

nodes.label: Mitochondria
nodes.description: Mitochondria are organelles found in cells that primarily serve as the source of energy production through oxidative phosphorylation under aerobic conditions. They contain an enzyme called ATP synthase in their internal mitochondrial membrane and are responsible for producing adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the universal energy currency, through a series of redox reactions involving an electrochemical gradient established across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Mitochondria have their own genetic material called mitochondrial DNA and are involved in various cellular processes, including energy production, apoptosis, iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis, heme and steroid synthesis, calcium homeostasis, and regulation of cellular redox state. They are essential organelles that play a crucial role in energy production and are targeted by mitophagy for removal. Mitochondria form specific regions of contact with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) called mitochondria-associated membranes (MAM).

nodes.label: Advanced Prostate Cancer
nodes.description: A type of prostate cancer that has spread beyond the prostate gland to other parts of the body. It was identified as having a moderate PAF among male cancers associated with excess body weight, with a rate of 14.9%. It is a type of cancer with a substantial burden attributable to excess body weight. A stage of prostate cancer characterized by its progression and the need for rapid and effective treatments. It includes both metastatic and non-metastatic forms, with the latter being sensitive to castration and the former being resistant. A type of prostate cancer that persists despite castration, characterized by the presence of androgen receptors and the ability to resist treatments such as enzalutamide, abiraterone, apalutamide, and darolutamide. A type of prostate cancer that has spread beyond the prostate gland and is affecting one in every nine men in the USA, being the second leading cause of cancer-related death.

nodes.label: Overweight
nodes.description: A condition characterized by excess body weight, associated with an increased risk of cancer at several sites including kidney, endometrium, colon, prostate, gallbladder, and breast in post-menopausal women. It contributes to 5% of all cancers in the European Union, 3% in men and 6% in women, corresponding to 27,000 male and 45,000 female cancer cases yearly. A condition characterized by excess body weight, linked with several chronic diseases including colorectal cancer among men. Not specifically linked with colorectal cancer risk among women. A condition characterized by excess body weight, defined by the body mass index (BMI) as BMI ≥ 25-29.9 kg/m². It is associated with an increased risk of several diseases and mortality when combined with obesity. Overweight individuals are at risk of colorectal cancer (CRC) and other health issues related to obesity. A medical condition characterized by excess body weight. It is defined by a body mass index (BMI) of ≥ 27 kg/m². In the context of the text, overweight is managed using oral naltrexone extended-release/bupropion extended-release (naltrexone ER/bupropion ER) in the presence of at least one bodyweight-related comorbidity.

nodes.label: Radical Resection
nodes.description: A surgical procedure involving the removal of a tumor and surrounding healthy tissue to ensure complete tumor removal and reduce the risk of recurrence. In this context, it is performed after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer. A surgical procedure used to manage patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) who have received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) and did not experience a significant downstage of the tumor. In the study, 1,693 patients underwent this procedure, and the median follow-up time was 44.0 months (interquartile range = 4-107 months).

nodes.label: BRG1
nodes.description: A subunit of SWI/SNF complexes that activates SOX10 expression and interacts with SOX10 to activate expression of OCT6 and KROX20. It recruits SOX10 to the MPZ locus and its expression is dependent on SOX10 in immortalized Schwann cells. Dominant negative BRG1 inhibits expression of MPZ and MBP in these cells. A chromatin remodeling factor that is essential for melanoma cell proliferation in vitro and for normal melanocyte development in vivo. It forms a complex with BRG1 and CHD7, and is actively recruited to a set of MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) at active enhancers by combinations of MITF, SOX10, TFAP2A, and YY1. BRG1 also regulates the dynamics of MITF genomic occupancy.

nodes.label: Erenumab
nodes.description: A fully human monoclonal antibody that inhibits the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor, used for the prevention of episodic migraine. Erenumab is administered via subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks for up to 5 years and has shown significant reduction in monthly migraine days (MMD) by an average of 5.0 days from baseline, with 65%, 42%, and 26% of patients achieving ≥50%, ≥75%, and 100% reduction in MMD, respectively, at week 64. It has a consistent linear portion of the clearance from 70 mg to 210 mg and a nonlinear PK profile from 1 mg to 70 mg, similar to other human immunoglobulin G2 antibodies. Erenumab is generally well tolerated with an acceptable safety profile.

nodes.label: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
nodes.description: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to insulin resistance or pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction. It is a common, chronic disease affecting nearly 6% of the adult US population and a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Wisconsin as well as the country. It involves underlying defects such as impaired insulin secretion, insulin resistance, and exaggerated postprandial hyperglycemia. Treatment includes controlling blood glucose levels, using multiple classes of oral medications like sulfonylureas, biguanides, thiazolidinediones, and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, and considering insulin for those who have failed oral therapy. It is associated with increased risk of developing from impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG), and is linked with microvascular manifestations and cardiovascular events. Metformin is a commonly prescribed treatment for this condition. A potential adverse effect associated with the use of statins, characterized by the development of this condition.

nodes.label: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
nodes.description: A rare and severe immune system disorder characterized by excessive activation of lymphocytes and macrophages, often associated with disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria infection. It is a life-threatening disease associated with aberrant macrophage overactivation, in which infections can be a leading cause in immunocompromised hosts. The condition is diagnosed based on the fulfillment of five out of eight diagnostic criteria, including fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, hemophagocytosis, low/absent NK-cell-activity, and hyperferritinemia. Treatment typically involves chemo-immunotherapy with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine A, followed by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in certain cases. The condition can have primary and acquired forms, with the primary form often seen in childhood and caused by various mutations with genetic inheritance, hence called familial HLH.

nodes.label: CP690,550
nodes.description: An inhibitor targeting Jak3, developed for the treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis and currently in phase II clinical study. It has been reported to cause IL-10 overproduction by Jak3 and Stat6 deficient dendritic cells. A small molecule JAK inhibitor that specifically targets the JAK/STAT signaling pathway in rheumatoid synoviocytes, reducing IL-6 production and MAPK activation. It is used to investigate the molecular effects on the JAK/STAT pathways and to examine the role of JAK kinases in rheumatoid synovitis. A new JAK3 inhibitor that has shown efficacy in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and was studied for its effects on cytokine production and cellular signaling in human CD4(+) T cells. It almost completely inhibited the production of IL-4, IL-17, IL-22 and IFN-γ from activated CD4(+) T cells at the optimal concentration, but only had marginal effects on IL-2 production. It also inhibited anti-CD3-induced phosphorylation of STAT1, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5, and STAT6, but not the TCR-associated phosphorylation of ZAP-70.

nodes.label: Kidney
nodes.description: A pair of organs responsible for filtering waste products from the blood and producing urine, maintaining proper kidney function, and regulating electrolyte balance. They are essential for excreting sodium in response to natriuretic hormones, participating in the regulation of sodium and water homeostasis, blood volume, and blood pressure. The kidney is also involved in the metabolism of certain substances, such as sotorasib, and can be affected by conditions like tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), hypertension, and aging-associated renal injury. Pendrin, an anion exchanger, plays a functional role in the kidney, particularly in the transport of chloride, bicarbonate, and iodide. The kidney is one of the sites where excess body weight increases the risk of cancer.

nodes.label: Breast cancer
nodes.description: A type of cancer that affects the breast tissue, characterized by the presence of breast cancer cells and often leading to the formation of tumors. It can be diagnosed in both men and women, but is more common in women. The severity of the disease can vary widely, with some families being severely affected. Breast cancer can be classified into various subtypes based on the level of expression of certain markers, including luminal and nonluminal types. It can also be associated with specific genetic mutations, such as TP53 and FANCJ, and metabolic syndrome. Some subtypes, like claudin-low breast cancer (CLBC), are associated with early metastasis and resistance to chemotherapy. Breast cancer can be treated surgically, and adjuvant therapies, such as hormonal therapy and targeted therapies, may be used depending on the subtype and stage of the disease. Certain risk factors, such as red meat consumption and disruption of the circadian clock, have been linked to an increased risk of breast cancer.

nodes.label: Riboswitch
nodes.description: A type of metabolite-binding RNA domain that is typically located in noncoding regions of mRNA. It selectively binds its target compound and modulates gene expression. Riboswitches are present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including fungi and plants. They are non-protein coding RNA elements that utilize metabolite binding to control expression of their own transcript, and are often found in the 5' untranslated region (5'-UTR) of mRNAs. Riboswitches contain an aptamer, an RNA structure that folds to expose or sequester regulatory elements in the adjacent sequence through alternative nucleotide pairing, and an expression platform that regulates either transcription termination or translation initiation. They are involved at various regulation levels of gene expression, such as transcription attenuation, translation initiation, mRNA splicing and mRNA processing. Riboswitches are most commonly found in the 5'-untranslated regions of bacterial mRNAs and interact with metabolites to regulate the expression of the coding region via a secondary structural switch. They are vital components of many genomes and their distributions and mechanisms vary across different microbial groups. There are more than 30 known classes of riboswitches, each consisting of an aptamer domain and an expression platform.

nodes.label: Clinical Trials
nodes.description: Research studies designed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of various medical interventions, diagnostic tests, or preventive measures in humans. They have been conducted for conditions such as type 2 diabetes, atopic dermatitis, migraine, cluster headache, and T1DM, and have evaluated the use of different treatments, including natural food compounds, medications, and targeted therapies.

nodes.label: Dilated cardiomyopathy
nodes.description: A type of cardiomyopathy characterized by enlargement of the heart chambers and thinning of the heart muscle walls, often leading to left ventricular dysfunction, reduced pumping efficiency, and heart failure. It can be caused by mutations in genes such as alpha-myosin heavy chain (alphaMyHC) and beta-myosin heavy chain, and is associated with conditions like Barth syndrome, myotonic dystrophy type 2, and viral myocarditis. Early characteristics may include restrictive cardiomyopathy with no ventricular enlargement and prominent atria.

nodes.label: alpha-synuclein
nodes.description: A highly conserved 140 amino acid protein primarily expressed in neurons, involved in synaptic plasticity and neurotransmission. It is a major component of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, forming the main filamentous part and detected by staining with antibodies directed against amino-terminal and carboxyl-terminal sequences. Mutations in the alpha-synuclein gene have been linked to rare cases of familial Parkinson's disease, and overexpression of both wild-type and mutant forms can cause dopamine neuron death. Alpha-synuclein is a microtubule-associated protein and is found in the synaptic boutons of many nerve cells in the adult human CNS.

nodes.label: Isradipine
nodes.description: A calcium channel blocker of the dihydropyridine class, primarily used for the treatment of hypertension in children and adults. It has a half-life of 6 to 8 hours and is available in a powder-filled capsule. Isradipine can be used as monotherapy or in combination with other agents, and is effective in controlling hypertension. It is also used in the treatment of black hypertensive patients with essential hypertension, and has been shown to reduce the infarct size in a rat model of embolic stroke. Adverse effects include headache, flushing, dizziness, and tachycardia.

nodes.label: Basilar skull fractures
nodes.description: Basilar skull fractures are fractures of the lower part of the skull, making up about 20% of all skull fractures. They are mainly caused by high-velocity blunt trauma and falls from high heights. Depending on their precise location, they can be divided into frontobasal, laterobasal and frontolateral fractures. Clinical signs include cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea or otorrhea, periorbital ecchymosis, retroauricular ecchymosis and cranial nerve injuries. Fractures of the petrous bone can lead to conductive hearing loss, sensorineural hearing loss, dizziness and nausea due to a failure of the labyrinth. Neurological deficits or limited consciousness may require a CT scan to rule out a basilar skull fracture and accompanying pathologies. If vascular injury is suspected, a CT angiography should be performed. Treatment is usually interdisciplinary and depends mainly on the accompanying injuries and possible complications. A purely conservative approach with close controls is often sufficient. The surgical approach is primarily used to treat possible complications, such as intracerebral bleeding. A disorder involving fractures in the base of the skull, which can lead to symptoms such as hemotympanum, tympanic membrane perforation, and otorrhea or rhinorrhea. The study reviewed 46 cases of this condition in children to evaluate the incidence of CNS infection and the potential benefits of antimicrobial chemoprophylaxis.

nodes.label: Pax3
nodes.description: A gene required to expand a pool of committed melanoblasts or restricted progenitor cells early in melanocyte development. A paired homeodomain factor that regulates the development of melanocytes and binds to the main cis-acting element in the Mitf promoter. Its protein and mRNA levels decline after IL6RIL6 treatment, and overexpression suppresses Mitf promoter inhibition. A paired box protein that is an essential regulator of muscle and neural crest-derived cell types, including melanocytes. It recognizes the genes encoding microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (Mitf) and tyrosinase-related protein-1 (Trp-1) through distinct modes, which are differentially affected by disease-associated mutations. Pax3 has a paired domain and a homeodomain that contribute to target site recognition, with the paired domain being sufficient for TRP-1 recognition but requiring both domains for MITF element binding. Mutations associated with Waardenburg syndrome exhibit marked disparity in their effects on MITF and TRP-1 binding, and impact the ability of Pax3 to regulate reporter genes fused to either the MITF or TRP-1 promoters. A transcription factor that plays a crucial role in melanocyte development and function, influencing melanocytic proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, migration, lineage specificity, and differentiation. It is also involved in the development of diseases and syndromes resulting from either too much or too little Pax3 function. The Pax3 pathway may provide an ideal target for either stem cell or cancer therapies due to its key role in melanocyte stem cells and tumors.

nodes.label: Alendronate
nodes.description: An oral second generation bisphosphonate used for the prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis, often recommended based on an individual's risk factors and needs. It reduces subsequent fracture rate in osteoporosis confirmed by bone densitometry or by occurrence of fractures. Alendronate is approved for the treatment of osteoporosis and has been shown to decrease fracture risk. It is also used for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, with a recommended dose of 5 mg per day for persistently preventing bone loss in recently postmenopausal women with normal bone mass. Its effect on bone mass and biochemical markers is comparable to that of commonly recommended regimens of postmenopausal HRT. Alendronate is safe for long-term use and has an equivalent gastrointestinal risk and adverse event profile to placebo. It is used to treat postmenopausal osteoporosis, specifically for the reduction of risk of vertebral, nonvertebral and hip fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

nodes.label: Golodirsen
nodes.description: A phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO) subclass antisense oligonucleotide developed by Sarepta Therapeutics for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). It induces exon 53 skipping and received its first global approval in the USA for the treatment of DMD in patients with a confirmed mutation of the DMD gene that is amenable to exon 53 skipping, based on positive results from a phase I/II clinical trial. Golodirsen is currently in phase III clinical development for the treatment of DMD worldwide. A chemical compound used as a treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, specifically designed to increase dystrophin production through exon 53 skipping. It was administered in two parts of the study, with part 1 being a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 12-week dose titration and part 2 being an ongoing, open-label evaluation. Safety findings were consistent with those previously observed in pediatric patients with DMD. The study demonstrated that golodirsen was well-tolerated and induced exon skipping and novel dystrophin as confirmed by 3 different assays. An AON designed for DMD exon 53 skipping, recently approved by the FDA. A provisionally approved PMO-based drug for approx. 8% of all DMD patients amenable to exon 53 skipping. It is used to induce therapeutic exon skipping during pre-mRNA processing to restore the reading frame of the primary transcript of DMD, potentially slowing down the disease progression. A drug used in a first-in-human, multicenter, two-part, open-label, phase 1/2 trial to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of treatment among ambulatory patients with exon 53 skip-amenable Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). It increased dystrophin protein expression and exon skipping, and had no safety-related discontinuations or deaths.

nodes.label: Etidronate
nodes.description: A molecule from the past used in the treatment of osteoporosis, particularly in specific cases. It should be avoided as much as possible and strictly restricted to its legal indication including women with several vertebral crush fractures and severely decreased bone mineral density. A less potent bisphosphonate used for the treatment of osteoporosis, ranking third in the treatment order for postmenopausal women with existing fractures. A bisphosphonate class of drug that inhibits bone resorption by interfering with the activity of osteoclasts, bone cells that break down bone tissue. It was investigated for its effects on postmenopausal women stratified by fracture risk and its benefits and harms in the primary and secondary prevention of osteoporotic fractures. It was administered in randomized controlled trials for at least one year, either alone or with other anti-osteoporotic drugs and concurrent calcium/vitamin D. A drug used in the comparison between etidronate 400 mg/day versus placebo, etidronate 200 mg/day versus placebo, and etidronate at any dosage versus another anti-osteoporotic agent. It was administered in three dosing regimens: 400 mg/day, 200 mg/day, and at any dosage. It was compared to placebo and another anti-osteoporotic agent in various studies focusing on primary and secondary prevention. A medication used for the treatment of fractures, with doses of 400 mg/day being considered for comparison against placebo. The drug is evaluated for its effects on various types of fractures, including non-vertebral, clinical vertebral, hip, and wrist fractures. The evidence regarding etidronate's impact on these fractures varies in certainty, ranging from moderate to very low.

nodes.label: Stroke
nodes.description: A medical emergency caused by the interruption of blood flow to the brain, leading to potential nerve damage and disability. It can occur due to blockage or bleeding in the brain vessels, and is a major concern in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). The risk of stroke in TIA patients is higher in those with a higher ABCD(2) score. Thyronamines, specifically 3-T(1)AM, have shown potential as a prophylactic or acute treatment for stroke due to their ability to induce hypothermia. A medical condition characterized by a sudden interruption of blood supply to the brain, leading to potential neurological deficits. It can occur as a consequence of a transient ischaemic attack (TIA). The risk of stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation increases with age. The ARISTOTLE trial evaluated the efficacy of apixaban and warfarin in preventing stroke.

nodes.label: Sotorasib
nodes.description: A small molecule that selectively and irreversibly targets the KRAS G12C mutation, functioning as a first-in-class KRAS G12C covalent inhibitor in clinical development for the treatment of tumors with the KRAS p.G12C mutation. It has shown promising results in the phase II CodeBreak 100 trial for non-small cell lung cancer, leading to responses in more than a third of patients and a median progression-free survival of almost 7 months. Sotorasib has been implicated in triggering checkpoint inhibitor immune-related adverse events, specifically hepatitis, in patients with KRAS G12C-Mutant NSCLC. It has undergone comprehensive nonclinical safety assessments and has shown no genotoxicity or off-target effects in vitro, with no direct effect on embryo-fetal development in rats or rabbits. However, it is associated with renal toxicity in the Sprague Dawley rat, characterized by degeneration and necrosis of the proximal tubular epithelium localized to the outer stripe of the outer medulla (OSOM).

nodes.label: Glioma
nodes.description: A type of brain tumor that includes various subtypes such as astrocytomas, anaplastic astrocytomas, glioblastomas multiforme, oligodendrogliomas, and mixed oligoastrocytomas. It is a neoplastic tissue that can be further classified into different grades based on their aggressiveness. Gliomas can contain mutations in the p53 and PTEN genes, with PTEN mutation being more common in GBMs and associated with both genetic pathways. They are the most frequent primary brain tumor and often overexpress the oncogenes EGFR and PDGFR, containing mutations and deletions of the tumor suppressor genes PTEN and TP53. MicroRNA-214 is found to directly target the 3' UTR of UBC9 and inversely correlate with its expression levels in glioma tissues and cells. Overexpression of miR-214 suppresses the endogenous UBC9 protein and affects T98G cell proliferation. Glioma cells include human glioblastoma T98G cells and human glioma U251 cells. They are associated with recurrent mutations in IDH1 or IDH2, along with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cholangiocarcinoma, and chondrosarcoma. Progression to higher tumor grade is associated with contrast enhancement on MRI. The majority of gliomas harbor mutations in the genes encoding isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 or 2 (IDH1/IDH2). Gliomas are characterized by the proliferation and invasion of glioma cells, with microRNA-128 and COX-2 involved in the pathogenesis of glioma.

nodes.label: Ctf4
nodes.description: A protein involved in sister chromatid cohesion, DNA replication, and the formation of the replisome progression complex (RPC), linking the MCM2-7 helicase to DNA polymerase alpha. It is a central member of the replication fork, interacts with the GINS component of the RPC, and is essential for the association of RPCs with DNA polymerase alpha. Ctf4 is also involved in the Fork Protection Complex (FPC) and is required for viability, S phase progression, sister chromatid cohesion, endoreplication, and coping with replication stress. It is a yeast protein that links the Cdc45-MCM-GINS (CMG) DNA helicase to DNA polymerase alpha within the replisome and is a component of the replisome, identified as a Dia2-binding protein. Ctf4 is ubiquitinated by SCF(Dia2) and is essential for the association of RPCs with DNA polymerase alpha.

nodes.label: Atrial Fibrillation
nodes.description: A cardiac arrhythmia characterized by an irregular and often rapid heart rate, typically affecting the atria. It is a non-valvular form, meaning it does not involve heart valve abnormalities. Atrial fibrillation can increase the risk of stroke, blood clots, and heart failure, and is associated with an increasing prevalence and a need for safe and effective stroke prophylaxis. It is often managed with medications such as anticoagulants, and can be divided into two groups: paroxysmal AF and persistent AF. Atrial fibrillation is the focus of stroke prevention treatments discussed in the text, including the comparison of various oral anticoagulants like VKAs, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and aspirin. The ARISTOTLE trial, which enrolled 18,201 patients with atrial fibrillation in 39 countries, studied the use of apixaban and warfarin for reducing stroke and other thromboembolic complications.

nodes.label: Ischiopagus twins
nodes.description: A type of conjoined twins characterized by connection at the hip region. In this study, 4 pairs of ischiopagus twins were managed, with 2 cases having direct involvement of the nervous system at the site of union. One pair had end-to-end union of their spinal cords, while another pair had a fused dural sac without joined neural elements. One child from this pair developed syringomyelia 2 years after separation. Nine of the 12 children (75%) had bony abnormalities of the spine, commonly hemivertebrae in the thoracic spine, and six manifested scoliosis.

nodes.label: Cardiomyopathy
nodes.description: A group of diseases affecting the heart muscle, leading to its abnormal structure and function. It can be familial hypertrophic, caused by an Arg403-->Gln missense mutation in the alpha-myosin heavy chain, or exacerbated by overexpression of cardiac G(s)alpha and chronic enhancement of sympathetic drive. It can also be associated with mutations in troponin subunits, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), and restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), and be characterized by altered calcium handling in the form of changes in the Ca²+ sensitivity of contraction. Cardiomyopathy can present as heart failure and/or arrhythmia and can be caused by dystrophic cardiomyopathy. It can also be a consequence of targeted ablation of ILK from the murine heart and its spontaneous occurrence in the absence of ILK. In some cases, cardiomyopathy can be associated with muscular dystrophies, natriuretic peptide family genes and their biological functions, and X-linked patterns of inheritance.

nodes.label: Neurofibromatosis
nodes.description: A group of genetic disorders that primarily affect the cell growth of neural tissues, with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) being the most common type accounting for about 90% of all cases. It is one of the most frequent human genetic diseases, with a prevalence of one case in 3,000 births. The expressivity of NF1 is extremely variable, with manifestations ranging from mild lesions to several complications and functional impairment. A serious, common, genetically determined neurological disorder affecting both sexes and all races and ethnic groups. It has a prevalence of about 1:4000 births and is characterized by complications that can occur in any of the body systems in tissues of ectodermal, mesodermal and neural tube origin. There are two major forms, NF1 and NF2, with NF1 having a more variable and complex disease phenotype. The NF2 gene is only expressed in tissues of ectodermal origin and its expression is more uniform both within and between families. The recent discovery and isolation of the gene responsible for the NF1 mutation has practical applications in the field of molecular genetics which could modify the approaches for diagnosis, treatment and prevention of NF. A group of rare genetic disorders that can affect all races equally at an incidence from 1:3000 (NF1) to a log unit lower for NF2 and schwannomatosis. The research community is reporting an increasing number of malignant cancers that carry mutations in the NF genes, leading to a general interest increase in both the research and pharma community. An autosomal dominant disorder identified in the study as one of the most frequent forms of hereditary pathology in Kostroma Province. It involves the growth of tumors along nerves and can affect multiple body systems. A neurocutaneous systemic disease occurring in 1:2500 to 3300 live births, with a prevalence comparable to cystic fibrosis or Down's syndrome and more common than muscular dystrophy. It involves intracranial, bony, and extracranial anomalies, including optic gliomas, acoustic neuromas, macrocephaly, absence of the sphenoid wing, facial asymmetry, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and cafe-au-lait spots. The study reviews the experience with 257 cases seen since 1972. A group of rare tumor-suppressor syndromes including neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2 (NF1, NF2) and schwannomatosis. These diseases affect the nervous system more severely than any other type of neoplastic disease. They are characterized by a greater tumor burden, monogenic or complex genetics, and distinct clinical and pathophysiologic features. The tumor biology involves alternation of growth phases and growth pauses, with variable correlations between genotypes and phenotypes, and common new mutations and genetic mosaics. A group of at least two different autosomal dominant disorders, including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), characterized by various manifestations such as café au lait spots, lentigines, neurofibromas, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, and other tumors of the central nervous system. NF1 represents 95% of neurofibromatoses cases, with an incidence of 1 for 3,500 newborns and a prevalence of 1 for 4,500. NF2 has an incidence of 1 for 33,000-40,000 newborns. Different neurofibromatoses are characterized by different prognosis, complications, and genetic counseling.

nodes.label: Basal ganglia
nodes.description: A group of nuclei in the brain, including the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and subthalamic nucleus, that plays a critical role in movements, sleep, and mental behavior. It is involved in motor control, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and other functions, and can be affected by anatomical lesions in secondary dystonia. Disorders of the basal ganglia, such as Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease, can affect sleep. The entopeduncular nucleus is one of its major output stations, and it receives widespread cholinergic innervation. It is also involved in the development of corticostriatal circuits involved in motor control and can display topographical organization and massive funneling of neuronal projections toward the globus pallidus, suggesting the formation of correlations between the spiking activities of pallidal cells. Ischemic lesions in the basal ganglia may occur, potentially promoting the occurrence of mood disturbances in CADASIL patients. Hyperintense signals on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in patients with liver cirrhosis and NCPF, dystonia-choreoathetosis CP, and secondary dystonia are often attributed to the deposition of paramagnetic substances, such as manganese (Mn), which can be caused by hepatocellular failure and/or portosystemic shunting. Angiotensin converting enzyme is found in high concentrations in the caudate nucleus and putamen, suggesting that the enzyme may be involved in processing neuropeptides that occur in high concentrations in these structures. The basal ganglia is also involved in the pathophysiology of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) along with the orbitofrontal cortex and anterior cingulate gyrus. It is visualized during MRI-guided deep brain stimulation surgery using convective-enhanced delivery of autologous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the volume of distribution (Vd) is calculated based on T2-weighted MRI scans. The external globus pallidus (GPe) is also included in the basal ganglia.

nodes.label: PD-L1
nodes.description: A ligand that interacts with the programmed death-1 (PD-1) receptor, producing T-cell anergy and stifling the antitumor immune response. It is involved in immune checkpoints and is exploited by cancers to evade anti-tumor immune responses. PD-L1 is targeted by anti-PD-1 human antibodies, such as Keytruda, and is expressed on the surface of tumor cells, allowing them to suppress T lymphocyte antitumor activity and evade immune surveillance. It is also upregulated by certain mutations, such as KRAS G12V, and is associated with better response to immunotherapy in specific cancer types, like mTNBC.
