PD-L1 is a protein involved in the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint and can be regulated at different levels to modulate the anti-tumor immune response.

nodes.label: Down's syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, and other medical issues. A disease present in 2 patients with permanent congenital hypothyroidism and a normal sized and shaped thyroid gland. A genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delays, and distinct physical features. It is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. A genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, distinctive physical features, and increased risk of certain health conditions such as heart defects and leukemia. A genetic disorder characterized by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, and increased risk of certain medical conditions. Prenatal screening for this condition using serum markers such as inhibin-A, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), unconjugated oestriol (uE3), and human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) is discussed in the text.

nodes.label: AIS
nodes.description: A complex curvature of the spine of unknown etiology, characterized by a curvature of the spine that is diagnosed during adolescence and has no known cause. It is associated with genetic factors, skeletal immaturity, and specific genetic polymorphisms such as rs11063714 and rs1805149 in the NTF3 gene. AIS is also linked to melatonin and abnormal peripheral leptin signaling.

nodes.label: Phase Ib study
nodes.description: A phase Ib study conducted to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), pharmacokinetics (PKs), and antitumor activity of escalating doses of tivozanib with a modified (m)FOLFOX-6 regimen in patients with advanced gastrointestinal tumors. The study confirmed the MTD for tivozanib with mFOLFOX-6 as 1.5 mg and observed an ongoing clinical complete response, 10 partial responses, and 11 prolonged stable diseases. A phase Ib study evaluating the safety, recommended phase II dose (RP2D) and efficacy of pexidartinib, a CSF-1R inhibitor, in combination with weekly paclitaxel in patients with advanced solid tumors. Part 1 involved 24 patients receiving escalating doses of pexidartinib with weekly paclitaxel, while part 2 involved 30 patients with metastatic solid tumors to examine safety, tolerability and efficacy of the RP2D. The study also assessed pharmacokinetics and biomarkers. The recommended phase II dose (RP2D) for pexidartinib was determined to be 1600 mg/day.

nodes.label: Mouse Organic Cation Transporter 3 (mOCT3)
nodes.description: A cloned form of Organic Cation Transporter 3 (OCT3) found in mice, expressed in mouse embryonic kidney cell lines. It is membrane potential dependent and pH independent. Its activity is inhibited by various compounds including TPA(+), serotonin, diazepam, and ketamine. The Vmax of mOCT3 is acutely regulated by the p56(lck) tyrosine kinase. It is present in mouse renal proximal tubules.

nodes.label: Epidermal growth factor receptor
nodes.description: A protein involved in cell growth and division, signaling pathways, and cancer therapy. It is targeted by monoclonal antibodies such as cetuximab, panitumumab, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors like gefitinib and erlotinib. High expression in tumor cells can predict the benefit of cetuximab therapy. Mutations in the gene can lead to resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Overexpression is common in nonsmall cell lung cancers, and blockade of the receptor has been studied to improve chemotherapy outcomes. The epidermal growth factor receptor pathway is a known target in cancer therapy for lung carcinomas, with several limitations in mutation testing.

nodes.label: Cyclophosphamide
nodes.description: A chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of various types of cancer, including breast cancer, often administered in combination with other chemotherapeutic agents such as fluorouracil, epirubicin, and trastuzumab. It is also used in immunochemotherapy regimens for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and as a broad-spectrum immunosuppressant in the treatment of severe Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with organ involvement. Cyclophosphamide is typically administered at a dose of 500 mg/m², either in a dose-dense manner or every 21 days, and has been shown to be effective in inducing apoptosis of activated lymphocytes and suppressing the immune response, thereby reducing inflammation and preventing organ damage.

nodes.label: Cancer
nodes.description: A group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells, potentially affecting various organs and systems in the body. It includes different types such as oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, rectum, breast, lung, and prostate cancer. Risk factors for developing certain types of cancer include alcoholic beverages, excess body weight, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Clinical depletion in cancer patients is a result of metabolic disturbances as a consequence of the cancer and has negative effects on the course of the disease and on the treatment. Altered eating behavior, food aversion, decreased food intake, and loss of body weight may indicate the presence of clinical depletion. Various types of cancer can be treated with immunotherapy targeting the PD-1 pathway, and immune checkpoint inhibitors can be used to regulate the activity of the immune system and mount a stronger response against cancer cells.

nodes.label: Human Organic Cation Transporter 3 (hOCT3)
nodes.description: A cloned form of Organic Cation Transporter 3 (OCT3) found in humans, expressed in human embryonic kidney cell lines. It is membrane potential dependent and pH independent. Its activity is inhibited by various compounds including TPA(+), serotonin, diazepam, and ketamine. The Vmax of hOCT3 is acutely regulated by the p56(lck) tyrosine kinase. It is present in human cells and its activity is regulated by calmodulin.

nodes.label: Baloxavir marboxil
nodes.description: An oral cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor developed by Roche and Shionogi, which blocks influenza virus proliferation by inhibiting the initiation of mRNA synthesis. It received its first global approval in Japan for the treatment of influenza A or B virus infections in February 2018. The active ingredient of Xofluza, used to treat influenza and approved in Japan under the SAKIGAKE Designation System. A new influenza drug that targets the endonuclease function of the viral PA polymerase subunit and prevents the transcription of viral mRNA. It is available under the trade name Xofluza and has shown greater reductions in viral loads compared to oseltamivir in clinical trials. A prodrug of baloxavir acid, it is a small molecule inhibitor of the polymerase acidic (PA) protein subunit of the influenza virus polymerase complex. It acts to block influenza virus replication by inhibiting the cap-dependent endonuclease activity of the PA protein. It is approved in the USA for the treatment of acute uncomplicated influenza in patients ≥ 12 years of age who have been symptomatic for ≤ 48 h. It is effective in improving influenza symptoms and reducing viral load more rapidly than oseltamivir. It has activity against influenza A and B viruses, including strains resistant to neuraminidase inhibitors, and is well tolerated. An antiviral flu treatment, approved for prevention of influenza.

nodes.label: Type 2 Diabetes
nodes.description: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to defects in insulin production, insulin action, or both. It is associated with obesity, chronic low-grade inflammation, and a risk factor for pancreatic islet dysfunction. Type 2 diabetes is managed using oral antidiabetic drugs and insulin, and is often managed with medications like metformin, dapagliflozin, and insulin. Lifestyle interventions, including exercise and dietary-induced weight loss, are highly effective in preventing or delaying its onset. It is a major risk factor for cognitive decline and late onset Alzheimer's disease, often associated with apolipoprotein E4 (E4).

nodes.label: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
nodes.description: A group of drugs used in cancer treatment, including ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, tremelimumab, pidilizumab and atezolizumab, which are associated with a significantly increased risk of all grade and high-grade colitis according to a meta-analysis. Immunomodulatory agents that aim to relieve tumour-mediated immune-cell suppression by targeting immune checkpoint proteins such as programmed cell death-1 (PD-1), programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4). They have shown impressive results in a range of solid cancers, particularly melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer. A class of drugs used to treat cancer by enhancing the immune system's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells, but their effectiveness can be impaired by cancer cell immune evasion mechanisms.

nodes.label: Traumatic brain injury
nodes.description: A type of brain injury caused by external force, often resulting in long-term cognitive deficits and reduced quality of life. It can lead to axonal injury, accumulation of amyloid precursor protein (APP), and generation of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides, which are hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Epidemiological evidence suggests a link between TBI and AD, implying that TBI has neurodegenerative sequelae. A type of brain injury caused by external force, leading to neuronal damage and altered lysosomal biogenesis in activated microglia. A type of injury involving the head that can lead to short-term mortality, often characterized by severe symptoms such as abnormal pupil reaction and low Glasgow Coma Scale scores. The Abbreviated Injury Score (HAIS) greater than 3 indicates severe TBI. Prospective epidemiological cohort study in Switzerland included patients with HAIS >3.

nodes.label: Penetrating spinal cord injury
nodes.description: A type of spinal cord injury caused by a foreign object penetrating the spinal cord, often resulting in severe neurological damage and requiring surgical intervention. It can be diagnosed through spinal X-rays or myelography, and its prognosis can be improved with immediate and multidisciplinary management.

nodes.label: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy
nodes.description: A recessive form of neuropathy, caused by mutations in a close homolog of myotubularin (hMTMR2). A heterogeneous group of inherited disorders of the peripheral nervous system, characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness and atrophy, sensory loss, and decreased deep tendon reflexes. It includes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease 1C as a subtype. A genetic disease associated with mutations in the myotubularin family of genes. It is one of the two forms of Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy that are associated with mutations in the myotubularin family of genes. A neurological disorder characterized by mutations in dynamin 2, leading to various clinical manifestations such as mild to moderately severe symptoms, a classical Charcot-Marie-Tooth phenotype, and a mean age at onset of 16 years with a large variability ranging from 2 to 50 years. Electrophysiological data indicate intermediate or axonal motor median nerve conduction velocities (NCV) ranging from 26 m/s to normal values in four families, and less pronounced reduction of motor median NCV (41-46 m/s) with normal amplitudes in two families. Co-segregation of Charcot-Marie-Tooth with neutropaenia was observed in Australian and Belgian families carrying two different mutations affecting the same amino acid (Lys558). Early onset cataracts were also observed in one of the Charcot-Marie-Tooth families. An autosomal dominant inherited disorder affecting peripheral nerves, characterized by intermediate or axonal NCV, and a classical mild to moderately severe phenotype. It can be associated with neutropaenia or cataracts. A neurological disorder characterized by phenotypic variability, affecting 15 members of a large Czech family. It is caused by mutations in the Dynamin 2 gene (DNM2) and can manifest as an autosomal dominant centronuclear myopathy or an autosomal dominant (AD) Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease. The phenotype shows mild to moderate impairment with relatively preserved upper limbs and a very broad range of the onset of clinical symptoms from an early onset around the age of 12 to the late onset during the fifth decade. Electrophysiology shows an intermediate type of peripheral neuropathy. Motor median nerve conduction velocity varies from 36 m/s to normal values with signs of asymmetrical affection of peripheral nerves. A neurological disorder characterized by mutations in dynamin 2 (DNM2), leading to dominant intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy type B and causing defects in clathrin-mediated endocytosis and myelination. It is associated with different mutations in DNM2 compared to autosomal dominant centronuclear myopathy.

nodes.label: Emanuel syndrome
nodes.description: A genetic disorder characterized by multiple congenital anomalies and developmental disability, caused by the presence of a supernumerary derivative chromosome containing material from chromosomes 11 and 22. It is associated with a 3:1 malsegregation of a parental balanced translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22, which is the most common recurrent reciprocal translocation in humans. Congenital anomalies are common, including ear pits, micrognathia, heart malformations, and cleft palate. Vision and hearing impairment, seizures, failure to thrive, recurrent infections, particularly otitis media, and psychomotor development delay are also frequently observed. Most individuals eventually learn to walk with support, but language development and self-care abilities are severely impaired. An aneuploid syndrome caused by partial trisomy 11;22. A rare chromosomal disorder characterized by severe mental retardation and multiple anomalies, caused by chromosomal imbalance due to a supernumerary derivative chromosome 22. It is associated with prenatal biochemical screening characteristics and ultrasonographic markers, including increased NT, low PAPP-A, intra uterine growth restriction, posterior fossa, cardiac and bowel abnormalities. An inherited chromosomal abnormality resulting from 3:1 meiotic segregation from parental balanced translocation carrier t(11;22)(q23;q11), mostly of maternal origin. Characterized by mental retardation, microcephaly, preauricular tag or sinus, ear anomalies, cleft or high arched palate, micrognathia, congenital heart diseases, kidney abnormalities, structural brain anomalies and genital anomalies in male. Also associated with supernumerary der(22) syndrome in a female patient with cleft palate, maldeveloped corpus callosum and hind brain with normal internal organs, arachnodactyly, hyperextensibility of hand joints, abnormal deep palmar and finger creases, extra finger creases and bilateral talipes. A syndrome caused by an unbalanced translocation of the constitutional t(11;22), which can be transmitted to the progeny. A syndrome associated with complex small supernumerary marker chromosomes (sSMC), specifically the derivative chromosome 22 (der(22)t(11;22)). It accounts for 82% of complex sSMC cases and is characterized by the presence of a centric minute-shaped chromosome derived from an acrocentric chromosome. Detailed cytogenetic analyses are important for identifying this syndrome, especially in patients with idiopathic mental retardation. A disorder caused by an unbalanced form of the constitutional t(11;22)(q23;q11) translocation, characterized by clinical symptoms. Its prevalence is estimated to be 1 in 110,000 in the general population, with approximately 1063 cases in Japan. A genetic disorder caused by a derivative chromosome der(22)t(11;22)(q23;q11.2), characterized by intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, and distinctive facial features. A rare chromosomal disorder characterized by multiple congenital anomalies and developmental disabilities. Affected children are usually identified in the newborn period as the offspring of balanced (11;22) translocation carriers. A rare anomaly associated with multiple systemic malformations such as micrognathia and congenital heart disease. It is also associated with supernumerary chromosome, which consists of the extra genetic material from chromosome 11 and 22. The frequency of this syndrome has been reported as 1 in 110,000. Patients with Emanuel syndrome may have seizure disorders. A genetic disorder characterized by numerous anomalies, including facial dysmorphism, microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, developmental retardation, congenital heart disease, genital anomalies, and others. It is the most frequent type of recurrent non‑Robertsonian translocation. Over 100 patients with Emanuel syndrome have been described in the literature. A genetic disorder characterized by a supernumerary marker chromosome der(22) t(11; 22) (q23;q11), which was diagnosed in a fetus through genetic analysis and confirmed by next-generation sequencing (NGS) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). The syndrome is associated with a derivative chromosome and may cause Dandy-Walker malformation.

nodes.label: ADAMTSL4
nodes.description: A gene associated with autosomal-recessive isolated ectopia lentis, a condition characterized by the subluxation of the lens due to the disruption of the zonular fibers. ADAMTSL4 is involved in the formation or maintenance of the zonule and colocalizes with fibrillin-1 in the extracellular matrix (ECM) of cultured fibroblasts. It is a secreted glycoprotein that binds fibrillin-1 microfibrils and accelerates microfibril biogenesis. ADAMTSL4 is expressed in ocular tissues such as the ciliary body, sclera, cornea, and retina and is commonly associated with isolated ectopia lentis, often through mutations. It is located on chromosome 11q23.1 and has a transcript NM_019032.4. ADAMTSL4 is the most important known causative gene in isolated Ectopia Lentis and can have significant implications for patient management and risk assessment for family members.

nodes.label: Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
nodes.description: A government agency responsible for approving new drugs and medical devices for public use in the United States, ensuring the safety and effectiveness of pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and other products. It has approved various medications, medical devices, and treatments for different conditions, including cystic fibrosis, obesity, heart failure, migraine, and cancer. The FDA has also granted 'Orphan Drug' approval for drugs intended to treat rare diseases or conditions.

nodes.label: Pruritus
nodes.description: A symptom characterized by an intense itching sensation, often associated with skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis. It can be measured using scales like the Pruritus Visual-Analogue Scale and improved through treatments like dupilumab, lebrikizumab, and nemolizumab. Pruritus is one of the most common symptoms in dermatology and general medicine, severely impairing the quality of life of affected patients.

nodes.label: apixaban
nodes.description: A type of NOAC (Non-Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Contraceptives), an anticoagulant drug that may be associated with the most substantial medical cost reduction relative to warfarin. A novel oral anticoagulant used for stroke prevention in AF, shown to be superior to warfarin in the ARISTOTLE trial and associated with more effective reduction of stroke when compared with aspirin in the AVERROES trial. It has a similar reduction in the rate of ischemic stroke and better tolerability than warfarin. A medication used to treat and prevent blood clots, especially in patients with atrial fibrillation. It has benefits over warfarin that are consistent across patient risk of stroke and bleeding as assessed by the CHADS2, CHA2DS2VASc, and HAS-BLED scores.

nodes.label: Cisplatin
nodes.description: A platinum derivative and chemotherapeutic agent used in various cancer treatments, including metastatic breast cancer, locally advanced head and neck cancer, and non-small cell lung cancer. It is administered intravenously at a dose of 60 mg/m² on day 1 and is known to have nephrotoxic effects. Cisplatin is also used in combination with other drugs like VM-26, topotecan, necitumumab, pemetrexed, gemcitabine, and LC-0296. It causes DNA damage and can induce vomiting via calcium-dependent release of multiple neurotransmitters and can induce intracellular Ca2+ elevation. It is also used to treat DNA lesions in fluorescent protein vectors and to increase the sensitivity of head and neck cancer cells.

nodes.label: AzgA
nodes.description: A gene encoding a hypoxanthine-adenine-guanine transporter in Aspergillus nidulans, which has been cloned by a novel transposon methodology. The null phenotype of azgA is defined by a number of mutations, including a large deletion. The protein encoded by this gene is involved in purine catabolism and is induced by uric acid and repressed by ammonium in mycelia. Its transcription depends on the pathway-specific UaY zinc binuclear cluster protein and the broad domain AreA GATA factor. AzgA is not closely related to any other characterized membrane protein, but many close homologues of unknown function are present in fungi, plants, and prokaryotes but not metazoa. A gene encoding a transporter protein found in Aspergillus nidulans, characterized in this study for its role in purine transport. Bulky groups at position N3 have a detrimental steric effect on substrate binding, while similar substitutions at C2 or N9 are fully or partially tolerated. The adenine-guanine-hypoxanthine transporter from Aspergillus nidulans. It has substantial amino acid sequence similarity to the AtAzg1 and AtAzg2 proteins in Arabidopsis. The major fungal purine transporter identified in the text, which is present in fungi, bacteria and plants. It has a topological model built based on the crystal structure of the Escherichia coli uracil transporter UraA. The model consists of 14 transmembrane, mostly α-helical, segments (TMSs) and cytoplasmic N- and C-tails. A distinct compact core of 8 TMSs, made of two intertwined inverted repeats (TMSs 1-4 and 8-11), is topologically distinct from a flexible domain (TMSs 5-7 and 12-14). A putative substrate binding cavity is visible between the core and the gate domains. Several residues critical for purine binding and/or transport are identified in TMS3, TMS8 and TMS10, including Asn131, Asp339, Glu394 and Asp342.

nodes.label: KRas G13D
nodes.description: A point mutant of the KRas gene with an aspartic mutation at codon 13, associated with lower metastatic efficiency and aggressiveness in colorectal cancer models compared to KRas G12V.

nodes.label: Type 1 Diabetes
nodes.description: A chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by high blood sugar levels due to the body's inability to produce insulin, caused by the body's immune system attacking and destroying the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. It is associated with certain antimicrobial immune responses and can be delayed by T cell-directed therapy such as teplizumab. Known risk factors include genetic predispositions and environmental triggers. It affects both adults and children age ≥8 years and is measured by C-peptide levels. Clinical stage 3 refers to the onset of the disease, while stage 2 indicates preclinical disease. Treatment with teplizumab has been shown to preserve β-cell function and reduce the need for insulin in newly diagnosed patients. Prevention strategies are under discussion, and clinical trials are ongoing to explore the potential of immunotherapies like teplizumab in delaying the onset of the disease or improving clinical outcomes.

nodes.label: Hypertension
nodes.description: A medical condition characterized by persistently elevated blood pressure, often serving as a risk factor for heart failure (HF). It is associated with overweight or obesity and is improved by exercise training in individuals with high normal blood pressure. Hypertension is a cardiovascular risk factor associated with increased SBP, linked to declined regional CBF in aging AβPP/PS1 mice. It is also a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Excess body weight is an established risk factor for hypertension, along with diabetes and cardiovascular disease. A risk factor for AD that can be decreased by SV therapy. A major risk factor for central nervous system (CNS) disorders like stroke and Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by robust microglial and astrocyte activation, neuroinflammation, and impairment of hippocampal neurogenesis. It is associated with over-activity of the renin angiotensin system (RAS) and brain inflammation related to AD. The study examines the effect of hypertension and RAS on glial activation and hippocampal neurogenesis in a rat model of chronic hypertension. A medical condition for which isradipine is used as a therapy, and where amlodipine may be considered in the management of this condition in patients with heart failure. It is also mentioned as a bodyweight-related comorbidity in the context of managing obesity or overweight with oral naltrexone extended-release/bupropion extended-release (naltrexone ER/bupropion ER).

nodes.label: gp210
nodes.description: A membrane-spanning glycoprotein and a major component of the nuclear pore complex. It exists as dimers and larger oligomers. Dimeric gp210 is resistant to SDS and can be isolated from cell extracts by immunoprecipitation and from purified rat liver nuclear envelopes by velocity sedimentation and gel filtration. Larger oligomers of gp210 can be obtained by gel filtration and denaturing electrophoresis, but they are dissociated by reduction and heating in the presence of SDS. gp210 is proposed to be organized into the pore membrane as a large array of gp210 dimers that may constitute a luminal submembranous protein skeleton. An integral membrane protein of nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) that has a large lumenal domain and a small COOH-terminal tail exposed to the cytoplasm. It plays an early role in nuclear pore formation and its tail-binding partner(s) mediate pore dilation. Inhibition of gp210 tails blocks NPC assembly and nuclear growth, leading to the accumulation of gp210 and some nucleoporin p62, but failing to incorporate nup214/CAN, nup153, or nup98. These nuclei are also defective for nuclear import of lamin B3 and show the accumulation of novel arrested structures including 'mini-pores'. A major constituent of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) with possible structural and regulatory roles. Its C-terminal domain (CTD) follows a transmembrane domain and a massive (approximately 200 kDa) N-terminal region that resides in the lumen of the perinuclear space. It adopts an extended, largely unordered conformation in water, containing a significant amount of left-handed polyproline type II (PII) helical structure. The CTD's conformation is altered by high pH, charged detergents, and the hydrogen bond-promoting reagent trifluoroethanol (TFE). A region containing an SPXX motif in the CTD becomes specifically phosphorylated during mitosis. A membrane-integral nucleoporin (Nup) of vertebrates, previously considered a candidate anchor for nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) within the nuclear membrane. A gene or protein involved in the assembly and maintenance of vertebrate nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) within the lipid bilayer of the nuclear envelope (NE), along with POM121. They are the only known anchoring sites of vertebrate NPCs and are excellent candidates for initiating the NPC assembly process. gp210 is also found to be present in severely depleted cells, suggesting extensive redundancies in protein-protein interactions within NPCs. A 210-kD integral glycoprotein located in the nuclear envelope pore membrane, having a 1,783-amino acid amino-terminal domain, a 20-amino acid transmembrane segment, and a 58-amino acid cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal tail. Autoantibodies from patients with Primary Biliary Cirrhosis recognize a restricted region within the cytoplasmic tail of gp210. An integral glycoprotein of the nuclear pores that is frequently targeted by autoantibodies in patients with primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC). It consists of three main domains: a large glycosylated lumenal domain, a single hydrophobic transmembrane segment, and a short cytoplasmic tail. Autoantibodies from PBC patients primarily react with the cytoplasmic tail when recombinant rat gp210 expressed in Escherichia coli is used as an antigen. However, using human gp210 isolated from HeLa cells, the lumenal domain is identified as the major target. The protein is digested with papain or endoglycosidase H for immunoblotting analysis and is present in a 64 kD glycosylated amino-terminal fragment.

nodes.label: Nemolizumab
nodes.description: A humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-31 receptor A, used to reduce pruritus in patients with atopic dermatitis (AD) after a 16-week administration period. It is administered subcutaneously at a dose of 60 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W) in combination with topical treatments. Nemolizumab provides continuous improvement in pruritus, signs of AD, and quality of life (QoL) for up to 68 weeks, with a favourable safety profile.

nodes.label: Cohesion
nodes.description: A biological process involving the cohesin complex and established by the acetyltransferases Esco1 and Esco2, essential for faithful chromosome segregation during cell division. It involves the binding of cohesin to chromatin, with dynamic behavior observed in G1 phase and stabilization during S-phase. Cohesion is coordinated by Elg1, Ctf4, and Ctf18, which may regulate the relative movement of the replication fork with respect to the cohesin ring. It is also involved in the formation of topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops by extruding chromatin loops until it encounters CTCF, with the cohesin unloading factor WAPL and its PDS5 binding partners controlling the length of loops.

nodes.label: Food Neophobia
nodes.description: A reluctance to try new foods, common in children and older people, but less studied in the adult population. It is associated with sociodemographic factors and chronic diseases, particularly in males. It is more prevalent among females regarding healthy foods.

nodes.label: Insulin
nodes.description: A hormone produced by the pancreas that regulates blood sugar levels, primarily by facilitating the uptake of glucose into cells. It is involved in activating mTORC2 and stimulating Akt phosphorylation, and its deficiency leads to impaired insulin action and glucose intolerance. Insulin is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes, often in combination with other drugs like pramlintide, and is administered as an injectable form in combination with metformin for managing type 2 diabetes. It is also used in the definition of prevalent and incident treated diabetes, along with oral antidiabetic drugs, in the Women's Health Initiative. Insulin is a canonical regulator of leptin secretion and is involved in insulin signalling, specifically activated downstream of the insulin receptor in adipocytes. It has no significant effect on PDS expression in FRTL-5 cells and does not depend on dapagliflozin's efficacy for secretion and action.

nodes.label: Globus pallidus
nodes.description: A structure within the basal ganglia of the brain, involved in motor control and movement regulation. It is divided into two parts, the internal (GPi) and external (GPe) segments, and is richly concentrated with neuropeptides and endocannabinoids such as enkephalin, substance P, neurotensin, orexin, somatostatin, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptides. These molecules exert excitatory or inhibitory effects mainly by modulating GABAergic, glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission, as well as many ionic mechanisms. The spontaneous firing activity of globus pallidus neurons is closely related to the manifestations of Parkinson's disease. It shows intermediate density of cholinergic innervation and receives widespread cholinergic innervation, and is targeted for deep-brain stimulation in the treatment of dystonia, with the internal globus pallidus (GPi) specifically stimulated. It is also involved in Parkinsonism, epilepsy, and the pathophysiology of akinesia and resting tremor, and is affected by increased iron deposition in patients with PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN) and by anatomical lesions in secondary dystonia. In neurological diseases, the levels of neuropeptides and endocannabinoids and their receptors in the globus pallidus change, suggesting their potential use as targets for treatment.

nodes.label: Colon cancer
nodes.description: A type of colorectal cancer that affects the colon, with international variations in incidence rates. Genetic predisposition and dietary habits contribute to its development. Vegetables are associated with lower risk, while meat consumption increases risk, but these associations are not fully explained by fiber content or fat content alone. Phytochemicals, mutagenic compounds, and physical activity also play roles. Colorectal adenomatous polyps share a similar spectrum of risk factors with colon cancer, with tobacco smoking being a clear and consistent risk factor for adenomas. It is assessed in a national cohort of patients who underwent colectomy for Stage I-III CC in the 2004-2020 National Cancer Database. It is one of the many human cancers associated with the deletion or mutation of the PTEN gene. Being overweight or obese in adolescence was associated with an increased risk of colon cancer in both men and women, with significant associations from a BMI of 23.4 kg/m2 for overweight and 23.6 kg/m2 for obesity. The risk increases with higher BMI, and inter-gender differences suggest potential mechanistic differences. Ubc9 expression is increased compared to their normal tissue counterparts in this type of cancer. It was found that being overweight or obese in adolescence was associated with an increased risk of colon cancer in both men and women. The risk was statistically significant from a BMI of 23.4 kg/m2 for overweight and 23.6 kg/m2 for obesity. It is one of the cancers investigated in the context of prospective cohort studies, where no association with fat consumption was found. It is a type of cancer that affects the colon, with an increased risk associated with obesity in men and a weaker or no association observed in women. It is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, for which colectomy represents the standard of care.

nodes.label: Randomized Controlled Trial
nodes.description: A type of clinical trial in which participants are randomly assigned to either the treatment group (apixaban or warfarin) or the control group (placebo). The ARISTOTLE trial was a randomized controlled trial comparing the efficacy and safety of apixaban with warfarin for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. A research design used to evaluate the efficacy of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in enhancing the effects of virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET) in acrophobia. The study recruited 64 college students with significant fear of height and randomly allocated them to either an active-stimulated group or a sham-stimulated group. A research study design used to test the effectiveness of internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (ICBT) in reducing fear related to dental phobia and injection phobia in children and adolescents. It involved 33 participants and compared ICBT to a control group on a waitlist. A research design used to evaluate the efficacy of augmented reality exposure therapy and traditional in vivo exposure therapy in treating spider phobia. The study involved three comparison groups, pre- and post-treatment assessments, and a one-month follow-up assessment. The results indicated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in both treatment groups compared to the waitlist control group.

nodes.label: p16(INK4a)
nodes.description: A tumor-suppressor gene involved in the regulation of cell division and senescence, particularly in response to stress imposed by inadequate culture conditions. It is part of the p16(INK4a)/Rb pathway and its expression can be inhibited by the introduction of Bmi-1 or p16(INK4a)-specific short hairpin RNA. p16(INK4a) is also involved in the pathogenesis of glioblastoma multiforme through homozygous deletion, and is upregulated in keratinocytes derived from chronologically and prematurely aged epidermis. It is a protein that mediates telomere-independent senescence in normal cells and is involved in the carcinogenic pathway of HPV-induced SCCs in the anogenital tract and head and neck region, as well as a potential biomarker for HPV-negative, p16(INK4a)-positive cancers. Its expression is regulated by Bmi-1, which is a direct transcriptional target of c-Myc, and its promoter activity is reduced by Bmi-1 overexpression.

nodes.label: Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
nodes.description: A type of cancer affecting the head and neck region, characterized by the overexpression of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Commonly treated with agents targeting the EGFR family.

nodes.label: Calcium channel antagonists
nodes.description: A class of drugs used to treat heart failure due to systolic dysfunction. They can be divided into two generations based on their chemical structure and pharmacological properties. First-generation agents include nifedipine, verapamil, and diltiazem, while second-generation agents are primarily dihydropyridine derivatives such as amlodipine, felodipine, isradipine, lacidipine, nilvadipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, and others. Second-generation agents are characterized by greater selectivity for calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, a longer duration of action, and a smaller variation in plasma concentrations between trough and peak levels. A heterogeneous group of pharmacologic agents used for managing cardiovascular disorders such as hypertension, ischemic heart disease, supraventricular arrhythmias, CHF secondary to diastolic dysfunction, myocardial reinfarction, and prevention of atherosclerosis. They include verapamil, diltiazem, nifedipine, nicardipine, isradipine, felodipine, nimodipine, amlodipine, and bepridil. Differences in tissue selectivity are responsible for the variations in hemodynamic and electrophysiologic properties, clinical uses, and side effect profiles of these agents.

nodes.label: Control group
nodes.description: A group used as a reference for comparison in various studies, representing normal or healthy conditions. This group can consist of volunteers without cognitive impairment, healthy individuals, or patients without certain medical conditions, such as endometriosis or aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. They are used to assess differences in various parameters, such as biomarker levels, symptom occurrences, or treatment responses compared to other diagnostic groups or patient populations.

nodes.label: MOPED
nodes.description: A multi-omics resource for human and model organisms, MOPED (Multi-Omics Profiling Expression Database) provides consistently processed data for gene, protein and pathway expression through a web-based interface. It includes metadata detailing experimental design and analysis methods, and integrates multi-omics data through direct links between genes and proteins, further connecting to pathways and experiments. MOPED now contains over 5 million records, information for approximately 75,000 genes and 50,000 proteins from four organisms (human, mouse, worm, yeast). It includes new features such as pathway expression, Pathway Details pages, experimental metadata checklists, experiment summary statistics and more advanced searching tools. MOPED enables querying for genes, proteins, experiments, pathways and keywords of interest and is enhanced with visualizations for comparing across different data types. In the future, MOPED will expand the number of organisms, increase integration with pathways and provide connections to disease.

nodes.label: EGFR Mutations
nodes.description: A genetic alteration detected in lung cancer patients, specifically in exon 19 and exon 21, which include mutations such as ex19del, L858R, and T790M. These mutations are sensitive to targeted EGFR inhibition and valuable companion diagnostic biomarkers for guiding personalized treatment.

nodes.label: Alagille syndrome
nodes.description: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in Jagged1 (JAG1), a ligand in the Notch signaling pathway, affecting multiple organ systems including the liver, heart, eyes, vertebrae, and face. It is characterized by a spectrum of mutations in the JAG1 gene, including frameshift, missense, splice site, nonsense, whole gene, and partial gene deletions. The disorder is associated with midface anomalies and aberrant craniofacial growth, and can also be caused by mutations in the NOTCH2 receptor gene. Renal manifestations are a minor feature in this disorder. Alagille syndrome is a heterogeneous disorder, and there is no apparent relationship between genotype and clinical phenotype.

nodes.label: Rivaroxaban
nodes.description: An oral factor Xa inhibitor that was found to be non-inferior to warfarin in thromboprophylaxis and with similar bleeding in the ROCKET-AF trial. It is a new Xa inhibitor leading in distribution among other Xa inhibitors, with a 12-hour half-life period and similarity in pharmacological profiles to other Xa inhibitors. It is used for the treatment of thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) and as a direct oral anticoagulant for the prevention of stroke in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF), deep venous thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism. It has demonstrated non-inferiority compared with warfarin for reducing the risk of stroke or systemic embolism (SE) in patients with AF, as shown in the pivotal phase III trial ROCKET AF. It is also used in conjunction with dabigatran for emergency reversal. Its medical cost reduction associated with usage instead of warfarin was estimated to be -$89 in a patient year for NVAF patients aged ≥75 years.

nodes.label: Overall survival (OS)
nodes.description: A measure of the total time a patient lives after diagnosis or treatment, often used to evaluate the effectiveness of different treatment strategies and disease characteristics. It can refer to the time from the start of treatment until death due to any cause, the time from diagnosis until death, or the time from treatment initiation until death. OS is a common endpoint in clinical trials, especially in oncology, and can be measured as median OS or 10-year OS rate. It is used to assess the impact of various factors, such as MGMT promoter methylation status, local tumor invasion, and International Prognostic Index (IPI) scores, on patient outcomes.

nodes.label: Medulloblastoma
nodes.description: A malignant brain tumor of childhood, primarily affecting the cerebellum, that develops as a result of inappropriate Hedgehog (Hh) signaling. It is one of the most common types of embryonal tumor in the pediatric population, accounting for 20-25% of all brain tumors in children. Medulloblastoma is associated with haploinsufficiency of Ptch and mutations in the PTCH gene, as well as the expression of BMI1 and PCGF2 genes, and their potential target, MYC oncogene. It is characterized by genomic amplifications and deletions, including MYC amplification and isochromosome 17q, and epigenetic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes such as RASSF1A, HIC1, and CASP8. Mutations in Hh pathway genes lead to ligand-independent pathway activation, and the hedgehog (Hh) pathway is aberrantly activated in medulloblastoma. The most frequent type of embryonal tumor in the pediatric population, it is a type of advanced solid tumor and a malignant brain tumor affecting children, comprising at least 4 distinct clinicogenetic subgroups. It is also characterized by the down-regulation of PCDH10 gene, involving cell proliferation, cell cycle progression, and cell migration. Medulloblastoma has been studied in relation to the hedgehog inhibitor therapy, specifically targeting Smoothened, and has been analyzed for differential gene expression and response to sonidegib treatment. The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, it can be detected in both adult and pediatric patients, with various histological variants and age/sex groupings. Comprehensive analysis of the genome and epigenome is required for identifying key tumor suppressor genes involved in its development.

nodes.label: REGEN-COV
nodes.description: A subcutaneous antibody combination consisting of casirivimab and imdevimab, used to treat early asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection and prevent progression to COVID-19. It significantly reduced the relative risk of developing symptomatic COVID-19 by 31.5% compared to placebo. A subcutaneous antibody combination consisting of casirivimab and imdevimab, approved for Covid-19 prevention. It significantly reduces the risk of hospitalization or death in high-risk individuals with Covid-19. REGEN-COV has been shown to prevent symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection and overall infections, both symptomatic and asymptomatic, with a risk reduction of 81.4% and 66.4%, respectively. Among infected participants, REGEN-COV reduces the duration of symptomatic disease, decreases maximal viral load, and shortens the duration of detectable virus. The study's clinical trial number is NCT04452318. A combination of the monoclonal antibodies casirivimab and imdevimab, previously known as REGN-COV2, which has been shown to markedly reduce the risk of hospitalization or death among high-risk persons with coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19). It is administered by means of a subcutaneous injection and was evaluated in a randomized controlled trial involving participants at high risk for infection due to household exposure to a person with SARS-CoV-2 infection. A medication used to treat COVID-19. It has been shown to reduce the duration of symptomatic disease and the duration of a high viral load among infected participants. Subcutaneous REGEN-COV prevents symptomatic Covid-19 and asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection in previously uninfected household contacts of infected persons. No dose-limiting toxic effects of REGEN-COV were noted. A brand name for the combination of neutralizing therapeutic monoclonal antibodies casirivimab and imdevimab, approved by the FDA for prophylactic post-exposure therapy in individuals at high risk of progressing to severe COVID-19. It has been used for treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19 in adults and children 12 years or older with exposure to SARS-CoV-2 at high risk for progression to severe COVID-19. A therapeutic antibody cocktail consisting of two human IgG1 monoclonal antibodies, REGN10933 and REGN10987, that targets the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike protein. It has shown great promise in reducing the SARS-CoV-2 viral load in COVID-19 patients enrolled in clinical studies. A combination of two monoclonal antibodies, casirivimab and imdevimab, approved for emergency use authorization (EUA). It is used for postexposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in adults and children 12 years of age and older who are at high risk for severe disease. It is not a substitute for vaccination against COVID-19.

nodes.label: Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
nodes.description: A heterogeneous group of rare monogenic conditions characterized by joint hypermobility, skin and vascular fragility, and generalized connective tissue friability. Comprises 13 clinical subtypes, with mutations identified in 19 different genes. Includes vascular subtype caused by a molecular defect in collagen type III, and other subtypes caused by defects in type V collagen, type I collagen, LH1, FKBP22, or ZNF469. A group of inherited connective tissue disorders with a worldwide prevalence of 1 in 2500 to 1 in 5000 births irrespective of sex or ethnicity, characterized by 14 subtypes each with characteristic phenotypes and associated genes. Pathogenic variants in COL5A1 and COL5A2 cause the classical EDS subtypes, while pathogenic variants in COL3A1 cause vascular EDS.

nodes.label: Conjoined twins
nodes.description: A rare congenital condition where two individuals are connected at birth, typically involving shared organs or body parts. There are various types of conjoined twins, including ischiopagus and pygopagus, which may present neurosurgical challenges. Over a 40-year period (1964-2003) at Red Cross Children's Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa, 23 pairs of symmetrical conjoined twins were managed, with 16 (70%) being separated. A rare congenital anomaly where two individuals are joined together, with the more common types including the thoracopagus type involving fusion at the chest and often involving the heart. Severe mortality and morbidity are associated with this condition. A medical condition characterized by two babies being joined together during development, often requiring specialized prenatal, delivery, and postnatal care. The study analyzed 40 cases of conjoined twins, with various types of fusion between fetal structures, including thoracophagus, paraphagus, omphalo-ischiophagus, omphalophagus, and cephalophagus. A rare condition where two individuals are joined together at birth, specifically in this case, the cephalothoracopagus type involving fusion of heads, thoracic and upper abdominal cavities. The exact mechanism for development is unclear and appears to involve an alteration in the normal developmental process of monozygotic twins. A rare form of monozygotic twinning that occurs when there is incomplete division of the embryonic disc after day 13 post conception, leading to a very high risk of perinatal morbidity and mortality. Prognosis depends on the site and extent of fusion and the degree of sharing of vital organs. Most conjoined twins die in utero or in the early neonatal period, but less severe cases can be successfully separated. A rare type of monozygotic twins that occur due to an incomplete embryonic division on postconception day 13 to 15, resulting in eight different types of conjoined twins being described in the literature. The management of the condition depends on the site and extent of the union.

nodes.label: Surgery
nodes.description: A medical procedure involving incisions or manipulations on the body to address a medical condition, often performed to remove diseased tissue, relieve effects of scarring, or treat coexisting carcinoma. It can involve the removal of tumors from the rectum, the treatment of severe valve regurgitation, the separation of conjoined twins, or the management of various medical conditions such as chordoma, rectal cancer, and subclinical hyperthyroidism. The optimal time interval between certain procedures, such as chemoradiotherapy and surgery, is under investigation and can vary depending on the specific condition and treatment approach.

nodes.label: Dorsal part of granular insular cortex (dGIrvs2)
nodes.description: A region of the cerebral cortex located rostroventrally adjacent to the rostralmost part of secondary somatosensory cortex (dGIrvs2) in rats, receiving proprioceptive signals from jaw-closing muscle spindles (JCMSs) via the caudo-ventromedial edge (VPMcvm) of ventral posteromedial thalamic nucleus (VPM).

nodes.label: Notch signaling pathway
nodes.description: An evolutionarily conserved signaling pathway in which Jagged1 (JAG1) is a ligand, and mutations in JAG1 lead to Alagille syndrome. It is involved in various developmental processes and diseases, including cell fate determination, craniofacial development, and cancer. Important components include the Hairy-and-Enhancer-of-Split-7 (HES7) gene and genes causing spondylocostal dysostosis (SCD) such as DLL3, MESP2, and LFNG. It has a tumor suppressor role in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and is associated with cell fate decisions in astrocyte and neuronal lineages.

nodes.label: SOX10
nodes.description: A transcription factor involved in the direct conversion of mouse and human fibroblasts to functional melanocytes, and a global regulator of gene expression in the melanocyte lineage. It is also a Sry-related high mobility (HMG)-box transcriptional regulator that promotes differentiation of neural crest precursors into Schwann cells, oligodendrocytes, and melanocytes, and is essential for survival and proper differentiation of neural crest cell lineages, playing an important role in the generation and maintenance of melanocytes. SOX10 is linked to melanoma initiation and progression, and is involved in the melanocyte lineage and chromatin organization.

nodes.label: Heart Failure
nodes.description: A chronic medical condition involving the heart's inability to pump blood efficiently, often associated with hypertension. It includes subtypes such as HF with reduced ejection fraction and HF with preserved ejection fraction. It is characterized by the failure of the heart to pump blood effectively, leading to symptoms such as shortness of breath and fluid retention. It is diagnosed and managed using biomarkers like natriuretic peptides (NPs), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and NT-proBNP. The diagnostic accuracy of NPs can be challenging in overweight and obese patients due to an inverse relationship between obesity and NPs. It is a major healthcare burden in the United States and worldwide, characterized by reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Managed with various drugs such as beta blockers, diuretics, aldosterone antagonists, ACEI's, and ARBs. Entresto has been approved for use in HFrEF patients as an alternative to these drugs. It is a potential outcome of impairment of proteasomal function in several cardiac proteinopathies. It is a condition in which the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs. It is one of the composite endpoints used to assess CVD risks in the study. It is a chronic condition affecting the heart's ability to pump blood effectively. It is a medical condition contraindicated for the use of both rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, two anti-diabetic drugs. It is associated with an increased risk when these drugs are used. It is evaluated using logistic regression and recurrent neural network models with UMLS terminology. It is a broad term for a condition where the heart is unable to pump blood effectively, leading to various symptoms and complications. It is divided into two types: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF) and Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF). It is a medical condition characterized by the symptoms and signs of a failing heart, often diagnosed using echocardiographic tests. There are challenges in confirming the diagnosis, and wave-mixing serves as a potentially beneficial screening tool.

nodes.label: Lrictor(KO)
nodes.description: A mouse model with a knockout of the rictor gene in the liver, used to study the effects of mTORC2 deficiency on insulin signaling and hepatic lipogenesis. These mice are unable to respond normally to insulin, fail to inhibit hepatic glucose output, and have defects in insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation and insulin-activated mTORC1 activity.

nodes.label: Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1
nodes.description: One of the two main types of Myotonic Dystrophy, characterized by muscle weakness and wasting, particularly affecting the muscles of the face, neck, and limbs. It involves a novel RNA-mediated disease process where the RNA rather than protein product of a disease gene has deleterious effects on muscle cells. The disease affects the biogenesis of other cellular RNAs, particularly influencing alternative splicing, leading to a complex set of signs and symptoms. The genetic lesion does not eliminate an essential muscle protein but induces a defect of RNA processing that is potentially reversible. A form of muscular dystrophy resulting from an expanded trinucleotide repeat in the myotonic dystrophy protein kinase gene. A clinically and molecularly defined form of myotonic dystrophy, also known as Steinert's disease. It is the most common form of adult onset muscular dystrophy and is characterized by several clinical and genetic features in common with Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2. A type of muscular dystrophy characterized by muscle weakness and myotonia. Recent advancements have led to a greater understanding of its pathogenetic pathways. A form of Myotonic Dystrophy, characterized by early conventional MRI findings such as hyperintense white matter lesions, primarily located in the anterior temporal lobe. It also shows widespread cortical and subcortical involvement of gray and white matter, affecting all lobes, brainstem, and cerebellum. Neuroimaging studies have identified neuronal and glial damage. A type of myotonic dystrophy, characterized by adult-onset muscular dystrophy. It is one of the two main types of myotonic dystrophy, the other being Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2. It shares clinical and genetic similarities with Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2, but they are distinct disorders requiring different diagnostic and management strategies. Understanding of the molecular pathogenesis has led to the classification of both types as 'spliceopathies', focusing on RNA rather than proteins. A type of myotonic dystrophy (DM) that is considered more severe than DM Type 2 (DM2) in terms of milestone events, but it is unknown whether this applies uniformly to all features. It is associated with earlier occurrence of disability and motor milestones compared to DM Type 2. Men are at greater risk for disability, use of ankle braces, and diabetes, while women are at greater risk for needing walkers or malignancy. The age-related risk of milestone events is greater in DM Type 1 than in DM Type 2, except for diabetes.

nodes.label: Muscular dystrophy
nodes.description: A heterogeneous group of inherited genetic disorders characterized by progressive muscle weakness and degeneration, affecting skeletal muscle primarily. These disorders can cause exercise intolerance, cardiac involvement, and varying degrees of severity, with some forms leading to premature death. They are caused by mutations in diverse genes, including those that encode proteins maintaining membrane strength, participating in membrane repair, or being components of the extracellular matrix or the nuclear envelope. Each muscular dystrophy shows distinguishing features in the magnitude and type of inflammatory response, indicating disease-specific immunomodulatory molecules. Some forms, like Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), are associated with up-regulation of sphingolipid de novo biosynthesis pathway transcripts in skeletal muscle.

nodes.label: Myocarditis
nodes.description: An underdiagnosed cause of acute heart failure, sudden death, and chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, characterized by non-specific symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnoea, and palpitations. It can be caused by viral infections, rheumatic carditis, Trypanosoma cruzi, and bacterial infections like diphtheria. The short-term prognosis varies by cause, and those who initially recover might develop recurrent dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure later on. Cardiac MRI and endomyocardial biopsy can aid in identifying myocarditis, predicting cardiovascular event risk, and guiding treatment. The pathogenesis of chronic dilated cardiomyopathy after viral myocarditis is complex and influenced by host and viral genetics, as well as environmental factors. A disorder characterized by inflammation of the myocardium, which can lead to myocardial edema. T1-mapping may serve as a complementary technique to T2-weighted imaging for assessing myocardial edema in this condition. A disease entity characterized by myocarditis, affecting 7 abnormal regions with mean ECV values ranging from 39-56%. It is associated with the measurement of diffuse disease and abnormal regions. A type of inflammation affecting the heart muscle, often associated with checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy. A viral infection of the heart muscle characterized by inflammation, often caused by cardiotropic viruses such as enteroviruses, parvovirus B19, and human herpes virus 6. It can lead to acute and chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy (DCMi). A manifestation of diphtheria, involving inflammation of the myocardium, which is the most serious and common cause of mortality in affected patients. A disease characterized by inflammation of the heart muscle, observed in a newborn infant infected with Coxsackie virus B3.

edges.description: (-)-OSU6162 and pridopidine are members of a new family of compounds referred to as dopaminergic stabilizers.
In Escherichia coli, 2-hydroxy-dATP elicits G.C-->T.A transversions, but to a lesser extent compared to HeLa extract.
Chromatin regulator EZH2 is regulated by androgen and strongly expressed in early prostate morphogenesis and during puberty.
AZD7442 has been found effective among immunocompromised individuals (ICIs) in reducing SARS-CoV-2 infection and severe disease in ICIs, which can lead to COVID-19.
Acneiform eruptions are caused by the use of epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors, specifically cetuximab.
The study supports the role of p53 in the progression of adenomas.

Advanced Prostate Cancer is a specific type of Prostate Cancer that has spread beyond the prostate gland and is affecting one in every nine men in the USA, being the second leading cause of cancer-related death.
Albinism is associated with the enzyme tyrosinase, which is produced by the tyrosinase gene (TYR) and involved in the melanin biosynthetic pathway.
A missense mutation in a highly conserved position of the tyrosinase (TYR) gene deduced protein causes albinism in donkeys.
Both Alu and B1 mobile elements have a similar origin from the 7SL RNA gene duplication.
Amphiregulin activates the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) when present in exosomes, leading to increased cancer cell invasion.
A mutant KRAS allele, as found in DLD-1 colon cancer cells, is a risk factor for increased AREG levels and greater invasive potential in exosomes.

Anaplastic astrocytoma can progress to glioblastoma, a type of brain tumor characterized by a highly anaplastic phenotype with marked proliferative activity and lack of glial fibrillary acidic protein expression.
Anaplastic astrocytoma is a subtype of glioma that can progress to glioblastoma multiforme.
Anaplastic astrocytoma is a subtype of astrocytoma with higher grade of malignancy.
Antibiotics are usually used to treat the EGFR inhibitor-associated skin rash, but they have prominent side effects over long-time use.
Antibiotics are used to treat EGFRi-associated rash as part of prophylactic treatment.
Mitochondria are organelles in plant leaves of Arabidopsis thaliana responsible for producing ATP and being the major source of ATP in the dark in leaves.

Dupilumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of atopic dermatitis based on published efficacy shown in controlled prospective studies.
Dupilumab, an anti-IL-4 receptor α-chain antibody, is used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis with strong evidence supporting its clinical efficacy.
B1 and Alu are sequence-homologous interspersed elements.
BCNU wafer implantation is associated with temozolomide, as it is often used in conjunction with temozolomide as part of the Stupp protocol for treating glioblastoma.
BCNU wafer implantation follows chemoradiotherapy as part of the Stupp protocol for treating glioblastoma.
BCNU wafer implantation is associated with recurrent glioblastoma, as patients with recurrent glioblastoma frequently receive this treatment.
In normal B-cell development in germinal centers, the expression of BMI-1 and EZH2 PcG genes is separated, while Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg (H/RS) cells co-express both genes.
BMI-1 is expressed in all histologic types of gliomas.
BRG1 interacts with MITF to form a complex and actively recruit BRG1 to a set of MITF-associated regulatory elements (MAREs) at active enhancers.
BRG1 interacts with SOX10 to activate expression of OCT6 and KROX20.
SOX10 was required to recruit BRG1 to the MPZ locus.
Nausea is a symptom that can occur due to fractures of the petrous bone in a basilar skull fracture.
Clinical trials are being conducted to evaluate the safety, efficacy, and optimal use of belimumab as a potential therapeutic target and diagnostic/prognostic marker for lupus patients.

Future studies include determining the role of belimumab in early SLE, as well as in renal or CNS involvement, and it has shown overall steroid-sparing ability and benefits on musculoskeletal and mucocutaneous organ systems, suggesting a reduction in the use of corticosteroids.

Belimumab is being investigated as a potential treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by inflammation and damage to various organs and tissues.
Belimumab has shown clinical benefit in two large-scale, multicenter phase III trials leading to US Food and Drug Administration approval for patients with serologically positive systemic lupus erythematosus who have active disease despite standard therapy.
Belimumab was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in March 2011 for active autoantibody patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) despite standard therapy.
Belimumab is being studied as a potential therapeutic agent for Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients.
The FDA approved belimumab for use in treating systemic lupus erythematosus.

If belimumab is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), its US market launch is expected in 2011. The FDA is a government agency responsible for approving new drugs and regulating their marketing and distribution in the United States.
Ixodes ricinus is one of the main tick vectors for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato.
Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, a group of related bacteria that are pathogens of medical and veterinary relevance, are transmitted by the vector Ixodes ricinus.
Bulevirtide (BLV) has prevented the progression to cirrhosis in patients with chronic hepatitis delta (CHD)
Bulevirtide (BLV) is a therapeutic intervention used to treat chronic hepatitis D.
Obesity is a common comorbidity of psoriatic patients, for which treatment with bupropion is indicated.
Inhibition of pro-inflammatory signaling pathways by CP690,550 could be important in the treatment of RA
CP690,550 has shown efficacy in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.
Calcium channel antagonists are being investigated for prevention of atherosclerosis.
Calcium channel antagonists have been a focus of interest in the treatment of heart failure due to their potential beneficial effects.
Calcium channel antagonists include isradipine as one of their components.
Cephalothoracopagus is a specific type of conjoined twins where they are fused with their heads, thoracic and upper abdominal cavities.
Surgery is not attempted in cases of cephalothoracopagus due to the poor prognosis associated with the condition.
Headache in patients with CADASIL was usually referred to as migraine.
CADASIL is caused by mutations of the NOTCH3 gene.

The cholinergic innervation is distributed in the basal ganglia of the human brain, which includes the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and subthalamic nucleus.
The level of cholinergic innervation was of intermediate density in the globus pallidus.
The cholinergic innervation is distributed in the globus pallidus, a component of the basal ganglia in the human brain.
Cholinergic innervation targets parts of the globus pallidus.
Surgery is the first choice for treating chordoma, involving the removal of the tumor.
Christianson syndrome is associated with the neurological disorder epilepsy, often co-occurring with other symptoms such as intellectual disability and ataxia.
Bulevirtide has received conditional approval as a treatment for chronic hepatitis D (CHD)
Echocardiography was used in the study to assess cardiac fusion in conjoined twins, particularly in cases with thoracic sharing.
Ischiopagus twins are a type of conjoined twins characterized by connection at the hip region.
The terms 'DMD' and 'Duchenne muscular dystrophy' are used interchangeably to refer to the same disease.
DMD is the genetic abbreviation for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, indicating that they are the same condition.
DMD is another name for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a rare, genetic disease caused by mutations in the DMD gene.
DMD is a specific type of Duchenne muscular dystrophy characterized by severe muscle weakness and degeneration.
Changes in DNA methylation patterns are an important characteristic of human cancer.

DNMT1 interacts directly with the H1 C-terminal domain of some, but not all, murine H1 subtypes, leading to the recruitment of DNMT1 and DNA methylation of the H19 and Gtl2 imprinting control regions in ES cells.

The study compares dabigatran etexilate and apixaban for thromboprophylaxis following hip or knee replacement surgery, assessing various clinical parameters in two groups of patients who received each medication.
Dapagliflozin has been compared with placebo in clinical trials to assess its efficacy in reducing glycosylated hemoglobin values and fasting plasma glucose levels in patients with type 2 diabetes.
Clinical trials are research studies conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of dapagliflozin in managing type 2 diabetes.
In cases where patients with type 2 diabetes cannot tolerate metformin, dapagliflozin can be used as an alternative for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

When used in combination with other antidiabetic drugs, dapagliflozin provides complementary therapy via its unique mechanism of action.
